knowledge-and-decisions-1980.context_blurb:
In 1980 the economist Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions, a long book about a short question: who knows the facts, and who gets to decide? He built it on an essay by Friedrich Hayek, and Hayek himself came to call it the best general economics book in many years.

Hayek's starting point was simple. The facts an economy depends on, about tastes, skills, nearby materials, broken machines and this season's crops, are spread among millions of ordinary people. No office or computer holds them all, so no small group of planners can ever know enough to run a whole economy.

Hayek made the case in an article in the American Economic Review in September 1945: The Use of Knowledge in Society. His famous example is tin. When tin grows scarce, whether because a mine has flooded or because some new use has appeared, its price rises, and manufacturers in a dozen industries use less of it without ever learning why. No planning board could gather into one office the separate reasons millions of people have for wanting tin; the price carries that knowledge in the only form in which it can travel.

Sowell asked the same question of every institution. He put markets, elected legislatures and courts through one identical test: which facts can the process actually pick up, and which is it blind to? That is why the book is no slogan of markets good, government bad; the answers differ institution by institution.

Sowell worried about a widening gap between the people who know the particulars firsthand, the farmers, tradesmen and shopkeepers, and the people who hold the power to decide, the planners and theorists who work at a distance.

Gasoline in 1973 shows the stakes. The Arab oil embargo was a real shock, but Washington also held down what American oil and gasoline could legally sell for, and drivers waited hours in lines although national stocks were adequate. On Sowell's account the cap silenced the one signal that would have told drivers to stretch a tank and refiners to run harder. When price may not ration a scarce good, something else must, and in the autumn of 1973 Oregon's governor, Tom McCall, could not move the price, so he rationed by calendar. Cars with plates ending in an odd number could fill up on odd-numbered days and even plates on even days, a rule other states soon copied.

Sowell carried the argument into education. Racial preferences in admissions, he argued, can place a student in a program whose other students arrived much better prepared. The admissions office never checks how this particular student would do at this particular program's pace, and the issue, in his account, is the fit, not the student's ability.

In 1980 the book won the prize of the Law and Economics Center, whose citation called it a landmark for helping readers understand how the market process and the process of government differ.

In December 1981 Hayek, then eighty-two, reviewed the book in Reason magazine under the title The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year.

Sowell himself was proud of it, but when an interviewer asked him in 2018, as he approached eighty-eight, he named a shorter and more readable book of 1987 as his own personal favorite: A Conflict of Visions.

long-term-capital-management-and-the-199.context_blurb:
Long-Term Capital Management, founded in 1994 by the former Salomon Brothers bond trader John Meriwether, was the most celebrated hedge fund of the 1990s. Among its partners were two of the world's most famous financial economists. In 1998 it nearly brought down Wall Street, and its rescue set a precedent that critics say grew into every bailout since.

The fund's star partners, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on pricing options. LTCM used their kind of advanced mathematical model to place its trades. Its collapse a year later taught the world that complex math models do not guarantee safety in markets.

The fund's power came from borrowing. It held about $125 billion of positions on only about $4.7 billion of its own capital, roughly twenty-seven borrowed dollars for every dollar of its own. Using borrowed money to multiply a bet in this way is called leverage: it magnifies profits when trades go well and magnifies losses just as fast when they go badly, since the loans must be repaid either way.

For four years the strategy earned very high returns. Many of LTCM's trades bet that the small price gap between two almost identical bonds would close. Then, on August 17, 1998, Russia defaulted on its debts, investors everywhere fled to the safest assets, and the price gaps widened instead of closing. The fund nearly went bankrupt and had to be rescued to stop the damage from spreading.

The models had promised that a move that large would come only once in many centuries. What they missed is that disasters strike far more often than models fitted to quiet years predict.

LTCM had no depositors and no small savers, nothing the Federal Reserve is supposed to protect. Yet the New York Fed stepped in, and its justification was the banks: those that had traded with LTCM were so exposed that a disorderly sale of its positions could cascade into the whole banking system.

The New York Fed's president, William McDonough, summoned Wall Street's chiefs, with his deputy Peter Fisher running the details. On September 23, 1998, fourteen banks agreed to pool about $3.6 billion of their own money, not taxpayers', to take over the fund and unwind its trades slowly.

There had been another offer. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, joined by AIG and Goldman Sachs, offered $250 million for the fund, a deal that would have wiped out LTCM's partners; the talks collapsed, and the banks' rescue came instead. Free-market critics prefer private buyouts like Buffett's because they do not teach big firms that the government will save them next time.

Critics saw the danger in that lesson. A rescue that shields risk-takers from loss encourages them to gamble more boldly in future, which economists call moral hazard, and LTCM extended the expected safety net from banks to private investment funds.

Each rescue is announced as just this once. Yet first a big bank, then an investment fund, then an insurance giant, then a money-market fund was saved, and the circle of firms considered too big to fail keeps quietly widening.

march-2020-emergency-cuts-and-unlimited-.context_blurb:
In March 2020, as COVID-19 reached the United States and markets panicked, the Federal Reserve did in a few weeks what it had taken years to do after 2008, and then went further. Austrian economists see that month as the moment a whole new level of central-bank power became normal.

The first move came on Tuesday, March 3, between scheduled meetings: an emergency cut of 50 basis points, half a percentage point, taking the target range to 1.00 to 1.25 percent. It was the first surprise cut since the crisis of October 2008.

Twelve days later, on Sunday, March 15, the Fed cut by a full percentage point more, to a range of zero to 0.25 percent, and kept rates there for two years.

On March 23 it went further, promising to buy government bonds and mortgage securities in whatever amounts were needed, with no set limit. Critics called it money printing. Their warning was the old one: when far more dollars chase the same goods, prices across the economy eventually rise.

For the first time in its history the Fed also began creating money to buy bonds issued by individual companies such as Apple, Ford and AT&T. Austrian critics, among them Peter Schiff, called it a dangerous step, because the central bank was now choosing which companies to prop up.

In April the buying stretched to riskier debt: company bonds rated investment grade until the pandemic, then downgraded to junk by the rating agencies. Wall Street calls such downgraded bonds fallen angels.

On April 9 the Fed also opened a Municipal Liquidity Facility to buy the bonds of states and cities. Together with the corporate programs, that meant the central bank itself now decided which companies and local governments got credit, a job traditionally left to legislatures.

To run its corporate bond buying, the Fed hired BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, which also ran huge bond funds of its own. Critics on left and right saw the cozy relationship between an official body and the industry it works with as a case of regulatory capture.

All of these programs rested on Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, a clause added in 1932 that allows emergency lending to almost any borrower, beyond the usual banks, in what the law calls unusual and exigent circumstances.

The Fed's balance sheet, about $4.2 trillion before the crisis, swelled to a peak of about $8.9 trillion in the spring of 2022, the biggest expansion in its history, and inflation followed in 2021 and 2022.

Economists at the Mises Institute drew the lasting lesson: emergency programs seldom get packed away once the crisis passes. They set a new, higher institutional baseline, and the next crisis response will start from that elevated level instead of returning to normal.

milton-friedman-brooklyn-to-nobel-1976.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman was born in Brooklyn in 1912 to poor immigrant parents and grew into the most famous economist of his age. Small, quick and cheerful in argument, he taught at the University of Chicago for three decades and put one stubborn question to every policy: what actually happened? In 1976 that habit won him the Nobel Prize.

His most quoted saying is that rising prices, in every country and century, come down to money. Prices climb across a whole economy, he argued, when the money supply grows faster than the goods it chases, so the blame belongs to whoever prints too much money, not to greedy shopkeepers or bad weather.

With his wife Rose, a trained economist herself, he took that view to ordinary readers after moving from Chicago to Stanford's Hoover Institution. Their best-selling book Free to Choose, also a ten-part public television series in 1980, argued that people spending their own money spend it more carefully than government experts spending it for them, because nobody guards a stranger's money as well as his own.

His first great scholarly book, on the consumption function (1957), attacked a Keynesian rule that a family spends a fixed share of whatever comes in. A worker plans his spending around the income he expects over many years, Friedman saw, so he reads a one-time bonus as a one-off and saves most of it. Economists call this the permanent income hypothesis.

Friedman also fought the draft. In 1969 Richard Nixon asked a commission chaired by Thomas Gates to study a volunteer army, with Friedman as a member. When General William Westmoreland, the Army's chief of staff, told the panel he did not want to command an army of mercenaries, Friedman asked whether the general would rather command an army of slaves. A draft forces young men to serve at whatever pay the state sets; a volunteer is paid enough to choose the job. The 1970 report urged an end to conscription.

With Anna Jacobson Schwartz, a full partner in the work, he wrote A Monetary History of the United States (1963), tracking the nation's money from 1867 to 1960. Its sharpest lesson for central bankers came from the 1930s: when banks are failing in a panic, never let the money supply collapse.

The Swedish academy's prize named three achievements: his analysis of consumption, his work in monetary history and theory, and his demonstration of how hard it is to stabilize an economy.

Before that history appeared, the common story said the market had collapsed by itself in 1929 and government had come to the rescue. Friedman and Schwartz measured instead. Between the summer of 1929 and the spring of 1933, they showed, the stock of money in America fell by about a third while thousands of banks failed. In their account the Federal Reserve did far too little, and an ordinary downturn became the Great Depression.

As president of the American Economic Association in 1967, Friedman attacked the Phillips curve, the idea that a bit more inflation could permanently lower unemployment. The trade works only while workers are fooled, he said. Once people come to expect the inflation and build it into their wage demands, unemployment drifts back to where it started, a level he called the natural rate. The 1970s, with high inflation and high unemployment at once, were widely read as the test his argument passed.

His consumption theory still does policy work. Suppose Congress mails a one-time rebate to every household to lift spending. An economist who follows Friedman expects much less spending than the sponsors hope, because the check changes this year's cash but not the long-run income a family budgets against.

Friedman and Ludwig von Mises both blamed central banks for deepening the century's worst slumps, yet each distrusted the other's method. Mises reasoned from principles of human action that, in his view, no statistic could ever overturn. Friedman insisted that an economic claim must stand or fall on measured series, such as the money stock, prices and output, that another researcher can check for himself. Austrians reply that numbers mean something only inside a theory, and the quarrel is still alive.

misess-disciples-the-chain-that-carried-.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises taught in Vienna between the wars and in New York after them. Through the postwar decades, when most universities ignored the Austrian school, its ideas survived because of a chain of people he trained or inspired: students, teachers and writers who passed the tradition from one generation to the next and carried it across the Atlantic.

The first great link was Friedrich Hayek, who went to work under Mises in a Vienna government office in 1921 and later called him his teacher. Hayek saw a market price as a signal that condenses the knowledge and wishes of countless people who trade. No central planner, he argued, could ever collect everything that prices already know, and that insight helped win him the Nobel Prize in 1974.

Murray Rothbard, a New Yorker who joined Mises's seminar at New York University in 1949, made a plain point about incentives. The more a government taxes and regulates, the smaller the reward for effort, so people produce less: they work, save and invent less than they otherwise would.

Israel Kirzner, who studied under Mises at NYU in the 1950s, put one activity at the center of the school in Competition and Entrepreneurship, published in 1973. The entrepreneur, Kirzner argued, is the person alert to opportunities everyone else has missed, a gap between prices or a want nobody is meeting, and that alertness is the true source of profit and of an economy that moves forward.

From the New York seminar, Mises's students carried the school's central teaching about prices into American colleges. Every price, they taught, tells how scarce a thing is, how much people want it and what it costs to make, knowledge scattered across millions of minds that no one person could ever pull together. Hans Sennholz, for one, taught it for decades at Grove City College in Pennsylvania.

Rothbard then set out to restate Mises's whole system for American readers. His two-volume treatise Man, Economy, and State (1962) swept from choice and prices through capital and money to the business cycle.

A year later Rothbard published America's Great Depression (1963), which applied the Austrian business cycle theory to the 1930s. In his account the Federal Reserve's easy money fed the false boom of the 1920s, and President Hoover's interventions stretched the 1929 crash into a decade-long slump.

The journalist Henry Hazlitt carried the method to the general public. His Economics in One Lesson (1946) stayed a best seller for decades. It boils the subject down to a single rule in the spirit of Bastiat: judge a policy by tracing all its effects on all groups of people, later as well as now, not just the visible benefit to one group today.

George Reisman, another graduate of the NYU seminar, went the other way. His Capitalism (1996), more than a thousand pages long, tried to fuse Mises's economics with the Objectivist philosophy of the novelist Ayn Rand into one grand system. Most economists at work today favor short, tight arguments, because a short argument can be tested against reality one claim at a time, while a vast system is hard to check piece by piece.

nationaloekonomie-1940-the-german-precur.context_blurb:
In 1940, as France fell to Hitler's armies, Ludwig von Mises, the Austrian economist, brought out the biggest book he had yet written. He wrote it in German, in neutral Switzerland, for a German-speaking world that was now closed to him. The story of that book, and of its second life in English, is a lesson in stubbornness.

Mises had taught at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva since 1934, after leaving Vienna. His treatise, Nationalökonomie, came out in Geneva in 1940 from a small Swiss house, Editions Union.

Then almost nobody read it. Nazi Germany and the Austria it had swallowed were closed to an author whose books had been blacklisted since 1933, and Switzerland, though neutral, was far too small a market to carry a thick German treatise. The book drew almost no notice.

That summer Mises fled to the United States and spent nine years rewriting and enlarging the book in English. Yale University Press published the result in 1949 as Human Action: A Treatise on Economics.

The two are not one book in two languages. They cover the same ground, from praxeology, the science of human action, to economic calculation, the business cycle and government intervention, but Human Action is longer and more polished, and it answers postwar American debates over Keynes, the New Deal and the Cold War.

For decades the German original was almost impossible to find. A German publisher reprinted it in 1980, and the Ludwig von Mises Institute in Auburn, Alabama, founded two years later, has since made both books freely available to any reader.

Read side by side, the two books teach a lesson about books themselves. A great work can meet almost no readers at first and still survive, because one determined author was willing to write it again in a new language for a new world.

north-korea-the-arduous-march-and-the-on.context_blurb:
North Korea, officially the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, is the last country on earth still run as a strict command economy. Since its founding in 1948 the state has owned the farms and factories, and planners have set the prices. Its record, a great famine, prison camps that still operate and a glaring gap with its southern twin, is the calculation debate played out on living people.

One family has ruled it for three generations: Kim Il-sung, his son Kim Jong-il and his grandson Kim Jong-un. The founder's official creed, Juche, set out in his speeches from 1955 on, teaches total national self-reliance: the country must stand alone and lean on no one, neither China nor the Soviet Union.

Floods and the loss of Soviet aid in the mid-1990s tipped the planned food system into a famine that the state calls the Arduous March. Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises had long since explained why a fully planned system so often ends in shortage. Free prices carry knowledge of what is scarce and what people need, scattered across millions of minds, and no planner can gather all that knowledge in one office.

Pyongyang keeps its records sealed, so outside scholars can only estimate the deaths above the normal rate. The standard range runs from about 600,000 to 2.5 million, in a country of some 22 million.

The regime also holds political prisoners in kwanliso, camps tucked away in the mountains of the north that Pyongyang has never acknowledged. Escapees and commercial satellite photos supply nearly all outside knowledge of them, and the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea, an American non-profit, publishes reports that set the two side by side.

The camps follow a rule the regime calls three generations of punishment. When one person is accused of a political crime, his parents, his brothers and sisters, his children and even his grandchildren can be imprisoned too, on the theory that disloyalty runs in the blood.

Mises opened the socialist calculation debate in 1920, and Hayek carried it on: without market prices, planners are blind. A famous nighttime satellite photograph of the Korean peninsula now illustrates it in countless textbooks. South Korea blazes with light, while North Korea lies nearly dark except for a glow around Pyongyang.

After the Second World War Korea was split at the 38th parallel, and the two halves began at similar living standards. The South chose markets, trade and private business; the North chose full planning. About seventy-five years later the average South Korean is roughly thirty times richer than the average North Korean, by the Bank of Korea's estimate.

The Austrian explanation is the calculation problem itself. Without market prices a state cannot weigh food, fuel, land and labor against one another, so it cannot allocate food or resources rationally across a whole nation, however hard its planners work.

After more than seventy years, the longest-running experiment in pure planning has produced chronic shortages of food and a great famine in the 1990s.

Its neighbors chose differently. China opened to private business under Deng Xiaoping from 1978, Vietnam began its Doi Moi reforms in 1986, and Cuba has cautiously let citizens run small businesses. All three keep one-party Communist rule but allow markets beneath it; only North Korea remains a pure command economy.

oskar-lange-and-market-socialism-the-rep.context_blurb:
Could socialism work if its planners were clever enough? Between the world wars that question split economists into two camps, in what became known as the socialist calculation debate. On one side stood the Austrians Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek. On the other stood the Polish economist Oskar Lange, whose market socialism was meant to beat the Austrians at their own game.

Mises opened the fight in 1920. Where the state owns every factory and farm, he argued, there are no market prices for steel, machines or land, so planners have no way to tell what to produce or in what amounts; they are guessing in the dark. Mises framed this as the problem of economic calculation, and Hayek later deepened it into what economists now call the knowledge problem.

In 1936 and 1937 Lange, then teaching at the University of Chicago, published his reply. The state would own the factories and mines, but people would still buy their everyday goods in real markets, and a central planning board would price machines and raw materials by imitating what a market would charge. He called the plan market socialism.

Lange granted that Mises had a point about pricing machines and raw materials, but he offered a way around it. The planning board would find the right prices by trial and error: announce a price, watch for shortages or surpluses, then nudge it up or down until supply and demand matched, just as a real market would.

The same faith in steering from the center shows up in budgets. A number of today's economists hold that taxing and spending should follow only what the economy seems to need at the moment, whether or not the books balance. Critics in the Austrian school, at the Mises Institute and beyond, answer that a government released from any duty to balance its budget tends to spend too much and to pay for it with inflation.

Hayek answered Lange on two fronts. First he edited Collectivist Economic Planning (1935), a volume that gathered translated essays by Mises, Enrico Barone and others, framed by his own opening and closing chapters, and it became a founding text for the Austrian side.

Then he changed the shape of the whole argument. The problem, Hayek said, is dispersed knowledge, not just price arithmetic. The facts that matter, about local conditions, shifting tastes and the circumstances of a particular time and place, live in millions of separate heads, and only market prices pull them together quickly enough to act on.

He made that case in 1945 in a short essay on the use of knowledge, printed in the American Economic Review, and it has stood ever since as the classic Austrian reply to every plan to run an economy from the top.

Mises and Hayek also saw a circle in any plan to borrow prices from capitalism. The prices a planner hopes to copy come from markets that socialism has already abolished, so there is nothing left to copy.

For decades many economists believed Lange had beaten Mises on paper. Hayek's essay named exactly what planners could not do and prices did automatically, gathering scattered knowledge, and that obstacle has been known ever since as the knowledge problem. The planned economies of Eastern Europe collapsed in 1989 and the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, moving the debate from theory into history. Lange did not see it; after serving as Poland's ambassador to the United States, he rose high in Communist Poland and died in 1965.

New socialist blueprints have kept appearing since Lange, from David Schweickart's economic democracy to the 21st-century socialism of Venezuela. Austrian critics say all of them share one gap: like Lange's board, they assume someone can gather what only prices know, and none of them answers Hayek's knowledge problem.

phil-zimmermann-pgp-and-the-munitions-li.context_blurb:
In the early 1990s strong encryption, the mathematics that keeps a message secret, was mostly a tool of governments and their spy agencies, and Washington treated it as a weapon. Phil Zimmermann, an American programmer, decided that ordinary people deserved it too. The fight that followed helped make it legal to publish code like the software that runs Bitcoin.

Encryption scrambles a message so that only someone holding the matching secret key can read it. In 1991 Zimmermann finished a free program that let anyone encrypt email, and he gave it a deliberately modest name: Pretty Good Privacy, or PGP.

He knew the government wanted such code kept inside the country, so he made sure that no one state could block it. He released it onto the internet, and within weeks copies had spread to computers all over the world.

By 1993 federal investigators were treating Zimmermann as a possible arms exporter. They relied on the Arms Export Control Act, under which strong encryption sat on the US Munitions List beside tanks and missiles.

Under that law, sending the program by email to someone in another country counted as the same act as shipping a rifle, or even a missile, overseas.

Zimmermann answered with a piece of legal theater. In 1995 MIT Press published PGP's entire source code as an ordinary printed book. Printed pages were not something the law could treat as a weapon, and a buyer abroad could simply scan the pages back into a computer.

The book stood on freedom of speech, applied to code as a kind of writing: if source code is speech, the government cannot forbid printing and selling it.

In January 1996, after nearly three years, the government dropped the investigation without ever filing charges.

Later federal cases brought by the programmers Daniel Bernstein and Peter Junger went further, holding that computer source code is speech protected by the First Amendment. Without that protection, Satoshi Nakamoto's open publication of Bitcoin's code in 2008 might have drawn the same kind of investigation.

The cypherpunks drew a lesson about timing. Once software is already everywhere, on thousands of computers in dozens of countries, no government has any way left to take it back, because nobody can un-publish a program.

potosi-silver-and-the-price-revolution-1.context_blurb:
In 1545 Spanish prospectors found a mountain of silver, the Cerro Rico above the town of Potosí, in what is now Bolivia. Within decades Potosí was one of the largest cities in the world. For the next century its silver, with more from Mexico, flowed to Europe, and it taught the world a lesson about money that economists still argue over.

Twice a year armed galleons gathered at Havana and crossed the Atlantic together to Seville, loaded with silver bars and coins for the Spanish king, with pirates and English raiders on their trail. Historians call these convoys the Spanish treasure fleets.

The flood of silver pushed Spanish prices for food and clothing higher every year. A general rise in prices, caused by far more money pursuing the same goods, is called inflation.

Between 1500 and 1650 prices across Europe rose several times over, roughly fivefold or sixfold by modern estimates, and the climb tracked the arrival of American silver. The lesson is that when the supply of money grows much faster than the supply of goods, prices rise.

Then came the puzzle. By 1600 Spain held more silver and gold than any nation in Europe, yet its workshops were closing, its royal treasury went bankrupt again and again, and Dutch and English competitors were winning its farmers' customers. The country with the most silver was growing poorer, not richer, because the flood raised Spanish prices faster than prices abroad and made Spanish goods too dear to sell.

Spanish scholars saw it happening. Catholic priests and teachers of law, most of them at the ancient university of Salamanca, studied prices, money and interest some two hundred years before Adam Smith. Historians call them the School of Salamanca.

In 1556 one of them, the theologian Martín de Azpilcueta, gave the first clear European statement of the idea: where money is plentiful it buys less, so an increase in money raises prices and a decrease lowers them.

Today that idea goes by the name of the quantity theory: the quantity of money governs what money is worth. Irving Fisher put it into an equation in 1911, and economists still use it to warn that a central bank which prints money to cover a government's deficits only drives prices higher.

The standard textbook says economics began with Adam Smith in 1776. Murray Rothbard's history of economic thought, published in 1995, traced it back to the Salamancans and earlier scholastics, showing that the textbook story skips real economic thinking that came centuries before Smith.

For today's central banks the Salamancans offer a warning: printing more money does not make a nation richer in real goods. Extra coins can lift prices without baking one extra loaf.

Frédéric Bastiat would split the Spanish paradox into what is seen and what is not seen. The seen was the galleons of silver arriving at Seville. The unseen was Spanish industry hollowed out and the savings of ordinary Spaniards quietly debased.

prices-and-production-1931-hayeks-lse-le.context_blurb:
In February 1931 Friedrich Hayek, a young Austrian invited by Lionel Robbins, gave four lectures at the LSE in London. Published that year as Prices and Production, they carried the Austrian theory of the business cycle to English readers, won Hayek the school's Tooke Chair, and set him on a collision course with John Maynard Keynes.

Behind the lectures lay an Austrian conviction. Picture a few officials in a capital like Soviet Moscow trying to plan how much bread, shoes, nails and winter hats fifty million people will need next year. The job is nearly impossible, because no small group can know what all those millions of people, with their different jobs, climates and tastes, actually want.

Prices do what planners cannot. If a great copper mine floods and copper's price shoots up, factory owners hunt for other metals or ways to use less, because the price is telling them information about what has grown scarce.

Hayek's lectures set out what is now called Austrian business-cycle theory, built on Ludwig von Mises's 1912 book on money and credit. Booms and busts, it holds, come from banks lending at interest rates held too low, not from sudden changes in investors' moods. The trigger, in Hayek's view, is a surge of easy credit that the banks themselves create, not the "animal spirits" that Keynes would later blame.

The real damage, Hayek argued, is not simply that prices rise. Cheap credit fools businesses into starting long, roundabout projects, such as mines, factories and machines that take years to pay off, which the real pool of savings cannot finish. The whole structure of production is bent out of shape.

To show production moving through stages, from raw materials like iron and lumber through factories and finishing to goods on a shelf, Hayek drew a triangle whose base stood for consumer goods and whose sloping side climbed through the earlier stages. Austrians have called it the Hayekian triangle ever since.

That led to Hayek's most startling conclusion. The boom, with its false signals and misplaced projects, was the disease; the bust was the painful correction, the market discovering its errors and moving resources back where they belong. Stimulus that prolongs the boom, in this view, only prolongs the illness.

Mises and Hayek predicted how every such boom ends. When a central bank pushes rates far below their natural level, the boom ends in a bust: once the cheap credit dries up, many of the projects it started collapse.

The lectures also started a famous quarrel. In 1931 and 1932 Hayek published a harsh review, in two parts, of John Maynard Keynes's Treatise on Money (1930) in the journal Economica, and Keynes struck back by attacking Prices and Production.

Then Keynes stepped away from the fight in 1932 and spent four years rebuilding his ideas. The result was The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936), the founding book of Keynesian economics.

public-choice-journal-founded-1966.context_blurb:
For most of the twentieth century, economists split the world in two. In the market, bakers and shopkeepers chased their own interest; in government, officials supposedly served only the common good. In the 1960s a band of economists in Virginia refused to accept that split, and in 1966 they gave their movement a journal of its own.

The school, whose leaders were Gordon Tullock and James Buchanan, is called public choice. Its founders pointed out the obvious: people in government want things too, such as reelection, bigger budgets and better jobs.

Tullock, a lawyer by training, founded the journal in 1966 at the University of Virginia under a long and clumsy title, Papers on Non-Market Decision Making. A few years later it was renamed Public Choice, and the short name spread until it labeled the whole field.

The movement grew up in a single state. Buchanan's research center began at the University of Virginia, moved to Virginia Tech, and in 1983 followed him to George Mason University, where it thrives today. All three universities are in Virginia.

The school's central assumption is that the people who staff government respond to incentives like everyone else and often act in their own interest. Voters, officials, lawmakers and regulators get no halos; economists study them the way they study shoppers.

In 1986 the field won its highest honor when Buchanan received the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, the economics Nobel, for his work on the constitutional and contractual foundations of political decision-making. Tullock, his partner on The Calculus of Consent (1962), never shared it.

The journal's pages built a whole vocabulary for how politicians, officials and voters actually behave: rent-seeking, the waste of lobbying for privileges that Tullock analyzed in 1967; logrolling, or vote-trading; the behavior of bureaucracies; constitutional political economy; and expressive voting.

regulatory-capture-at-the-sec-harry-mark.context_blurb:
Bernie Madoff was one of the most respected men on Wall Street. In December 2008 he confessed that his investment business had been a fraud for decades, the largest of its kind in American history. The most troubling part of the story is that a mathematician had told the government watchdog the truth years before, and nobody acted.

Madoff's scheme was an old one. He promised steady returns but never truly invested the money; he paid earlier investors with cash from newer ones and kept the rest. A fraud like that, which lasts only as long as fresh money keeps flowing in, is called a Ponzi scheme.

Harry Markopolos, a Boston financial analyst with a gift for mathematics, began studying Madoff's results in 2000. No real fund, he saw, could post such a steady profit month after month whether markets rose or fell. For about eight years he sent warnings to the SEC, the Securities and Exchange Commission, which guards investors for the federal government. The agency ignored him, and the fraud kept running for years.

His most famous report, sent in November 2005, was titled "The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud" and listed 29 red flags. He was right: Madoff's fund was a Ponzi scheme, using money from new investors to pay the old ones.

When the fraud collapsed in the 2008 crash, the losses on paper came to about $65 billion. Free-market thinkers draw a blunt lesson: a government watchdog can miss even an enormous fraud, so investors still have to think for themselves instead of trusting a regulator's seal.

Afterward the SEC's own inspector general wrote a long report on what the agency had missed. One failure it named was that young staff had been handed cases too complicated for their training; a single call to check Madoff's trading would have shown he was not making the trades he claimed.

Madoff was no fringe operator. Early in the 1990s he had served as chairman of NASDAQ, the major stock market, a post that made him an honored establishment figure years before anyone knew of the fraud.

After the collapse Markopolos told his story in a book whose title says it all: No One Would Listen (2010).

The $65 billion figure counted years of invented profits printed on clients' statements. Counting only the real cash that investors had handed over and lost, the damage came to about $18 billion.

Since 2010 the SEC has paid whistleblowers 10 to 30 percent of the fines their tips produce. Paying a percentage rather than a flat sum lines up the incentives: the bigger the fraud a whistleblower exposes, the bigger his reward, so insiders have reason to speak up sooner.

Why would a regulator ignore detailed warnings again and again? Public-choice economists, following George Stigler, look first at the staff's own career incentives, which pulled them away from tough fraud detection. Taking on a former NASDAQ chairman meant risk and embarrassment, while ignoring an outsider's complaint cost them little.

The case teaches a habit of mind. When an agency keeps doing nothing about a well-connected figure, ask whose career interests are served by not investigating him.

robert-conquests-great-terror-1968-the-v.context_blurb:
Robert Conquest was a British historian and poet who set out, in the middle of the Cold War, to count the dead of Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union. Many Western professors scoffed at his numbers. Then the Soviet Union fell, its secret archives opened, and the records showed that Conquest had been right.

Stalin's regime shot or imprisoned millions of its own people during the 1930s and starved millions of Ukrainian villagers in the famine of 1932 and 1933. Wherever communism was tried, from Russia to China and Cambodia, it brought death on the scale of tens of millions; the Black Book of Communism (1997) puts the toll at 65 to 100 million.

The worst years were the Great Terror of 1936 to 1938, when the secret police seized and killed vast numbers of people, among them loyal Communists, veteran revolutionaries, generals and factory bosses. The lesson is grim: a state that owns everything, the land, the factories and the press, and that no voter can remove, can aim its violence at anyone, with nothing to stop it.

In 1968 Conquest published The Great Terror, the first serious study of the purges published in the West, built from defectors' testimony, smuggled documents and close reading of what the Soviet press let slip. His sharpest attention went to the two worst years, 1937 and 1938. When the archives finally opened, the secret police's own records showed about 680,000 people executed in those two years, the scale Conquest had described.

For two decades afterward, a group of Western scholars around Sheila Fitzpatrick and Arch Getty argued that Conquest had counted too many dead and blamed Stalin too much personally, stressing local pressures and bureaucratic chaos instead. It was known as the revisionist school.

The argument was settled by the Soviet collapse in December 1991. The NKVD, Stalin's secret police, had kept careful books, and when researchers read them, its own records vindicated Conquest's execution estimate almost exactly. Stalin's handwriting even appeared on execution lists.

Conquest had already turned to the countryside. His second great book, The Harvest of Sorrow (1986), told the history of the 1932 to 1933 famine in Ukraine, a famine brought on by Stalin's forced seizures of grain, in which millions of peasants died. Ukrainians call it the Holodomor, death by hunger.

From 1981 Conquest worked at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, in California, where he guided a generation of scholars of the Soviet Union. In 2005 he received America's Presidential Medal of Freedom.

san-francisco-rent-control-diamond-mcqua.context_blurb:
In 1994 San Francisco voters approved Proposition I, bringing small apartment buildings of two to four units, built before 1980, under rent control. Nearly identical buildings just outside the rule stayed free of it. That accident of law gave economists a natural experiment in what rent control really does.

The classic study of it came from three Stanford economists, Franklin Qian, Tim McQuade and Rebecca Diamond. Using address-level records on every San Francisco rental, they compared the newly controlled buildings with their uncontrolled neighbors over two decades.

Their paper appeared in September 2019 in The American Economic Review, the flagship journal of the American Economic Association.

What happened to the newly covered buildings? Their owners found every exit the law allowed. Some converted units into condominiums, some tore buildings down and rebuilt them as new, unregulated housing, and some moved family members in. Together these moves cut the rental housing in the newly covered buildings by about 15 percent.

Fewer apartments for rent meant higher prices on the ones still available. Across the city, rents rose by about 5 percent as a result, raising costs for every tenant still looking for a home.

Tenants who already held protected leases saved a great deal, so the result was mixed, and Diamond described it plainly: the policy amounted to a transfer of wealth away from future renters and toward the tenants it protected today, not a fix for the city's housing shortage.

The finding was not new in theory. In 1946 Milton Friedman and George Stigler, two young economists who would both win Nobel Prizes, had predicted exactly this supply response in a short pamphlet published by the Foundation for Economic Education, Roofs or Ceilings? The Current Housing Problem.

segwit-and-taproot-the-two-big-soft-fork.context_blurb:
Bitcoin has no chief executive and no board that can change its rules. Its software runs on thousands of computers around the world, and an upgrade happens only if the people running them choose to adopt it. Two big upgrades of the past decade, SegWit and Taproot, show how that works, one after a bitter fight and one almost in silence.

The computers that check Bitcoin's rules are called nodes. A rule change can be gentle: older nodes still accept the new blocks as valid, so the network stays one chain. That backward-compatible kind of change is called a soft fork. A sharper change, which old nodes reject, can split the chain in two.

The rules that matter most never change at all. Only 21 million bitcoins will ever exist, and no person or company can alter that alone. That is the basic difference from the dollar: a central bank can issue new dollars at its own discretion, while nobody can create bitcoins beyond the cap.

From 2015 to 2017 the community fought the Block Size War over how large each block should be. SegWit, short for Segregated Witness, moved signature data out of the main part of each transaction, fixing an old flaw and adding room in every block. One faction wanted much bigger blocks instead, and on August 1, 2017, it split off with a hard fork to create a separate coin with larger blocks, Bitcoin Cash. SegWit itself activated that August.

Why does an upgrade need so many people? Because nobody runs Bitcoin: no single person or company is in charge, so a change takes effect only if enough miners and users install it. If most refuse, it simply never happens.

The second big upgrade, Taproot, activated in November 2021, after more than nine in ten miners signaled support. It brought in Schnorr signatures, named for the German cryptographer Claus-Peter Schnorr, which can combine several signers into one. That shrinks the signatures in each transaction and gives away less information about who is spending.

A student might ask why Ethereum is updated so often while Bitcoin hardly changes. A veteran Bitcoin coder would answer with Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem: thousands of separate miners, node runners and wallet makers must all accept new rules, and no central architect can safely rewrite the rules of a system spread across so many hands.

The contrast between the two upgrades carries a lesson. The blocksize fight finished in a split and an angry postmortem, while Taproot, a real change to the mathematics of signatures, passed almost without argument. Bitcoin developers conclude that decentralized consensus can deliver careful technical progress whenever the community broadly agrees.

smoot-hawley-tariff-and-the-collapse-of-.context_blurb:
In June 1930, as the Great Depression was taking hold, President Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, which raised American taxes on imported goods to their highest level in about a century. It became the most famous trade blunder in modern history, and it shows Frédéric Bastiat's seen and unseen at work on a world scale.

Canada, France and other trading partners retaliated with new tariffs. When countries trade blows like that, trade shrinks and both sides end up poorer, because each loses the goods it bought cheaply and the markets where it sold.

The act is named for the two Republicans who steered it through Congress: Senator Reed Smoot of Utah, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, and Representative Willis Hawley of Oregon, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.

Economists saw the danger coming. In May 1930 a petition signed by about one thousand of them, 1,028 names in all, appeared in the New York Times urging Hoover to veto the bill. He signed it anyway.

Congress built the law line by line, setting a separate duty for everything from watches to cheese, as each member defended the businesses back home. In the end it raised duties on more than twenty thousand separate goods.

Country after country closed its doors, among them Canada, France, Britain and Germany. Between 1929 and 1934 total world trade shrank by about two-thirds, the greatest peacetime collapse of commerce on record.

Bastiat had mocked this kind of protection in 1845. His mock petition to the French parliament came from the candlemakers, who begged lawmakers to shut out an unfair foreign rival, the sun, whose free light was ruining their trade.

The seen effects of Smoot-Hawley were cheering factory owners and foreign goods vanishing from the shelves. Bastiat's unseen ones took months or years to show: higher prices for every shopper, and lost sales for American exporters, whose foreign customers now faced retaliatory tariffs.

The cure came from changing who decides. The Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934, championed by Secretary of State Cordell Hull, let the president cut tariffs through bargains struck with other governments. A president bargains for the entire package at once, so no single local industry can block its own line, as it could in Congress.

After the Second World War the United States and 22 other countries signed the GATT, a broad accord on tariffs and trade, in 1947, which became the World Trade Organization in 1995. Such agreements calm tariff fights because each member promises the others not to raise its tariffs, so nobody has a reason to strike first.

Economists draw a general lesson from the 1930s. Raising tariffs during a downturn usually makes the downturn deeper instead of curing it. The actor and economist Ben Stein summed up the story in a famous classroom scene in the film Ferris Bueller's Day Off.

sowells-compared-to-what-reasoning-move.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell, who has worked at Stanford's Hoover Institution since 1980, built much of his career on a habit of mind that anyone can learn. When someone condemns an existing arrangement, Sowell asks what, exactly, would replace it, and whether that replacement has ever worked anywhere.

For decades he heard people call some market result, a low wage, a high price or a shortage, simply unacceptable. Most such claims, he said, collapse under a short question that almost nobody has an answer ready for: compared to what?

Picture a speaker at a public meeting who declares that the market has failed local families and the council should take over. Sowell's reply denies none of the hardship. It shifts the burden: the speaker must now name the particular institution he would put in the market's place, a city agency, a state board, a federal program, so that there is something real to weigh.

His book Applied Economics (2003) adds a second habit, thinking beyond stage one. When a state lifts its business tax, the first year's revenue does go up. Officials stop thinking there, Sowell says, because their horizon ends at the next election.

He then follows the same state a few years on. By stage two businesses have relocated to other states and new firms have settled elsewhere, so the state's tax base has shrunk and its revenue has fallen.

Economists have a name for the unfair comparison at the root of so many complaints. Measuring a real, untidy grocery store against an imaginary one where nothing is wasted and every shelf is full, and then calling the real store a failure, means comparing a real thing with a perfect fantasy instead of with other options that actually exist.

The economist Harold Demsetz named that habit in a 1969 paper. Writers, he noticed, set a working arrangement beside a paper ideal, see that reality falls short and pronounce it inefficient. Demsetz called it the nirvana approach, and later economists spoke of the nirvana fallacy.

Demsetz readily admitted that markets have flaws, but so do governments, so measuring either against perfection settles nothing. The real choice in policy, he wrote, is always between one actual institution and another actual institution.

His target included the great economist Kenneth Arrow, who had shown that a market might supply too little of something, such as new inventions, and then assumed that government would do better. Demsetz's complaint was that Arrow never checked: he had compared a real, flawed market with a government that existed only in imagination.

The move works on health care as well. A speaker says American medicine fails millions who cannot afford treatment and that the federal government should take it over. A Sowell-trained student disputes none of the hardship; he asks which existing public system is the model, Britain's, Canada's or the Veterans Health Administration's, and how it rations care, since each has a record that can be read.

James Buchanan urged economists to study politics without romance, treating officials as ordinary people rather than saints. Sowell's question attacks the same error from the opposite direction, and between them they enforce one rule: judge every institution, market or government, by the record it actually has.

The rule also exposes a common kind of reform proposal. Suppose a reformer would replace a country's private pensions with one state fund, run by independent trustees, shielded from politics and publicly audited. As an argument it has one flaw, however good the plan may be: the fund it describes exists nowhere yet, and a design on paper has never failed. An honest case would point to a state fund that has actually run for decades and show its record.

stephane-courtois-the-french-maoist-who-.context_blurb:
Stephane Courtois was born in 1947 at Dreux, west of Paris, and he grew up to become the French historian attached to the twentieth century's grimmest arithmetic. In 1997, working with European scholars from a dozen countries, he edited a thick volume that went regime by regime and counted the dead of communist rule: labour camps, engineered famines, purges, killing fields. Harvard University Press carried it into English, and the topline figure it reached has become the baseline number in any serious argument about the century.

That total was staggering: about 85 to 100 million people, dead not in battle but at the hands of the governments that ruled them. Courtois's own breakdown put China near sixty-five million and the Soviet Union near twenty million, with the remainder spread across Cambodia, Vietnam, North Korea, Africa and Afghanistan.

In May 1968 Paris nearly came apart: students threw up barricades, millions of workers walked out, and Charles de Gaulle's government wobbled. Courtois, a student then, was pulled into the fever and took up Maoism, the creed the fiercest of his classmates had borrowed from the upheaval Mao had unleashed in China. Reports out of Cambodia and the Soviet Union broke that faith during the 1970s, and the convert became the accuser. Courtois had himself been a Maoist student militant in 1968 before becoming the leading French counter-historian of communism, and that arc is why his indictment landed with a weight no outsider's could carry.

Long before the book he had made himself an archive historian. France's national research agency, the CNRS (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), the state body that puts permanent researchers on salary, hired him. That salary bought him years inside French Communist Party records, the files of the Comintern that Moscow once used to steer communist parties abroad, and, after 1991, the opening Soviet archives.

The Soviet chapter was the longest in the book. Its author, the French Sovietologist Nicolas Werth, had the first of the communist states to cover, seven decades of it, from Lenin's first camps in 1918 to the collapse in 1991, and he drew on the Soviet archives opened after 1991.

The sharpest fight over the book broke out among its own authors. Werth and Jean-Louis Margolin, who had covered Asia, sent a public dissent to the Paris daily Le Monde. Neither man disowned his own chapter's archival work; what both refused was Courtois's equating of communist and Nazi crimes in the introduction, a moral comparison each thought the documents did not license. Thirty years on, the country-by-country totals have held, and the quarrel over the framing has not.

teachers-union-public-choice-from-friedm.context_blurb:
In 1955 Milton Friedman published a short essay on how government should handle schooling, and it ended up putting millions of American children into classrooms their parents picked. He was not arguing that the state should stop paying for education. He was prising apart two jobs that had been welded together for a century: funding schooling versus producing it. A government can pay for a service, Friedman pointed out, without being the only body allowed to provide it.

The mechanism follows from the distinction. Rather than assigning a child to the building nearest his address, the state hands the money to the family. Parents can take the money to any approved school, public, charter, private or religious, and a school now has to be worth choosing before it sees a cent. In the American version that certificate carries a name of its own, a school voucher, worth a fixed sum each year, good for tuition at any school on the state's approved list and worth nothing at all if the family never spends it.

The capital ran the test. Congress set up a scholarship for low-income Washington families in 2004, and the federal Department of Education studied the results for more than a decade. Patrick Wolf, an education professor at the University of Arkansas, led a team comparing children who won the scholarship lottery against children who entered and lost, about as clean a comparison as school research gets, since the draw and not the parent decided who went. The winners finished school more often: higher graduation rates, by a margin big enough to count as statistically significant.

Thomas Sowell found a second natural experiment inside New York City's building rules. Some old school buildings there hold two schools at once, a district school and an independent charter such as a Success Academy campus, sharing the stairwells and the gym, drawing pupils from the same handful of blocks. Because both sit under one roof on one street, the neighborhood and building are the same, so those cannot explain any score gap. That is what makes a shared roof so useful: you can rule out the building and the neighborhood as reasons for any score gap, which leaves how each school is actually run. In his 2020 study of charter schools and their enemies, Sowell reported that in matched-building comparison after comparison, the charter pupils came out ahead.

The politics shows itself fastest when the doors close. The Chicago Teachers Union struck in 2012 and again in 2019, and each time roughly three hundred thousand children sat at home. A family with money bought a few weeks of private school or a tutor, while families whose kids can only attend the public schools had nothing to buy, and those were disproportionately the poorest households in the city.

Terry Moe at Stanford named this pattern in public-choice terms in a 2011 study of American teachers' unions. A union bargains hard for its members' pay, tenure and job security, which is precisely what a union exists to do, and the result is a special-interest group getting more from the system than the average voter does.

California showed the arithmetic in 1993. Proposition 174 would have given families a voucher; the California Teachers Association spent tens of millions of dollars to beat it and outspent the other side by something like ten to one. Far more families stood to gain a little than teachers stood to lose a lot, and the measure was still crushed. The lesson sits in one line: a small group that stands to lose a lot fights harder than a big crowd that stands to gain a little.

Mancur Olson's rule tells you why. A small, organised body with a great deal at stake out-manoeuvres a vast, scattered one with a little at stake, because organising costs money and only the concentrated side finds it worth paying. In American schooling the group that fits the shape is the teachers' union, which signs up members, negotiates the contracts, funds candidates and turns out voters in school-board elections almost nobody else attends. James Buchanan's public-choice school would stop you there, before analysis curdles into accusation. The question worth pressing is not whether teachers are good or bad people, since most of them are decent: it is which organized interest is best positioned to shape the rules.

the-1929-crash-black-thursday-and-black-.context_blurb:
The 1920s had been the finest stretch American investors had ever seen. The Dow climbed from about 63 in the summer of 1921 to 381 in the first days of September 1929, and ordinary people borrowed money to join the ride, certain it would never end. When prices climb on excitement and borrowed money, economists call it a speculative bubble, and this was the largest anyone had yet built.

The index everyone watched had been published since 1896 by the newspaperman Charles Dow and followed a short list of big industrial firms: the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Buying into it was absurdly easy. A broker might let a customer put down as little as a tenth of a share's price in cash and lend him the rest, so a hundred dollars could hold a thousand dollars of stock, an arrangement known as buying on margin.

The break came in the last week of October 1929, on two days traders named for ever afterwards: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday, the twenty-fourth and the twenty-ninth. On the Tuesday the selling went beyond anything the exchange had machinery for. About sixteen million shares changed hands, so many that the tape printing prices fell hours behind the market, and the index surrendered nearly twelve percent in a session; no day topped that volume for almost forty years.

Irving Fisher of Yale, perhaps the most respected economist in the country, had told an audience on 15 October that American share values stood on what he called a permanently high plateau. Two weeks later the plateau gave way, and the slide did not stop with the crash. Banks failed, factories shut, a quarter of the American workforce lost work, and the index kept falling until July 1932, by which time it had given up about 89 percent of its September 1929 value.

A crash is not a depression, and that was the puzzle Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz set out to settle in 1963. Earlier panics, 1907 and 1920 among them, had brought savage downturns and then recovery. What stretched this one across a decade, they argued, was the Federal Reserve allowing the money supply to collapse by about a third while bank after bank went under and nobody lent the system the cash it needed to stay open. The comparison that makes their case is 1920. That slump was steep, with unemployment near twelve percent, and Warren Harding's government, which inherited it on taking office in March 1921, trimmed its own budget, printed nothing extra, and let prices and wages drop until firms could hire again. The whole thing was over in about eighteen months, which is why 1920 is the standard counter-example to the decade that followed 1929.

For anyone who had bought at the top, the arithmetic was brutal. The index did not close above its September 1929 level again until November 1954, a quarter of a century later.

the-2020-2024-inflation-abct-applied-to-.context_blurb:
When a government wants to spend money it does not have, a central bank can create it. What the 2020s settled is what happens next, and how long the bill takes to arrive.

In March 2020 the pandemic shut the American economy down and the markets came apart. The Federal Reserve answered by buying government debt and mortgage paper at a speed it had never attempted in a hundred and seven years of existence: in the first few weeks alone its purchases passed a trillion dollars. Its balance sheet, which is what it owns against the dollars it has put into the world, stood near $4.2 trillion before the pandemic and reached nearly $9 trillion at its peak in April 2022. The money supply followed. M2, the plain count of dollars sitting in current accounts, savings accounts and money funds, went from roughly $15.4 trillion in February 2020 to about $21.7 trillion by April 2022, a rise of more than two-fifths in two years and the fastest peacetime expansion the country has seen.

Prices were rising 1.4 percent a year in early 2021. As the country reopened they began to climb hard, and the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Jerome Powell, told press conference after press conference that the rise would fade on its own. The word he used, over and over through that year, was transitory. By June 2022 American consumer prices stood 9.1 percent above the year before, the steepest twelve-month rise since 1981, and the word had become a joke. Powell gave it up in November 2021, telling a Senate committee that it was probably a good moment to retire that word, and the rate rises began the following March.

None of this surprised people who count dollars for a living. Milton Friedman had put the rule into one sentence in a talk in India in 1963: inflation is always and everywhere produced by a faster rise in the money supply than in output, whatever particular story the newspapers hang on it. The analysts who called the 2021 inflation two years in advance were drawing on the Austrian school of Mises, Hayek and Rothbard, whose business-cycle work holds that a burst of new credit reaches consumer prices on a lag of twelve to twenty-four months. Peter Schiff and other hard-money writers made exactly that argument in the spring of 2020.

One school took the opposite view and got a public test. Stephanie Kelton and the modern-monetary-theory writers had argued that the real limit on money-financed government spending is physical, a matter of workers and factories and materials rather than of political will, and that the inflation limit was still comfortably distant. Then prices went from about one percent to over nine. Critics treated the sequence as a demonstration in real time: the inflation limit the theory had called comfortably distant had already been reached, and printing lots of new money really does drive up prices. The wider recognition is the one that survives every argument about shipping containers. A big enough increase in the money supply pushes prices up on a lag, whatever else is going on, and a shock to particular goods changes the shape of the rise rather than its source.

Putting the price level back cost something. From March 2022 the Fed lifted its target by 525 basis points in about sixteen months, the fastest tightening in four decades. The only comparable episode in living memory is Paul Volcker's 1979-1982 campaign, which drove rates near 20 percent and brought two downturns in order to break the inflation of that era.

the-bennett-hypothesis-federal-student-a.context_blurb:
In February 1987 Ronald Reagan's Secretary of Education published a short and rude essay in the New York Times accusing American colleges of pocketing the aid that Congress was sending to students. William Bennett's argument has outlived the row it started, and most of the evidence gathered since has gone his way.

The mechanism takes one move to see. Suppose Washington hands each undergraduate a new ten-thousand-dollar grant. The colleges know precisely how much more a family can now pay, and the seats in the good schools have not multiplied, so tuition prices go up by about the same amount. The money was meant for the student, but in the end most of it reaches colleges, through higher tuition, which is why the net cost of attending barely moves. Economists call the claim the Bennett Hypothesis: a subsidy handed to buyers in a market where supply is tight and demand is stubborn ends up captured by the sellers.

The thirty-year record is startling. Between 1987 and 2017, after allowing for inflation, tuition at American public four-year colleges climbed about 213 percent and at private ones about 129 percent, outrunning the price of food, cars and housing. Over the same decades one stream of money expanded step for step with that climb: federal student loan and Pell Grant programs, enlarged at each reauthorisation of the higher-education law. The debt is the other side of the same ledger. Federal student loans outstanding have grown from roughly a hundred billion dollars in the 1990s to about $1.7 trillion, a burden now heavier than all the credit-card balances in America put together.

Two pieces of work put numbers on the mechanism. A New York Fed team led by David Lucca compared each extra dollar of government-backed lending with the published price tags, using the moments when loan limits jumped, and found that a $1 increase in subsidized federal loans led to about a $0.60 increase in sticker tuition. Grey Gordon and Aaron Hedlund then built a model of the whole American tuition market covering the years 1987 to 2010 and asked how much of the rise the expansion of aid could explain. The answer their simulation gave was essentially all of it, a result that leans on the model's assumptions but points the same way as the Fed's measurement.

Bennett's own answer is the one critics still give: cheap government-backed student loans let colleges keep raising tuition, with the taxpayer closing the gap and nobody on campus facing a buyer who can simply walk away. Richard Vedder laid the pattern out in a 2004 book on why college costs too much, years before the measurements arrived, and the spending figures show where the extra revenue went. American colleges took on more than half a million new administrators and professional employees between 1987 and 2012, roughly eighty-seven every working day, so that the ranks of such staff more than doubled, twice as fast as the number of students grew, and the celebrated climbing walls and luxurious dormitories came out of the same pot. The aid builds administrative bureaucracy and amenity competition, not classroom capacity.

The pattern is not confined to campuses. Section 8 housing vouchers producing rent increases in tight rental markets is the same machinery in another market: give a tenant more to spend where no new flats are going up, and the landlord takes the difference. Health-insurance subsidies and the homebuyer credit of 2008 have been read the same way. That leaves one question worth asking before any buyer-side subsidy is voted through, and it is not whether the cause is good. It is who has the market power to price against the newly-enhanced payment capacity.

the-broken-window-applied-to-war-and-dis.context_blurb:
Every generation rediscovers the idea that smashing something is good for business, and every generation gets the same answer out of a pamphlet written in 1850. Frederic Bastiat's broken-window chapter supplies the tool. The twentieth century supplied the tests.

The first test arrived with peace. More than eight million American soldiers were home by the middle of 1946, and federal spending fell off a cliff: from about eighty-four billion dollars in 1945 to roughly thirty billion the next year, a cut of close to two-thirds inside twelve months and the largest peacetime fall ever recorded. Alvin Hansen of Harvard, whom colleagues called the American Keynes, had already told the public what to expect. The economy would be slipping back into depression as wartime spending was withdrawn, because on his reading it was the war budget that had ended the slump of the 1930s. It did not happen. Unemployment stayed around 4 percent through 1946 and 1947 as private buyers and private investors took up the men and the materials the government had released.

Henry Hazlitt, a journalist rather than a professor, brought out a short book for ordinary readers that same year and made Bastiat's method the spine of it: Economics in One Lesson. The demobilisation, he pointed out, was The broken window run backwards, since destroying the government's spending did not impoverish the country, because the labour and the steel were freed for somebody else to use. That is exactly where they went. The men and the dollars were absorbed by private demand and investment within months of the transition, which is what Bastiat's reasoning predicts and what the gloomier forecasts had ruled out.

The error came back on 14 September 2001. Three days after the towers fell, Paul Krugman wrote in the New York Times that the destruction might do the economy some good, with so much new building now required. He later stepped away from the framing, but the column is the standard modern example of the broken window fallacy. Bastiat's question is the one almost nobody asked at the time. The steel, the concrete and the skilled trades that went into rebuilding lower Manhattan were not idle before, so what the country gave up was other new office buildings and other homes those workers and materials could have produced instead.

Hurricane Katrina got the same treatment and deserves the same answer. Rebuilding the Gulf coast cost something like a hundred billion dollars, and by late 2006 the people of Louisiana and Mississippi had the same houses they had before, minus a year of alternative economic activity plus deaths and injuries. A hundred billion dollars of labour and material that replaces what existed cannot also build what did not.

The family of claims is a large one: that the September 11 attacks were good for business, that the Second World War cured the Depression, that a hurricane would lift the Gulf economy. Each makes the identical mistake, treating Destruction and production as if they were one quantity, when a country that rebuilds what it had is poorer than a country that builds something new on top of it.

the-constitution-of-liberty-1960.context_blurb:
By the late 1950s the argument looked settled. The state ought to take over more of the economy, and the only question left was how much. Friedrich Hayek spent the decade writing the other case, this time not as an attack but as a design. The Constitution of Liberty appeared from the University of Chicago Press in 1960, and the tradition it defends, in which people make their own choices instead of a committee making them for everybody, is classical liberalism.

He wrote it at Chicago but not in the economics department, which had not wanted him. His chair sat in the Committee on Social Thought, the small interdisciplinary unit that later housed Saul Bellow and Allan Bloom, and he finished the manuscript there in 1959.

The book opens by narrowing a word that everybody uses loosely. Liberty, as Hayek means it, is not wealth, not political voice and not power over one's circumstances. It is the absence of coercion by another person, the condition of not being made to serve somebody else's will. The definition is deliberately thin, and the thinness is the point, because a word that means everything desirable cannot be defended against anything. He laid the argument out in three parts: the first on why freedom is worth having, titled The Value of Freedom, then one on freedom and the law, then one on freedom in the welfare state.

The legal argument turns on a distinction that two identical fines can illustrate. A fine for running a red light comes from a rule set down in advance and applied to everybody alike; a fine imposed because an official decided on the spot that you owed him one comes from somewhere else entirely. The difference between the two is the rule of law versus administrative discretion, even when the money leaving your pocket is exactly the same. The last part asks why a free order outperforms a planned one, and Hayek's answer is not that people are wise. It is that the value of an innovation cannot be known before someone is free to try it, which means a planner would have to know the discovery already in order to permit it.

The book ends with a postscript that surprised half its readers. Hayek refuses the label most of them had assumed fitted him, in a chapter called Why I Am Not a Conservative, and claims instead the older British name Edmund Burke had used of himself, an Old Whig. The reasoning is sharp. A conservative wants to hold the present position, while Hayek wanted to move toward more freedom. The objection he presses is that conservatism has no positive program, only a resistance to change from wherever society currently stands, which makes it a brake rather than an alternative.

One story about the book is better known than anything in it. In 1975, as the account goes, Margaret Thatcher silenced a colleague who was recommending a middle way by producing the book from her bag, striking it on the table and declaring that this was what her party believed. The gesture was about the thing the book presses, that individual liberty and free markets are what makes a free society possible. The anecdote comes from John Ranelagh's 1991 history of the Thatcher circle, and the Margaret Thatcher Foundation's own archive note calls it a little too perfect, perhaps, to be true. That caution is the lesson about evidence: vivid political anecdotes should be flagged as reported testimony, not treated as settled historical fact.
