the-cypherpunk-mailing-list-hughes-may-g.context_blurb:
In the autumn of 1992 three Bay Area engineers began meeting in a house in Oakland and then opened a mailing list, and what they argued about was whether ordinary people could have privacy that no government could overrule. Eric Hughes was a Berkeley mathematician, Timothy May a retired physicist, John Gilmore the fifth employee at Sun Microsystems. The hacker and writer Jude Milhon gave the group its name, and it stuck: the cypherpunks.

The tool they pressed on everybody was cryptography (scrambling messages with a code), which until then had belonged to armies, embassies and banks; what this group wanted was a schoolteacher able to use it on a home computer without asking anyone's leave. Their reason for thinking it urgent fits in one line: a state that reads every message can control people, since one that knows everything you say to your friends can decide which friends you keep.

May's own road to the argument ran through semiconductors. In the late 1970s his job was to work out why memory chips kept corrupting themselves, and the answer proved to be alpha particles thrown off by traces of radioactive material in the packaging, flipping bits at random. He fixed it, the company he fixed it for was Intel, and the stock options left him rich enough to retire in his thirties and think full-time.

The claim the list existed to defend was political, and it was about permission. Ordinary people should be able to use unbreakable codes without asking permission, which in the early 1990s was close to illegal, since American export rules then treated strong encryption as a munition. The list also had a rule about how to win an argument. Hughes put it in three words at the close of his manifesto in March 1993, and the movement adopted them as a standard: 'Cypherpunks write code.' Essays were welcome; shipped software was the only thing that counted.

Geography helped. The Oakland meetings sat inside an hour's drive of Stanford and Berkeley, two of the strongest centres of cryptography in the world at the time, one of them the home of public-key cryptography and the other Hughes's own graduate school. By the late 1990s the list had gathered the people who would build the pieces of Bitcoin: Adam Back, Wei Dai, Hal Finney, and Nick Szabo, authors respectively of a proof-of-work postage stamp, a bankless currency sketch, a reusable proof-of-work system and a design for scarce digital tokens. Julian Assange was on the list as well.

Sixteen years after Oakland the payoff arrived in an email. On 31 October 2008 someone calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto posted to a cryptography list descended from Gilmore's old server, and what he posted was a white paper for Bitcoin, a design for electronic cash passed peer to peer, with no bank in the middle, kept honest by proof-of-work. Looking back, the bet those founders made in an Oakland living room is the thing worth naming: that mathematics and code could give ordinary people privacy the government could not take away, rather than privacy granted by a parliament or licensed by a company.

the-fatal-conceit-1988-hayeks-last-book.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek published his last book in 1988, at eighty-nine, under the title The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism, and it reads as the compressed summary of nine decades of thinking. The conceit of the title is a species of pride, and the book's question is what exactly the planners had been proud about.

The pride lay in an assumption about what a committee can know. They thought a small group could plan what millions of people need, which sounds like competence until somebody asks where the knowledge would come from. Hayek's reply runs the other way round. The information is spread across millions of people making their own choices, held as local circumstance and private preference and practical skill, and it changes faster than any office could gather it.

Hayek would not call the thing he was defending capitalism, since the word suggests a scheme somebody invented for the benefit of people who own capital. His own name for it is the extended order of human cooperation: an arrangement in which strangers across a continent trade with one another by customs and rules no committee ever wrote. The first chapter explains where those rules come from, and its title is the argument in three words: Between Instinct and Reason. Morals, on this account, are a third thing, neither animal impulse nor the conclusion of anybody's reasoning, but an inheritance from cultural evolution. He opens with David Hume's remark that morality is not something our reasoning worked out. The claim it supports is worth holding onto: long-tested traditions can be wiser than any single clever planner, because a rule that survived many generations was tested against more cases than one mind could imagine.

The mistake Hayek names is a specific one, and it is a good engineer's mistake. A man who can design a bridge or an aircraft naturally supposes an economy could be laid out the same way, from a drawing, and the reason it cannot is that the market uses more dispersed knowledge than any single mind or committee could hold. Prices are how that knowledge gets gathered and used without anyone possessing it. The rules that make such an order possible, property and honest trade and keeping a contract and the family, were drafted by nobody either. They spread the way traits spread under natural selection, only through customs and habits instead of genes, and Hayek's word for the process is cultural evolution. The whole argument has a standard name in economics, one he had given it decades earlier: the knowledge problem.

The target is not only Moscow. Hayek wrote as Soviet planning visibly failed, but he aimed the same charge at friendly Western technocracy, at demand management and the confident official with a model. The move that joins the two is this: both treat the evolved order as though a rational designer could grasp and improve on the knowledge it embodies. One honest caveat belongs with the book itself. Hayek fell ill in 1985 and his editor, William Warren Bartley, prepared much of the manuscript; Bruce Caldwell, who now edits the collected works, has argued from the diction that the finished text owes more to Bartley's pen than an ordinary edit would explain. The scholarly conclusion is a rule about sources rather than about Hayek: that a heavily rewritten manuscript should be read as a joint editor-author work, with specific passages flagged as uncertain, while the core argument stays unmistakably his.

the-free-banking-era-and-the-national-ba.context_blurb:
Andrew Jackson refused to recharter the Second Bank, and from 1837 until the Civil War no institution stood above the banks at all. Banks were chartered by the states under state laws, and each printed paper of its own. Historians call the period the free-banking era.

Hundreds of different bills circulated, and a New York shopkeeper handed a note drawn on a bank in Georgia had two questions: is that bank still open, and what is its paper really worth? The answer came from a subscription trade press, printed banknote reporters, which listed every known bank and the discount its notes were fetching, ninety cents on the dollar from a distant bank and nothing at all from a failed one. Some banks earned their discount. In Michigan and Indiana a few put their redemption offices deep in the woods, where a noteholder would have trouble reaching them, and the joke was that the only customers for miles were the local wildlife; the term for such a bank is a wildcat bank.

The Civil War ended the arrangement, and it ended for the oldest reason there is. The Bank of England dates from 1694, when William III needed money for his war with France, and America's first chartered bank of 1791 was built partly around the debts of the Revolution; the pattern is ancient and the motive is to make it easier to borrow the huge sums a war costs. Salmon Chase, Lincoln's Treasury Secretary, designed the national banking laws of 1863 and 1864 to create a captive market for government bonds, and in passing they solved a real problem, because the country had no single trusted paper currency before them. Federally chartered banks could now issue one uniform note against Treasury bonds held in reserve. State paper was not forbidden outright. In 1865 Congress taxed it at 10 percent, which was enough to make state note issue commercially pointless, and within a couple of years it had gone.

The textbooks used to call the free-banking decades chaos. In 1983 two economists at the Minneapolis Fed, Arthur Rolnick and Warren Weber, went back to the failure records of the leading free-banking states and found something duller: they were modest and comparable to later regulated eras, which is now the standard revisionist finding. What the national system lacked was left out on purpose. Congress omitted a lender of last resort, because critics feared the concentration of power that would come with one. When the panics of 1873, 1893 and 1907 arrived there was nobody to supply emergency cash, and J. P. Morgan had to organise the 1907 rescue himself, which became the main argument for creating the Federal Reserve in 1913. The war produced one more currency worth knowing. The Treasury, short of gold, printed paper backed by nothing but the government's promise, and its reverse side was printed in green ink: greenbacks, which traded below gold during the fighting and returned to par when convertibility came back in 1879.

The Austrian reading of the episode is about the reporters rather than the banks. Nobody was ordered to rate a bank's paper and no agency published the discounts; merchants priced risky notes low and sound notes high, and a trade press collected those prices and sold them. That is an emergent order, with prices carrying each bank's reputation: the price system doing a job that looks as though it must need a regulator. It is the argument Hayek would make about prices in general in 1945, on a small scale and eighty years early.

the-halving-and-the-21-million-cap.context_blurb:
Every currency has an issuance rule, and in almost all of them the rule is a committee. Bitcoin's rule is arithmetic, written into the software before anybody used it.

When Satoshi Nakamoto started the network on 3 January 2009, the software paid the miner who added a block a brand-new reward of 50 BTC. That payment was never meant to last. Every 210,000 blocks the reward is cut in half automatically, and with a block arriving every ten minutes or so that comes to about one cut every four years. The community's name for the event is the halving. The first came in November 2012 and took the reward to 25 bitcoins, the second in 2016 to 12.5, the third in 2020 to 6.25, and the fourth in April 2024 to 3.125.

Halve a number for ever and the total converges. Summing the whole series gives Bitcoin's final supply of 21 million bitcoins, a figure fixed on the first day the software ran. The point of a shrinking reward is not to punish miners but to keep new supply scarce and predictable forever, so that anybody can work out today how many coins will exist in forty years. Following the curve, the last new coin is mined around 2140, after which miners are paid out of transaction fees alone. The unit at the bottom matters too: a bitcoin divides into a hundred million pieces, each one a satoshi, which is how a currency limited to twenty-one million units can still price a cup of coffee.

What makes that number unlike any other monetary rule in history is who may change it. Milton Friedman spent his career arguing that money growing faster than goods must push prices up, and his remedy was a rule for a central bank; Bitcoin went further, because the cap cannot be raised by any committee, politician, or emergency vote. Lifting it would mean persuading every user on earth to run different software, and anyone who did would be running a different currency.

The objection from the other side of the profession is not about inflation at all. Keynesian economists, Paul Krugman among those who have pressed it, argue that a fixed supply forces prices and wages down in a slump, making debts heavier. If the quantity of money cannot grow when demand collapses, prices and wages have to fall instead, and a debt fixed in money grows heavier as they do. Austrians answer that the falling prices are the adjustment and that elastic money only postpones it. The argument is live, and a reader can follow both halves of it.

the-law-when-legal-force-is-used-for-plu.context_blurb:
Bastiat published The Law in June 1850, six months before he died, and it is the shortest statement of his politics. It opens with a claim about purpose: the law exists to defend three things a person holds before any government exists, which are life, liberty, and property.

Everything else follows from what happens when the law is turned to some other purpose. Use it to take what one man has earned and hand it to another, and the law becomes a tool for legal robbery. Bastiat called that spoliation legale, and every English edition since 1859 has rendered the phrase as legal plunder. He offers a test anybody can apply to a proposed statute, and it is one question: does the law take from some persons what belongs to them and gives it to other persons to whom it does not belong? His second test is sharper still, which is to see whether the law lets one citizen do to another what he could not do himself without committing a crime.

He names the French examples of his own day without flinching. One is the socialism of the national workshops, guaranteed employment paid for out of everybody's taxes; the other is protectionism, the tariff that moves money from every shopper to a sheltered producer. He even binds the two to communism in one image: the three are one plant at three stages of its growth. The cost he thought worst is not financial. When a state plunders by statute for long enough, citizens stop asking whether a thing is right and ask only whether it is permitted, and that decay of the ordinary moral sense is corruption, the private version of the move the law itself has been making.

One sentence out of the pamphlet has been quoted ever since by people who never read the rest. He described the state as a great fiction through which each person tries to live at the expense of everyone else, a line he had first used in an essay of 1848. In America the pamphlet has never been out of print since 1950, kept there by the small institute at Irvington-on-Hudson that Leonard Read founded in 1946 with Henry Hazlitt's help: the Foundation for Economic Education.

Strip the pamphlet down to one claim and this is it: Law exists to protect life, liberty, and property, not to redistribute them. That is a statement about what law is for rather than a policy programme, and a reader who accepts the premise still has to argue every case out for himself.

the-mises-privatseminar-1920-1934-vienna.context_blurb:
From 1920 to 1934 the most important economics seminar in Europe had no university behind it, no fees, no examinations and nothing to show for attending. It met every other week in an office belonging to the Austrian Chamber of Commerce in Vienna, and it belonged to the man who worked there as the chamber's economist: Ludwig von Mises. The law faculty in Vienna let him lecture without a salary, but his paid work and the seminar's room were in the same building, which is the institution the circle met inside: the Austrian Chamber of Commerce (Handelskammer).

The register of that room is the point. Two of the regulars became famous beyond economics: Friedrich Hayek and Oskar Morgenstern, one of whom shared the 1974 Nobel while the other launched game theory with John von Neumann in 1944. Gottfried Haberler and Fritz Machlup sat there too, and so did people from outside the subject altogether, among them the sociologist Alfred Schuetz, who argued that economics rests on the meanings people give their own actions. That mixture was the seminar's method as much as its membership, because other fields ask questions economics alone would never think to ask.

What Mises himself argued in that office became the school's central claim. No committee of officials in a capital city can plan an economy well, however clever or well-intentioned its members, and the reason is not arithmetic. Millions of people have information the planners never see, about what they want, what they can do and what a thing costs them, and almost none of it is ever written down.

In 1931 Lionel Robbins, the young head of economics at the London School of Economics, brought one of the seminar's regulars to London; Hayek joined the School that year, and the Austrian tradition travelled with him into English. The lesson in that is small and real: personal contact and one open door can carry ideas across borders. Vienna had a second room of the same kind. A mathematical colloquium met in those years with John von Neumann and Kurt Goedel among its debaters, hosted by a member of the Vienna Circle whose father had founded the Austrian school with his Principles of Economics in 1871: Karl Menger the younger, son of Carl Menger.

The seminar ended because the city did. In the spring of 1934 Mises left for a professorship at the graduate institute for international studies in Geneva, and the Privatseminar stopped; he moved on to New York in 1940 as the German army approached the Swiss frontier. Most of the others faced the same problem, since its members were Jews or liberals who had to flee Central Europe as the Nazis rose, and the annexation of Austria in March 1938 made staying impossible. They landed where they could, and the school was transplanted almost by accident. Machlup, who had left on a Rockefeller fellowship in 1933 and never returned, taught at Buffalo and then held chairs at Johns Hopkins, Princeton and New York University and pioneered the study of knowledge and information as an economic subject. Haberler went to Harvard, Morgenstern stayed at Princeton, and Hayek was already in London.

the-nyu-seminar-1945-1969.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises reached New York in 1940 with very little, and no American university would give him a paid chair; his free-market economics was unfashionable to the point of embarrassment. New York University made him a visiting professor and paid him nothing, an arrangement that lasted twenty-four years, and from 1945 to 1969 he ran a Thursday-evening seminar there that was the American successor to his Vienna circle.

Somebody had to pay him. The William Volker Fund of Kansas City covered much of the salary, as it did for Hayek at Chicago, and Lawrence Fertig, a Madison Avenue advertising man who admired the work, made up the rest out of his own pocket. The reason private money was needed at all is the uncomfortable part: Universities would not hire scholars whose ideas they disliked. What the arrangement shows is something a reader can use: Even unpopular ideas can survive if some people value them, which is also how a tradition gets carried for a generation by a few donors and one unpaid room.

Two of his standing arguments ran through the whole twenty-four years. The first was about inflation: when a government creates a great deal of new money, prices climb, and the loss is not spread evenly, because the ones hurt most are People with savings and people on fixed incomes, whose claims are fixed in a money being diluted. The second was Hayek's, argued in 1945 and shared by the whole school: an official in a capital cannot know which bakery is short of yeast this morning or whose tractor broke last night. The name for that permanent gap between what a planner can gather and what an economy runs on is The knowledge problem.

The students did the carrying. Murray Rothbard, who arrived in 1949 and stayed through the 1960s, wrote a treatise in 1962 that opens not with charts but with one man alone on an island, and builds trade and prices and money up from his choices a step at a time. The point of starting there is To show that every trade and price begins with individual choices. Israel Kirzner took his doctorate under Mises and built the Austrian account of the entrepreneur, published in 1973. The engine of new firms and better prices is neither capital nor luck but Alertness to opportunities other people have overlooked, the noticing of a gap between what a thing sells for here and what it would fetch over there.

Hans Sennholz, Mises's first American doctoral student, spent his whole career teaching at Grove City College in Pennsylvania, and that mattered more than it sounds: Austrian ideas kept a foothold in a few colleges even when mainstream departments ignored them. The same pattern held across the emigration. Mises taught in New York, Hayek at Chicago, Machlup at Princeton and Haberler at Harvard, several of them into the late 1960s, and the effect of those long careers is the plain one: They carried Austrian ideas into a whole new generation of English-speaking students. Mises gave his last seminar in December 1969 and died in 1973 at ninety-two; nobody took over the room, and American Austrian economics had no dedicated graduate programme again until the 1980s.

the-phillips-curves-death-and-friedmans-.context_blurb:
In 1958 a New Zealander working in London, Bill Phillips, plotted British wages against unemployment across the years from 1861 to 1957 and found a pattern: low unemployment went with fast-rising wages, high unemployment with wages that hardly moved. The relationship took his name and is called the Phillips curve.

A correlation in old data became a policy instrument in the 1960s, when Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow redrew it as a menu, with prices on one axis and joblessness on the other. Turn the dial one way for fewer unemployed, the other way for slower prices: the inflation-unemployment trade-off, which American policy treated for a decade as a choice available to whoever held office. In December 1967 Milton Friedman stood up at the American Economic Association and said the trick works once. As soon as people see prices rising they bargain for it, so in the long run the trade-off between inflation and unemployment vanishes. Edmund Phelps had reached the same conclusion that year on his own, and the work was part of what the Nobel Prize honoured when it went to him in 2006.

What the two of them put in place of the menu was a baseline. However much a central bank prints, unemployment drifts back to a level set by real things, by skills and the matching of workers to jobs and the institutions of the labour market, and that baseline is the natural rate of unemployment. Monetary expansion can push below it only for as long as people are fooled. That makes one variable central: people's expectations of future prices matter a lot, because a worker who expects prices up five per cent next year asks for the raise before the prices arrive. The 1970s then settled the argument in the rudest way available. America got high prices and high unemployment at the same time, a combination the curve said could not occur, and the word coined for it is stagflation. By 1979 the country had roughly six per cent of its workers idle and eleven per cent inflation together.

Part of the explanation is political rather than theoretical. Arthur Burns, chairman of the Fed through the 1970s, was leaned on by Richard Nixon to keep money loose into the 1972 election so that the electorate would feel prosperous that November. Burns obliged, Nixon took forty-nine states, and the decade paid for it, which is the lesson: a central bank that helps politicians in the short run creates bigger inflation later. Phillips himself had built something else worth remembering. In 1949 he made a machine of tanks and pipes in London in which coloured water stood for money moving through the British economy; turn a valve and watch the consequences flow. The reason no such machine can forecast an economy is the Austrian point in physical form: real economies are made of millions of people making choices, not smooth flows.

The Austrians agreed with Friedman and then went further. Murray Rothbard, following Mises's account of the cycle, accepted that expectations undo the trade-off but pressed a deeper claim: every attempt to fine-tune with monetary expansion eventually produces the same distortion-and-liquidation cycle. Cheap credit does not merely lift prices; it misdirects investment into projects the available savings cannot finish, and the stagflation Friedman diagnosed is what the liquidation of those projects looks like.

the-roman-denarius-debasement-64-ad-274-.context_blurb:
For four centuries the Roman world priced everything in one small silver coin, the denarius, first struck around 211 BC in the war against Hannibal. A soldier on the Rhine drew his pay in it, a tax official in Egypt counted it into chests, a baker in Ostia made change with it. Under Augustus the coin held about ninety-eight parts silver in a hundred, and that purity is precisely why a stranger in a strange market would take it.

The trouble began with an emperor who needed money in a hurry. In 64 AD, with much of Rome burnt and his own household spending enormous, Nero ordered the mint to drop the silver to roughly ninety-three parts and shave the coin's weight a little; the metal left over was his to spend. His successors liked the trick too much to stop. For two hundred years the mints took a little more and poured in copper, until under Gallienus in the 250s and 260s only about five percent silver remained, a copper slug under a silver wash so thin it rubbed off inside a purse.

Debasement is a tax nobody has to vote for. Each thinner coin went out at its old face value, and the men closest to the mint spent it first, before the price of bread had caught up. By the time the coin reached a farmer in a provincial town, prices had climbed and it bought less than it used to. Austrian economists call that a hidden tax on money holders: the ruler keeps the silver he no longer puts in the coin, and every saver pays the difference without ever seeing a bill.

In 301 AD Diocletian met the resulting price rises with law rather than with better coin. The Edict on Maximum Prices named a ceiling for over a thousand items, from grain and wine to shoes and a day's wage, and death for any seller who went above it. Where governors actually enforced it, sellers hid their goods or stopped bringing them to market, because a decree cannot make wheat easier to grow. The record of the months that followed is blunt: merchants withdrew goods from public sale, black markets emerged, and shortages appeared. Stack a cap on coin that has already been thinned and the shape of the outcome never varies: shortages and black markets, because the underlying debasement is untouched.

The script has reruns. On August 15, 1971 Richard Nixon cut the dollar's last tie to gold and in the same broadcast froze pay and prices for ninety days, which is why Austrians file Nixon's 1971 wage and price freeze on top of dollar debasement as the Roman story in American dress. Caracas ran it again: Venezuela's central bank has printed on an enormous scale since 2013 while Nicolas Maduro's government has capped the legal price of food and medicine and prosecuted grocers who charged more, and the shelves emptied as millions of people walked out of the country.

Nero and Maduro stand nineteen centuries apart, and the Austrian reading of both is one move. Prices are signals, not the thing itself; suppressing the signal does not fix the cause. That is Friedrich Hayek's way of putting a point Ludwig von Mises had made more narrowly before him: a price tells everyone where something has grown scarce, and a ceiling silences the price without producing one extra sack of grain, so the scarcity returns as an empty shelf.

the-soviet-gulag-solzhenitsyns-accountin.context_blurb:
The Soviet state's own clerks called it the Main Camp Administration, Glavnoye Upravleniye Lagerei in Russian, and the abbreviation they wrote on the paperwork became one of the darkest words of the twentieth century: Gulag. More than four hundred camps lay strung through the Siberian forests and the Arctic north, and from the 1920s under Lenin to the 1950s under Stalin the state fed them with men and women arrested for a careless joke, a friend abroad, a doubt spoken aloud. Prisoners felled timber and dug ore in cold that killed, and the whole machine is what Russians mean by the Gulag.

Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn had been inside it. Arrested in 1945 over a private letter mocking Stalin, he served eight years, and after his release he gathered testimony from more than two hundred fellow prisoners while hiding the manuscript from the secret police and sending pages west on rolls of film. The Nobel Prize in Literature came to him in 1970 for the ethical force of that work. His three volumes, mapping the system region by region, are called The Gulag Archipelago.

Published in Paris from 1973, the book did two things at once. For Western readers who had been assured the camps were a minor blemish, it supplied the truth about the Soviet camps, written by a man who had counted the barracks himself. And what it chiefly revealed, page after page, was the vast scale of Soviet prison camps and mass killings, not a few labour colonies for criminals but a system built into the state from 1918 onward. Moscow answered fast. In February 1974, two months after the first volume appeared, the Soviet government stripped him of citizenship and flew him to Frankfurt; he lived in Vermont from 1976 and went home to Russia in 1994.

Two historians put numbers on the thing. Robert Conquest wrote The Great Terror, published in 1968, out of private letters, memoirs and the testimony of refugees, counting Stalin's purge of 1937 and 1938, and the secret police's own records, opened after 1991, list about 680,000 people shot in those two years alone. Anne Applebaum, writing Gulag: A History out of those same archives in 2003, totalled every prisoner who entered the camps from 1930 to Stalin's death in 1953 at about 18 million, with between 1.5 and 1.7 million deaths documented inside the camps.

The book also changed minds where nobody expected it. In Paris a knot of young thinkers from the left, Andre Glucksmann and Bernard-Henri Levy among them, broke publicly with Marxism after reading it and started saying out loud that such regimes produce camps rather than paradise; the French press called them the Nouveaux Philosophes. Conquest's own history carries a second lesson. For twenty years specialists called his count Cold War inflation, and then the opened archives matched it almost exactly, which shows that honest outside estimates can be closer to the truth than a closed regime's official numbers. Against a record of that size, the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition refuses the move that files the camps beside the West's own twentieth-century failures as though the two were of a size.

the-treasury-revolving-door-rubin-paulso.context_blurb:
The top money job in the American government is Secretary of the Treasury, and for a quarter of a century several of its holders arrived from the same few blocks of New York. Robert Rubin spent twenty-six years at Goldman Sachs, ran the Treasury from 1995 to 1999, then joined Citigroup's executive committee for a decade. When a bank chief takes the Treasury and later goes back to a top-paid seat in the industry he was regulating, the name for the move is the revolving door between government and Wall Street.

Henry Paulson joined Goldman in 1974, became its chief executive in 1999, and held the Treasury from July 2006 to January 2009, which put him in the chair when Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers went down. He drove a seven-hundred-billion-dollar rescue through Congress in a matter of weeks, and taxpayer money spent to keep a private firm from failing is a bailout. The insurer AIG, which had sold protection on housing debt it could not cover, took the largest rescue of all, around a hundred and eighty billion dollars, and much of it passed through to the banks holding the other side of those contracts, Goldman's share coming to roughly twelve point nine billion. Rescues of that shape carry the danger economists call moral hazard: banks will take even bigger risks next time, since they expect another rescue.

Timothy Geithner ran the New York Fed from 2003 to 2009 and the Treasury from 2009 to 2013. In March 2014 he went to Warburg Pincus as its president, which is a private-equity firm. Janet Yellen chaired the Federal Reserve until 2018, and over the following two years she collected about seven million dollars in speaking fees, most of it from Wall Street firms including Citadel and Goldman Sachs, before becoming Treasury Secretary in 2021.

Two economists put the pattern into words. Simon Johnson, who had been the International Monetary Fund's chief economist, wrote in The Atlantic in May 2009 that the banks had grown powerful enough to help draft the rules meant to bind them, supplying the language, the staff and the advice that legislators used, which is regulatory capture. In 2012 Luigi Zingales of Chicago, an Italian-born defender of markets, argued that American finance had slid out of competition into crony capitalism, where the biggest firms win by political connection instead of by better products, and he titled the book A Capitalism for the People.

The pattern is not confined to finance. Scott Gottlieb ran the Food and Drug Administration from 2017 to 2019 and took a seat on Pfizer's board in June 2019, months after stepping down, which is the revolving door again in another industry. What makes capture work is not a bribe. The pool of qualified candidates comes from the industry and expects to return to it, so the career interests of a perfectly honest official already lean the industry's way before anybody asks a favour.

State the public-choice claim carefully. Four Treasury secretaries between 1988 and 2013 — Nicholas Brady, Rubin, Paulson, Geithner — all four had come from Wall Street houses or from the New York Fed, every one lawfully nominated and confirmed. The pattern is institutional-incentive selection, not individual character. Pay is part of what does the selecting: in a 2014 study of American lobbyists, Marianne Bertrand and two colleagues, Matilde Bombardini and Francesco Trebbi, found that connections to politicians earned a more consistent money premium than expertise did. A reader can judge the practice as he likes; the move to recognise is the selection effect.

the-vienna-intellectual-context-of-the-1.context_blurb:
Vienna between the wars held the densest few square miles of thinking in Europe. In one city you could find the Vienna Circle, gathered around the philosopher Moritz Schlick, meeting weekly to rebuild philosophy on logic and observation; the mathematician Kurt Godel proving things nobody had thought provable; the economists of Mises's circle arguing about planning; and novelists and composers in the coffee houses between them. The politics were just as sharp, with the Social Democrats running a programme they called Red Vienna and the classical liberals arguing against it.

Mises's argument was about knowledge, not motives. A family can plan its week because one person holds the whole of it in his head. A country cannot be run that way, because no committee can know what every person wants or what every thing is worth. What a planner would have to replace is the ordinary thing that coordinates millions of strangers with nobody in charge: market prices.

Godel's result had a similar shape, and some writers have set the two side by side. In 1931 he showed that no system of mathematics can prove everything true that lies within it: a few truths always sit out of reach of the rules. Mises and Hayek were pressing a similarly shaped point about an economy, that no small group can ever plan a whole economy -- they can't know enough.

The Circle was no political ally of theirs. Most of its members simply wanted knowledge put on a scientific footing, but one of them, Otto Neurath, pressed for the economy to be run on a plan as well, a position belonging to socialism. Karl Popper, close to the scene without ever joining the Circle, went his own way on method. His 1934 book argued that an idea counts as science only if it takes a risk, which means you can say in advance what evidence would show it false, and on that test he judged Freudian psychology and Marxism to fail where Einstein's physics passed. He named the test falsifiability, and he aimed it squarely at the Circle's verificationism.

Then the scene ended, and it ended the way free thought usually ends: a dictator takes over and shuts down free debate. The Anschluss of March 1938 brought Nazi Germany into Austria, and within months the universities had expelled their Jewish scholars. Rudolf Carnap had seen it coming and left in 1935 for the University of Chicago, which became the North American home of logical positivism. Godel got out in early 1940 by an absurd route: east on the Trans-Siberian Railway, through Japan, and across the Pacific by ship. He spent the rest of his working life at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where Einstein became his walking companion.

time-preference-a-good-now-is-worth-more.context_blurb:
Offer a child one cookie now or two tomorrow and he takes the one now. Offer a lender a hundred dollars back today or a hundred dollars back next year and he asks for a hundred and five for the wait. Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk built his 1889 book on this plain fact about human beings, and the name it goes by is time preference.

It explains why anybody pays interest at all. If you lend me a hundred dollars for a year and I hand back exactly a hundred, handing back the same sum after a year does not make you whole. What you gave up, and what the extra payment buys back, is a year of consuming the money now instead of later. The size of the preference varies enormously, with the cookie-grabbing child at one end and a grandmother who skips a cruise so a grandchild can spend the money in thirty years near the other, yet the Austrian claim is that every chooser holds some positive preference for a good sooner over the same good later, because a promise of an apple a thousand years out is worth nothing to a man who will not be there to eat it.

Mises made it the root of interest rather than a quirk of certain people. In Human Action he split the market rate into three parts: a core that comes from time preference alone, a slice covering business risk, and a slice covering expected inflation. The core he called originary interest. Strip away the add-ons and what sets the base rate is how much people prefer having money now over later, not the productivity of tools and not the supply of gold. Frank Fetter had made the pure case first, in 1904, and Rothbard later built his whole theory of interest on it.

Boehm-Bawerk pushed the idea into capital. A people who save can build what a people who eat everything cannot: tools that make tools, work chains ten years long, a net before you fish. He called those long chains roundabout production, and every extra link means more waiting and more consumption deferred. So of two countries with the same people and the same land, one saving hard for a generation and the other spending every dollar and borrowing to spend more, the capital-heavy economy ends up being Society A -- lower time preference lengthens the sustainable structure of production, since resources not eaten today are the only resources a ten-year project can use.

This is also where it becomes a theory of the slump. Suppose a central bank holds short-term rates far under the level at which real saving and real borrowing would balance. Entrepreneurs read the cheap credit as a message that consumers have deferred a great deal of consumption, and they start factories and subdivisions and mines on that reading, when in truth nobody deferred anything. In the Austrian account it lies to entrepreneurs about time preferences, and the bust is the correction, the stage at which half-built projects get written down and the economy falls back to a shape real preferences will support.

Boehm-Bawerk had given three reasons for interest in 1889: that goods would be more plentiful later, that people undervalue what they will want tomorrow, and that a good in hand today is better for starting production. Fetter, Mises and Rothbard kept only one of the three as the root of pure interest, the undervaluation of future needs relative to present ones, treating the first as a preference effect in disguise and the third as a fact about productivity rather than about time. Hans-Hermann Hoppe carried the variable into politics in his 2001 book Democracy: The God That Failed, arguing that elected leaders face a short horizon, spend now and bill the unborn, and that over generations such high time preference yields rising debt, weaker manners, and a general decline in long-term thinking. That last argument is Hoppe's own and much disputed; the mechanism he borrows from 1889 is not.

us-milk-supports-and-government-cheese.context_blurb:
Congress ordered Washington to hold up the price of one farm product in the Agricultural Act of 1949, and the order has outlived every politician who voted for it. The method was simple: whenever farmers made more than buyers wanted at the supported price, the federal government bought the surplus and stored it. The product is milk (and derivative dairy products), bought mostly as butter and processed cheese because those keep and fluid milk does not.

The warehouses tell the rest. By 1981 the Department of Agriculture owned over 500 million pounds of processed cheese, aging in refrigerated caves and depots across Wisconsin, Missouri and Kansas while reporters worked out how to describe a government with a cheese mountain. Rather than dump it, Ronald Reagan's administration began handing the bricks out through food banks that same year, and the yellow blocks turned up in so many poor neighborhoods that American English gained a phrase: 'Government cheese'.

Milton and Rose Friedman used the program to show the shape of the politics, in Free to Choose, which they published in 1980. Roughly a hundred thousand dairy farmers take most of the gain, often tens of thousands of dollars in a single year, while more than three hundred million shoppers pay a few cents more for milk and cheese and butter. That is the public-choice pattern of concentrated benefits with dispersed costs, and it explains why the dairy lobby fights every reform while the people paying for it never form a lobby at all. The theory behind the pattern got its classic statement in 'The Logic of Collective Action' by Mancur Olson, published in 1965: a small group with a large stake per member organizes easily, and a vast group with a tiny stake per member does not.

The machinery has changed names, not direction. The 2014 Farm Bill retired the old bulk-buying apparatus and put in an insurance-style scheme that pays a farmer whenever his margin, the milk price minus his feed costs, falls under a level he picks, known since as The Dairy Margin Coverage (DMC) system. The payment mechanism is new; the guarantee of above-market income for dairy producers is seventy-five years old.

vincent-ostrom-polycentric-political-sys.context_blurb:
In 1973 a husband and wife set up a small research workshop at Indiana University in Bloomington, and it is now among the most respected groups in the field: Vincent and Elinor Ostrom. He was a political scientist, she an economist, and their subject was how real villages, cities and water districts actually solve shared problems, rather than how a textbook says one authority on top ought to solve them.

Vincent's word for the arrangements he studied was polycentric political systems: school boards, water districts, city councils and courts, each holding real authority of its own, instead of a single hierarchy issuing orders downward. In 1961 he put the idea into the American Political Science Review with two co-authors, the economist Charles Tiebout and the political scientist Robert Warren. The paper had a target. American urban reformers of the 1950s wanted the cities and their suburbs merged into single giant governments with one mayor and one police force and one school system, and the Ostrom-Tiebout-Warren paper was written against the metropolitan-consolidation movement, which held that fragmented local governments should be merged. Their evidence ran the other way, since the patchwork of little towns and special districts often delivered services more responsively, experimented more, and left a citizen more ways to complain or to move.

In 1971 he turned the same lens on a famous piece of institutional design, arguing from the Federalist Papers that the American founders' choice of federalism was a deliberate polycentric institutional design, splitting authority between the nation and the states, the cities and the courts, so that nobody ever held the whole of it. Later in his career he watched the drift run the other way, through the New Deal, the Great Society and the security state, and warned that centralization was eroding the polycentric constitutional structure the founders designed.

Elinor's half of the work drew the recognition. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, for showing that irrigation groups, fishing fleets and hill villages the world over manage water and pastures and forests successfully with neither state ownership nor private title. Vincent died on 29 June 2012, and the date is striking because his wife Elinor Ostrom had died on June 12, 2012, seventeen days earlier. Forty years of a shared research programme ended inside a fortnight, and the workshop at Indiana still carries their name. The parallel with Friedrich Hayek's argument of 1945 is exact: the knowledge needed to run a place is held locally, and overlapping local authorities can use it in a way one central office cannot.

western-intellectual-apologists-duranty-.context_blurb:
A recurring pattern of the twentieth century was the public defense of totalitarian governments by Western intellectuals of real standing, and three names carry it.

The American muckraker who had exposed city-hall corruption in The Shame of the Cities in 1904 visited Soviet Russia in 1919, two years after the revolution, and came home telling the financier Bernard Baruch that he had been over into the future and that it worked. He printed that version in his 1931 autobiography; the more famous wording, that he had seen the future, comes from a letter to a friend in April 1919. His name was Lincoln Steffens.

Sidney and Beatrice Webb were British socialists of the Fabian tradition, which wanted socialism by gradual reform instead of revolution, and in 1895 they helped to found the London institution that still teaches economics today: the London School of Economics. They toured the USSR in 1932 and published a two-volume defense of it in 1935 under the title Soviet Communism: A New Civilisation? The second edition of 1937 made one change that mattered. It dropped the question mark. It did so at the height of Stalin's Great Terror.

Walter Duranty, the New York Times man in Moscow, took the 1932 Pulitzer and then denied the Ukrainian famine while the Welsh reporter Gareth Jones was describing it accurately. The line of his that gets quoted most often applied a kitchen proverb to several million deaths: 'You can't make an omelette without breaking eggs'.

Friedrich Hayek spent part of The Road to Serfdom in 1944 on the question of why so many professors and journalists and novelists excused planning. His answer named neither bribery nor flattery but a professional habit of mind. These were people trained to admire orderly rational administration, and what drew them was the appearance of central planning as a rational-administrative project, while the market coordination they could not see went unnoticed. The tenth chapter of that book carries the title everybody quotes, 'Why the Worst Get on Top', and argues that such a state rewards exactly the traits those readers were slowest to recognise.

The archives have been open for a generation now and have confirmed the famine and the camps, yet Duranty keeps his prize, the Webbs' book sits uncensored on the shelf, and Steffens's line still stands in his celebrated autobiography. Historians in Hayek's tradition draw one conclusion from that, and it is a claim about institutions rather than about individuals: the Western intellectual class has never systematically confronted its 20th-century apologetics record. Individual figures have been criticised plenty; the prestige structures around them have barely moved.

yang-jishengs-tombstone-2008-the-archiva.context_blurb:
Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward ran from 1958 to 1962. Peasant families were pushed off their own plots into vast collectives called people's communes, village grain was carted away to the cities and sold abroad for machinery, and men who should have been in the fields were melting iron pots in backyard furnaces to make bad steel. In the villages that had grown the food, the result was the worst famine in history -- tens of millions starved. Grain output crashed, and over the next four years came a famine that killed tens of millions of China's peasants.

The party denied that any famine was happening, and a schoolboy in Hubei province believed it. Yang Jisheng was in the Communist Youth League at the time, and in 1959 the man he called his father, in truth the uncle who had raised him, starved to death in the family's village. He understood only later that his father had been one of tens of millions, and the discovery became his life's work. He spent his career at Xinhua, the state news agency, and used the access those credentials gave him to spend seven years quietly reading provincial party archives.

His book came out in Hong Kong in 2008 as Tombstone, a title meant both for his father and for the millions with no marker at all. The figure he reached was about 36 million. His method mattered as much as his number. Basil Ashton and Judith Banister, working in the 1980s, had already put the dead in the tens of millions by weighing later census counts against the births that should have happened, reasoning downward from national totals, while Yang, a Xinhua insider, did what no outsider could and drew on internal party archives that no outsider could see, alongside the official population figures. The count from the bottom up confirmed the older estimates and added detail province by province.

Farrar, Straus and Giroux brought out an abridged English edition in 2012, cut from two Chinese volumes to one and translated by Stacy Mosher and Guo Jian, under the title Tombstone: The Great Chinese Famine, 1958-1962. In 2013 the Manhattan Institute gave the book its Hayek Prize, named for Friedrich Hayek, and Yang flew to New York to accept it. Harvard's Nieman Fellows then chose him for their 2016 Louis M. Lyons Award, which honours journalists for conscience and integrity, and this time officials of Xinhua told him he was forbidden to travel to receive it. Tombstone is still banned from publication on the mainland. For the Austrian and classical-liberal tradition Yang's work is the Chinese counterpart to Robert Conquest's vindication by the Soviet archives, except that this count came from an insider reading the regime's own paperwork.

1973-oil-shock-and-us-gasoline-price-con.context_blurb:
In October 1973 the Arab oil producers cut off shipments to the nations that had sided with Israel during the Yom Kippur War, and world oil prices roughly quadrupled within months. Americans remember that winter for something else: hour-long lines at gas stations that had simply run dry. Milton Friedman, Murray Rothbard and other economists in Bastiat's tradition argued that the lines came from a law in Washington as much as from the embargo.

Start with the plain economics of a cut-off. When the biggest oil exporters stop selling to a nation, buyers who still need fuel for their cars, trucks and factories bid against one another for what is left, and the price shoots up. Now imagine a government that forbids sellers to raise prices during a shortage, say with a hurricane on the way. Drivers rush to fill up at the old price, long lines snake down the road, and the pumps run empty faster than before. In the 1970s many states fell back on odd-even rules, letting cars whose plates ended in an odd number buy only on odd dates, while stations hung out NO GAS signs.

That is what Friedman and his followers saw in 1973. The United States was already living under federal ceilings on the price of gasoline, part of the wage-and-price controls Richard Nixon had imposed in 1971. The ceiling barred the pump price from rising to match the shrunken supply, so instead of charging more, stations simply emptied, and the shortage was rationed by queuing. Europe ran a natural experiment. West Germany and Switzerland had no price controls; their prices jumped, drivers cut back, and the pumps stayed full with no lines at all.

Rothbard sorted the episode into Bastiat's two columns. The seen was the low price painted on the pump. The unseen was the hours burned waiting in line, the gasoline private importers refused to bring in at a loss, and the deliveries that never happened. Behind that lay Friedrich Hayek's 1945 insight that the knowledge a market runs on is scattered among millions of ordinary shoppers, whose daily choices about price, taste and budget tell farmers and refiners what to supply. Hand all those choices to one office in the capital and it would guess wrong about what people actually want, leaving shortages in one place and waste in another. Milton and Rose Friedman made the gas lines a showcase of their 1980 television series and book, Free to Choose.

The Austrian economists put the lesson in one sharp phrase: a price cap does not abolish the cost of something scarce, it changes the currency the cost is paid in. A cost that would have been paid in money, to a seller, is paid instead in time spent in line, and nobody collects it. The caps outlived Nixon, because Presidents Ford and Carter both left them standing. On January 28, 1981, a week after taking office, Ronald Reagan used an executive order to end the last federal controls on domestic crude. Once producers could sell at real market prices, oil flowed freely, prices soon began to fall, and the lines never came back.

The pattern had already repeated. In 1979 the Iranian Revolution toppled the Shah, Iran's oil stopped flowing, and world prices spiked for the second time in the decade. The lines came back, and California's were the worst, because federal price caps still held and a federal formula divided gasoline among the states by what each had used in earlier years, which left fast-growing California with an allotment based on its smaller past use. From both episodes Rothbard drew a lesson sharper than the word shortage. Under a ceiling the shortage shows up in two dimensions at once, in space as empty pumps and in time as hours of queueing, and lifting the ceiling ends both.

airline-deregulation-1978-the-low-cost-c.context_blurb:
For forty years, from 1938 to 1978, a federal agency in Washington, the Civil Aeronautics Board, chose which American airlines flew which routes and set the price of every ticket. Its defenders called it a shield. Its critics, led by the Cornell economist Alfred Kahn, called it a textbook case of what George Stigler named regulatory capture: a regulator that ends up serving the industry it is supposed to police.

No airline could cut a fare without the Board's permission, so the established carriers never had to fear a cheaper rival, and they gained the most from the arrangement. The Board gave the public a different reason. It warned that open skies would unleash ruinous competition, a fare war that would bankrupt carriers and leave small towns stranded. Because big price gaps were treated as dangerous, airlines competed on meals, seat width and schedules instead of fares.

The shield worked too well. Between 1950 and 1974 outside firms filed 79 applications to start a scheduled airline, and the Board granted none of them; after 1960 it barely bothered to hold hearings on such requests. A few upstarts lived beyond its reach. California's Pacific Southwest and Texas's Southwest flew only within their home states, and the Board's power covered only flights between states, so it could not touch them. Free to set their own prices, they charged 30 to 60 percent less than the regulated carriers and filled more of their seats.

The cozy side of the system came out in public. Robert Timm, who chaired the Board until 1974, made it his aim that the scheduled airlines earn a 12 percent return, and he was caught accepting a Bermuda golf holiday from the very carriers he oversaw. Senator Ted Kennedy's subcommittee referred him to the Justice Department, and its 1975 hearings put the cheap fares of the in-state airlines on display. In 1977 Jimmy Carter put Kahn himself in charge of the Board. Kahn, a lifelong Democrat, joked that all airplanes looked alike to him; to him, he said, every one of them was simply a marginal cost with wings. A marginal cost is what one more passenger adds to a flight that is leaving anyway, and Kahn's point was that fares should follow it.

In the Board's day, service to small towns was paid for invisibly: travelers on crowded routes were overcharged, and the extra money propped up the lightly used ones. When deregulation ended that hidden transfer, Congress created the Essential Air Service program, paid for openly as a line in the federal budget. The lesson is Bastiat's. The cost had always been paid, by unseen passengers elsewhere, and deregulation dragged it into daylight, where lawmakers had to vote on it.

The Airline Deregulation Act, largely Kahn's design, passed both houses by enormous margins, and Carter signed it in October 1978. Those votes hid a bitter fight, and economists still point to who lost it. The fiercest resistance came from the established trunk airlines and the pilots' union, the Air Line Pilots Association: the very parties that forty years of protection had sheltered, an industry defending its own regulator. The consumer champion Ralph Nader, by contrast, backed deregulation.

anthony-downs-and-the-median-voter-theor.context_blurb:
Anthony Downs was an American economist who turned the tools of economics on politics. His Stanford doctoral thesis, written under Kenneth Arrow and published in 1957 as An Economic Theory of Democracy, asked what voters and parties do if they behave like ordinary people pursuing their own ends. His answers helped found public choice, the branch of economics that studies political behavior through incentives.

Start with one voter among a hundred million. The odds that his single ballot decides the election are about as good as a lottery jackpot, while reading up on every candidate eats whole evenings. So a sensible citizen spends very little time on research: study costs real hours, and one vote almost never settles anything. Downs's best-known idea concerns parties. When two parties compete along a single line of opinion, each keeps edging toward the citizen who stands exactly in the middle, since whoever wins that voter wins the majority. This is the median-voter theorem.

Downs made the theorem famous, but its mathematical proof had appeared nine years before his book, when the Scottish economist Duncan Black published it in 1948. The theorem explains a familiar grumble about American elections: by voting day the two big parties often sound alike on many issues, because both are chasing the same voter in the middle. Third-party campaigners like to say there is not a dime's worth of difference between them.

Downs's second big idea comes from the arithmetic of a single vote. Because one ballot among millions almost never flips the result, the private return to becoming an informed voter is near zero, even if society as a whole would gain from informed citizens. Sensible voters therefore skimp on studying bills, candidates and budgets. Downs called this rational ignorance, meaning that most voter ignorance is a reasonable response to incentives, not stupidity.

Arrow had found a deeper trap in 1951. Imagine three friends each ranking three choices for lunch. Arrow proved that no voting rule can satisfy a short list of basic fairness conditions for every possible set of rankings: some patterns of preference make every rule fail. The result, his impossibility theorem, helped earn him a Nobel Prize. Downs, meanwhile, turned to a very concrete urban headache, traffic, and wrote about cities for decades, later from the Brookings Institution in Washington. His law of peak-hour expressway congestion says that widening a highway invites more driving until the new lanes fill up again.

In 2007 the economist Bryan Caplan pushed Downs's argument further in The Myth of the Rational Voter. A mistaken vote costs the voter nothing personally, so voters indulge pet beliefs they would never risk acting on when buying groceries or a used car. Caplan concluded that voters are not merely uninformed but systematically irrational, because holding a wrong belief costs them nothing in private, a move he called rational irrationality.

asic-evolution-cpu-to-specialized-silico.context_blurb:
Bitcoin is secured by mining, a worldwide race in which computers grind through a hashing puzzle and the winner adds the next block of transactions. Since Satoshi Nakamoto released the software in January 2009, the machines in that race have changed four times, each generation more specialized than the last. The story shows an industry remaking itself, with no planner in charge, around the price of electricity.

At first, in 2009 and 2010, everyone mined on the same chip: the CPU, the ordinary processor inside every laptop and desktop. Satoshi mined that way, so did the cryptographer Hal Finney, and so could any hobbyist at home, winning 50 bitcoins a block. Then, in 2010, miners discovered that the graphics chip in a video-game card, the GPU, built for the parallel arithmetic of shading pixels, could run the hashing puzzle fifty to a hundred times quicker than a CPU. Word spread on the forums, gamers turned their rigs into round-the-clock money mints, and GPUs ruled mining through 2010 and 2011.

Next came FPGAs, chips that can be rewired after they leave the factory to perform one particular circuit. FPGA mining lasted only about a year before the first ASICs, chips built to run nothing but Bitcoin's SHA-256 hashing, shipped from Butterfly Labs and Avalon in early 2013. Every new generation won for the same reason: it did each calculation with less energy, so miners still running older gear could no longer cover their power bills. The ASIC is the extreme of that trade-off. Set against a laptop's general-purpose processor, it is vastly faster and cheaper per calculation, but it is good for nothing else, and because its silicon is fixed when it is made, it can never be repurposed.

By 2015 hobbyists could not keep up. Giant mining farms in China, many in Sichuan and Inner Mongolia, packed warehouses with ASICs thousands of times faster than any home computer, and the chief chipmakers, Bitmain and its rivals MicroBT and Canaan, were Chinese as well. Its defenders argue that this narrowness makes Bitcoin more secure, not less. A miner who has sunk millions into chips that can do nothing else has no way to walk away from Bitcoin and reuse his hardware, so his fortune rides on the network's survival. Critics call this centralization; defenders call it aligned incentives.

Then, in 2021, China banned Bitcoin mining outright, though more than half the world's hash power sat inside its borders. Over the following months, millions of machines were packed up and shipped to places with cheap, often stranded power: wind and gas in Texas, coal in Kazakhstan, geothermal heat in Iceland and the great Itaipu hydroelectric dam in Paraguay. Within nine months the network's total hash power had hit new records. No central planner ordered the move; entrepreneurs reading their electricity bills steered it themselves.

bastiat-inside-mises-s-human-action.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises, a Vienna-trained economist, left Austria in 1934 for a teaching post in Geneva and moved on to New York in 1940 as the Nazis overran Europe. His 1949 masterwork, Human Action, became the English-language anchor of the Austrian school. Mises saw in it the formal version of the reasoning Frédéric Bastiat had used in plain French a century earlier: trace what is seen, and then what is not seen.

The school began in 1871 with Carl Menger, a Vienna professor who taught that value is subjective. Only a person, with his own tastes and needs, can say what a thing is worth to him. A hungry child prizes a candy bar more than one who has just eaten lunch, so there is no single true price for the candy; it is worth different amounts to different children. While teaching in Geneva, Mises wrote the first, German version of his treatise, Nationalökonomie, published in 1940. When the journalist Henry Hazlitt urged an English translation, Mises chose to rewrite the book for Americans instead, and the result was Human Action.

Mises had made his name in 1920 with a paper on economic calculation under socialism. Where no one owns the factories, land and machines, they are never bought or sold, so no real market price ever shows what they truly cost, and planners are left with nothing to show them which projects deserve the resources. Friedrich Hayek pressed the point further in 1945 with an article for the American Economic Review titled The Use of Knowledge in Society: the scraps of local knowledge in millions of heads can never be gathered by any central planner. The same school traced great downturns such as the Great Depression not to markets gone mad but to central banks pushing interest rates below the level where saving and borrowing would naturally meet.

In 1946 Henry Hazlitt, who wrote editorials for the New York Times, boiled Bastiat's method down to one rule in Economics in One Lesson. Look at a policy's effect on every group, he taught, not just the group it is meant to help, and over the long run as well as the short. Mainstream economists ignored Bastiat for decades, largely because of Joseph Schumpeter, the Austrian-born Harvard economist. In his History of Economic Analysis, published after his death in 1954, Schumpeter wrote that he did not consider Bastiat a bad theorist; he considered him no theorist at all.

Murray Rothbard, the leading Austrian of the generation after Mises, answered Schumpeter in his last great work, the two-volume An Austrian Perspective on the History of Economic Thought, released by the publisher Edward Elgar in 1995, the year Rothbard died. Its pages take Bastiat seriously as a thinker in his own right, far more than a clever pamphlet writer. Read together, Bastiat's essays, Mises's Human Action and Rothbard's Man, Economy, and State of 1962 teach one move with growing rigor. Mises called his method praxeology: because human action is purposive, economic reasoning has to follow every choice through its whole chain of consequences, the unseen as well as the seen.

bitcoin-as-a-scarce-digital-commodity-th.context_blurb:
Across history, people in far-apart places have settled on gold and silver as money. The Austrian school, beginning with Carl Menger in 1871, argued that this was no cultural accident but a matter of what the metals are like. In the Austrian reading, Bitcoin's fixed supply is an engineering answer to the oldest failure of money: the people who issue it debasing it.

Shells from West African beaches, the huge stone discs of Yap, Roman gold, Chinese silver bars and the shell-bead belts of North America look nothing alike. Yet every one of them shared a single trait: each was hard to produce more of, so it held its value, while goods that were easy to make flooded the market and lost theirs. In 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin with a hard limit in its code: no more than 21 million coins can ever exist, and no central bank, committee or future programmer can raise it.

Menger asked why one good, rather than another, becomes money. Its beauty, size or toughness matters less, he answered, than its marketability: the good that the most people accept most readily in trade gradually becomes the money everyone uses. Historically, high marketability went hand in hand with difficulty of production. Mines from Nevada to South Africa and Australia add only about 1 to 2 percent each year to all the gold ever dug up and still held in vaults and jewelry, and Austrian economists see that slow growth as the real strength of a gold standard.

Gold is only relatively scarce, because its stock keeps creeping upward. Bitcoin is the first money whose code fixes a final ceiling on the total, a property called absolute scarcity; no metal and no paper currency ever had one. Saifedean Ammous, in The Bitcoin Standard, popularized a yardstick for how hard a money is to inflate: divide the whole supply already in existence by the new supply added each year. That figure, the stock-to-flow ratio, stands at about 60 for gold, and the higher it climbs, the harder the money.

Bitcoin's ratio keeps rising because of the halving. Each time another 210,000 blocks are mined, roughly once in four years, the miner's reward is cut in half, so after about thirty-three halvings the reward rounds down to nothing and new issuance ends around the year 2140; miners will then live on transaction fees alone. In 2019 a Dutch analyst writing as PlanB turned stock-to-flow into a price model that forecast very high prices after the 2020 halving. It looked accurate for a while and then missed badly from 2021, a reminder that a formula tuned to old prices may not forecast new ones. The monetary idea of hardness survived; the price forecast did not.

The Austrian case for Bitcoin is narrower than world conquest. Every past currency, from Diocletian's Roman denarius to the Weimar mark of 1923 to the paper money issued since 1971, lost value through the same channel: debasement by the authority that issued it. Bitcoin's cap closes that channel, because no one holds the power to decide the supply. The whole line of argument traces back to one book, Carl Menger's Principles of Economics, published in Vienna in 1871, and every later Austrian work on money builds on it.

bretton-woods-1944-the-dollar-gold-ancho.context_blurb:
In July 1944, with the Second World War still raging but nearly won, delegations from forty-four Allied nations spent three weeks at a resort in New Hampshire's White Mountains, designing the money system for the postwar world. The arrangement they built anchored the world's currencies on the dollar, and the dollar on gold, and it lasted until 1971. Austrian economists argue that its end was written into its design.

The delegates met from July 1 to July 22 at the Mount Washington Hotel, in the New Hampshire village of Bretton Woods, which gave the system its name. Every Allied currency was pegged at a set rate to the American dollar, while the dollar itself was fixed by law to gold at $35 an ounce, so foreign central banks could turn in their dollars at the American Treasury for gold at that price. The conference also founded two institutions to run the system, both still at work today: the International Monetary Fund, to keep exchange rates stable, and the World Bank, to finance the rebuilding of a shattered world.

Britain's delegation was led by John Maynard Keynes, who pushed a rival plan. His design called for a reserve money belonging to no single country, issued by a new International Clearing Union to square the trade accounts of nations, and he named that currency the bancor. The American design, drafted by the Treasury official Harry Dexter White, won instead. Its aim in tying everything to a dollar anchored in gold was to keep exchange rates steady and to stop governments from printing money without limit, since any country that inflated would see its currency strain against its fixed rate.

White's own story turned dark. In 1948 the former Soviet courier Whittaker Chambers named him before a congressional committee. From 1995 the National Security Agency released files from the Venona project, a wartime effort that had cracked Soviet cables, and they identified White as a Soviet source under the code names Jurist and Richard. The episode exposes a hidden risk in letting a small circle design the world's money: a handful of insiders, pursuing aims no one else can see, can write rules that bind all the rest.

The gold promise held for twenty-six years after the war. On Sunday evening, August 15, 1971, Richard Nixon announced on television that the gold window was closed, and from then on the dollar was a paper currency backed only by the government's word. Austrian writers such as Murray Rothbard and Saifedean Ammous argue that the collapse was arithmetic, not bad luck. To supply the world with the dollars it needed, the United States had to keep running deficits in its own currency, and once the dollars it owed abroad outgrew its gold, the peg was doomed, whatever leaders said or did.

Strictly speaking, Bretton Woods was never a classical gold standard like Britain's before 1914, when ordinary people could hand paper money across a bank counter for gold coins. Private citizens had no such right; only foreign central banks could swap their dollars for the metal, which made it a gold-exchange standard.

buchanans-1986-nobel-prize.context_blurb:
In October 1986 the Nobel prize in economics went to a single winner, James Buchanan, who had grown up in Tennessee and now taught in Virginia at George Mason University. His achievement was to turn the ordinary tools of economics on government itself. The prize put public choice theory on the world's academic map.

For much of the twentieth century, economists pictured politicians and bureaucrats as selfless servants maximizing the public welfare. Buchanan and his colleague Gordon Tullock called that a fairy tale: officeholders chase votes, agencies chase larger budgets and voters chase benefits, all pursuing their own interests just as people do in markets. The branch of economics built on that insight is public choice. The Swedish academy worded its citation with care, naming the idea rather than the school: it honored Buchanan for developing the contractual and constitutional foundations of the theory of economic and political decision-making.

On December 8, 1986, at sixty-seven, Buchanan gave his Nobel lecture in Stockholm under the title The Constitution of Economic Policy. Its point was that arguing about this or that tax rate misses the prior question of what rules frame the arguing, so policy should be judged by the rules that govern choices and not only by the outcomes of particular choices. What public choice adds about people in government is plain: officials and politicians react to rewards and penalties exactly as shoppers and business owners do.

Many economists disliked that framing, because it strips away the comfortable assumption that officials always act for the public good. When the prize was announced, Paul Samuelson reportedly grumbled that it was really for political science, which was exactly Buchanan's point: the wall between the economics of markets and the economics of politics was itself the mistake. The British economist Ronald Coase, who won the Nobel in 1991, noticed that if bargaining were free, neighbors would settle any quarrel over noise or smoke on their own. In real life bargaining costs time, effort and lawyers. Coase called that friction a transaction cost, and it helps explain why companies exist at all, and why the law's assignment of property rights matters so much.

By the 1990s this rules-of-the-game tradition, often called new institutional economics, had won three Nobels: Buchanan in 1986, Coase in 1991 and the economic historian Douglass North in 1993. In 2009 Elinor Ostrom of Indiana University joined them, the first woman to win the economics prize, for demonstrating that ordinary communities can govern shared pastures, fishing grounds and irrigation canals by themselves, with neither state ownership nor privatization. The tradition also explains everyday politics. A senator backs a bridge back home that enriches a handful of local firms and costs every taxpayer a few dollars, because the benefits fall on a few who notice and reward him, while the costs are spread thin over many who barely notice. Tullock, Buchanan's co-author on The Calculus of Consent in 1962 and the pioneer of rent-seeking analysis, never won a Nobel, a sore point among public-choice scholars.

Whether the subject was a constitution, a property right, a court system or a village's rules for a shared fishery, Buchanan, Coase, North and Ostrom all built on a move Buchanan had made decades earlier: treating institutions themselves as serious objects of economic study. The rules of the game, he insisted, deserve as much analysis as the play within them.
