ppp-loans-2020-the-concentrated-benefit-.context_blurb:
When the COVID-19 lockdowns began in March 2020, Congress passed the CARES Act, a relief package of about 2.2 trillion dollars, the largest in American history at the time. One of its programs, the Paycheck Protection Program, or PPP, offered small businesses loans that would be forgiven if they kept their workers on the payroll. It became a lesson in seeing both the seen and the unseen.

To a shop owner the money felt like a gift, but a government earns nothing by selling products. Every PPP dollar came from taxes and from borrowing that future citizens will have to repay.

The whole package was paid for with borrowed money, much of it absorbed by a Federal Reserve creating new dollars, while relief checks went to nearly every household. Over the next two years the predictable side effect arrived: sharp inflation, as everyday prices rose fast.

The MIT economist David Autor and his colleagues later used payroll records to measure what PPP achieved. They estimated that each job it preserved cost taxpayers about $170,000 to $257,000 for every year the job was kept, far more than the workers' own yearly pay.

They also asked where the money ended up. About 72 percent, they reported, went to business owners and shareholders rather than to workers, because most of the firms that received it would not have laid anyone off in the first place.

The rollout showed Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem at work. No central agency could know which of millions of firms truly needed help in April 2020, so the money flowed to whoever already banked with a big lender. Well-connected clients were funded in days, while many minority-owned and country businesses got nothing in the first round.

A second pandemic program offered a comparison. Extra unemployment benefits, $600 a week under the CARES Act, went only to workers who had actually lost their jobs, so for each job they protected they cost far less than PPP, which paid nearly every business whether it had lost customers or not.

A defender can point to the millions of owners who received forgivable loans, and a critic in Bastiat's tradition grants that those seen beneficiaries were real. The unseen cost is roughly $600 billion of public debt for firms whose employees would have kept their jobs anyway, a bill that future taxpayers now carry.

prices-as-knowledge-signals-the-core-aus.context_blurb:
Friedrich Hayek's short 1945 essay in the American Economic Review is the most cited text of the Austrian school. In eleven pages it answers a question that sounds simple and is not: how can an economy use knowledge that is scattered among millions of heads and that no planner could ever collect? Its answer is the price system.

Hayek's title says exactly what the paper is about: the use of knowledge in a society too large for any one mind.

Its central story is about tin. Suppose that somewhere in the world tin suddenly becomes scarce. Within days every user of tin is saving it, though no one has given an order and only a few people know the cause, because the rising price carries the message to all of them.

Most economists, Hayek said, made the same slip: they imagined a single wise planner who knew every fact. But the knowledge an economy runs on is dispersed. It never exists in one place, only as scattered and incomplete bits held by separate people.

Hayek called the person who holds such knowledge a man on the spot: the mechanic who knows this particular lathe, the shopkeeper who knows these particular buyers, the captain who knows this particular port. That knowledge of time and place cannot be written into a report and mailed to headquarters in time.

The essay was a reply. In 1936 and 1937 Oskar Lange had argued, in On the Economic Theory of Socialism, that a central planning board could play at markets: set prices, push them up when queues formed and down when goods went unsold. Hayek answered that the board would still lack the scattered knowledge that real prices gather.

Hayek's knowledge problem is the other side of Ludwig von Mises's 1920 calculation problem. Without market prices for factories, land and machines, Mises argued, socialism has no way to weigh what one production plan costs against another, such as whether a railway should be built of steel or of aluminium.

In 1974 Hayek won the Nobel Prize in economics, and the news startled people for an odd reason. He shared it with the Swedish economist Gunnar Myrdal, a social democrat whose views on central planning were nearly the opposite of his, and each spent his prize lecture disagreeing with the other.

In 1979 drivers across America again waited in lines around the block, buying gas only on odd or even days according to their license plates. In Hayek's terms the trouble was a federal ceiling on gasoline prices, left over from the 1973 controls, which broke the signal that would have called forth more supply. When President Reagan lifted the controls in January 1981, the lines soon vanished.

In 1980 Thomas Sowell stretched Hayek's essay into a full theory of how societies use knowledge, in markets, law, science and daily life. Hayek praised the result, Knowledge and Decisions, as the finest economics book he had come across in years.

Austrian economists apply the same argument to the biggest price of all. The interest rate, the price of having goods now rather than later, is not set by a market of lenders and borrowers but by a Federal Reserve committee that gathers eight times a year. In the Austrian view that committee holds it below the rate the market would set. That breaks the signal telling businesses which long projects real savings can support.

In 1948 Hayek gathered his key essays into Individualism and Economic Order, built around the 1945 essay and its forerunner, Economics and Knowledge, a talk he had first given to the London Economic Club in the 1930s.

public-sector-unions-fdrs-warning-and-wi.context_blurb:
Most Americans picture unions bargaining with private companies. Since the 1960s, though, the most heavily unionized workers in the country have been government employees, and economists in the public-choice tradition argue that bargaining with a government is a very different game. Even Franklin Roosevelt, a hero of the labor movement, saw the problem.

A strike at a shoe store hurts the owner, but customers can buy shoes down the street. If a whole city's police force went on strike on the same day, the people hurt most would be the ordinary citizens who need protecting, because nobody else can take the officers' place.

In 1937 Roosevelt wrote to Luther Steward, head of the National Federation of Federal Employees, that collective bargaining as usually understood cannot be carried over into government service, and he called a strike by public employees unthinkable and intolerable. Roosevelt, the champion of private-sector unions, opposed collective bargaining by government workers.

The difference, he explained, lies in who the employer is: in government service it is the whole people, speaking through laws passed by Congress, and no official at the table can fully bind it. Public-choice economists draw the contrast more sharply. A private union faces a private employer out to make a profit, whose pay offers must be weighed against profits and the firm's survival. A government union faces officials spending other people's money.

By 2010 about 36 percent of government workers belonged to unions, against about 7 percent in private jobs, because public employees make up a compact, organized group while the taxpayers who foot the bill are scattered and unorganized.

In 2011 Wisconsin's new governor, Scott Walker, pushed through Act 10. Among other things it stopped the automatic deduction of union dues from public workers' paychecks and required unions to win a recertification vote every year, so that paying dues became each worker's own yearly choice rather than something taken from his pay without asking.

The fight was fierce. Weeks of protests filled the state capitol, and fourteen Democratic senators fled to Illinois, because without them the Senate lacked the quorum, the minimum number of members present, needed to pass Act 10. The walkout delayed the law but did not stop it.

Afterward the Wisconsin Education Association Council, the state's biggest teachers' union, saw a majority of its paying members leave within a few years. The drop suggests that many members had been paying only because the dues were taken automatically, not because they wanted to.

In 2018 the Supreme Court carried the voluntary principle nationwide. An Illinois state worker named Mark Janus objected to paying the "agency fees" that unions charged non-members, and on June 27 the Court ruled five to four in Janus against AFSCME that no public worker could be forced to pay them.

The cost of past bargains shows up in public pensions. CalPERS, the fund for California's state employees and the biggest public pension fund in the nation, carries large unfunded promises that remain a long-term worry for the state.

Public-choice economists point to what sets government unions apart. A public union spends members' dues on campaigns to put governors and legislators in office, and then those same officials negotiate its contracts, so the union helps pick the officials who sit across the table from it.

When a union has helped choose its own bargaining partner, the usual picture of two independent sides breaks down. In effect the group is bargaining with itself, while the taxpayers who pay the bill have no seat at the table.

regulatory-capture-case-studies-icc-cab-.context_blurb:
Washington creates agencies to police powerful industries on the public's behalf. Again and again, though, economists have watched those agencies end up serving the very industries they were meant to restrain. The Chicago economist George Stigler gave the pattern its name in 1971, regulatory capture, and three old American agencies became its classic cases.

The first is the Civil Aeronautics Board. From 1938 the CAB assigned every airline its routes and fixed its fares, and flying stayed a luxury of the well-off. Then the Airline Deregulation Act, signed by Jimmy Carter in 1978, freed carriers to pick their routes and price their own tickets. Ticket prices dropped, and many more ordinary people could afford to fly.

Taking rules away from an industry in this way is called deregulation. Its champion at the CAB was the Cornell economist Alfred Kahn, who chaired the board in 1977 and 1978 and helped take it apart.

The oldest case is the Interstate Commerce Commission, created by Congress in 1887 to protect farmers and shippers from the railroads' rates. The historian Gabriel Kolko argued that the big railroads had themselves pushed for the ICC, hoping a friendly regulator would hold rates up and keep new lines out. That is regulatory capture: the industry ends up running its own regulator.

The Federal Communications Commission, created in 1934, hands out broadcast licenses, each a slice of the airwaves that no rival may legally use. License holders hired lobbyists to block new stations and to slow cable television for years, which shows how a license granted by government can become a protected privilege its holders fight to defend.

Deregulation spread. Two years after the airlines, the Motor Carrier Act of 1980 freed trucking, ending decades of ICC control over the rates and routes of the big rigs, and freight costs fell.

Capture has a familiar channel. An official oversees a drug maker for years, quits for a well-paid job at that company, and later someone from the company takes a post at the agency. People call this back-and-forth the revolving door.

Before the 2008 crash, the bank supervisors missed the risks piling up in mortgage lending. Post-crisis critics singled out the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which oversees national banks, and the Office of Thrift Supervision, which oversaw the savings-and-loans behind some of the worst mortgage books, pointing to staff who passed back and forth between those supervisors and the banks under their watch.

Why does capture happen so often? The most common reason is that the regulators come from the industry they oversee and expect to return to it, so they come to share its view. The Princeton political scientist Marver Bernstein had described the life cycle back in 1955: an agency is born full of zeal and grows old as the industry's partner.

The ICC, the CAB and the early FCC tell one story. In each case the industry's established firms captured the agency and used it to keep new competitors out.

Stigler said capture shows in outcomes, not intentions. The strongest visible sign is an agency that blocks new companies from entering while it protects the profits of the firms already there.

His 1971 paper, "The Theory of Economic Regulation," launched half a century of testing, much of it carried on by his student Sam Peltzman and their followers. In the reading of that Chicago tradition, study after study, from transport and broadcasting to banking and licensing, has largely vindicated the theory across every major agency examined.

ron-paul-end-the-fed-and-audit-the-feder.context_blurb:
Ron Paul is a Texas doctor who delivered babies before he went to Congress, where he served on and off from 1976 to 2013. No modern American politician did more to put Austrian economics before ordinary voters. His target, for four decades, was the Federal Reserve.

Paul's basic complaint was simple. The Fed can create new dollars whenever the government wants more to spend, and when it prints too many, each dollar buys less over time. Economists call that steady erosion of money's buying power inflation.

After the 2008 crash, which he blamed on the Fed, Paul wrote a book for general readers in September 2009. It became a best seller, and its title said it all: End the Fed.

On the House floor Paul built speech after speech on three Austrian economists, citing them constantly: Ludwig von Mises, Friedrich Hayek and Murray Rothbard, who was also his personal friend.

As early as 2003 Paul told the House that house prices were swelling into a bubble that would end in a crash. He laid the blame on Alan Greenspan's low-rate policy: the Fed chairman, Paul said, had kept money cheap for years, and cheap money was inflating the bubble. Five years later the crash came.

In February 2009 Paul filed the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, which would have opened the Fed's books to a complete audit by Congress's own investigators at the GAO. At rallies and on signs the bill went by a three-word slogan: Audit the Fed.

The bill drew remarkable support. About 320 of the 435 House members signed on as co-sponsors before Senate leaders scaled it back to a one-time audit of the Fed's emergency lending, folded into the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

His book made three charges: that the Fed violates the Constitution, that printing money from nothing is morally wrong, and that it damages the real economy. For the economic charge Paul leaned on Mises and Hayek. The Fed, he argued, creates the very boom-and-bust cycles that Austrian business-cycle theory predicts, because artificially low interest rates lure businesses into mistakes that must end in a bust.

In 2011 the Mises Institute in Alabama gave him its highest award, named for his late friend: the Rothbard Medal of Freedom.

His constitutional case rested on Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress the power to coin money and regulate its value. In Paul's view that power belongs to Congress and cannot legitimately be handed over to an independent agency like the Fed, created in 1913.

Paul's biggest legacy is not a law but a shift in what counts as normal. Before his presidential campaigns of 2008 and 2012, criticism of the Fed lived on the fringes of politics; afterward, calls to audit the Fed or curb its powers became an ordinary position in Republican primaries.

sarbanes-oxley-2002-the-small-cap-ipos-t.context_blurb:
In 2002 Congress passed one of the biggest overhauls of American corporate rules in decades, named for its two sponsors in Congress, Michael Oxley of the House and Paul Sarbanes of the Senate. It was meant to stop the next great accounting fraud. Critics argue it also did something nobody intended: it made it much harder for small, young companies to sell shares to the public.

The trigger was Enron, the energy giant that hid enormous losses with accounting tricks and went bankrupt in 2001, wiping out thousands of workers' jobs and savings. After a scandal like that, lawmakers usually answer with new rules that force companies to prove their financial reports are honest.

Two collapses drove the law: Enron, the energy trader that failed in December 2001, and WorldCom, the phone company that failed the next summer, in July 2002, once its padded profits came to light. Sarbanes-Oxley was the response to Enron and WorldCom alike.

One section requires the chief executive and the chief financial officer of every large public company to sign, each quarter, a statement that the numbers are true, and a false signature can mean prison. The idea is to make real people legally responsible, so that no one can hide behind the company and claim he never knew.

Another section proved the most expensive to obey. Section 404 makes managers set up, test and personally vouch for a system of controls over their company's accounts, and it can cost even a small public firm one to two million dollars a year.

Over the following years many listed companies vanished, through mergers, buyouts or delisting, and fewer new ones replaced them. By the count of a widely cited study led by Gustavo Grullon, about 4,300 American companies remained listed by 2016, down from roughly 7,300 twenty years earlier.

The general lesson is about fixed costs. A bill of about a million and a half dollars barely dents a company earning billions but can sink one earning fifty million, so a regulation with a large fixed cost of compliance lands hardest on the smallest firms and shields the giants from newcomers.

Critics in Bastiat's tradition grant the seen benefit, fewer Enron-style frauds, and point to an unseen cost borne by ordinary savers. Promising young companies now stay private far longer, funded by venture capital and private equity, so retail investors have lost access to their early growth, which is reserved for wealthy accredited clients; the public can buy in only after most of the gains are gone.

self-custody-and-not-your-keys-not-your-.context_blurb:
Owning bitcoin is not like owning dollars in a bank. What you really own is the power to move coins, and that power is a secret. Twice in a decade, at Mt Gox in 2014 and at FTX in 2022, millions of people learned the hard way what happens when someone else holds that secret for them.

Every Bitcoin wallet rests on a secret number known only to its owner. With it, the owner signs a message proving he controls the coins, and the network accepts the transfer. That secret number is the private key: without it nobody can move the coins, however powerful he is, and anyone who steals it can move them all at once.

Most people buy bitcoin on an exchange and leave it there. But the exchange, not the customer, holds the private keys. If that exchange halts withdrawals or collapses, the customer discovers that all along he owned only a claim on the exchange, a promise to be paid in bitcoin, not the coins themselves.

The Bitcoin teacher Andreas Antonopoulos, author of the textbook Mastering Bitcoin (2014), drove the point home at conference after conference with a short rule: if they're not your keys, they're not your coins.

The safest storage is a hardware wallet, a small device, sold under brands such as Trezor, Ledger and Coldcard, that keeps the keys on a chip that never touches the internet. Its owner connects it only long enough to approve a payment on the gadget's own screen, so online hackers can never reach the keys.

If that device is lost or broken, a backup saves the day. The standard called BIP-39, written in 2013, lets an owner rebuild every key from twelve or twenty-four ordinary English words, all taken from one standard list of 2,048.

The first great lesson came in February 2014, when Mt Gox in Tokyo, then the biggest exchange in the world, halted withdrawals and went bankrupt, and about 850,000 customer coins vanished. Savers concluded that coins left on someone else's website can disappear whenever that company fails.

The lesson came again in November 2022, when the exchange FTX collapsed under its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, with billions of dollars of customer money gone. A New York federal jury convicted him of fraud, and in 2024 a judge gave him a 25-year sentence.

In both collapses, some customers lost nothing at all: those who had withdrawn to wallets of their own, holding the private keys themselves instead of leaving their coins with the exchange.

Careful holders go one step further with a multisig wallet, which splits the power to spend across several keys kept in different places. Coins can be spent only when enough of those keys agree, for example any two out of three, so no single stolen or broken device is fatal.

Bitcoin writers set Mt Gox and FTX side by side and press a definitional point. If you cannot sign for a coin, it is not your money in any meaningful sense; you own only a claim on whoever can sign, and you take the loss when he fails.

social-security-the-retirement-check-and.context_blurb:
Social Security, created in 1935, sends monthly checks to tens of millions of retired Americans. It is one of the most popular programs in the country. It is also a favorite case for economists who ask Bastiat's question: besides what the money does, what would it have done otherwise?

The very first monthly check went to Ida May Fuller, a retired legal secretary in Ludlow, Vermont, in January 1940. It was for $22.54, and she had paid in a mere $24.75 during her years of work. She lived to 100 and collected about $22,900 in all, because the first retirees paid in for only a few years while a huge generation of workers paid the taxes.

That points to how the system works. Today's workers pay the taxes that fund today's retirees; nobody's money is saved up for his own old age. In 1950 about sixteen and a half workers supported each person collecting, but with fewer babies and longer lives, by 2024 the number had fallen to about 2.7.

The law calls the payroll tax a "contribution," which sounds voluntary, yet anyone who refuses to pay can go to prison. Milton and Rose Friedman argued in Free to Choose that calling a forced tax a contribution disguises what is really going on, and that a private company advertising that way would be in trouble with regulators.

The courts agree about what the tax buys. Ephram Nestor, who came to America from Bulgaria in 1913, paid Social Security taxes for two decades. In 1956 the government deported him for his old Communist Party membership and stopped his benefits. Four years later the Supreme Court ruled that paying the tax buys no property right, and that Congress may change the benefits whenever it chooses.

Each year the program's trustees report when its reserve, the trust fund, will run out. In its 2025 report the depletion date arrived a year sooner than before: 2034. The law forbids the program to borrow, so once the reserves are gone, incoming payroll taxes would cover only about 81 percent of the benefits promised.

Other countries tried a different path. In May 1981 Chile, under the labor minister José Piñera, allowed workers to quit the government pension and put a tenth of their pay into a private retirement account. Switching was optional for those already in the old system, but workers within five years of retirement could not switch, since an account opened so late could not grow enough.

In January 2005 President George W. Bush made personal accounts his chief domestic goal, but Congress never voted on a bill. Support collapsed when voters concluded that the plan would cut the guaranteed benefit for everyone except the lowest earners.

A congressman can point to the 67 million Americans who receive a check each month. Critics in Bastiat's tradition accept the facts but call the defense incomplete. They demand a comparison with what forty-five years of the same payroll taxes would have grown into in each worker's own account. That comparison is contested, since a private account carries market risk and no built-in guarantees, which is why the argument is about the counterfactual rather than a simple verdict.

sowells-late-career-charter-schools-and-.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell, the Black American economist long based at Stanford's Hoover Institution, is known for plain-spoken books, packed with data, that question popular beliefs about race, poverty and policy. In June 2020, the month he turned 90, he published one about schools that are publicly funded but run independently of the district and its unions.

The book is Charter Schools and Their Enemies. In it Sowell argued that charter schools were teaching poor city children far better than the traditional schools nearby.

Critics of charters often say their students do well only because their families are richer or more motivated. Sowell set out to remove that objection with a careful design. In New York City he compared the test scores of charter students with those of traditional-school students who shared the very same school buildings, or lived in the same neighborhoods, so that income, race and neighborhood could not explain the difference.

Many of those charters, including the Success Academy network in Harlem and the Bronx, admit students by public lottery whenever applications outnumber places, with no entrance tests or interviews. The fairness argument for a lottery is simple: every family gets an equal chance, whoever it knows.

The results were striking. The best Harlem charters posted test scores comparable to those of wealthy suburban schools, with children drawn from the same neighborhoods as the much lower-scoring pupils in the traditional schools next door.

When opponents pointed to the flaws of one particular charter, Sowell answered with his trademark question: compared to what? The real alternative for these children is not some perfect public system that exists only in theory, but the traditional schools they would otherwise attend, with the results those schools actually get.

Why, then, do charter families so often lose political fights? Sowell borrowed Mancur Olson's logic of collective action. Teachers' unions are concentrated and organized, with money and votes to deploy, while charter parents are scattered and unorganized, so policy tilts toward the unions.

Still writing at 93, Sowell published Social Justice Fallacies in 2023. The movement's recurring mistake, he argued, is assuming that any gap in outcomes between groups must have been caused by unfair discrimination, without testing the many other possible causes.

stockholms-twenty-year-apartment-queue.context_blurb:
Stockholm is the case every economics teacher reaches for when a class asks what happens if a government simply fixes a price by law. Sweden has capped apartment rents since the 1940s, and the capital's housing bureau, Bostadsformedlingen, hands out most first-hand rental contracts from one strictly first-come queue. The cap is popular. The queue is two decades long.

A rent held below what renters would gladly pay does not conjure apartments; it makes them scarce. Money for new building goes where returns are legal, old rental blocks get sold off flat by flat, and a long waiting list forms because too few apartments get built. Sweden's version of the cap even has a name written into the law: bruksvardeshyra, or utility-value rent. Each year the national tenants' union sits down with the landlords' association and bargains an official rent for every class of flat, scored on the building's age, size and address rather than on what a renter would actually pay.

A first-hand contract at a central address took about 20 years of accumulated queue time by the early 2020s, and the most sought-after streets have been documented well past thirty. Young Stockholmers answer the only way the rules allow. The bureau takes no one under eighteen, so the usual advice is to join on the eighteenth birthday itself, knowing that a central flat may take until nearly forty to come.

Ride the cap for a decade or two and the stock itself goes. Owners sell controlled units off as owner-occupied flats, maintenance slides, and new money drifts to the one segment where prices are free, so there are far fewer to rent, and long waiting lists appear. Assar Lindbeck, the Swedish economist who chaired the committee that awards the Nobel in economics, wrote that apart from bombing, rent control was the most efficient method anyone had found for destroying a city, and the law he was describing was his own country's.

Demand does not evaporate when the official price refuses to move; it goes underground. Stockholm police files and the Swedish research institute Timbro have both traced an illegal second-hand sublet market, in which a sitting tenant passes his controlled flat along at three to five times the legal rent.

Friedrich Hayek's point about all of this was not that caps are unkind but that a price is information. The number on a flat tells a builder what is worth building and tells a renter what he is truly willing to give up; cap it and the message stops being sent, while the flats still have to reach somebody. So the rationing job moves elsewhere: where a price is forbidden to clear a market, some other mechanism must do it -- typically queueing, connections, black markets, or exit. Soviet bread lines, the American petrol queues of 1973, wartime ration books and Stockholm's two-decade list are the same machinery, and not one of them carries the information a price carried.

term-limit-resistance-why-incumbents-opp.context_blurb:
Three Americans in four want a cap on how long a member of Congress may serve, and Congress has never passed one. That gap is not a puzzle about public opinion. It is a lesson about who gets to write the rules, and the economists who worked it out gave their field a name: public choice.

Term limits are simply a ceiling on the number of terms one person may hold a single office, and America already has one at the top. Franklin Roosevelt won the presidency four times running, from 1932 to 1944, and in 1951 the states ratified the Twenty-Second Amendment so that nobody could repeat the feat.

States then tried to do the same to their own delegations. Arkansas voters barred long-serving incumbents from the ballot, and in 1995 the Supreme Court struck that law down by five votes to four in US Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton. The qualifications for sitting in Congress, the majority held, can be changed only by amending the Constitution, never by one state acting on its own.

The public has been asked for decades. Gallup, Pew and others keep putting the question to American voters, and support comes back at about 75 to 83 percent, with Republicans, Democrats and independents agreeing, which almost no other issue manages. No amendment has ever come close to the two-thirds of both chambers needed to send one out to the states. James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock had explained why in 1962, in a book on the calculus of consent, by splitting political choice into two levels: the constitutional and the post-constitutional. At the first level people pick the rules before knowing which office, if any, each of them will hold, so a rule that binds whoever wins looks fair to all sides. At the second level the people choosing already hold the offices, and the identical rule now takes something from them personally.

California tried it at state level first. In November 1990 voters there passed Proposition 140, capping how long anyone could sit in the Sacramento legislature, and a dozen states copied the idea within four years. Political scientists then went to see what the capitols were actually like afterwards. Lawmakers now arrived, learned a little and left, so the people who knew how a budget really gets written were no longer the elected ones. Day-to-day power drifted toward the executive branch, lobbyists, and permanent legislative staff, none of whom face any limit at all.

Put the question to a congressman of thirty years' standing and the reply is standard: elections are the real term limits, and the voters can throw him out whenever they please. The trouble is the record. Long-serving incumbents almost always win, so real elections barely limit anyone, with sitting House members returned better than nine times out of ten.

Switzerland shows the reverse. Its national executive is a council of seven, chosen by the parliament, and the presidency rotates through the seven once a year, so no one person ever piles up the staff, the perks and the favours that make an office hard to give up. That is a constitutional-level anti-consolidation rule that survives because it was set from the start, written in before any sitting officeholder had to vote to shorten his own tenure.

Buchanan's point generalises, and it is arithmetic rather than cynicism. When a reform's cost lands on the officeholders whose votes must pass it, while the benefit goes to future citizens or future challengers, it has the shape of a term limit, which is why campaign-finance reform in the US Congress has had the same unhappy history. So the careful forecast is gloomy and usually right: the reform will typically fail to pass regardless of majority support. The way out, when there is one, is the Swiss way: get the rule written at the founding, before anybody holds the office it binds.

the-1974-nobel-prize-and-the-pretence-of.context_blurb:
In the autumn of 1974 a cable from Stockholm caught Friedrich Hayek on a trip to Salzburg. The Swedish academy had given him the economics prize, an award it had never handed to anyone from his school of thought. He was seventy-five, his health had been poor for years, and the world had just handed his old argument a vindication nobody had wanted.

The timing is the point. Through the mid-1970s American prices at the pump and the grocery store climbed hard while factories closed and unemployment rose. Economists had to coin a word for it, stagflation, out of stagnation and inflation, because the models of the day insisted that rising prices and rising joblessness could not arrive together.

Hayek's standing argument was about information rather than motives. His name for the permanent gap is the knowledge problem: the facts an economy runs on sit scattered through millions of separate heads, change by the minute, and no committee in a capital city can ever collect them. The knowledge problem is why he thought planning fails even when the planners are brilliant and well intentioned, because the failure lies in the arithmetic of information and not in anybody's character.

On 11 December 1974 he stood up in Stockholm and spent the lecture attacking his own profession. He called it The Pretence of Knowledge, and the title is the charge: economists had begun to behave as though a national economy could be driven like a machine, with every lever read off a dial. A physicist can watch a stone fall and name the spot where it will land, because stones obey fixed laws and people do not, so copying the methods of physics without its subject matter is what Hayek had been calling scientism since the 1940s.

Where, then, do the missing facts sit? Not in any government's filing cabinets, Hayek insisted. The knowledge that decides what gets made, and for whom, is dispersed across millions of individual minds, held as local habit and hunch, and it reaches the rest of us only as prices. He had argued exactly that in a 1945 paper on how knowledge spreads through a society. The target of the Stockholm lecture was the tradition founded by John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936, which taught governments to manage total demand with public spending and cheap credit.

The lecture closes on a warning rather than a theorem. A student of society who forgets the limits of his own knowledge, Hayek said, turns into an accomplice in the fatal striving to control other men, and at last the destroyer of a civilisation that no brain designed but that has grown from the free efforts of millions of individuals.

The prize he won was not one of Alfred Nobel's. The 1895 will endowed five; Sweden's central bank added the economics award in his honour much later, and the first went in 1969 to Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen for the mathematical machinery still used in modelling a whole economy. Hayek's was the sixth, shared with the Swedish welfare-state economist Gunnar Myrdal, who was reported to be furious at the company. Twelve years later the committee gave the 1986 prize to James Buchanan, who had shown that politicians and officials chase re-election, bigger budgets and their own jobs much as business owners chase profit, the insight that founded public-choice economics. Hayek wrote one more book himself. The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism appeared in 1988, when its author was eighty-nine, and argues that socialism rests on the belief that a designing mind can build institutions better than the slow trial and error of a market order.

the-2020-24-everything-bubble-across-ass.context_blurb:
Cheap money never stays in one place. Between March 2020 and the end of 2021 the Federal Reserve held short-term rates at zero and bought trillions of dollars of bonds, and the price of nearly everything a person could own went up at the same time.

The hedge-fund manager Jesse Felder had a name ready. Around 2018 he popularised the everything bubble, meaning a rise that turns up in houses, shares, art and collectibles together because one cause is driving all of them, unlike the dot-com mania that lifted a single sector. Housing was the most visible of them. The Case-Shiller index, built by Karl Case and Robert Shiller to track American house prices, rose about 45 percent in the thirty months from January 2020, and its fastest twelve-month gain, about 20.8 percent in April 2022, is the highest reading in the series since it began in 1987.

Shares did the same thing. The S&P 500, which follows the five hundred largest American companies, bottomed near 2,237 on 23 March 2020 and topped out around 4,796 at the turn of 2022, more than doubling in under two years, a climb of a little over a hundred percent. Bitcoin went much further, because its supply cannot be stretched to meet new demand: no more than twenty-one million coins will ever exist. From roughly $4,000 in the March 2020 panic it reached about $69,000 in November 2021, a seventeen-fold rise.

Further out along the risk curve things got strange. In January 2021 a Reddit board called WallStreetBets organised hundreds of thousands of small traders to buy two struggling firms that short-sellers had bet against, a mall video-game chain and a cinema operator, and the share prices of GameStop and AMC Entertainment left anything the businesses earned far behind. The same flood of money reached digital art. So-called non-fungible tokens, ownership records kept on a blockchain for cartoon apes and pixel portraits, sold to the tune of about $25 billion in 2021, and within two years the market had fallen by more than ninety percent.

Wall Street built a vehicle for the mood. A cash shell would list itself first and then take a private startup public by merging with it, sparing the startup the usual listing process and its awkward questions. These were SPACs -- special-purpose acquisition companies, and they raised well over a hundred and sixty billion dollars in 2021 before all but disappearing by 2023. Individual reputations rode the same wave. Cathie Wood's technology fund climbed far faster than the market, which made her famous, and then fell about eighty percent from its February 2021 peak, which is the whole lesson in miniature: the same concentration that made it rise fast can make it crash just as hard.

Richard Cantillon, an Irish banker who made his fortune in Paris in the 1720s, had described the shape of all this three centuries ago. New money does not arrive everywhere at once, he wrote: whoever receives it first spends it at yesterday's prices and gains, while whoever receives it last meets tomorrow's prices and loses. That is the Cantillon-effect pattern of first-receiver benefits followed by later-receiver adjustment. The 2020s went through it in order, with asset prices first in 2020 and 2021, consumer prices next, and the bust after that. When the Fed raised rates hard in 2022 the falls were worst exactly where the cheap money had pushed hardest: Bitcoin -78%, ARK Innovation ETF -80%, and the meme-stock complex -90%+. Houses and the broad share indexes held up better, because the tightening came after their peaks and never took back the whole climb.

the-berlin-wall-1961-89-the-calculation-.context_blurb:
Germany came out of the Second World War cut in two, a free republic in the west and a communist state in the east, with the old capital divided inside the eastern half. For twelve years a Berliner could still walk from one side of the city to the other. The walking went one way.

Between 1949 and the summer of 1961 about 3.5 million East Germans left through Berlin, something like a fifth of the entire population, and those who went were disproportionately young, trained and able. On the night of 12 August 1961 Walter Ulbricht's government unrolled barbed wire in the darkness and then poured concrete: the Berlin Wall. It encircled West Berlin rather than following the frontier between the two Germanys, and it ran about 155 kilometers, some ninety-six miles, of concrete, watchtowers, trenches, patrol roads and a raked sand strip where a single footprint showed. It stood from 1961 to 1989, twenty-eight years and three months.

The design answers one question: which way was it meant to stop people? The machine guns in the towers, the mines and the dog runs all faced East, at East Germans, because nobody expected an army from the other direction. Nine days after the wire went up, Ida Siekmann jumped from her fourth-floor flat on Bernauer Strasse, where the building stood in the East and the pavement in the West, and died of the fall. She is the first name in the memorial's register, and what her death shows is that people were willing to risk death rather than stay trapped inside. The Berlin Wall Memorial has documented about 140 confirmed deaths at the Wall itself, with several hundred more along the wider border between the two Germanys.

Holding the line took more than concrete. The Ministry for State Security, the Stasi, kept one uniformed officer for roughly every 180 citizens and recruited about twice that number of unpaid informers, neighbours, colleagues, sometimes husbands and wives reporting on each other, which gave East Germany the heaviest surveillance of any modern state. A government that needs that much watching is telling you something: it had to spy on its own people constantly to hold control. The direction of travel never changed either. In February 1989, months before the end, border guards shot Chris Gueffroy, a twenty-year-old who was the last person shot dead at the Wall, and he was going the way everybody went: from communist East Berlin to free West Berlin.

When the regime fell the files stayed. The Stasi had left millions of pages on ordinary citizens, and a law passed in December 1991 gave every East German the right to read his own file and to see which friends and relatives had written in it. That is why opening such an archive matters once a police state collapses: it lets people see who spied on them and makes the informers publicly known, so the knowledge belongs to the victims instead of the state.

The economists had worked out the shape of this long before. In 1920 Ludwig von Mises published the case that central planning cannot work out what anything ought to cost, since without markets there are no prices to tell a planner what people actually want, and Friedrich Hayek carried the argument forward for the next fifty years. The Wall turned that argument into masonry. Given an open border and twelve years in which to compare the two systems, three and a half million people had already answered, and the regime's reply was a line of inward-facing guns. When people are free to compare, they choose the market side and the planned economy has to wall them in.

the-broken-window-the-shopkeepers-son-an.context_blurb:
In July 1850, five months before he died, Frederic Bastiat published the pamphlet that holds his whole method, and its first chapter became the most reprinted page in economics. A boy smashes a pane of glass in his father's shop, and the neighbours gather round to explain why this is really good news.

They begin with a proverb about the ill wind that blows nobody any good: everybody has to make a living, and what would become of the glass trade if panes were never broken? Then they name the beneficiary. The money goes to the glazier, who now has a job he would not otherwise have had, and from him it travels on to the glassworks and beyond. Bastiat gives the figure exactly, because the whole argument turns on it. The new pane costs six francs.

What the consoling story leaves out is where those six francs were already going. The shopkeeper had plans for them, and the plans die with the window: he could have spent that money on something new instead of just replacing what he had, which in Bastiat's telling is a new coat from the tailor. The tailor's lost sale is every bit as real as the glazier's gain, and nobody sees it, because it never happens. Bastiat's name for that missing half of the ledger is the unseen. Then he does the accounting. Before the accident the till held six francs and the frame held glass; afterwards only the glass is there, and so the community is exactly one window poorer.

The move transfers to any policy that destroys something. After the World Trade Center fell in 2001 and Paul Krugman suggested in print that rebuilding might lift the economy, Austrian and classical-liberal writers answered straight out of this chapter. The resources spent rebuilding could no longer be spent on other new construction, so the offices that would have gone up in Queens are the loss nobody records. The purest modern case is American. In the summer of 2009 the federal government paid people three or four thousand dollars to trade in an older vehicle, and the trade-in had to be wrecked on purpose, its engine killed with sodium silicate: Cash for Clunkers put something like six hundred and ninety thousand working cars beyond use.

The title of the pamphlet is the whole rule, and it survives as a habit of mind: whatever a policy or a headline shows you, go looking for the unseen effects it hides. Milton Friedman spent a decade teaching that habit to a mass audience. Free to Choose, the book he wrote with his wife Rose in 1980 and the ten-part series that went with it on public television, took the method through schooling, welfare, consumer safety and inflation. His argument throughout was that the everyday decisions of a life, the school, the job, the shopping, belong in ordinary people's hands, not central planners' hands.

the-continental-1775-1781-not-worth-a-co.context_blurb:
A government at war that cannot tax has one other way to pay. On 22 June 1775 the Continental Congress, which had no taxing power of its own since only the thirteen states could tax, voted to print two million dollars of paper backed by the promise of a country that did not yet exist. The money was Continental currency, and everybody called the bills Continentals.

The arithmetic was hopeless from the start. Congress printed roughly two hundred to two hundred and forty million dollars over the course of the war, depending on how the reissued bills are counted, while the gold and silver coin circulating in all thirteen colonies in 1775 has been put at no more than about ten million dollars. In the summer of 1781 a paper dollar fetched about a cent in silver, and by December it fetched nothing at all; barbers were said to be papering their shop walls with the bills. The language kept the memory for a century, in the phrase 'not worth a Continental.'

Somebody always holds the paper when it dies. Here it was soldiers' families and small savers who held Continentals as savings: a man paid in Continentals sent them home, and what his wife had put by evaporated while he was away. A farmer who took the paper for grain grew poor, and a farmer who insisted on coin was denounced as a profiteer. Congress and several states answered in 1777 and 1778, not by stopping the press but by fixing what goods might cost and what work might earn, which is to say wage and price controls, evaded within months and abandoned inside a year. Some states went further and compelled shopkeepers to take the paper at its printed face value on pain of punishment, which is what legal-tender laws do; sellers hid their best goods or left the market instead.

Twelve years later the men who had lived through it wrote the lesson into the founding document. Section 10 of its first article forbids any state to emit bills of credit, the eighteenth-century term for exactly the sort of paper Congress had issued, while Section 8 confines the federal power to coining money and regulating its value. That hard-money clause was not borrowed from a book. Madison, Hamilton and the rest had watched their own currency die, so the conviction behind the clause is an empirical lesson drawn from a catastrophe they had personally lived through.

France ran the same experiment a decade later with the same tools, and added the guillotine. The revolutionary paper issued against confiscated church land, the assignat, met refusal with legal-tender decrees, ceilings on prices and finally capital punishment, and it collapsed anyway, because none of those measures touched the printing. Bastiat's two columns catch the American case exactly. Seen: government paying soldiers; Unseen: soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed. The payment is an act anybody can point to, while the destruction of what the recipient had saved stays invisible until it is complete.

the-endangered-species-act-perverse-ince.context_blurb:
Richard Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act on 28 December 1973, and hardly anybody disagreed with the purpose. The trouble sits in the design. When a listed species turns up on private land, federal regulators can forbid the owner to log, plough or build on much of it, and nothing in the statute pays him for what he loses.

Rural landowners worked the logic out quickly, and the folk answer runs to three verbs: shoot, shovel, and shut up. The reasoning is cold and perfectly rational given the rule. A man who kills the bird, buries it and tells nobody keeps the use of his land, so no one knows the animal was there, and no inspector ever comes to draw a boundary across his pasture.

The best-studied case is a bird. The red-cockaded woodpecker nests in mature southern pines, and in a 2003 paper Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael showed that owners of land near known colonies in North Carolina were felling their pines young. The behaviour inverts the law's purpose, and the law produced it: destruction of mature pines before the birds could arrive, because a tree old enough to hold a woodpecker's nest has become a liability rather than an asset.

Public choice has a name for the shape of this. Each American gets a small, pleasant share of the benefit of a protected species, while a handful of particular owners carry the whole cost in lost income, which is concentrated costs combined with dispersed benefits, Olson's famous pattern run in reverse. The obvious remedy is to pay. If the government buys the restriction instead of imposing it, the owner signs a contract limiting what he may do with his land in exchange for money, which is a conservation easement. The law professor Jonathan Adler has argued for years that compensation turns a landowner from the species' enemy into its keeper.

Elinor Ostrom's work points somewhere else again. She spent a career documenting how groups really do protect a shared resource, and her answer is neither a federal designation nor private indifference but local landowner cooperatives with genuine ownership of the conservation problem, with clear boundaries, rules the members write themselves and a real stake in the result.

The general class of failure has a name too: perverse incentives, where a rule creates individual incentives whose combined effect defeats the rule's own purpose, as with the Delhi cobra bounty or a driving ban that makes families buy a second car. The lesson a legislator ought to read before voting is the plain one: a rule that loads its whole cost on one owner makes him dodge it before it hits, which is why the woodpecker's best protection may be a cheque rather than a prohibition.

the-federal-reserve-act-of-december-23-1.context_blurb:
The United States had done without a central bank since Andrew Jackson's day, and the bank panics kept coming. In December 1913 Congress passed a law creating one, and Woodrow Wilson signed it two days before Christmas: the Federal Reserve. The Federal Reserve is the body that settles how much money exists in America and what borrowing costs, and it has done so ever since.

The design tried to answer an old fear, that a single city would own the nation's credit. So the system was spread around the country, each district with its own Reserve Bank owned by the member commercial banks in it, and the number of districts drawn under it was twelve, from Boston and New York to Dallas and San Francisco. The new system took over the paper money too. Before 1913 individual chartered banks printed their own bills; the Act created the paper that over the next decades replaced theirs and that Americans still carry, formally called Federal Reserve Notes, backed at first partly by gold and today by the assets the Fed holds.

How the plan was written is part of its history. A handful of the richest bankers in America travelled in November 1910 by private railway car to a hunting club on Jekyll Island in Georgia, describing themselves as a duck-shooting party so that nobody would ask questions, and drafted the scheme that became the Aldrich plan. The obvious objection to a design made that way is not complicated: the bank might quietly serve those few insiders more than ordinary people. Three years later the bill went through Congress under the names of two Democrats who had long argued for a currency that could stretch and shrink with business: Owen and Glass, a senator from Oklahoma and a congressman from Virginia. Not everybody was persuaded. Charles Lindbergh senior told the House from the floor that the bill would set up the most gigantic trust on earth, and the fear underneath his objection was that control over money would put unelected bankers in charge behind the scenes.

The date itself drew comment. The Senate passed the bill on 19 December, the House approved the final version 298 to 60 on the 22nd, and the Senate followed 43 to 25 on the 23rd, when Wilson signed it; critics said the holiday calendar had cut the debate short, though most members were there to vote. As for what the new bank does from day to day, it buys and sells in the open market: buying adds reserves to the banking system and pushes rates down, selling drains reserves and pushes rates up, and the instrument it trades is Treasury securities.

One famous story about Wilson needs handling with care. A quotation circulated long after his death in 1924, attributing to Wilson on his deathbed a confession that he had unwittingly ruined his country by creating the Fed. Historians who went looking cannot find it. The 'unwittingly ruined my country' confession has no verified source and is likely invented, and the honest practice is to quote only what can be checked. Wilson did write, in a book published in 1913, about the hidden sway of concentrated financial power, which is a different and documented passage. The Act as passed gave the Fed no numerical goal at all, only a phrase about furnishing an elastic currency, and Congress wrote no targets into the law until 1977, when it told the Fed to pursue two things at once: maximum employment and stable prices.

the-friedman-hayek-relationship-and-mont.context_blurb:
In the first ten days of April 1947 Friedrich Hayek gathered thirty-nine economists, historians and philosophers at the Hotel du Parc, standing on a hillside called Mont Pelerin above Lake Geneva. Central planning was the respectable opinion almost everywhere that year, and what the group met to defend was the older tradition of classical liberalism (limited government plus free markets). Milton Friedman, thirty-four years old and a year into his Chicago job, was in the room.

The Statement of Aims they adopted opens by declaring that the central values of civilisation are in danger, and it singles out one threatened possession as the most precious of all: freedom of thought and expression. Against the tide of planning, entrenched in the Soviet Union and spreading through the welfare states of western Europe, the thing the group existed to defend was free markets and individual liberty. They nearly called themselves something else. The plan had been to name the society for two nineteenth-century liberal writers, Lord Acton and Alexis de Tocqueville, until Frank Knight objected to gathering under two Catholic aristocrats and Mises worried that the pair's old mistakes would stick, so the hillside's name went on the letterhead instead.

Somebody paid for the ten days, and the bill came to a little over eighteen thousand Swiss francs. Ninety-three per cent of it was settled by a Swiss commercial bank, the Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, with smaller sums from an American fund, from the Bank of England and from a free-market institute in New York. Three years later Hayek moved from London to Chicago, where Friedman had taught since 1946, and for twelve years the two worked on one campus without sharing a department. Hayek's chair sat in The Committee on Social Thought, an interdisciplinary body, and part of his salary came from outside grants.

Admiration did not mean agreement. Friedman's 1953 essay on method said a theory earns its keep by the accuracy of its predictions alone, however unrealistic the assumptions behind it look, and Hayek rejected that standard for his own subject. His objection, which he called a critique of scientism, is that treating economics as measurement makes the unmeasurable vanish, since the local and tacit knowledge that makes a market work is exactly what no statistic records. Friedman returned the compliment in the other direction. He supplied the introduction for the fiftieth-anniversary printing of Hayek's wartime bestseller, and admired its author for fifty years, but one piece of his economics he called false, and said so in print repeatedly: Hayek's account of how booms turn into busts. Examining American cycles from 1879 to 1988, Friedman reported no significant link between the length of a boom and the depth of the slump after it.

Both men wanted the money supply out of political hands, and each published a different answer. Friedman's rule, set out in 1959, kept the central bank but tied it down: let the quantity of money grow at a fixed low rate each year and leave it alone. Hayek went further in 1976 and proposed abolishing the monopoly instead, letting private banks compete to issue currencies, so that a saver could simply walk away from any money being debased. The state of the argument in their own lifetime is visible in one award. In 1974 the Nobel committee split the economics prize between Hayek, who held that central planning could not work, and the Swedish social democrat Gunnar Myrdal, who had spent a career arguing for it. That shared award tells you that serious economists still disagreed at the deepest level about whether planning was possible.

the-hayek-keynes-exchange-1931-1932.context_blurb:
In 1931 a thirty-two-year-old Austrian joined the London School of Economics and picked a fight with the most famous economist alive. The result was the central economic argument of the century, conducted in print, in a journal, with impeccable manners and no mercy whatever.

The quarrel began as a book review. In August 1931 Economica carried the first half of a long and hostile essay: Friedrich Hayek reviewing John Maynard Keynes, and specifically the Treatise on Money that Keynes had brought out the year before. Keynes replied in November, Hayek rejoined, and the second half of the review appeared in February 1932. Underneath the technicalities lay a practical disagreement about the Depression then wrecking both their countries: Keynes said governments should spend more; Hayek said that would make things worse later, because the spending would prop up the very malinvestments a slump exists to clear away.

Hayek's technical charge was that Keynes had built a theory of money with no theory of capital attached and had ignored an entire continental literature on interest: the Wicksell-Mises tradition on interest and the natural rate, the Swedish and Viennese work on which Hayek's own account of booms and slumps rested. Keynes largely declined to answer the technicalities. He turned instead on Hayek's own book of 1931, Prices and Production, which he called a frightful muddle and an example of a remorseless logician starting from one mistake and ending in Bedlam.

The counter-attack came from a third party. Keynes arranged for his Cambridge colleague Piero Sraffa to review Prices and Production, and Sraffa's 1932 piece argued that without money there is no single natural rate of interest to be found but a whole multiplicity of commodity rates. Hayek answered that June, and professional opinion swung away from him for a generation. The episode shows how much weight one well-aimed notice can carry: a well-placed critical review can shift a whole field's views. The feud also had a geography. Keynes and his students were at King's College in Cambridge while Hayek and Lionel Robbins taught in Houghton Street, so the fight that framed British economics until the war ran between Cambridge and the London School of Economics.

Then came the decision Hayek regretted for the rest of his life. When Keynes brought out the General Theory in 1936, he wrote no review of the General Theory at all. His explanation afterwards was partly tactical: Keynes was famous for changing his mind about his own earlier positions, having already moved twice, so a long technical review seemed likely to be answered by yet another new book. By the time it was clear this one would stand, the Keynesian revolution had swept the profession with no serious Austrian reply in print.

The whole exchange, with the letters and Sraffa's attack, was collected in 1995 as a volume of Hayek's collected works, under a title that gives away the contents: Contra Keynes and Cambridge. The coda is worth as much as the argument. When the London School was evacuated to Cambridge in the war, Keynes found Hayek rooms at King's and a school place for his son, and the two men took turns on fire-watch duty on the chapel roof at night. Hayek remembered that hospitality as one of the pleasures of his life, which carries the useful lesson: people can differ deeply about ideas without becoming personal enemies.

the-liberty-fund-collected-works-bastiat.context_blurb:
Bastiat wrote in French, which means English-speaking readers have always depended on whoever was willing to translate him. For most of the twentieth century that was one small outfit at Irvington-on-Hudson in New York state: the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE), started by Leonard Read in 1946, which kept three works in print, the pamphlet on law, the Economic Sophisms and a volume of selected essays. Those editions were good, and they covered a fraction of what he wrote; most of his letters, his journalism and his speeches in the National Assembly had never appeared in English at all.

The bigger job was taken on later by the Liberty Fund in Indianapolis, endowed by the lawyer and businessman Pierre Goodrich for exactly this purpose. Its collected works of Bastiat, six volumes edited in English by David Hart with Jacques de Guenin and Jean-Claude Paul-Dejean as general editors, is the first full scholarly edition in the language. What such an endowment demonstrates is private funding keeping ideas alive across generations, with no committee and no grant programme deciding which dead economist deserves a reprint. Volume three, published in 2017, carries the famous essay of 1850, titled in that edition 'What Is Seen and What Is Not Seen', along with the satirical Sophisms and the candlemakers' petition for a law against the sun.

That essay is the one with the window. A boy breaks the pane in his father's shop, the father hands a glazier six francs, and the neighbours congratulate the town on the work created. Bastiat points back at the till: the six francs can no longer be spent on anything else. Follow the francs and the accounting comes out flat, because nothing new has been created. A coat not ordered from the tailor is every bit as real as a pane ordered from the glazier, and the town ends one window poorer than it began.

Much of the corpus is free now. David Hart, the edition's English editor, also built the Online Library of Liberty, a classical-liberal archive that puts Bastiat's writings in front of anybody with an internet connection and no money at all.

the-modern-democratic-socialist-revival-.context_blurb:
Bernie Sanders of Vermont ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and again in 2020, describing himself as a democratic socialist, and the organisation most associated with the revival grew from roughly six thousand members in 2014 to some ninety-two thousand seven years later: the Democratic Socialists of America. Its best-known elected figures include Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib.

The policy package usually travels together: a fifteen-dollar federal wage floor, rent control in expensive cities, government-set prices for prescription drugs, and a single tax-funded health plan covering everybody in place of private insurance. That last piece carries a name Sanders made famous, Medicare for All. On the arithmetic, the standard promise is that the rich will pay. The country holds only so many rich people, and confiscating their whole fortunes would still leave the bills unpaid, so the remainder falls on middle-class and poor families, through higher taxes or inflation, which is a statement about sums rather than about anybody's intentions.

The useful exercise is to name what each critic would say, which is a different thing from deciding who is right. On a wage floor set well above what small shops can pay, the classical move is Bastiat's, from 1850: seen-versus-unseen -- the worker priced out of the labor market is the hidden cost, the visible beneficiary being the worker whose wage rises. On rent control the argument runs back to a 1946 pamphlet by Milton Friedman and George Stigler, and what critics have pressed hardest ever since is the supply response: capped rents mean fewer apartments over time. A rent held below the cost of supplying housing makes supplying it less attractive, and the shortage lands on tenants who have not arrived yet.

On government-set medicine prices the oldest version of the objection is Mises's, from an essay of 1920. Earlier critics of socialism had argued about morals or politics; Mises made a mechanical argument about the informational role of prices, claiming the thing could not work however saintly the planners were, because a price carries information about scarcity and urgency that no committee can manufacture. Hayek extended the point in 1945, and applied to a government negotiating what a medicine may cost it becomes the knowledge problem, applied to which new drugs get researched: nobody at the table knows which research lines a lower price will quietly stop funding.

Accuracy cuts both ways here. What Bernie Sanders and other American democratic socialists propose in the 2020s is not the Soviet arrangement, and the honest description of the difference is this: his plan sets prices in some sectors but leaves ownership private, putting government-set prices in place of market prices in labour, housing, medicine, energy and schooling. That is a smaller claim than planning every factory, and the critics' mechanism is the same one at a smaller scale. What all this leaves is a habit rather than a conclusion. The habit is to identify the reasoning move a specific critic would press, without demanding you share the critic's verdict, so that a reader can follow the chain and then decide for himself. One more thing follows from Mises's argument being mechanical rather than political: the reasoning moves apply the same way regardless of the label the advocate uses, whether the word on the banner is socialism, reform, social democracy or consumer protection.

the-panic-of-1907-and-j-p-morgans-privat.context_blurb:
The United States of October 1907 had no central bank, and when the panic came nobody's job was to stop it. Theodore Roosevelt's government had no tools for the purpose. The rescue was organised instead by a group of wealthy private bankers, using their own money, with the seventy-year-old J. P. Morgan at the head of it.

The trigger was a failed squeeze. Otto and Augustus Heinze tried to squeeze the short-sellers of United Copper Company stock, the scheme collapsed on 16 October, and depositors began pulling money out of every institution connected with the brothers. The largest casualty went down on 22 October and gave the episode its other name. The Knickerbocker was no ordinary bank: it took deposits like one but lived under looser reserve rules and could speculate far more freely, because it was a trust company, and the third largest of them in New York.

Morgan's method was personal in a way no institution could be. He called the presidents of the other banks and trusts to his personal library at 219 Madison Avenue, the building that is now a museum, and by his son-in-law's account locked the doors until each man had written a cheque. Told that the New York Stock Exchange would have to shut, he answered that the shock would be too great, and he raised about $25 million in 15 minutes from the men in that room to keep it open. He also decided who lived. The Knickerbocker he judged beyond saving and let go; another large trust facing a run he judged solvent and backstopped with a private syndicate, and it survived: Trust Company of America.

Washington helped with money rather than with rules. The Treasury Secretary, George Cortelyou, pushed thirty-five million dollars of federal deposits into New York institutions, a vast sum for the era, and the modern word for public money used to prop up failing firms is a bailout. What the whole week demonstrated was an absence. In a run, even a sound institution holding good loans can be destroyed if nobody will lend it cash overnight, and the thing the country did not have was a lender of last resort.

The politics took six years. Congress set up a national monetary commission chaired by Senator Nelson Aldrich, which spent four of them studying European central banks and produced the Aldrich Plan of 1911, and the stated reason for wanting such an institution was straightforward: so there would be a lender of last resort during future bank panics. The structure it drafted became law in December 1913 as the Federal Reserve Act. Charles Kindleberger, the economic historian, later used the 1907 rescue as the pivot of his book on panics, and his verdict on Morgan's night in the library sums up why the Fed exists. That was the last time an individual acted as a central bank in a major crisis, and nobody could reasonably be asked to do it again.

the-powell-2024-pivot-and-the-second-inf.context_blurb:
The Federal Reserve held its policy rate at five and a quarter to five and a half per cent for fourteen months from July 2023, waiting for the post-pandemic inflation to come down. On 18 September 2024 it began cutting, and the size of the first move surprised the markets: 50 basis points, an oversized cut, where a new easing cycle traditionally opens with half of that. A central bank that swings from one direction to its opposite is said in the financial press to have made a pivot. Jerome Powell had prepared the ground at Jackson Hole the month before.

The justification was not that inflation had reached the target. Consumer prices had come down from the peak above nine per cent to about two and a half, with the core measure stickier at around three, so the committee pointed somewhere else: labor-market cooling, with unemployment ticking up, vacancies shrinking and hiring slowing. The outcome the Fed was aiming at has a name of its own, and two years of its messaging had been staked on it: the soft landing, meaning inflation back at target without a recession on the way.

The reason anybody worried about an early cut is a memory from the 1970s. Arthur Burns raised rates, watched inflation fall, and then cut again the moment growth slackened, in order to protect jobs; inflation returned, worse than before, within a few years. The lesson economists took from it is blunt: cutting rates too early can trigger a second, worse inflation wave. Clearing up that second wave fell to Paul Volcker, who took the chair in 1979 and pushed short-term rates to about twenty per cent by 1981. Loans for houses, cars and businesses became punishing, unemployment went above ten per cent, and prices finally settled, which is the trade-off in plain sight: very high interest rates can crush inflation but hurt borrowers first.

Whether the landing was soft is the live question. Inflation above nine per cent in 2022 came down while the Fed lifted rates from almost nothing to above five per cent, and the deep recession most forecasters expected did not arrive. If that holds, one reading of the whole period is vindicated: the Fed's aggressive 2022-23 tightening successfully broke inflation without recession -- the soft-landing thesis. If a second wave appears instead, the Austrian reading of the cycle wins the argument, and nobody gets to declare the result in advance. The institutional question runs alongside. Powell was appointed by Donald Trump in 2018 and reappointed by Joe Biden in 2022, his term as chairman ended in May 2026, and Kevin Warsh succeeded him.

Austrian and monetarist critics read the pivot as an instance of a standing pattern rather than a single error: central banks tend to cut rates before inflation is fully broken because the political cost of continued unemployment exceeds the political cost of eventual re-emerging inflation. The two costs arrive at different times, and the later one lands after the officials responsible have moved on. Underneath the week-by-week commentary sits an older dispute that this cycle is actually testing: whether monetary expansion produces consumer-price inflation on a long and variable lag, as monetarists and Austrians argue, or whether it can be neutralized by supply-side responses, as MMT and some New Keynesians argue. The 2020s are the largest natural experiment on that question since the 1970s, and no verdict is in yet.

the-salamanca-school-16th-century-spanis.context_blurb:
Salamanca is an old university town in western Spain, and in the 1500s its lecture halls were loud with Dominican friars and Jesuit priests arguing about the New World. Spain had just conquered a hemisphere, treasure fleets were coming home, and these theologians had to work out what counted as a just price, a just wage and a just war. Historians gave the group a name: the School of Salamanca.

Their founder was Francisco de Vitoria, a Dominican friar who held the chair through the 1530s and 1540s until his death in 1546, and who treated trade and conquest as matters a Christian was obliged to get right. Silver was the puzzle he handed his students. It came home from the Americas by the shipload, kings and captains and merchants spent it across Europe, and the stock of bread and cloth and grain for sale had not grown to match, so prices in European towns roughly doubled inside a single lifetime. When new money chases a fixed pile of goods, the result is inflation, and the Salamanca men watched it arrive in real time.

One of them traced the rise to its source. Martin de Azpilcueta, whom students called Doctor Navarrus, was writing a handbook for priests who hear confessions when he set the rule down in 1556: where money is scarce goods are cheap, and where money is plentiful goods are dear, which is the earliest clean statement of what later economists called the quantity theory of money. The flood he was watching poured out of one mountain, the Cerro Rico above Potosi in what is now Bolivia, whose ore doubled prices across Spain inside his own working life. Four centuries later Milton Friedman reached the same finding and compressed it into one line, that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon, which is why Austrians enjoy noting that a confessor's manual got there first.

A Jesuit of the same school pushed in another direction. Across six volumes published between 1593 and 1609, Luis de Molina argued that a just price is not the labour or the cost poured into a thing, but whatever willing buyers and willing sellers would settle on in a market working normally, which puts value in the buyer's head three centuries before Carl Menger said so in Vienna. All of it then dropped out of the textbooks, which begin in 1776 with Adam Smith, as though nobody had thought hard about money earlier. In 1995 Murray Rothbard devoted two volumes to the history of the subject in order to put back what that opening had dropped: medieval scholars who studied prices and money in monasteries and universities. The point is not that Smith stole anything. It is that market ideas were being worked out for centuries before they became famous in English.
