the-sowell-trilogy-on-the-intellectuals.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell wrote three books that work as a single argument. The Vision of the Anointed came out in 1995, and its subtitle names the habit the book is about: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy. In 1999 came a book on two rival ideas of fairness, one asking only that everyone play by one set of rules, the other asking that society reach back and even out the hands life dealt, and Sowell called it The Quest for Cosmic Justice, because the second standard is what a man would choose if he were designing the universe from scratch. Intellectuals and Society followed in 2010.

The 1995 book lays its pattern out in four stages. First a problem is announced as a crisis. Second, a remedy is adopted on a promise, while critics warn of damage. Third, the damage arrives. Fourth, the remedy's champions call the critics simplistic and demand proof of cause, often adding that things would have been worse without the remedy, a claim offered in a form nobody can check. What bothers Sowell about the crisis stage is not the suffering it describes. It is that nobody first asks the obvious question, whether the trouble had already been getting better for years, in which case a remedy dropped onto an improving trend can collect the credit for the trend.

The 1999 book aims a different objection at a different target. Suppose a campaign asks the government to repay every group for the wrongs done to its ancestors, until outcomes finally come out level. Sowell grants that the wish is decent, and still objects that nobody has the knowledge to weigh each group's past without new injustice, which is Hayek's knowledge problem carried into the moral realm, since the circumstances of all those groups across generations and continents are scattered, contested and in most cases simply gone.

The 2010 book supplies the mechanism, and it opens by narrowing a word. By an intellectual Sowell means neither a clever man nor a well-credentialled one: an intellectual is a person whose occupational output is ideas themselves. An engineer who publishes superb papers is not working as an intellectual while he lays out a span, because his work ends in a bridge that either stands or falls. A surgeon faces the same discipline, and so does a battle commander, who can pay for one bad judgment with his life. Where the product is ideas alone, the verdict falls instead to the peers who read the work and praise it.

Sowell's cleanest illustration is Britain between the wars. Its leading writers and thinkers campaigned through the 1930s against rearmament, while Germany rearmed at speed, and when the bill came due in 1939 not one of them lost any standing for it. His account of why the pattern survives is structural, not personal, and it reaches intellectuals as a class: nothing in their occupation punishes a prediction that turned out false. Hence the question he would have a listener fire back on being told that all the experts agree: which experts, and what happens to them if they turn out wrong? The argument is about the feedback loop, not about anybody's honesty or intelligence, and a reader can accept the mechanism and still disagree with Sowell on any particular policy.

the-universal-reach-bastiat-as-economics.context_blurb:
Frederic Bastiat farmed at Mugron, in the Landes of southwestern France, for most of his adult life, and only at the very end of it did he become a public writer. Everything that made him famous, the sophisms, the pamphlet on law, the unfinished Harmonies, came out between 1844 and 1850, so his major writing career ran about five years before tuberculosis killed him on Christmas Eve of 1850.

He wrote the way he did on purpose. Other economists of the century, Antoine Cournot among them, built their arguments out of equations that only a trained scholar could follow; Bastiat chose plain prose aimed at the general reader, so that a farmer in his own district could check the reasoning himself.

Taken together, the discipline has three parts, and they are worth stealing. One is that plain prose. Another is to open with something a reader can picture, a shopkeeper's broken pane, a new railway line, a row in the chamber of deputies, before any lesson is drawn, which is starting with a concrete scene. The third is the turn that does the work. Describe what everybody sees and applauds, name what the other side has left out, and then drag into daylight the unseen consequences: the tailor whose sale never happened because the shopkeeper spent his money on glass, the worker priced out of a job, the shopper paying extra for a protected good.

Later writers took the method up whole. Henry Hazlitt, an American journalist, worked through tariffs, rent control, price controls and public works chapter by chapter in a slim 1946 book called Economics in One Lesson, and it has outsold every other popular Austrian title in English. Thomas Sowell wrote the most sustained modern version in 1980, weighing grand political claims against what ordinary people actually know when the moment comes to decide, in Knowledge and Decisions.

The method has limits, and Bastiat's admirers say so first. Seen-and-unseen is a superb tool for an argument about trade barriers or make-work schemes, but it does not by itself equip a reader for monetary theory and business-cycle analysis, where the tradition sends you to Menger, Mises and Hayek for money, to Bohm-Bawerk for capital, and to Buchanan and Tullock for the behaviour of governments.

the-vienna-university-economics-traditio.context_blurb:
Economics at the University of Vienna was taught inside the law faculty, and in 1873 Carl Menger took its chair and held it for thirty years. He had founded the Austrian School two years earlier on a simple claim about trade: when two people swap willingly, each side valued what it got more than what it gave up, which is how a voluntary swap leaves both sides better off with nobody tricked.

Menger had two first-rate students in that first generation. One was Friedrich von Wieser. The other resigned as Finance Minister of Austria-Hungary in 1904, took a parallel Vienna chair the same year, and taught until he died in 1914: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk. His seminar from 1905 to 1914 is one of the strangest rooms in the history of the subject. In it sat the young Ludwig von Mises, the future Austrian Social Democratic foreign minister Otto Bauer, and Rudolf Hilferding, later the Marxist finance minister of Weimar Germany, all hearing the same lectures. What the men out of that room spent their lives arguing over was whether a small group of officials can plan a whole nation's economy well.

Mises took his Vienna doctorate in 1906 and his licence to lecture in 1913, and in the 1920s he ran a private seminar of his own, which is where the young Hayek came in. His case against planning is an information case. A market throws off millions of small local facts every day, and no central office can invent them: they lack the millions of local price signals that markets produce. Abolish bargaining and bidding and shopping around, hand every price to a committee, and the thing that vanishes overnight is prices that reveal what people really want.

Hilferding's own career supplied the other half of the lesson. He was finance minister while the German central bank printed marks by the ton to cover debts and reparations, and bread priced in the hundreds of marks in the spring of 1923 was priced in the hundreds of billions by that November: prices shoot up because each unit of money loses value.

The Vienna chair passed in 1922 to Hans Mayer, who stood outside the front rank of the tradition, so the school's real home became those private seminars. The city's part in the story closed with the 1938 Anschluss with Nazi Germany, when German troops came in, the police arrested opponents, and the universities pushed out Jewish and dissenting professors. Mises had already left for Geneva in 1934. The tradition's centre moved to London, then to Chicago and New York, and later to George Mason University in Virginia.

transitory-powells-2021-miscall-and-retr.context_blurb:
Through most of 2021 American prices climbed faster than they had in forty years, and the officials in charge had a word ready. Jerome Powell, chairman of the Federal Reserve, Janet Yellen at the Treasury, and most of the Fed's rate-setting committee told press conferences and congressional hearings from spring through autumn that the rise was transitory. The case rested on three supports: the low base of 2020, the tangled state of global supply chains, and a claim about the American job market, namely that continuing slack in employment made wage-price spirals unlikely.

The background mechanism is not complicated. The Federal Reserve can create dollars and lend them to banks, so when it creates a great many very fast, more money chases the same goods on the same shelves: prices go up -- your money buys less. Across 2020 and 2021 the money supply grew by better than a quarter, which is not a quantity that any amount of labour-market slack absorbs.

Warnings came from inside the tent. In February 2021 Larry Summers, a Democrat who had been Treasury Secretary under Bill Clinton, wrote in a newspaper column that the size of the new $1.9 trillion package created a serious risk of inflation from too much new money chasing the same goods. Fed officials dismissed him publicly, and within a year he looked right. Monetarists in Milton Friedman's line and Austrians in Mises's pressed the stronger version of the same point: when the money supply grows a lot, prices eventually rise no matter what supply chains do, because a one-time monetary expansion works through prices over a lag of a year or two.

Meanwhile the policy stayed loose. With inflation already running at 6.2 percent, the Fed held its main rate at zero and went on buying bonds by the billion each month, and keeping credit cheap and plentiful into a rising price level is what the term easy money describes. On 30 November 2021 Powell told the Senate Banking Committee that it was probably a good time to retire the word, with the index at 6.8 percent that month. Six months after the retraction the cycle peaked, and the reading was 9.1% in June 2022, the highest since 1981. The Fed then raised rates hard through 2022 and 2023.

Two lessons get drawn from the episode, and they are different sizes. The mild one, which almost everybody accepts, is that officials often stick with a story too long even as the evidence turns against it. The Austrian tradition after Mises and Hayek presses a sharper one, that central banks reason from supply-shock stories that flatter their own past decisions and dismiss monetary explanations that would embarrass them, since the institution offering the supply-chain account was the same institution that had created the money. Judy Shelton's case gets filed alongside it. A hard-money economist nominated to the Fed's board, she lost a Senate cloture vote in November 2020, and Austrian writers read that as evidence that nominees who challenge the Federal Reserve's usual easy-money views often fail confirmation.

venezuela-2013-present-the-modern-social.context_blurb:
Hugo Chavez came to power in Venezuela in 1999 promising what he called socialism for a new century, ruled until his death in 2013, and left Nicolas Maduro a machine with three moving parts: legal maximum prices on everyday goods, state ownership of the big industries, and a central bank that would print whatever the treasury needed.

The price caps came first. The state fixed what food and fuel could be sold for and told shopkeepers to obey or face jail, but the fixed price was often below what the goods cost to produce or import, so each sale lost money, and shelves went empty -- shops stopped stocking things that lost money. What shoppers found missing was not a list of luxuries: it was widespread shortages of flour, chicken, toilet paper, and medicine. The government called it a capitalist conspiracy and sent soldiers to make shops sell at the legal price anyway.

Then the money went. To pay its bills the Maduro government printed bolivars on a scale that took a loaf of bread from a few units to millions and then to billions, and shoppers carried their cash to market in bags, which is hyperinflation. For 2018 Venezuela's own central bank put the annual rate at about 130,000% per year, and the International Monetary Fund's estimate was about ten times higher: the Weimar wheelbarrow replayed in Latin America a century later.

People left. By 2024 the United Nations counted one of the biggest peacetime movements of people in modern history, with families walking south into Colombia and Peru and on to Brazil: about one quarter, some 7.7 million people, out of a country that had been middle-income. Those who stayed built a workaround nobody legislated. Shopkeepers began quoting prices in a currency they trusted, and relatives abroad sent money by phone, so the country ended up pricing goods in US dollars and receiving remittances via Zelle from relatives abroad, a dollarization from below.

The theory came first by ninety years. An Austrian economist had published a paper in 1920 arguing that with no private ownership of farms and factories a country has no real markets, and with no markets no real prices, and with no prices nothing to tell a planner whether steel is scarcer than sand; the author was Ludwig von Mises. His point is about knowledge rather than character: central planners cannot know what dispersed market prices would signal about scarcity and value, however honest they are.

What Venezuela adds is not a new argument but a new kind of evidence. The Soviet collapse and Mao's famines happened in closed countries behind a Cold War, hard to see even from inside, while this one is happening now, on smartphone video, in a Western Hemisphere country a plane ride from Miami. For most of the last century Mises's critics could call his claim untestable hand-waving. The Venezuelan record answers that: the socialist calculation problem is not an abstract academic dispute; it is an observable, current phenomenon.

walter-durantys-pulitzer-and-gareth-jone.context_blurb:
Walter Duranty ran the New York Times bureau in Moscow from 1922 to 1936 and took the 1932 Pulitzer Prize for Correspondence for his glowing dispatches on Stalin's Five-Year Plan. Across 1932 and 1933 Stalin's government seized grain from Ukrainian villages until several million peasants had starved to death, a famine Ukrainians call the Holodomor, and Duranty assured the world's most influential readership that no famine was happening. The reporting served the government causing the famine, because the denial carried the authority of the paper of record.

Instead of the word famine he used a phrase that has outlived him as the specimen of its kind: widespread mortality from diseases due to malnutrition. There was, he wrote in March 1933, no actual starvation.

One reporter went and looked. In March 1933 a young Welshman, once private secretary to David Lloyd George, walked through Soviet Ukraine without a minder, saw one starving village after another, crossed out, and told the story at a press conference in Berlin on 29 March. His surname was Jones. Malcolm Muggeridge had filed similar accounts from Ukraine in the Manchester Guardian that same month. Two days after the Berlin conference, Duranty answered in print, and what he called the account of a man who had walked the ground himself was a big scare story. The Soviet authorities then banned Jones from returning, which is what a government does when the truth would show that the government's own policies caused the famine. The regime plainly preferred the correspondent who filed the comfortable version, because his stories protected the government's image abroad. In August 1935, one day before his thirtieth birthday, Jones was shot dead in Inner Mongolia, and his family has argued ever since that the killing may have been arranged.

The prize stayed where it was. Ukrainian-American groups pressed the case hard from the 1980s onward, and in 1990 a signed editorial in the Times itself called his articles some of the worst reporting to appear in the paper. In 2003 the Pulitzer Board reviewed the award. It found that the 1931 work fell seriously short, concluded that there was no clear and convincing evidence of deliberate deception, and declined to withdraw the prize. The 2019 film Mr. Jones put the whole story in front of a mass audience. What a student should carry away is narrow and useful: winning a prize does not prove the reporting was true.

why-gold-the-convergent-monetary-propert.context_blurb:
Ask why money kept turning out to be metal and one historical fact jumps out. Egypt along the Nile, imperial Rome, Han China and Mansa Musa's Mali all picked the same substance for their highest-value money without consulting one another, and the substance was gold. Austrian and Bitcoin-standard writers argue that the convergence is evidence about physics rather than culture, since separate peoples kept choosing the same metal because the metal kept passing the same tests.

Those tests are usually listed as six. Money has to last, to travel, to split, to be interchangeable unit for unit, to be checkable, and to be hard to make more of. The checkable one is the merchant's problem: handed a purse of coins by a stranger in 1300, you need to tell by eye and by weight whether the things are genuine, and that property is recognizability.

Run the other candidates through the list and watch them fail. Diamonds are rare and hard and lovely, and they fail on divisibility -- diamonds cannot be split without loss of value, because a one-carat stone is worth far more than two half-carat stones, while half a gold coin is worth exactly half. Seashells, cowries and fired clay tokens all served as money somewhere, and they fail on scarcity -- they can be gathered or fired at will, which European traders proved by shipping cheap Indian Ocean shells into West Africa until the local currency was worthless. Even fool's gold fails on the scales: the yellow mineral that fooled many a prospector is iron pyrite, roughly a quarter as dense as gold, so a balance catches the swap at once.

Gold's hardest property to beat is the last one, and it has a number. The measure Saifedean Ammous put at the centre of The Bitcoin Standard in 2018 is the stock-to-flow ratio, which sets the ratio of existing above-ground stock to annual new production. What the ratio tells you is how hard it is to make more of it, which protects its value over time, and on that scale gold sits near sixty while silver sits near twenty-two and farm commodities are far lower. Gold's number rests on one physical fact, which is that essentially all the gold ever mined is still around, so annual production adds only about 1.5% to the total stock, because the metal does not corrode and a coin buried in 500 BC comes out of the ground shiny.

So the argument sets an engineering standard rather than a preference. Gold's monetary role reflects its physical properties, not cultural accident -- so any successor must beat gold on at least one property without losing others. Bitcoin was built in 2009 to that standard, matching gold on durability and interchangeability while adding finer divisibility, instant portability by wire, and verification by code, with a supply capped at 21 million units. Whether it holds up is an argument about engineering, which is the kind of argument evidence can settle.

youre-right-we-did-it-bernankes-friedman.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman spent years on the Great Depression and came out with a charge against an institution rather than against the market. The slump that began with the 1929 crash turned into a decade of shut banks and hungry families, he argued, because the Federal Reserve stood by while thousands of banks failed and a third of the nation's money supply disappeared, so the central bank made the crash worse instead of stopping it. He and Anna Schwartz set the case out at length in 1963, in a book titled A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960. What the Fed had done, on their account, was that it allowed the money supply to contract about 33% by failing to act as lender of last resort during bank failures.

In November 2002 the University of Chicago held a two-day conference for Friedman's ninetieth birthday, and a Fed governor named Ben Bernanke, who had spent two decades at Princeton studying this exact episode, spoke with Friedman and Schwartz sitting in the audience. He said he would abuse his status as an official representative of the Fed, and then conceded what the Fed had caused, which was the worst economic catastrophe in modern American history. The critique he accepted was the Friedman-Schwartz one, that the Fed caused the Great Depression by failing to lend to banks in the crisis. His closing words to the two of them were that they had been right, that the Fed had done it, that the Fed was very sorry, and that thanks to them it would not do it again.

Six years later he was chairman when the housing bubble burst. Banks had lent against houses suddenly worth less than the loans, and the Fed created new money to take the bad debts off them and keep them standing while homeowners lost their houses, which is a bailout. On the 1930s test he passed, since no cascade of bank failures was allowed to run. Austrian critics say he failed a different test, because he launched massive quantitative easing and zero interest rates that his critics argue mispriced capital and seeded a later inflation wave.

Friedman died in 2006 and never saw any of it. Anna Schwartz lived until 2012, and in an October 2008 interview with the Wall Street Journal she assessed the chairman who had apologised to her six years earlier, saying that he was fighting the last war, with tools meant for the 1930s, against a crisis of trust in banks' balance sheets. Set the two moments side by side and the recognition is uncomfortable rather than cynical: the lesson learned from one crisis can itself become the mistake that causes the next crisis.

a-conflict-of-visions-1987-constrained-v.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell, an American economist, set out in 1987 to explain a puzzle every newspaper reader knows: why do intelligent, well-informed people keep reaching opposite conclusions about the same policies? His book A Conflict of Visions argued that the quarrel starts before any facts are weighed, in each side's picture of what human beings are. It became one of his most-cited works.

Picture two friends arguing about a city's traffic. One wants clever experts put in charge to plan it properly. The other is skeptical: he doubts that any handful of planners could hold the knowledge of every driver, every street and every day's surprises. Sowell traced quarrels like that to rival views of human nature. Some people believe that the right rules and enough schooling could make us very nearly perfect; others believe we carry permanent limits, such as selfishness, ignorance and weakness, that no rulebook will ever erase. Sowell called these pictures visions because they come before any argument, shaping which policies feel obviously right and which feel obviously naive.

He named the two pictures with one pair of words: the constrained vision and the unconstrained vision. The constrained vision sees human nature as having real limits that we must work around. Knowledge is scattered among millions of people, self-interest never goes away, and good rules grow slowly through trial and error. In this vision, which runs through Adam Smith, Edmund Burke, the American Federalists and Friedrich Hayek, politics means designing rules that channel imperfect people, not finding the wise and handing them power.

The opposite picture, the unconstrained vision, holds that human nature is flexible and can be improved by new and better institutions. Sowell traced it through William Godwin, the French revolutionaries, John Kenneth Galbraith and John Rawls; in it, politics means identifying those who see correctly and empowering them to act. Sowell's own most-quoted line sums up the constrained side: in his telling there are no solutions at all, there are only trade-offs, so every choice gives up one good to gain another. He paired it with a two-word challenge, "Compared to what?" Any policy must be judged against the real options on the table, not against a dream, so a critic who calls a policy bad has to name the actual alternative he prefers.

Sowell spent the next twelve years building the idea into a trilogy. The second volume, The Vision of the Anointed (1995), held the unconstrained vision up against modern American social policy and diagnosed what happens when self-congratulation becomes a basis for policy. The third, The Quest for Cosmic Justice (1999), followed the same hope to its utopian end: the dream of remaking every outcome to match a picture of ultimate fairness.

What the first book holds back is as striking as what it says. Sowell lays out each vision at its strongest, follows both through named thinkers and applies them to real policy fights, and then deliberately declines to declare which vision is right. His aim was to teach readers to recognize which vision is speaking. That restraint explains why economists and activists so often seem deaf to each other on the very same issue, even when neither side is short of facts. Each side is reasoning from a different picture of what human beings essentially are. To one, talk of trade-offs sounds like a failure of will; to the other, talk of solutions sounds like naive utopianism.

americas-great-depression-1963-the-austr.context_blurb:
Murray Rothbard was a New York economist of the Austrian school, the tradition of Ludwig von Mises. In 1963, at thirty-seven, he published America's Great Depression, a 361-page reexamination of the worst slump in American history. Where most accounts blamed the free market and the crash of 1929, Rothbard pointed at Washington instead: at the central bank and at the White House.

Between 1929 and 1933 thousands of American banks failed and nearly a quarter of workers lost their jobs. Rothbard named two culprits, the Federal Reserve and President Herbert Hoover. The Fed's cheap credit through the 1920s built a boom that was bound to bust, and Hoover's activism after October 1929 turned what should have been a short cleanup into a decade-long depression.

For the boom Rothbard blamed one man above all: Benjamin Strong, governor of the New York Fed and the dominant force in the system. After Britain returned to gold in 1925 at its old prewar rate, Strong worked hand in glove with Montagu Norman of the Bank of England and kept American credit loose, partly to help Britain hold on to its gold. For the long bust he blamed Hoover. Weeks after the crash, in November 1929, Hoover summoned great industrialists such as Henry Ford and Pierre du Pont to the White House and pressed them to promise not to cut wage rates. Rothbard argued that this high-wage policy blocked the very adjustment that had ended earlier American depressions in eighteen months or less.

Austrian writers point to a natural experiment, the forgotten depression of 1920 and 1921. That slump was savage, with unemployment near 12 percent and output down about a sixth, yet Warren Harding's government slashed federal spending and allowed wages and prices to drop. Within about a year and a half prices had reset and the recession was over. Hoover chose the opposite path. In June 1930 he signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, heavy duties on nearly every import. Trading partners answered with big tariffs of their own on American goods, world trade shrank further, and the American slump spread abroad. In January 1932 Hoover founded the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which lent more than a billion dollars in six months to failing banks and railroads. The long-run danger of such rescues is that firms come to expect a loan whenever they stumble, and so they take bigger risks in the future. Franklin Roosevelt kept the agency and enlarged it.

This record overturns the schoolbook picture of Hoover sitting idle until Roosevelt arrived. Rothbard, and later Amity Shlaes in her 2007 book The Forgotten Man, found that Hoover himself had run large spending and price-support programs; Rothbard even called him the founder of the New Deal. His deeper move came from Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Credit made artificially cheap lures savings into projects that only look profitable while rates are held down, and when rates return to normal those projects stand revealed as malinvestment. On this reading the 1929 crash was not the disease but the correction, the unavoidable liquidation of errors the Fed had planted in the 1920s. The book was a companion to Rothbard's great treatise of 1962, Man, Economy, and State, a full textbook of Austrian economics; America's Great Depression applied its framework to a single historical case.

That same year Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published their Monetary History, which also blamed the Fed, but for shrinking the money supply by about a third once the crash had come. Rothbard faulted the Fed for the opposite error, committed across the whole decade before: expanding credit through the 1920s to prop up Britain's return to gold, and so seeding the malinvestment that had to bust. One account explains the contraction after the crash; the other explains the boom that came before it.

anti-price-gouging-laws-michael-munger-j.context_blurb:
In 2005 Hurricane Katrina tore across the Gulf Coast and left thousands of Mississippi homes without electricity. John Shepperson, a Kentuckian, saw a chance to help and to earn something: he bought nineteen generators, rented a truck and drove them about 600 miles south. The Duke University economist Michael Munger made what happened next the classic case against laws that punish price gouging.

Picture a town without power: refrigerators warm up, food spoils, hospitals go dark. Shepperson planned to sell his generators at roughly double what he had paid. That price is what made the long drive worth his while, and so it gave the town generators it otherwise would never have had. But Mississippi's anti-gouging statute forbade selling necessities far above their normal price. When Shepperson arrived, police arrested him, seized all nineteen generators and held him in jail for four days, while the machines sat unused in police custody and families stayed in the dark.

Economists see a hidden cost in every arrest like that. Imagine a man who spends sixteen hours driving a truck full of ice into a storm zone and charges triple to cover his fuel, his time and his risk. Arrest him, and the next time disaster strikes, fewer people bring in emergency supplies, because the trip no longer pays. Munger told Shepperson's story in a 2007 essay for Cato Unbound, using the language of Friedrich Hayek's 1945 article The Use of Knowledge in Society, which argued that prices carry knowledge no planner could ever gather.

Seen through Hayek's eyes, the high Mississippi price was a message telling a man hundreds of miles away that generators were desperately needed there. By answering it, Shepperson moved scarce capital from a low-value use at home to a high-value use in the storm zone, and Mississippi's law cut the signal that made the move possible. Munger reframed the moral argument. People on the ground, he said, never get to choose between fair and unfair prices; their real choice lies between expensive supply that arrives and cheap supply that does not exist. The 1970s showed the same mess on a national scale. Federal price caps set under Nixon and kept under Carter held gasoline below the level where supply and demand would meet, and the shortage appeared as long lines at filling stations across the country.

When Hurricane Katrina drowned New Orleans in August 2005, the Federal Emergency Management Agency moved slowly, while Walmart trucks were delivering bottled water, food and diapers across Louisiana in a matter of days, often ahead of the official convoys, as the economists Sobel and Leeson documented. The difference lay in who could decide: Walmart's local managers had authority to act without waiting for orders from headquarters, and they knew what their own towns needed. Venezuela ran the opposite experiment for years. After Hugo Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro widened controls on basics such as milk, bread and medicine, capping prices far below what they cost to produce, and the result was chronic, severe shortages, empty shelves and mass emigration.

One lesson runs through every case. Where knowledge is scattered among many people, prices are what coordinate them, and a rule that cuts the price signal makes that coordination disappear. The seen result is that nobody was gouged; the unseen cost is thousands of people left in the dark for weeks.

austrian-business-cycle-theory-abct.context_blurb:
Why do economies boom for years and then crash? Austrian business cycle theory, or ABCT, is the answer worked out in Vienna by Friedrich Hayek and the older Ludwig von Mises. It treats the boom-bust cycle as a monetary event with an institutional cause: a central bank holding interest rates where they do not belong.

In 1936 Keynes traced the swings to changing moods, the lurch from hope to fear. Mises and Hayek blamed one policy tool used badly: interest rates pushed artificially low by a central bank. Mises first set out the idea in his 1912 book The Theory of Money and Credit. Hayek built on it in the 1920s and 1930s, with Monetary Theory and the Trade Cycle in 1929 and Prices and Production in 1931; the second made him world-famous at thirty-two and launched his great debate with Keynes.

Through the 1920s the two men warned that credit held cheap for an extended stretch would breed a boom of bad investments bound to collapse, and when the Great Depression followed the crash of 1929, their admirers saw Austrian Business Cycle Theory vindicated. Mises acted on his warning. In 1929 he turned down a top post at Austria's great bank, the Kreditanstalt, telling his fiancée that a great crash was coming; in May 1931 the bank failed and set off Europe's banking crisis. That forecast came straight from his own Austrian business cycle theory.

Here is the mechanism. A developer offered loans at 1 percent launches a housing development that will take fifteen years to finish, and builders in every long-lived industry do the same. When rates climb back to 4 percent, many of those projects stop making sense, and some are abandoned half-built. Austrians call such projects malinvestments: not foolish bets, but projects that would have been sound if the interest-rate signal had told the truth. The theory met a modern test when Alan Greenspan's Fed cut its key rate from 6.5 percent at the end of 2000 to 1 percent by the middle of 2003 and held it there for a year. Austrian analysts singled out housing, above all residential real estate, as the main sink for the malinvestment, because homes are bought with long mortgages and so respond to long-term rates more than any other big market.

Peter Schiff, an investment adviser who learned his Austrian economics from his father, Irwin, warned again and again on business television that a housing crash was coming, and studio guests often laughed at him. Arguing on Fox News on New Year's Eve 2006, he predicted that American real-estate prices would come crashing back to earth in 2007, and the crash arrived in 2007 and 2008. Rothbard read the 1920s the same way: the Fed under Benjamin Strong held rates artificially low, partly to help Britain back onto gold. In the Austrian account, cheap central-bank credit always fuels a boom that ends in a crash once the bad bets are exposed.

The policy conclusion follows. Suppose a lending boom leaves a town full of empty office towers that no buyer will take at boom prices. If the government buys them at those prices, the correction stretches out, since failed projects are propped up rather than cleared away. Clearing them frees capital and workers for uses people truly want, and Rothbard argued that the interventions of Hoover and Roosevelt prolonged the very depression they were meant to cure.

The yardstick behind it all comes from the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell. In a market where no central bank meddles, rates would settle where the saving people want to do matches the borrowing businesses want for real projects, and economists call that level the natural rate. Push the bank rate below it, and credit outruns real saving. Keynes's rival account, in his 1936 General Theory, made the driver psychological instead: spontaneous urges to act, swinging between confidence and panic, which he named animal spirits. For Keynes the cycle was psychological; for the Austrians it was monetary, with a specific cause and a specific cure.

bastiat-vs-proudhon-the-1849-50-debate-o.context_blurb:
Over the winter of 1849 and 1850, two Frenchmen fought a duel in print over one question: may a lender rightly ask for interest? One was Frédéric Bastiat, the free-trade economist. The other was Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, the socialist who had become the first thinker to call himself an anarchist. Their letters became the first popular statement of a theory the Austrian school would later make its own.

Proudhon had been famous since 1840, when he published a book asking what property is and answered in three words: property is theft. He meant property that draws rent or interest without labor, not a workman's tools, a distinction later socialists often blurred. At the end of January 1849 he opened the Bank of the People in Paris, which was to lend to workers without interest, paying in notes that members swapped for goods; once Proudhon was sentenced to prison, the bank was wound up. The debate ran almost entirely in Proudhon's own Paris daily, La Voix du Peuple, which he kept editing from his cell in Sainte-Pélagie prison, so Bastiat argued in front of Proudhon's readers.

Bastiat's case did not rest on lenders deserving a reward. Interest, he argued, is a price, the price of the lender's going without the use of his money for the term of the loan. On a loan of a thousand francs for a year, the interest pays for that year of doing without; a century later Austrian economists would call this time preference. He then pressed a consequence Proudhon would not accept. Force interest to zero by law, and savers simply stop lending and keep their cash, so savings no longer flow into loans and there is nothing left to borrow. Proudhon replied that he needed no force at all. Let mutual banks owned by their members multiply and compete freely for borrowers, he claimed, and competition among such lenders would drive the rate down to zero by itself. Bastiat answered that competition can push interest down only as far as the value people place on time, and no further.

In 1850 Bastiat gathered the exchange into a book from the Guillaumin house in Paris and gave it an ironic title borrowed from Proudhon's own slogan for free lending: Gratuité du crédit. The two editions do not match. Bastiat's runs to fourteen letters, opening with one by Proudhon's disciple Chevé and closing with a final reply from Bastiat that Proudhon refused to answer. Proudhon's rival edition, Intérêt et principal, simply left out Bastiat's closing letter and so contains thirteen.

The idea was set out in full, formal dress in Austria. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's Capital and Interest, Kapital und Kapitalzins in German, appeared in parts from 1884 onward, and he counted Bastiat among the theory's forerunners. Then in 1949 Ludwig von Mises, a Viennese exile teaching in New York, brought the argument to English readers at the heart of a thousand-page treatise, Human Action. The book presents time preference as a basic feature of all human choosing, present in anyone's weighing of today against tomorrow, and no mere quirk of capitalism.

bitcoin-as-fifth-amendment-money-the-mem.context_blurb:
Every bitcoin is controlled by a secret number so long that nobody could memorize it or copy it by hand without mistakes. In 2013 a handful of developers, among them Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak, published a free open standard, BIP-39, that turns the number into a short list of ordinary words. The result is a kind of wealth no earlier age could have imagined: money you can carry in your head.

Nearly every wallet today turns its secret into a seed phrase, a sequence of twelve or twenty-four common English words that can be written on paper and locked away, and from which every key in the wallet can be rebuilt. The words all come from one fixed dictionary of exactly 2,048 English words, used alike by hardware makers such as Ledger and Trezor and by countless phone wallets, so a backup made by one wallet can be read by any other.

That makes a strange journey possible. Cross a border with no wallet, no paper and no phone, only the words in your memory, and customs officers can find nothing at all, because no search can read what is inside your head. Yet on the far side, any internet-connected computer can rebuild the wallet from those words, and the coins can move again.

The law has had to catch up. Police can seize a phrase written on paper, but when it exists only in memory, American defense lawyers argue that the state cannot force a person to say it aloud, and they cite the Fifth Amendment, which shields every person from being forced to bear witness against himself. Courts have split over phone and laptop passwords. Some judges refuse to compel a suspect to unlock a device; others order it under the foregone-conclusion doctrine, which holds that when the state already knows the material exists, where it is and that it is genuine, unlocking it reveals nothing new.

Because the standard was published free, for anyone to use without permission or fees, so many wallet makers adopted it that a user can move his funds between wallet brands without ever losing access. So if the company behind a hardware wallet shuts down for good, its owners need not panic. They simply restore their phrase into any other wallet that follows the same open standard, since no company's server ever held their coins.

Every earlier money sat somewhere physical, whether as metal in a pouch or a strongroom or as a number in a banker's books. A memorized phrase lets savings live inside the owner's own memory, with no physical or digital trace anywhere outside his head. That answers a specific threat. Gold sets off scanners, cash draws currency-sniffing dogs, and a bank balance can be frozen from a distant office, but a memorized phrase offers none of them a target: it blocks seizure by physical search, by currency detection and by remote freezing of accounts.

brics-and-the-dollar-alternative-movemen.context_blurb:
In 2001 Jim O'Neill, a British economist at the bank Goldman Sachs, coined a catchy label for four big emerging economies: Brazil, Russia, India and China, the BRICs. What began as an investment idea became a political bloc that now talks openly of trading without the US dollar. Austrian economists read its rise less as a story about rivals than as a story about the choices of the dollar's own issuer.

O'Neill picked the four because they had huge populations and plenty of room to catch up with richer countries, so their economies looked set to grow fast for twenty years. In 2009 the four began meeting as a formal group, and when South Africa joined in 2010 the forum became BRICS, a rival club to the older G7. On January 1, 2024, the bloc took in Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. Its members want trade channels of their own for a plain reason: they fear the United States could freeze their dollar reserves if it disagrees with them.

The fear had a precedent. When Russian troops crossed into Ukraine at the end of February 2022, Washington, the European Union, Britain and Japan froze roughly 300 billion dollars of Russian central-bank reserves held in Western banks, the largest such action in modern history, and every reserve holder outside the West took note. Russia and China moved fast. Their trade with each other now settles overwhelmingly in rubles and yuan, over 90 percent by Chinese customs figures, up from a small fraction before 2022, and India began paying for Russian oil in rupees and UAE dirhams.

The dollar's grip is loosening only slowly. Its share of central banks' reserves fell from 71 percent in 2000 to about 58 percent by 2024, yet no rival has caught up, and nearly nine in ten currency trades still involve a dollar. Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, France's finance minister in the 1960s, coined the famous name for that special position: the exorbitant privilege, the advantage of a country that can pay its bills in money it issues itself.

Debt is the other half of the story. The federal government of the United States now owes more than 34 trillion dollars, about as much as everything the nation produces in a year or more. Ludwig von Mises warned where such a road can end. When a government that cannot tax enough to carry its debts inflates instead, people at last see that the inflation will never stop and stampede out of money into real goods until the currency collapses; Mises called that final stage the crack-up boom. Central bankers have answered with the one neutral reserve that no government controls. Their gold purchases hit a fifty-five-year high of about 1,082 tonnes in 2022 and stayed above 1,000 tonnes in each of the next two years.

Analysts in the Austrian camp, among them Luke Gromen, Lyn Alden and Saifedean Ammous, read the gold buying and the debt together: a slow shift toward neutral assets is under way, but the dollar is not about to be replaced. Historians of fallen trading currencies, from the Venetian ducat and the Spanish dollar to the Dutch guilder and the British pound, see a pattern. Rivals lurk for decades, and what finally tips the balance is the issuing country's own conduct, overspending or seizing other nations' savings. In that reading, the BRICS story is less about the yuan or the rupee than about the choices Washington made.

buchanans-constitutional-political-econo.context_blurb:
James Buchanan, who won a Nobel for founding public choice, made one move that set his work apart: he split political argument into two levels. At the lower level, people fight over particular outcomes under the rules that already exist. At the higher level, they choose the rules themselves, and Buchanan believed most policy debates go wrong by mixing the two.

Picture children quarreling every recess over who gets the ball, when they could settle once and for all the rule for who gets it each day. Buchanan built a whole field on that second kind of choice and called it constitutional political economy, which examines the rulebook itself rather than each decision made under it. Haggling over whether a tax should be 20 or 25 percent makes each new law a fresh brawl that draws lobbyists and favor-seekers every time. Buchanan wanted the argument lifted one step, to the rules that govern how policy gets made, such as whether any tax increase should need a supermajority, because a rule binds majority and minority alike in a way no single policy fight can.

In 1985, the year before his Nobel, Buchanan and the Australian philosopher-economist Geoffrey Brennan published The Reason of Rules, the standard modern statement of why firm rules, rather than officials' goodwill, must bind government. Its key device asks people to pick the political rulebook as if they had no idea whether fortune would make them wealthy or poor, mighty or humble, so that the rules stay fair to whoever lands where. Buchanan and Brennan called this the veil of uncertainty, a cousin of John Rawls's veil of ignorance. The same book explained why a fixed rule, like a posted speed limit, beats letting officials judge case by case: fixed rules limit favoritism and let ordinary citizens plan their lives ahead, while wide discretion invites the abuse of power.

In 1977 Buchanan and Richard Wagner published Democracy in Deficit: The Political Legacy of Lord Keynes. They argued that for well over a century an unwritten constitutional norm of balanced budgets had disciplined American politicians. Once Keynes's teaching licensed deliberate deficit spending, that norm dissolved and deficits ratcheted upward ever after. For Buchanan the trouble was never this or that deficit; it was the loss of the rule that had restrained everyone.

The whole tradition grew from a 1962 book by Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, The Calculus of Consent, the founding text of public choice. It brought the economist's way of reasoning to bear on how constitutions are built, and it showed why bare majority rule cannot by itself protect a minority.

The move is easiest to see on a playground. Before the kickball teams are chosen, the whole class settles how score will be kept; once the teams exist, each side knows which rules help it. Judging a rule from the moment before you know your team moves the argument from picking winners to picking fair rules: from asking whether a policy is good to asking whether we would have agreed to the rules that produced it.

cash-for-clunkers-2009-690-000-used-cars.context_blurb:
In the summer of 2009, with new-car sales crushed by the financial crisis, Washington launched a scheme officially named the Car Allowance Rebate System. Buyers who traded in a running older car got a rebate toward a new, more fuel-efficient one, and the old car was destroyed. To economists in Bastiat's tradition it is a modern worked example of his oldest parable.

President Barack Obama signed the program into law in June 2009, with rebates of $3,500 to $4,500. So that no trade-in could ever be resold, the rules spelled out its fate: the dealer poured sodium silicate, a kind of liquid glass, into the oil to seize the engine, and then the car was crushed. Everyone knew the program by its catchy nickname, Cash for Clunkers, and it burned through its $3 billion in about two months.

The program matches the most famous parable in Bastiat's 1850 essay, the broken window: destroying a usable good does not create wealth, however busy the glazier's shop, or the car dealer's, may look. Some 690,000 running cars were destroyed, most of them in the cheap price range where low-income families and students shop. As Austrian economists predicted, the price of used cars climbed roughly 10 percent in the following year, according to the Manheim index of used-vehicle values.

In 2013 Ted Gayer and Emily Parker of the Brookings Institution found that most of the program's new-car sales were purchases buyers would have made in the next six to nine months regardless. People had just bought sooner to catch the rebate, an effect the two economists called pulled-forward sales. They also found no lasting gain in jobs, and carbon savings that cost far more per ton than official estimates of the harm carbon does. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, part of the Department of Transportation, wrote the program's rules and certified each car's destruction.

The seen benefit was obvious: a new car in a buyer's driveway. The unseen victims, critics from the Austrian and Chicago schools pointed out, were poor households who buy in the used-car market, which the destruction had thinned out, since they now found fewer cheap running cars, at higher prices.

Critics found the whole argument laid out long before, in 1946, by Henry Hazlitt, a financial journalist who wrote for the New York Times and later Newsweek, whose book Economics in One Lesson applied Bastiat's seen and unseen to make-work projects. Beyond the wrecked cars and the priced-out buyers lay a larger loss. Every one of those $3 billion had to come from a taxpayer or a lender, and the alternative goods and jobs that money could have supported, had it stayed with them, are the program's biggest unseen cost.

coase-1937-the-nature-of-the-firm.context_blurb:
In 1937 Ronald Coase, a twenty-six-year-old British economist at the London School of Economics, asked a question most of his profession had never thought to ask. If prices coordinate markets so well, why does so much economic life happen inside companies, where managers give orders instead? His answer launched a whole field and, more than half a century later, won him the 1991 Nobel prize.

He published the paper in the journal Economica under a plain title, The Nature of the Firm. The idea had begun years earlier on a traveling scholarship in 1931 and 1932, when Coase, still an undergraduate, toured America's great integrated companies to learn why so many tasks were handled within single firms. In Detroit he visited Ford, the giant carmaker of the day.

His answer was that using the market is not free. Finding partners, haggling, writing contracts and checking the work all cost time and money, so a carmaker keeps salaried workers rather than hiring someone new for each bolt tightened or letter typed: using the market for every tiny task carries its own hidden costs. The same costs set a company's size. A firm keeps bringing jobs in-house, such as cleaning, accounting or deliveries, until doing one more inside costs the same as buying it from an outsider, and there it stops growing.

Economists later built a whole subfield on that insight and named it after the quantity at its center: transaction cost economics. Oliver Williamson extended it into a study of markets and hierarchies and shared the 2009 Nobel. The burdens themselves, finding the right supplier, signing a contract, watching the work and going to court when things go wrong, are what economists call transaction costs.

Coase's idea also explains how industries change. When shipping and the internet made dealing with outside firms far cheaper, the boundary of the firm moved. Apple, which once built much of its own hardware, now designs chips in California and has contract factories in Asia build them, part of a broad shift away from vertical integration toward outsourced supply chains. His Nobel citation named two papers: the 1937 paper on the firm and a 1960 paper on social cost, which changed the economics of smoke, noise and neighborly quarrels by focusing on externalities and property rights.

For any deal, say a carmaker buying steel, Coase's framework asks one comparative question: why does this exchange happen inside a company instead of across a market? The answer always lies in the relative transaction costs of the two arrangements. Coase earned his commerce degree at the London School of Economics in 1932, and he credited his teachers there, especially Arnold Plant, who taught him to distrust the planning schemes then in vogue among British intellectuals.

corporate-income-tax-who-actually-pays.context_blurb:
Politicians like to talk about making corporations pay their fair share. Economists in the classical and Austrian traditions answer with a basic lesson about any tax: whoever writes the check to the government is often not the one whose income actually shrinks. The American corporate income tax is the clearest test of that lesson.

Congress's 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act lowered the federal rate on corporate profits from 35 percent to 21 percent, where it stands today. Milton Friedman liked to point out that a corporation is a legal fiction, not a human being, and so it cannot truly pay a tax at all. Every dollar of corporate tax comes out of the pockets of real people: workers, customers, or the company's owners.

Economists call the party the law names as payer the legal, or statutory, incidence of a tax. Once prices, wages and returns adjust, the party whose income really falls may be someone else, and that real-world burden is called the economic incidence. Applied to the corporate tax, Bastiat's question has a striking answer: much of the burden lands, unnoticed, on workers, through lower wages.

The reason is an asymmetry between the two great inputs of production. Capital is more mobile across borders than labor: money can leave a high-tax country, or demand a higher return to stay, while most workers cannot move abroad, so the burden slides onto the people who cannot leave. The standard modern study appeared in 2016 in the American Economic Review, where Juan Carlos Suárez Serrato and Owen Zidar used data on local job markets across the states to measure who really bears state corporate taxes.

Part of the burden does fall on the owners of capital, but those owners are not only the rich. Pension funds holding the retirement savings of teachers, firefighters and other public employees own enormous amounts of American stock, so the share that lands on capital hits ordinary retirement accounts too. The political trick, in this reading, is that corporate-tax talk names a legal payer the public is happy to punish while hiding the real people who carry the cost.

david-chaum-s-digicash-and-the-microsoft.context_blurb:
David Chaum, an American cryptographer, dreamed of digital money as private as cash in a pocket. In 1989 he founded DigiCash in Amsterdam to build it, and for a few years the world's biggest technology companies came calling. Its collapse in 1998 taught the cypherpunks the lesson that later shaped Bitcoin.

The foundation was a trick Chaum invented in 1982, the blind signature. A bank could certify a digital coin while, in effect, blindfolded, never seeing the particular coin it approved, so that when the coin was later spent at a shop nobody could trace it back to the person who had withdrawn it. His aim was to protect the buyer's privacy. Chaum expected banks and merchants to rush in. Instead the banks dragged their feet, few merchants signed up, and customers never came in numbers, because for most people paper money and credit cards already did the job well enough.

DigiCash's system used those blind signatures to let the bank confirm that a coin was genuine and had not been spent twice, without ever learning who had received it. The cypherpunks, though, saw one deep flaw, which they spent the next decade trying to remove: the system still required a trusted bank to issue and back the coins, and without a partner bank there were no coins at all.

In the mid-1990s Microsoft, racing to launch Windows 95, reportedly offered Chaum a nine-figure sum, widely cited as $100 million or $180 million, to build DigiCash into the new system. The big software firms wanted the technology because private digital payments promised to let their customers shop online with no bank standing between buyer and seller. Two other giants made offers too, Netscape, whose browser then ruled the young web, and the credit-card network Visa, and Chaum turned them both down.

DigiCash filed for bankruptcy in November 1998. That same month the cypherpunk Wei Dai sketched a form of digital money with no bank behind it, in which a network of computers jointly kept the books, and he called it b-money. Wei Dai, Nick Szabo and, a decade on, Satoshi Nakamoto all drew the same moral: even brilliant anonymous cryptography fails as money if the system still needs a central issuer who can be bought, bankrupted or shut down.

When Satoshi published the Bitcoin paper in 2008, he did not merely improve on DigiCash; he removed the piece that had killed it. Bitcoin keeps signatures and units of value but has no trusted issuer whose bankruptcy could freeze the currency, since new coins come from proof-of-work and a distributed network checks every transaction. Bitcoin historians press one more lesson. Chaum's refusals of Microsoft, Netscape and Visa were ordinary business choices, yet they doomed his whole system, because the operator of any trusted issuer, however brilliant, can sink an entire project through everyday business decisions.

deirdre-mccloskey-the-bourgeois-trilogy.context_blurb:
Deirdre McCloskey, a Chicago-trained historian of the economy, spent her teaching career at universities in Iowa and Illinois. Between 2006 and 2016 she published three books, the Bourgeois Trilogy, asking why ordinary people in one corner of the world suddenly grew rich after 1800. Her answer was not machines or money but words: how people talked about those who buy, sell and invent.

For most of history nearly every family was poor and often hungry. Then, from around 1800, first in northwestern Europe and later in America, incomes began climbing year after year, until a typical Western household was some thirty times richer than its forebears. McCloskey calls that leap the Great Enrichment. Her explanation centers on a change of attitude. In 1700 a European of standing would sneer at anyone in trade; by 1800 ordinary opinion had swung toward respect for shopkeepers, inventors and traders.

The middle volume, Bourgeois Dignity, published in 2010, carries a defiant subtitle, Why Economics Can't Explain the Modern World, because the usual inputs of capital, geography and institutions fail to explain when and where the enrichment happened. The final volume, Bourgeois Equality, published in 2016, puts her thesis right on its cover: How Ideas, Not Capital or Institutions, Enriched the World.

The shift she points to took place between about 1600 and 1800, above all in Holland and England, when merchants and inventors, long despised by nobles and churchmen, began to win moral respect, and millions of ordinary people started trying to invent things. Her one-word name for the missing ingredient is dignity: treating ordinary business people with real respect, so that innovation and trade were honored in everyday talk. Her story does not discard secure property, enforceable contracts or honest courts. In McCloskey's view the new respect for innovators works alongside good institutions instead of displacing them; she adds a missing ingredient to the list and removes none of the others.

Her interest in words began much earlier. In 1985 she published The Rhetoric of Economics, a short book that jolted her profession by showing that economists persuade one another with metaphors, stories and appeals to authority as much as with mathematics. To sharpen her later puzzle she sets Ming-dynasty China's stagnation beside Britain's Industrial Revolution: similar people, land, technology and trade, opposite results, because the culture around the merchant differed.

McCloskey borrows Bastiat's pattern. The seen inputs are capital, institutions and geography; the unseen factor that made them productive was the cultural legitimation of merchants and inventors, without which the same inputs stagnate. The scale of the result is staggering. A typical European before 1800 got by on some three dollars a day in today's money, as his ancestors had for generations; since then the real income of each person in the first industrial countries has grown about thirtyfold, roughly 3,000 percent.

diocletians-edict-on-maximum-prices-301-.context_blurb:
Rome's emperor Diocletian, in the year 301, faced prices that kept rising across his empire. For decades Rome had funded its soldiers' pay by debasing the silver denarius, melting old coins and mixing in cheap metal to stretch the silver. Diocletian's answer was the most famous price control of the ancient world, and it failed in a pattern that has repeated ever since.

His Edict on Maximum Prices set legal ceilings on more than a thousand goods and wages, from bread, wine and olive oil to boots, wagon wheels and haircuts. A merchant who asked more faced execution under the edict's own text; the Christian writer Lactantius recorded that much blood was shed over small and cheap things. Merchants would not sell at a loss, so they stashed their stock, shut up shop or quit producing, and Roman shoppers met empty shelves and shortages.

The emperor did not blame his own mint. The edict's preamble cursed the merchants instead, for their unbridled fury and their greed, though it was the cheapened coin that had driven prices up. Across the empire the result came fast: goods vanished from the public market, held back, sold only to family, or carried off to black markets in other cities.

Lactantius, a Christian who had suffered through the emperor's persecution, described the outcome in his account of how the persecuting emperors died. The edict was quietly allowed to lapse within about a decade, and Diocletian himself abdicated in 305, the only Roman emperor to step down of his own will. Bastiat's method reads the episode in two parts. The seen is the cheap official price cut into stone in the market square. The unseen is the seller who would rather hoard than sell at a loss, and the buyer who goes hungry as a result.

We know the edict so well because fragments of its stone tablets survive across the eastern Mediterranean, and the most complete copy is at Aphrodisias in southwestern Turkey, from which archaeologists have rebuilt hundreds of price lines. Murray Rothbard and Thomas Sowell treat it as the founding case of an error governments keep repeating: they blame merchants for price rises that the government's own debasement of the currency caused. The pattern recurs from Rome to Nixon's Washington and Maduro's Caracas, as rulers debase the money, blame the sellers, impose a ceiling and watch the goods disappear. The record from Lactantius and the inscriptions is plain: what followed the edict was vanishing goods and spreading shortage, until the law was abandoned.

economic-harmonies-bastiats-positive-the.context_blurb:
Frédéric Bastiat is best known for his sharp critical essays, but Economic Harmonies was his one attempt at a complete positive theory of how a free economy holds together. He was still writing and revising it in Rome when tuberculosis killed him on Christmas Eve 1850. Its argument set him against the most powerful idea of the socialists of his century.

Karl Marx would soon teach that workers and owners are class enemies locked in a fight that only one side can win. Bastiat looked at the same world of markets and drew the opposite conclusion: in a free society, people's interests are naturally in harmony rather than at war, because when exchange is voluntary one party's gain does not require another's loss.

His most famous passage on value imagines a pair of equally useful diamonds, one stumbled upon in a stream bed, the other hacked out of a mine through years of toil. Buyers want both equally, and Bastiat concluded that both have the same value, because value comes from the service a good renders to its user, not from the labor spent producing it. That idea runs straight to Friedrich Hayek, who argued in 1945 that prices work like a silent messaging system: each price tells buyers and sellers something no single planner could know, so millions of strangers coordinate without anyone giving orders.

For centuries economists had held that a thing's price came from the labor put into it. In 1871 Carl Menger and William Stanley Jevons, working independently, proposed instead that a good's worth depends on how badly someone wants one more of it, an idea called subjective value, which depends on the person rather than on the labor spent. Bastiat's diamonds had hinted at it a generation earlier. He began the book in Paris near the end of the 1840s and raced the disease to finish it, but at his death only ten chapters were complete; his friend Prosper Paillottet assembled the drafts and fragments of the rest into an expanded edition in 1851.

Bastiat's method runs through the book. Imagine a farmer's barn burns down and a neighbor cheers the work it creates for carpenters. The carpenters' wages are what everyone notices, while the plow the farmer had been saving for, now never bought and never built, goes unnoticed. Bastiat called this habit of mind looking at what is seen and what is unseen.

enver-hoxhas-albania-and-the-173-000-bun.context_blurb:
Albania is a small, mountainous country in the Balkans. For four decades one man, Enver Hoxha, ruled it as the most isolated state in Europe. Its fields and beaches are still dotted with little concrete domes, the leftovers of his fear of invasion, and they make a sharp lesson in what that fear cost the people who paid for them.

Hoxha took power in 1944 and held it until he died in 1985. Under him the state took nearly everything. Farm families were driven onto huge collective farms, private business was outlawed, food often ran short, and the borders were sealed. That system, in which a single ruling party owns and plans the whole economy, is communism.

Hoxha trusted no one, not even his fellow communists. He broke with Yugoslavia in 1948, siding with Stalin against Tito; with the Soviet Union in 1961, siding with Mao against Khrushchev; and with China in 1978, as Deng Xiaoping's reforms began. Each break left Albania more alone.

In 1967 the regime closed all the country's mosques, churches and monasteries, turned many into warehouses and gyms, arrested the clergy and banned even private prayer at home. No government anywhere had declared itself officially atheist before; Albania was the first.

The secret police, the Sigurimi, kept files on almost every family and paid informers to report on their neighbors, so a joke about Hoxha could cost years in prison. Such watching has one purpose. It makes people afraid to speak, and people who are afraid to speak cannot find one another, so no group can ever organize against the state.

Hoxha was convinced that an invasion could come any day. From the late 1960s into the 1980s his regime poured concrete into about 173,000 small pillbox bunkers on beaches, hilltops and farmland, in a country of only some 2.8 million people. That works out to roughly one bunker for every sixteen Albanians.

When the regime finally fell in the early 1990s, researchers opened the secret-police archives and camp records. Even with those papers, an honest death count is hard to reach, because regimes like Hoxha's hide deaths, record prisoners under false labels and burn their files before they lose power. Scholars still count thousands executed for political crimes and tens of thousands sent to labor camps.

In December 1990 Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, decided not to shoot the students protesting in the streets, and in March 1991 Albanians voted in their first multi-party election. Once the frontier opened, ordinary Albanians could finally see what it had hidden from them: how far their planned economy had fallen behind the free-market countries next door. Albania ended the communist era with the lowest income per person in Europe.

The French economist Frederic Bastiat taught that every choice has a cost you cannot see. A Bastiat-minded economist looks at the bunkers and asks what is missing beside them. Every ton of cement and every hour of labor that went into a bunker was a ton and an hour that never became a house, a school or a factory; economists call that lost alternative the opportunity cost. The invasion never came, but the houses were never built either.

ex-im-bank-and-boeing-the-concentrated-f.context_blurb:
In 1934, with the Great Depression at its worst, Franklin Roosevelt set up a federal lender by executive order: the Export-Import Bank of the United States (Ex-Im Bank). Its task was to use taxpayer-backed credit to help foreign customers buy American products, and it became one of the clearest cases of how a small, organized interest can keep a federal program alive.

Over the decades one customer came to dominate. One think tank reviewed the bank's lending over the years 2007 to 2013 and found that roughly two-fifths of its help went to the sales of a single company: Boeing, whose foreign airline customers bought jets with Ex-Im-backed financing. Critics nicknamed the agency the Boeing Bank, a textbook example of corporate welfare.

In June 2015 FreedomWorks, the Heritage Foundation and the Club for Growth beat Boeing and the bank's other big corporate allies in Congress. Lawmakers refused to renew the bank's charter, so it lapsed for about five months, and from July until December 2015 it could not sign new deals.

Boeing had warned that American exports would collapse without the bank. The bank's critics found no measurable fall in exports during the lapse, because Boeing kept selling airliners using ordinary commercial bank loans, which cost a little more than Ex-Im's guarantees but not enough to stop the deals.

In December 2015 Congress brought the bank back by folding its renewal into a big highway bill, the FAST Act. Few lawmakers wanted to vote against road money for their districts, so voting against Ex-Im suddenly became expensive; public-choice economists call this kind of bundling and vote-trading logrolling.

Why does the bank keep surviving? Mancur Olson's 'The Logic of Collective Action', published in 1965, explains the pattern. When a program hands large benefits to a few firms and spreads its cost thinly across millions of taxpayers, the few organize and lobby hard while the many barely notice. Boeing spends millions of dollars a year lobbying, but no single taxpayer spends a weekend fighting over his few cents' share.

fee-and-the-american-rediscovery-leonard.context_blurb:
In March 1946 the American businessman Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education, known as FEE, in Irvington-on-Hudson, New York. It was the first postwar American institution devoted to teaching free-market economics to ordinary readers, and it became the bridge that carried the old European classical-liberal tradition to a new American audience.

That same year Henry Hazlitt, a journalist who sat on FEE's founding board, published Economics in One Lesson. Hazlitt reduced economics to a single rule taken from Frederic Bastiat: in judging any policy, look at both its seen and its unseen effects.

Bastiat's best-known illustration of that rule comes from his 1850 essay on the seen and the unseen. A boy hurls a rock through a shopkeeper's window, and the neighbors comfort themselves that at least the glazier will get work. Bastiat showed what they missed: the money the shopkeeper must now spend on glass can no longer buy the new shoes he had planned on, so the shoemaker's lost sale is the hidden cost.

FEE helped make Bastiat an American author. In 1950 it published Dean Russell's English translation of The Law, the short book Bastiat finished months before he died in 1850. Bastiat argued that when a government seizes property from some citizens to hand it to others, the law itself becomes legal plunder. The law's true job, he said, is to protect every person's life, liberty and honestly earned property.

In 1958 Read wrote FEE's most famous essay, I, Pencil, narrated by an ordinary yellow pencil. Its cedar is logged in Oregon, its graphite is mined far away, its eraser comes from rubber trees and its metal band from brass, and the pencil boasts that no one anywhere could make it alone. Read's point was that a free market coordinates millions of strangers with no central planner directing them. If no one can plan a pencil, no single mind could ever plan a whole economy. Prices carry the signals, so the logger, the miner and the factory hand each respond to what things cost, and millions cooperate without anyone in charge; Milton Friedman later built a segment of his television series Free to Choose around the pencil.

Why build an institution rather than run campaigns? In his 1949 essay The Intellectuals and Socialism, Friedrich Hayek argued that a country's direction is set less by elections than by the ideas that schoolteachers, reporters and authors absorb and pass on, because politicians eventually follow them. Think tanks, magazines and reading programs for students, FEE's among them, aim at something campaigns cannot reach: they work, slowly, on what the public treats as common sense about economics.

friedman-1970-business-responsibility-is.context_blurb:
By 1970 American companies were being urged to take on causes beyond making money: cleaner air, better neighborhoods, social programs. Milton Friedman, the University of Chicago economist, answered with an essay people still argue over more than fifty years later. His question was simple: whose money is a company's boss spending, and on whose behalf?

The essay ran in the Sunday magazine of the New York Times on September 13, 1970, and its title said it outright: the social responsibility of business, Friedman wrote, is to increase its profits. Admirers and critics alike now call the argument the Friedman Doctrine.

It was not a new idea for him. The essay condensed and sharpened a chapter of Capitalism and Freedom, his 1962 book arguing at length for open markets and a small state.

Friedman began with a plain fact about who works for whom. A corporate executive is an employee of the shareholders, the owners of the firm, and their interests define his job: to run the business so it makes as much money as possible for them.

The chase for profit had limits, though. The executive must keep to the basic rules of society, Friedman wrote, both those written into law and those carried in ethical custom, so he was defending honest business, not fraud.

Then Friedman drew his sharpest line. An executive's own salary is his to give away, so he may donate it to whatever cause he likes. The company's money is different, because it belongs to the owners. An executive who spends the firm's funds on some cause its owners never approved is, in Friedman's words, spending someone else's money, like a self-appointed tax collector who charges the owners and then decides how the money gets spent.

Friedman also saw a problem of accountability, and later economists sharpened it. If managers are told to serve employees, neighbors, nature and owners together, nobody can hold them to account: with so many masters they answer to none, and any decision can be defended by pointing to whichever group it helped. One clear owner to serve is what keeps managers honest.

Friedman's essay remains the chief intellectual answer to ESG investing, the push for companies to steer profits toward environmental and social goals. In Friedman's terms, that is charity with someone else's money, handed out by executives whom no shareholder authorized to give it.

The rival view gathered strength. The Business Roundtable, a Washington group of top American chief executives, issued in August 2019 a statement on what a corporation is for that broke openly with Friedman's rule, and 181 CEOs signed it.

Business-school professors pressed the same case: Michael Porter of Harvard with his idea of "shared value," Colin Mayer of Oxford on what firms are for, and Rebecca Henderson of Harvard in her book Reimagining Capitalism. All three argue that the shareholder-only rule misses how companies create value over the long run, by caring for workers, communities and the environment. Friedman's side replies that shareholders are free to choose such goals themselves; what lacks a mandate is an executive imposing them.
