friedrich-von-wieser--who-he-was---oppor.context_blurb:
Friedrich von Wieser helped found the Austrian school of economics and became the bridge between its founder, Carl Menger, and the generation of Mises, Hayek and Schumpeter. He gave economics two of its most-used terms. Born in Vienna in 1851 as plain Friedrich Wieser, he died in 1926 a baron, a former cabinet minister and a member of the empire's upper house.

His closest colleague was family: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk, who had studied beside him, married Wieser's sister Paula. Wieser spent almost twenty years, from 1884 to 1903, teaching at the German-language university in Prague, where most people spoke Czech. In 1903 he came home to take over Menger's chair at the University of Vienna.

His first famous word came in 1884. When you drink one canteen of water after another, each brings you less benefit than the one before, and what drives price is the usefulness of the final unit you add. Wieser called that usefulness Grenznutzen, which in English is marginal utility; it is why a thirsty traveler in the desert pays a fortune for the first canteen and almost nothing for the tenth.

His second word names the true price of any choice. An hour at the movies is an hour you cannot spend earning money at a job, so whatever you pass over, the most valuable option you did not take, is what the choice really costs you. Wieser's German word for it was Alternativkosten, and its English form, opportunity cost, now appears in every economics textbook. A farmer who sows wheat on a field pays, in truth, with the barley he could have grown there instead.

Behind both words lay the Austrian discovery that value lives in people, not in things. Older economists said a good's worth came from the labor or the materials inside it. Wieser and Menger answered that a thing is worth however much a particular person wants it at that moment, and Wieser set out this subjective theory of value in his readable 1889 book Natural Value. Two collectors may offer fifty dollars and two dollars for the same baseball card, because value is not a fixed number but depends on each person's wants.

He also turned the labor theory upside down with his theory of imputation. The value of a train wheel does not begin with the hours of work and the coal that went into it. It begins with what the customer will use the finished product for, a working train, and is then credited back down the chain to the steel, the ore and the workers.

In 1917, halfway through the First World War, Emperor Karl I made Wieser his minister of commerce, in charge of the empire's trade, business and industry, a post he kept until the empire collapsed in November 1918. That same year the emperor raised him to the nobility, so Friedrich Wieser became Friedrich von Wieser, a baron, and gave him a seat in the imperial parliament's upper chamber, the House of Lords.

Wieser's students carried the school forward. One was the young Friedrich Hayek, who attended his Vienna seminars in the early 1920s. In a famous 1945 essay Hayek argued that planners can never collect the countless local details of who needs what, where and at what price, details that ordinary people and market prices carry through an economy, a limit now called the knowledge problem.

Another student, Joseph Schumpeter, watched cars replace buggies and electric bulbs replace gaslight. He argued that this constant replacement of old products and firms by new ones is the market's most important trait, and he called it creative destruction.

gottfried-haberler-prosperity-and-depres.context_blurb:
Gottfried Haberler (1900-1995) grew up in the Vienna of the Austrian school and spent most of his career at Harvard. He wrote the book a whole generation used to understand why economies boom and bust, and he carried Austrian ideas into the American mainstream, at a price some of his teachers resented.

He trained at the University of Vienna in the 1920s, and his two doctoral advisors were Friedrich von Wieser, of the generation after Carl Menger, and Wieser's younger colleague Ludwig von Mises. He also joined Mises's private seminar.

His early fame came from trade. David Ricardo had explained comparative advantage in 1817, the idea that each nation does best by specializing where its edge over others is largest, but Ricardo measured costs in hours of labor. In his 1933 book on international trade, Haberler restated comparative advantage in terms of opportunity cost, what a country gives up by making one good instead of another, a version Austrians could accept and the one trade textbooks teach today.

In 1936 Haberler moved to the United States, one of many Austrian-trained economists, among them Mises, Hayek and Fritz Machlup, who left Central Europe in the years when dictators took it over. What most of them brought with them was a belief in free markets and a deep skepticism of central planning.

Every economy rises through good years, crashes into a slump where factories close and jobs vanish, and then climbs back again; economists call that repeating rise and fall the business cycle. In 1937 the League of Nations, based in Geneva, commissioned Haberler to survey every serious theory of it. The result was Prosperity and Depression, whose title pairs the top of the cycle with its bottom, and it became the standard reference for a generation.

Strict Austrians, Mises among them, were unhappy with the survey. Haberler treated the Austrian theory as just one theory among several, all equally worth surveying, instead of presenting it as the correct account, and they saw that even-handedness as a first step toward compromise with mainstream economics.

Haberler also belonged to the Mont Pelerin Society, which Hayek founded in April 1947 at a meeting in the Swiss Alps above Lake Geneva, gathering defenders of classical liberalism such as Mises, Machlup and the young Milton Friedman.

After retiring from Harvard in 1971 he moved to Washington and joined the American Enterprise Institute, where he went on attacking inflation, protectionism and government controls on wages and prices until near his death.

hal-finneys-reusable-proofs-of-work-2004.context_blurb:
Bitcoin did not appear out of nowhere. For fifteen years before it, a loose band of programmers called cypherpunks tried to build digital cash, and each attempt got a little closer. One of the most important steps came in 2004 from the California programmer Hal Finney.

The story starts with the British computer scientist Adam Back. In 1997 he built Hashcash, which made anyone sending an email first solve a small math puzzle and attach the answer as a proof-of-work stamp, so that a spammer blasting millions of messages would be slowed down. But a Hashcash stamp could be used only once and could not be handed on to someone else the way a coin can.

In 2004 Finney took the idea further. His system turned each proof-of-work stamp into a token that could change hands again and again, and he named it Reusable Proofs of Work (RPOW).

Passing tokens around raised the hardest problem in digital cash: what stops someone from copying a token and spending it twice? Finney's answer was a trusted server that kept track of which stamps had already been spent and issued fresh ones to replace them. He ran it on an IBM 4758, a tamper-resistant chip, so users could check that the server was running honest, audited code.

The famous earlier attempt, DigiCash, built by the American cryptographer David Chaum in the 1990s, also routed payments through one trusted central server. Special hardware could not cure the deeper weakness both systems shared: dependence on one server that a government could switch off or an insider could corrupt.

Bitcoin took a different road to trust. Instead of special hardware, it trusts a public network of computers that all check one another's work.

Satoshi Nakamoto's 2008 white paper solved the double-spending problem without any central server. Its invention was a public ledger that many strangers keep in step using proof-of-work, so no single party can freeze the money or rewrite the record.

Satoshi launched Bitcoin on January 3, 2009. On January 12 he sent the first person-to-person transfer to Finney, recorded in block 170: ten bitcoin, written 10 BTC.

helicopter-ben-bernankes-2002-deflation-.context_blurb:
In November 2002 Ben Bernanke, then a governor of the Federal Reserve and later its chairman, gave a speech about a danger most Americans had never worried about: prices that fall instead of rise. The speech earned him a nickname for life, and six years later it read like a script for what the Fed actually did in the 2008 crisis.

Deflation means prices drop over time, so a dollar buys more next year than today. That sounds pleasant, but it can wreck jobs: people put off purchases hoping prices will fall further, sales dry up, and businesses lay off workers.

Bernanke's speech rested on one bold claim. A central bank issuing fiat money, paper backed by nothing, can always create more of it at essentially zero cost, so it can always push prices up if it truly wants to. Markets heard reassurance; Austrian economists heard a warning that nothing but political will stands in the way of printing.

To make the point vivid, he borrowed an image Milton Friedman had used: a helicopter dropping money over a town, the simplest picture of new money flowing straight into people's hands. Friedman had painted it in his 1969 essay The Optimum Quantity of Money as a thought experiment, not a policy. The press dubbed Bernanke "Helicopter Ben," and the name stuck.

Next came a menu of tools for a Fed that has already cut short-term rates to zero. At the head of the list was buying long-term Treasury bonds to push long-term interest rates down. In an extreme case, Bernanke added, a central bank could even pay for direct tax cuts by printing money. Austrian critics called that monetary financing of fiscal policy, the central bank simply creating new money to fund the government.

Austrian-minded critics attacked the speech as a road map to eventually debasing the dollar. The trio usually named is Bob Murphy of the Mises Institute, the investor and broadcaster Peter Schiff, and the commodities investor Jim Rogers.

Six years later, in November 2008, Bernanke, by then the Fed's chairman, launched the first program to buy mortgage-backed securities and long-term government debt on a vast scale, adding hundreds of billions to the Fed's holdings. It became known as QE1, for quantitative easing.

Its sequels followed. Between 2008 and 2014 the Fed carried out nearly everything the 2002 speech had previewed, chiefly through QE1, QE2, and Operation Twist, followed by a third round of buying.

Austrian and public-choice economists draw a lesson from the whole episode. When central bankers describe in public what they could do in a hypothetical crisis, they are often previewing exactly what they will do in a real one.

inflation-is-always-and-everywhere-a-mon.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman, the Nobel-winning Chicago economist, repeated one sentence for three decades: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. Behind those words lay a claim about cause and a century of evidence, and they won a long argument over why prices rise.

The picture is simple. Suppose a government doubles the money it hands out while the country produces exactly as much as before. Shopkeepers find extra dollars competing for an unchanged pile of goods, so they mark prices up: the cause is too much money for too few things to buy. Friedman's point was that a lasting general rise in prices comes from money, not from wages, weather or supply troubles. In his famous line, inflation is a monetary phenomenon.

He offered it as a tested finding, not a mere slogan. With Anna Schwartz he spent nearly ten years assembling American money and price figures reaching back to 1867, and in 1963 they published the results as A Monetary History. Friedman rested his claim on that century of money-supply-and-inflation data.

The book's most famous chapter, The Great Contraction, turned to the Great Depression. From 1929 to 1933 the quantity of money in America fell by about a third, and Friedman and Schwartz argued that this sudden collapse of the money supply is what made the Depression so deep. The lesson cuts both ways: when the money supply shrinks fast, businesses fail and jobs vanish along with it.

In a famous lecture in London, titled The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory, Friedman openly challenged the ruling school of his day, Keynesian macroeconomics, which treated money as a passive bystander.

The 1970s tested him. After Nixon cut the dollar loose from gold, and with the Fed creating money fast, prices climbed year after year, yet politicians and television reporters kept pointing elsewhere: at corporate greed, at union wage demands and at the oil sheikhs of OPEC. Friedman answered that all three were effects; the cause behind them was years of monetary expansion.

The decade also brought stagflation, rising prices and rising unemployment together, which the older textbooks had said could not happen and which Friedman had predicted. By the 1980s much of the profession had come around to his side of that argument.

The Austrians agreed that inflation is monetary but parted from Friedman on the details. Friedman watched a single statistic, the growth of the total money supply. Mises, Hayek and Rothbard focused on the way fresh central-bank credit distorts the structure of investment, building booms that later bust; in short, Friedman watched the aggregate, while the Austrians studied credit-driven malinvestment.

jiaozi-and-kublai-khan-the-first-paper-m.context_blurb:
Paper money was invented in China, roughly a thousand years ago. Within a few centuries two Chinese dynasties had shown both its convenience and its great danger, and a traveler from Venice had carried the astonishing story back to Europe.

The trouble began with iron. Under the Song dynasty, merchants in the busy trading region of Sichuan paid in heavy iron coins, sometimes a cartload for one deal. So they left their coins with trusted holders and traded the paper receipts instead, and those slips grew into paper money.

In 1023 the Song government took the system over, making the notes, called jiaozi, the first paper money issued by any government. At first they held their value. But the Song state fought long wars, first against the Jin kingdom in the north and later against the Mongols, and to pay for those military campaigns it printed far more notes than its reserves could back, until the paper lost most of its worth.

The Mongols conquered China, and in the late 1200s Kublai Khan ruled it from Beijing. He issued his own paper money, the chao, backed by no gold or silver, and ordered every merchant and peasant to accept it. A ruler free to print as he pleases, and to compel everyone to accept the result, tends to print more to pay his bills, and each note buys less than the one before.

The Venetian merchant Marco Polo, who served at Kublai's court in the 1270s and 1280s, devoted a chapter of his Travels, written in 1298, to the chao. He explained that the notes were made from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, stamped in vermilion with the imperial seal. Refusing them, he reported, was punishable by death.

To a European used to coins of gold and silver, the sight was dazzling. He compared the system to alchemy: the Khan, he marveled, had the secret of turning bark into wealth.

The magic did not last. Kublai died in 1294, and the emperors after him printed chao at will to meet each new crisis, so by the 1350s the notes were worthless and the Yuan dynasty itself was collapsing.

Modern Austrian economists draw a pointed conclusion from China's two-for-two record. The very first two government paper currencies in history both ended in hyperinflation, which suggests the failure is built into the incentives of paper money rather than being a modern accident.

Bastiat's lens sharpens the story. What Polo saw was the Khan seemingly turning bark into wealth; what nobody could see was the coming collapse in prices, already written into the arrangement, that would drain the wealth of every chao holder within a generation.

julian-assanges-cypherpunk-years-and-rub.context_blurb:
Long before he founded WikiLeaks, the Australian programmer Julian Assange spent years on the cypherpunk mailing list of the 1990s, alongside Eric Hughes, Tim May and other coders who believed privacy had to be built with mathematics. His early work shows how one idea from that world, that what many copies hold no one can seize, came to matter far beyond computers.

The cypherpunks wanted tools no government could switch off, even a powerful one. If a tool is to be beyond any government's off switch, no single person or place can control it, because any single point of control is a single point of attack.

Strong mathematics has one weakness it cannot fix. Picture a diary locked with a code no computer could ever crack; a bully can still threaten you until you open it yourself. Cryptographers grimly call this rubber-hose cryptanalysis, and Bitcoin holders face it too, because the weakest link is the person who knows the key, and force applied to him can break any code.

In 1997 Assange co-wrote an encryption program for hard disks named after that threat: Rubberhose. He meant it for human-rights activists at risk of capture and torture. Its trick was to hide several encrypted volumes on one disk, so a captive could surrender one password while the others stayed invisible; an interrogator could never prove that more hidden volumes existed. Cryptographers call this plausibly deniable encryption.

The idea outlived the program. Two widely used disk-encryption tools carried the hidden-volume design forward: TrueCrypt (2004) and VeraCrypt (2013).

In 2006 Assange founded WikiLeaks, a site for publishing leaked official papers. When governments tried to force it offline, it kept coming back, because its documents were mirrored across many independent servers in many different countries.

After WikiLeaks released secret US war logs and diplomatic cables, Assange faced arrest. In 2012 he took refuge in the Ecuadorian embassy in London and was granted asylum, and he lived inside it for seven years until Ecuador revoked his asylum in 2019 and British police arrested him there. He then spent years in Belmarsh prison until a plea deal freed him in 2024.

The thread that links the 1990s mailing list to WikiLeaks, and later to Bitcoin, is distributed censorship-resistance: what many independent copies preserve, no single power can seize.

kelo-v-city-of-new-london-2005-eminent-d.context_blurb:
Susette Kelo, a nurse, loved her small pink house by the water in the Fort Trumbull neighborhood of New London, Connecticut. In 2000 the city decided her street should make way for private redevelopment, and when she refused to sell, it moved to take her home anyway. Her fight reached the Supreme Court, lost there, and then won in a different arena.

Governments have a legal power to take private land. The Fifth Amendment allows it for "public use," provided the owner receives just compensation, and the power is called eminent domain. Historically public use meant a road, a school or a military base.

New London's plan was different. The land would go to a private developer for offices, shops and housing, built to complement a large new Pfizer research center next door. The city's stated public purpose was more jobs and a bigger tax base.

Critics said that stretched public use past breaking point, because the property was being handed to another private owner rather than turned into a park or a road.

In 2005 the Supreme Court sided with the city, five votes to four, in an opinion by Justice John Paul Stevens. Justice Sandra Day O'Connor wrote the main dissent and its most quoted warning: under this ruling, she argued, nothing stops a government from swapping a cheap motel for a luxury hotel, or a family home for a mall.

The promised revival never came. Pfizer closed its New London research center within about five years, around 2009 and 2010, and the cleared land where Kelo and her neighbors had lived sat empty for more than a decade.

Public-choice economists see a familiar story. A politically connected developer captured the government's taking power and turned it against scattered homeowners, each of whom lost a great deal but who had little ability to organize. Behind any stated public reason, they say, the analyst should look for the concentrated winner and the concentrated loser: who gains a great deal, and who pays a great deal.

The homeowners did have one organized ally. Their lawyers came from the Institute for Justice, a public-interest law firm that Clint Bolick and Chip Mellor founded in 1991 and that has become the country's leading property-rights litigator.

Then came the surprise. The backlash crossed party lines, and in the ten years after the ruling roughly 45 states passed laws or constitutional amendments limiting takings for private development. Normally a concentrated interest beats a dispersed one; here the dispersed side won, because the Institute for Justice's years of lawsuits, model bills and publicity organized the scattered homeowners into a force.

law-legislation-and-liberty-1973-1979-an.context_blurb:
In his seventies, long after The Road to Serfdom had made him famous, Friedrich Hayek set out to explain what kind of order a free society actually has, and why clever lawmakers keep misunderstanding it. The result was a three-volume work, published between 1973 and 1979, whose title joins three ideas that all begin with the letter L: Law, Legislation and Liberty.

Hayek's central picture contrasts a garden with a forest. In a garden a gardener places every flower by hand; in a forest every tree finds its own place with no planner at all. Both have order, but the forest's is a grown order that nobody designed on purpose, what Hayek called kosmos, as against the made order, taxis, of the garden.

He gave such grown systems a two-word name: spontaneous order. Human language, market prices and the common law all emerge from the separate choices of multitudes, each person following his own aims and local habits, and no one plans them. The scientist Michael Polanyi had used the same phrase in 1951, and Hayek acknowledged him.

Law can grow in exactly that way. In one tradition experts write a complete code and courts apply it word for word. In the other, judges settle actual quarrels one at a time and their successors follow the precedents, so the rules accumulate over centuries. Hayek admired the second, English common law, because like the market it has no single designer and draws on a great deal of local knowledge.

The idea was old. The Scottish philosopher Adam Ferguson had observed in 1767 that many institutions come from people's actions but not from anyone's plan, a line Hayek quoted often. Language, money and law grow out of many small everyday choices, without any one person planning the whole.

The opposite mistake has a name too. Looking at a slowly grown pattern such as language, law or prices and treating it as an engine that experts could take apart and rebuild is what Hayek called constructivist rationalism, the belief that reason can build a society from nothing.

Volume 2, published in 1976 and subtitled The Mirage of Social Justice, attacked a phrase people apply to market results. Hayek argued that social justice is a category mistake: justice belongs to the deliberate acts of persons, and a market's distribution of rich and poor has no single author. A misfortune that nobody chose, he argued, may be bad luck, but it makes no sense to call it unjust.

He wrote that volume partly in answer to a book that had put social justice at the center of political philosophy five years earlier: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls, the Harvard philosopher.

Volume 3, of 1979, is his most political. Fearing that majority-rule democracies were sliding from stable general laws into day-to-day bargaining, Hayek proposed a two-chamber legislature: one chamber, its members elected for long terms, to make the general rules, and another to handle ordinary government business.

Polanyi also named a kind of knowledge that fits Hayek's argument. An experienced physician recognizes appendicitis almost at a glance yet cannot list every clue; a carpenter steadies a warped board without being able to describe each finger's movement. Polanyi called this tacit knowledge, real skill passed on by practice that no manual can fully capture, and Hayek treated it as more proof that what an economy knows cannot be gathered in one place.

ludwig-von-mises-who-he-was.context_blurb:
Ludwig von Mises, born in 1881 in Lemberg, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and today Lviv in Ukraine, became the central figure linking the Austrian school of old Vienna to its revival in America. He spent his life arguing that markets coordinate what no government could, and he paid for his views with years of exile and decades without a paid professorship.

He took his doctorate in Vienna in 1906, and his strongest influences were the school's founder and its great theorist of capital: Carl Menger and Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk.

Vienna's university never paid him a professor's salary; it gave him only an unpaid lecturer's title. From around 1909 for twenty-five years his salary came from the Austrian Chamber of Commerce, the body that spoke for Austrian business, where he wrote policy papers on tariffs, labor law and money.

From 1920 to 1934 he also ran a private seminar in his office every second Friday evening. Its most famous member, Friedrich Hayek, later won the 1974 Nobel Prize for, among other things, the insight that market prices carry facts scattered across millions of people that no central planner could ever collect, an idea known as the knowledge problem.

In 1927 Mises founded a research body to study the ups and downs of the business cycle, with Hayek as its first director: the Austrian Institute for Business-Cycle Research. The Rockefeller Foundation later helped fund it.

Mises's most famous argument came in 1920. Under full socialism the state holds all the means of production, so they are never bought or sold and carry no genuine prices. Without real prices, Mises argued, planners cannot tell which uses of resources create the most value, and so they cannot plan rationally at all.

Prices, in his account, carry two messages at once: what people want and what things cost to make. Abolish free prices, as communist states did, and the planners can no longer tell what is scarce or what people truly need. In a free economy that knowledge comes instead from prices set by millions of buyers and sellers making their own decisions.

He also refused to call himself merely an economist. To Mises, economics was only one part of a larger science, built by deduction, of human beings acting with purpose, which he named praxeology from the Greek praxis, action, and he preferred to be called a praxeologist.

Mises left Vienna for Geneva in 1934, married Margit Sereny in 1938, and fled Europe for the United States in 1940; from 1945 to 1969 he led a seminar at New York University. He died in 1973. In October 1982 the American organizer Lew Rockwell founded a research institute in his name, with support from his widow Margit, Ron Paul, Henry Hazlitt and Murray Rothbard, and it has stood ever since in the college town of Auburn, Alabama.

medical-licensing-friedmans-capitalism-a.context_blurb:
Before a doctor may treat patients in America, a state must grant a license. Most people assume that rule simply protects patients. Milton Friedman argued that it also protects doctors, from competition, and economists since have tried to measure how much.

Friedman made the case in Capitalism and Freedom, published in 1962, a short defense of free markets for general readers that became one of the most widely read of the century. Its ninth chapter, on occupational licensure, argued that medical licensing holds down the supply of doctors and pushes up what they charge.

Who decides? In each American state the license is granted by the state medical board, a body staffed largely by physicians, so doctors decide how many new doctors may join them.

The modern system grew from a 1910 study. Abraham Flexner, an educator writing for the Carnegie Foundation, urged states to close small medical schools that missed strict new standards and to train doctors on the model of Johns Hopkins. School after school shut: the count fell from roughly 160 schools in 1904 to 66 by 1935. With fewer new doctors entering the field relative to a growing population, doctor visits grew more expensive.

The labor economist Morris Kleiner has measured licensing far beyond medicine. In the 1950s about one American worker in twenty needed a license; by 2008 more than one in four did, from hair braiders to interior designers. His studies find that people who hold a license earn more, by about fifteen percent on average, because new competitors are kept out, with little measurable gain in quality. Licensing, in his findings, mostly serves the existing practitioners.

The pattern has a name. In North Carolina, the dentists who controlled the state's dental licensing board went after mall kiosks where non-dentists offered cheap teeth whitening, though the kiosks harmed no one; in 2015 the Supreme Court ruled against the board. Turning the state's licensing power against competitors in this way is called rent-seeking.

Some states have tested the alternative. By 2024 about half of them let nurse practitioners, nurses with advanced clinical training, run their own primary-care clinics without a supervising doctor. Studies by RAND and others comparing those states with physician-only states keep finding lower prices for primary care with no measurable difference in quality.

Friedman did not want patients left in the dark about who was well trained. His proposal was certification rather than licensing: the state could certify that a practitioner had met a published standard, without forbidding anyone uncertified from offering services to adults who chose them.

Public-choice economists draw a default rule from all this. When nearly every seat on a licensing board belongs to the profession it oversees, the first suspicion should be that its entry restrictions serve those members' incomes more than public safety.

mining-pools-from-solo-miners-to-global-.context_blurb:
Bitcoin miners are computers racing to add the next block to Bitcoin's shared ledger, and the winner of each race collects a reward of new coins. As the race grew crowded, a lone miner's odds shrank toward nothing. Miners solved the problem without any boss telling them how: they formed pools, voluntary cooperatives that now stretch around the globe.

The first opened in November 2010, when a Czech programmer who went by the name Slush launched a service that let small miners combine their computing power and divide the winnings. That kind of service is called a mining pool. Slush's pool still runs today as Braiins Pool.

Inside a pool, a miner is paid by the share. A share is a partial hash, a result that would have won a block if the network's target were far easier to hit. It proves the miner did real work, so the pool can split each reward according to how many shares each member turned in.

Why join at all? The network as a whole finds a block only about once every ten minutes, and the prize is now about 3.125 coins. A miner with one or two machines holds a tiny ticket in a global lottery: alone, he might go months or even years without winning a single block. In a pool he trades that rare jackpot for a small, steady trickle of income, the same bargain an office lottery syndicate strikes when its members buy tickets together and split whatever wins. By the 2020s a handful of big pools, led by Foundry USA, directed most of the world's mining power.

That concentration carries a danger. If one miner or pool ever held more than half of the network's hashing power, it could rewrite the latest blocks, reverse its own payments and spend the same coins twice, or shut out transactions it disliked. Bitcoin developers call this a 51-percent attack.

In the summer of 2014 the danger looked real, when a pool called GHash.io briefly passed half of the network's power. No court or regulator stepped in. Instead, individual miners pulled their machines out of GHash.io on their own, and its operators publicly urged users to move to other pools until the pool had shrunk.

A public-choice economist reads that episode as a story about incentives. A pool operator's machines, fees and reputation are worth something only while people trust Bitcoin to stay honest. An attack would wreck the value of everything he owns, so his own self-interest pushes him back from the line. Nobody has to be a saint; the incentives do the guarding.

mmt-rise-and-fall-stephanie-keltons-defi.context_blurb:
Modern Monetary Theory, or MMT, is a school of thought that burst into American politics in the late 2010s. Its central claim sounds almost magical: a government that issues its own money can never go broke, so it need not fear deficits the way a family fears debt. In 2021 and 2022 the real economy put that claim to a live test.

The idea began with Warren Mosler, a bond trader turned hedge-fund manager. His 1990s pamphlet Soft Currency Economics argued that a state which issues its own money can never run short of it. Mainstream economists granted the narrow point and rejected the sweeping one: a government can always print more money, but each new bill buys less, so inflation is the real limit. The Australian economist Bill Mitchell later spread the name MMT.

That older lesson is simple. Flood an economy with newly printed money and prices rise, so each dollar buys less. Kept up long enough, heavy printing drives prices up until the money is worth only a fraction of what it was.

Stephanie Kelton, an economist at Stony Brook University and an adviser to Bernie Sanders, took MMT to a mass audience in her best-selling 2020 book The Deficit Myth. MMT holds that neither tax revenue nor the size of the debt limits a currency-issuing government; in its own account, only two things do, inflation and real resources, meaning the workers, machines and materials that money can hire.

Critics answer that the theory plays down the damage inflation does to the people least able to bear it. Rising prices hurt savers and the poor first, because their cash and wages lose value before they can protect themselves.

The criticism came from the left as well as the right. In 2019 Larry Summers, a Democrat and a former Treasury secretary, likened MMT to voodoo economics, the insult the elder George Bush had aimed at Ronald Reagan's tax-cutting plans during the 1980 race. Paul Krugman, a Democratic Nobel winner, wrote critiques of his own.

Austrian-school economists such as Robert Murphy pressed a deeper objection. MMT says new money is safe while there is unused capacity: idle workers, empty factories, machines standing still. Across an entire country's economy, the Austrians reply, no such pool sits waiting to be switched on; resources are always in some use, so fresh money bids prices up rather than raising production.

Then came the test. In March 2021 President Joe Biden signed the American Rescue Plan, a $1.9 trillion burst of spending paid for with borrowed and newly created money, and Larry Summers warned that it would push prices up hard. Over the next two years the United States suffered its worst price inflation in about forty years, which reached 9.1 percent in June 2022.

One camp, nicknamed Team Transitory, blamed the surge on supply-chain trouble, with container ships stacked up outside the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, rather than on the new money. Many MMT advocates took the same line.

MMT's critics draw a broad lesson from those years. A theory that had been argued over for decades in journals was tested in a matter of months, and a live test like that in the real economy can discredit a school of thought faster than years of debate.

new-york-citys-rent-control-since-1943.context_blurb:
No American city has controlled rents for longer than New York. It began in November 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, when Washington ordered a freeze on apartment rents that was meant to last only for the emergency. The war ended; the controls did not. Eight decades of New York's experience make it the longest-running test of what capping rents does.

A law that caps the rent a landlord may charge is called rent control. New York's freeze passed from the federal government to the state and then to the city, and a chain of laws kept it going, from the 1946 rent law through the 1969 stabilization law to the 1974 tenant protection act. By 2026 it had run for over 80 years.

Even economists on the left came to fear it. In 1971 Assar Lindbeck, a Swedish economist of the democratic left who taught at Stockholm University, wrote that rent control seemed to be the most efficient technique known for destroying a city, short of bombing it.

Frédéric Bastiat's test of the seen and the unseen explains why. The seen is the low rent printed on a lucky tenant's lease. The unseen is everything the cap prevents: apartments that are never built, repairs that landlords keep putting off, and empty units that owners hold off the market rather than rent at a loss.

In the 1970s whole blocks of the South Bronx burned. Critics of rent control tied the fires to a grim incentive. When a controlled building could no longer cover its mortgage and upkeep, an insurance payout for a total loss could be worth more to its owner than the building itself, so some owners burned their own buildings for the insurance money.

The classic critique had come long before. In 1946 Milton Friedman and George Stigler, two young economists and both future Nobel laureates, wrote the pamphlet Roofs or Ceilings? for the Foundation for Economic Education. Their title posed the choice: more roofs, or price ceilings.

Later research kept finding the same pattern. In 2019 Rebecca Diamond and her Stanford colleagues reported in the American Economic Review on San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control. They found that landlords converted, demolished or withdrew about 15 percent of the newly covered apartments from the rental market, destroying housing stock and shrinking supply.

New York tightened its rules again with a 2019 law known as the HSTPA, which held down rent increases, kept more units under regulation and made eviction harder. Within two years, critics of the law pointed to measurable results: more regulated apartments left empty, or warehoused, because the capped rent could not pay for renovating them, and less new rental construction.

Across eighty years the argument has stayed the same, from Friedman and Stigler through Lindbeck to the San Francisco study. A landlord whose rent is held below his costs has no reason to keep up his building, enlarge it or add new apartments, so the housing stock slowly decays and shrinks while the number on the lease stays low.

occupational-licensing-1-600-hours-to-br.context_blurb:
In much of America a worker needs the state's permission before he may work in certain trades, from cutting hair to arranging flowers. Supporters say such rules protect customers. Critics, from Milton Friedman to the public-interest lawyers of the Institute for Justice, have shown how often the rules protect the people already in a trade from newcomers, and how hard the rules are to repeal.

Melony Armstrong wanted to braid hair for pay in Mississippi. Before the state would let her open a shop, it required some 300 hours of costly classes for a related license, and the classes did not teach braiding at all. A rule that bars a person from a job until the state grants a permit is called an occupational license.

Such licenses have spread fast. In the early 1950s only about one American worker in twenty needed one. By the time Morris Kleiner and Alan Krueger published their survey in 2013, about three in ten reported holding a government license for their work.

In Texas, Isis Brantley had been braiding hair in Dallas since 1979. Police arrested her in 1997, because the state demanded a cosmetology course of 1,500 hours in which braiding was never taught. After eighteen years of fighting she won in federal court early in 2015, and that June the legislature took natural hair braiding out of the state's licensing rules entirely.

Louisiana was long the only state that demanded a license just to sell flower arrangements. The Institute for Justice took up the cause of Sandy Meadows, a widow fired from her flower-arranging job for lacking the license, in 2003, along with two other women. The heart of the case was the hands-on exam, which licensed florists graded, the very people the applicants would be competing against.

Why do bills to free such trades die in committee session after session? Mancur Olson explained it in The Logic of Collective Action (1965). A few who each gain a lot from a rule, here the licensed incumbents, have every reason to organize and lobby, while the many who each lose a little, the customers paying a bit more, rarely bother to fight.

In North Carolina, shopping-mall kiosks began whitening teeth far more cheaply than a dentist would. The state's Board of Dental Examiners, most of whose members were practicing dentists, sent the kiosk owners orders to stop, and the kiosks closed. When the Federal Trade Commission sued, the board said it shared the state's own shield against antitrust suits. In February 2015 the Supreme Court ruled six to three against it: a board controlled by active competitors in the trade keeps that shield only if the state really supervises it.

George Stigler had explained the pattern in 1971 in "The Theory of Economic Regulation." A trade is not the victim of regulation, he argued, but its customer, buying rules from lawmakers. Of all the favors a trade can buy, the most valuable is a rule that blocks newcomers from entering it, because a cash subsidy only draws in new rivals who compete it away, while a barrier to entry keeps them out for good.

In Capitalism and Freedom (1962), Milton Friedman began his chapter on licensing with doctors, describing the American Medical Association as possibly the most powerful trade union in America. He granted that a bad doctor can do real harm, yet he still opposed licensing. His alternative was certification: the state would certify which practitioners had met a published standard, warning cautious patients while leaving everyone free to choose and the uncertified free to practice.

paul-volcker-20-rates-and-breaking-the-1.context_blurb:
By the late 1970s American prices were climbing so fast that savings melted and every trip to the store cost more than the one before. In August 1979 President Jimmy Carter put Paul Volcker, a six-foot-seven, cigar-smoking banker, in charge of the Federal Reserve. Volcker broke the inflation, and his cure became nearly as famous as the disease.

With prices rising nearly 13 percent a year, his plan was blunt: push interest rates way up so that people and businesses would borrow and spend less, and starve the inflation of fuel.

He moved fast. On the evening of Saturday, October 6, 1979, the Fed announced that it would target the growth of bank reserves and allow rates to climb wherever that led. Reporters called the surprise the Saturday Night Special.

Volcker knew the cure meant a severe recession that would throw millions out of work. He accepted mass unemployment as the price of killing inflation, judging that half-measures would only drag out the pain.

Rates climbed toward 20 percent in 1981, and the prime rate had already touched 21.5 percent. Factories closed and farms failed; farmers protested outside the Fed, and homebuilders mailed Volcker lumber from houses that would never be built. In November 1982 unemployment peaked at 10.8 percent, the highest since the Great Depression.

But it worked. Inflation, 13.5 percent in 1980, had dropped to roughly 3 percent by 1983, and Paul Volcker became the name history gives the man who broke it.

Victory brought a long calm. For about two decades, from the middle of the 1980s to 2007, American prices stayed low and steady and the economy swung less wildly, an era economists call the Great Moderation.

The politics mattered as much as the economics. The worst of the recession arrived before the 1982 midterm elections, yet President Ronald Reagan refused to attack the Fed in public, and in 1983 he reappointed Volcker. That restraint supports a principle many economists hold: a central bank should be free of day-to-day political pressure.

Volcker's name came back after the 2008 crash. The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 included the Volcker Rule, which bars big commercial banks from gambling for their own account while they hold ordinary deposits insured through the government's FDIC. The reason is simple: if a bank loses its own gamble, the taxpayer-backed insurance ends up covering its depositors' losses, so the public would be carrying the risk of the bank's bets.

The whole story points to a two-part lesson about stubborn double-digit inflation. Breaking it takes a Fed chair willing to accept a severe recession and a president willing to give political cover for the recession's cost; without either one, the effort would likely have collapsed.

polands-balcerowicz-plan-1990-shock-ther.context_blurb:
For forty years Poland lived under communism, with prices set by decree and shop shelves often bare. When the regime fell in 1989, the country faced shortages and runaway inflation. Its new finance minister, the economist Leszek Balcerowicz, chose to leap from planning to markets in a single jump, with advice from the Harvard economist Jeffrey Sachs, and Poland became the most famous test of that approach.

The plan bearing his name took effect on the first day of 1990. Overnight the government freed prices on almost all goods, cut off the subsidies that had kept state companies alive, and opened the country to trade.

A switch made all at once like this is called shock therapy, for how hard and fast it hits ordinary people; the plan's other nickname comes from Balcerowicz's own name.

The first year hurt. Shops filled with goods missing for years. Prices, though, leaped ahead of wages, unemployment rose, and the economy shrank by about 12 percent in 1990.

Then Poland took off. From 1992 the economy grew year after year in an unbroken run that no other European country matched, a stretch known as the Polish growth miracle.

By 2019 the average Pole's real income was about three times what it had been at the 1990 low point, the largest sustained gain of any post-communist economy.

Russia took a different road. In the early years of Boris Yeltsin's rule it gave every citizen vouchers that stood for slices of state industry, but reform came piecemeal and without hard limits on state firms. In the critique pressed by defenders of the Polish plan, those halfway measures were captured by well-placed insiders, who gathered up the vouchers cheaply and emerged as the oligarchs.

Balcerowicz's deepest lesson echoes the calculation debate: reforms work as a package or not at all. He insisted that four things launch together: freed prices, hard budget limits so that failing state firms got no bailouts, a currency that could be freely exchanged, and open trade. Freed prices without hard budgets, for example, would never create real market discipline.

praxeology-economics-from-the-action-axi.context_blurb:
Most sciences test their claims by experiment. Ludwig von Mises argued that economics is different: its core laws can be worked out by logic from one undeniable fact about people. He called the science built on that fact praxeology, and his followers still defend it against economists who want every claim tested by data.

Mises took the name from praxis, the Greek word for action or deed; economics, in his view, is one branch of a broader science of all purposeful choice. The French sociologist Alfred Espinas had coined the word in 1890, and Mises adopted it in the 1940s.

Austrian economists since Carl Menger in the 1870s have taught with simple scenes. A shopper hands a baker a dollar and leaves with a loaf, and both walk away pleased, though neither was forced. Each valued what he received more than what he gave up; otherwise one of them would have kept what he had.

Mises built everything on the action axiom: human beings act purposefully, using scarce means to reach the ends they prefer. Even trying to deny it proves it, because the denier is spending scarce time and effort to reach a goal of his own.

Milton Friedman took the opposite road in his 1953 essay The Methodology of Positive Economics. The test of a theory, he wrote, is the accuracy of its predictions, not the realism of its assumptions.

Critics complain that no one can test Austrian claims as physicists test theirs. Mises's stock reply, found in Human Action and again in Theory and History, is that human action is not laboratory chemistry. Nobody can rerun 1929 with the money supply held steady and watch what happens, because in any real episode everything else changes at the same time.

Logic alone, Mises granted, cannot explain history. To explain a particular episode you also need what he called thymology: understanding what real people, in their own time and place, wanted and why they chose as they did.

Murray Rothbard carried the method into a giant treatise. The William Volker Fund asked him in 1952 to condense Human Action into a classroom textbook. The project kept growing, and ten years later it appeared as Man, Economy, and State (1962), more than a thousand pages running from consumer choice through money and banking.

That is why the Austrians say their main laws are true by logic once you grant that people act on purpose, with no laboratory needed to confirm them. Hans-Hermann Hoppe defended the claim in Praxeology and Economic Science (1988), expanded in 1995 as Economic Science and the Austrian Method.

The method shapes how the school reads history. Mises argued by logic in 1920 that a planned economy without market prices could not calculate. When the Soviet system collapsed at the end of the 1980s, his followers called it real-world confirmation of a point already proved, not a first test of whether the point was true.

Underneath it all lies a rule Mises inherited from Menger: only individuals choose, value and act. Claims about what a nation, a society or a social class wants must be traced back to individual people, or they mean nothing. The rule is called methodological individualism.

principles-of-economics-1871-mengers-fou.context_blurb:
In 1871 a Vienna economist named Carl Menger, who had spent years reporting on grain and stock prices for newspapers, published a slim book, Principles of Economics, in German Grundsätze der Volkswirtschaftslehre. Written at almost the same moment as similar work by William Stanley Jevons in England and Léon Walras in Switzerland, it helped launch what historians call the marginal revolution, and it founded the Austrian school.

Menger's starting point can be seen on any schoolyard. One child trades a quarter's worth of apple for another child's four-dollar sandwich, and both walk away happy, though nobody was fooled or forced. That works because value depends on what each person wants, not just on the price tag; each child wanted what he got more than what he gave.

A second insight explains why the first bottle of water means so much to a thirsty traveler and the tenth so little. Each extra unit adds less value than the one before, because the first meets the most urgent need and every later one a less urgent need. Economists name this pattern diminishing marginal utility.

Earlier economists had traced value to the work that went into producing a thing. Menger turned that around. A loaf does not gain its worth from the baker's sweat; it is valuable for its usefulness to the person choosing it, and bakers labor over it because people value bread.

His idea is known as the theory of subjective value: value lives not in the good but in the mind of the person judging it, which is why bread is worth far more to someone starving than to someone who has just eaten. Adam Smith, David Ricardo and Karl Marx had all held labor-based theories of value, and Menger did not refine them but replaced them.

The idea cracked an old puzzle. Why does a diamond fetch a fortune while water, without which nobody survives, sells for next to nothing? Menger said not to compare all the water on Earth with all the diamonds, but to look at the particular next unit that someone is actually weighing, the next glass against the next stone. Water is so plentiful that the next glass is worth little, and diamonds are so scarce that the next stone is worth a great deal.

Menger described this reasoning at the margin in plain words but never gave it a single name. The German word Grenznutzen, marginal utility, was coined more than a decade later by his follower Friedrich von Wieser, and the English term is a translation of it.

Menger used no equations, graphs or curves, because he saw economics as the study of human choice, not of numbers. Hayek, Mises, Rothbard and Böhm-Bawerk all followed him, so making the case in words rather than in mathematical models became a lasting mark of the Austrian school, while Jevons and Walras built the mathematical tradition.

Menger drafted a second volume on capital and interest but never published it. His follower Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk filled the gap with Kapital und Kapitalzins, Capital and Interest, whose volumes began appearing in 1884.

The founding book waited a long time for English readers. Only in 1950, nearly thirty years after Menger's death, did the Free Press publish James Dingwall and Bert Hoselitz's translation, with an introduction by the Chicago economist Frank Knight.

Karl, Carl Menger's son, born in 1902, chose mathematics over economics. He belonged to the Vienna Circle of philosophers and led a famous mathematics seminar in Vienna, and when the Nazis came he left for America, where he spent decades teaching at Chicago's Illinois Institute of Technology.

qe1-the-first-bond-buying-program-2008-1.context_blurb:
In the autumn of 2008, with the housing market collapsing and banks failing, the Federal Reserve tried something it had never done before. It created hundreds of billions of new dollars and used them to buy bonds. That first program opened a new age of central banking.

On November 25, 2008, the Fed said it would conjure up $500 billion and spend it on mortgage bonds held by troubled banks. Economists now call this first round of quantitative easing QE1.

In March 2009 the Fed enlarged the program, raising its purchases of mortgage bonds to $1.25 trillion and adding $300 billion of Treasury bonds and $200 billion of other agency debt. When QE1 came to an end in early 2010, its purchases had reached about $1.75 trillion.

Where did the money come from? When the Fed buys a bond from a bank, no truck of cash leaves a vault. The Fed simply types a larger number into the bank's reserve account, creating the money out of thin air.

At the moment Lehman Brothers failed, in September 2008, the Fed's balance sheet, everything the central bank owned, stood near $900 billion. When the program was over it had swollen to about $2.3 trillion, more than double.

Austrian critics read QE1 through an idea from the early 1700s. Richard Cantillon, an Irish-born banker who made a fortune in Paris, observed in his Essai sur la nature du commerce en général that new money does not fall evenly, like rain. It comes in at particular doors, a mine, a king's treasury, a bank, and those nearest the door spend it before prices adjust. The pattern bears his name: the Cantillon effect.

In QE1 the new reserves entered through the Fed's dealings with big financial firms, so the first receivers were banks and hedge funds, people working in finance, and those who already owned assets. Stocks and property rose sharply in 2009 and 2010 while wages stagnated.

Defenders of QE1, among them Bernanke, writing later, and the economist Paul Krugman, credit it with preventing a depression: by stabilizing the market for mortgage bonds and keeping mortgage rates low, they argue, it kept housing from crashing further. Whether that is right depends on a counterfactual no one can run.

"Quantitative easing" is a soft, technical name; critics say "money printing" is just as accurate. Run such a program for years and the most predictable long-run result is inflation, prices rising across the economy. The Bank of Japan had used the name for its own program from 2001 to 2006.

While the program ran, three Austrian-school voices warned most publicly that the Fed was printing money to pay for federal deficits and that the price rises, though delayed, were coming. They were Peter Schiff on television, Bob Murphy at the Mises Institute, and Jim Grant in his newsletter, Grant's Interest Rate Observer.

QE1 was sold as an emergency measure, but QE2 and QE3 followed, and then an even bigger round after the 2020 pandemic. The lesson of this balance-sheet era is that expanding the central bank's balance sheet has become a standing policy tool, not a measure saved for emergencies.

rent-control-the-apartment-building-that.context_blurb:
Rent control caps what landlords may charge for an apartment, usually to keep housing affordable for the people living there now. Its critics, from Frédéric Bastiat's tradition of the seen and the unseen, point to the people the policy never shows you: the families who would have lived in apartments that were never built.

In Bastiat's terms, a policy has effects you can see and effects you cannot. Freeze rents, and what everyone sees is current tenants paying less. The unseen effect is the apartment buildings developers would have put up but never do, because future rents are capped below what it costs to build.

Imagine a city that forbids any landlord ever to raise the rent. Twenty years later the old buildings are crumbling from neglect, and not one new apartment block has gone up, because there was no way to make money building one, so nobody tried.

Economics predicts the same result even for gentler caps that allow only tiny yearly raises while heating and taxes climb. Fewer new apartments get built, and the old ones fall into disrepair.

Stockholm shows the queue that follows. Its strict rent rules meant a renter could not simply find a first-hand lease on the open market; he joined the city's waiting list, and by the mid-2010s the average wait for such an apartment in central Stockholm was about 20 years.

The Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck, a man of the democratic left, put the lesson in its most famous form. Rent control, he wrote, seemed to be the most efficient way known to destroy a city, short of bombing it. A 2019 study by Diamond, McQuade and Qian of San Francisco's 1994 expansion found that affected landlords shrank their rental stock by roughly 15 percent, converting some apartments to condos and tearing others down.

Wherever strict rent control has run, in New York, Paris or Stockholm, an under-the-table payment appears. A would-be tenant slips cash to the landlord or the departing tenant just to get the cheap lease. That side payment is called key money.

In 2020 Berlin froze rents for five years across roughly a million and a half apartments under a law called the Mietendeckel, and in April 2021 Germany's Constitutional Court struck it down because a single state had no power to override national housing law. Had the freeze stood, the long-run problem was predictable: landlords stop building and repairing, so the supply of rentals shrinks.

Milton Friedman liked to note that in a free market no exchange happens unless both sides benefit. A rent cap breaks that rule, and its effects split cleanly: it helps the tenants who already have leases and harms most of all the would-be tenants who never get a lease at all.

In 1981 the Fraser Institute published Rent Control: Myths and Realities, a collection whose editors were Edgar Olsen and Walter Block, which found the same long-run pattern in city after city. Its most damaging result over decades is a collapse in new rental building combined with the steady decay of the older buildings.

Stockholm's twenty-year queue and New York's cracked-plaster walk-ups point to the same unseen family that never got a home. When a price is held below the level where supply meets demand, something other than price must decide who gets the scarce apartments: waiting lists, connections, key money. Economists call that non-price rationing.

ronald-coase-transaction-costs-and-socia.context_blurb:
Ronald Coase was a British-born economist who taught for decades at the law school of the University of Chicago, and in 1991 he received the Nobel Prize. He wrote only a handful of famous papers, but two of them changed how economists think about firms, pollution and the role of government. He kept working until he died in 2013 at the age of 102.

His first great question came in a 1937 paper on why firms exist. If markets coordinate strangers so well, what is the point of a company? Why not hire people one task at a time? His answer was that making a fresh deal for every task costs time and effort, so it is often cheaper to keep workers on hand.

Every market deal, Coase saw, carries costs beyond its price: searching for the right partner, haggling over terms, drawing up a contract, and making sure the other side delivers. Economists call these transaction costs, and a firm grows to do a job in-house wherever that is cheaper than paying them again and again.

Inside a firm, prices stop doing the work. Between firms, market bargains coordinate strangers; within one, coordination comes mostly from command, as the manager tells the employee what to do.

In 1960 Coase published his second landmark paper, The Problem of Social Cost, about spillover harms such as smoke or noise. Picture a factory whose smoke ruins a farmer's crops. If the law gives the farmer a right to unpolluted air above his fields, he can sue the factory, or he can make it pay him a fee in exchange for letting the smoke continue.

Before Coase, most economists followed the Cambridge economist Arthur Pigou, who said the state should tax such harms. Coase answered that, as long as bargaining is cheap, the factory and the farmer can bargain their way to an efficient outcome themselves.

The surprise was that the final result tends to be the same whichever side the law first gives the right to. What matters most is that the two sides can bargain cheaply, not who is handed the right first; the starting rights decide only who pays whom. George Stigler named this the Coase theorem in 1966.

Coase complained that many readers misread him as saying government should always stay out. He meant something subtler. When many people are harmed and bargaining among them is impossible, government action can be justified, but its own costs of running things, its transaction costs, must be counted too.

At the age of 100 he finished a final book, written with Ning Wang. How China Became Capitalist (2012) traced how China left Maoist planning behind and turned to markets once Deng Xiaoping's reforms began in 1978.

Both of his great papers share one move. Instead of comparing a real market with an imaginary perfect government, or the reverse, they compare institutional forms, markets, firms, private bargains and government, on their real terms, transaction costs included.

satoshi-nakamoto-and-the-white-paper.context_blurb:
On Halloween night 2008, with the world's banks in crisis, someone calling himself Satoshi Nakamoto posted a short message to a mailing list about cryptography. The message pointed readers to a paper of just nine pages describing electronic cash that needed no bank and no trusted middleman. Nobody knows who Satoshi was, but that paper launched Bitcoin.

The post, signed Satoshi Nakamoto, went to a list run by the cryptographer Perry Metzger, a well-known place for experts to pick apart new proposals. Its title called Bitcoin a peer-to-peer system of electronic cash, money that passes directly from one person to another.

Every earlier plan for online cash had needed a trusted company in the middle, keeping track of who owned what. Without one, what stops someone from copying a digital coin, as easily as copying any file, and spending it twice? This old puzzle is called the double-spending problem, and solving it without a central authority was Satoshi's great achievement.

His answer was a race. Machines all over the globe race to crack a difficult puzzle, and whichever wins adds the next block to the shared record of every transaction. Because each puzzle burns real electricity, rewriting old blocks later would cost more than it could ever be worth. The system is called proof-of-work.

When rival versions of the record appear, everyone follows the chain with the most honest computing work behind it. That combination of proof-of-work with the longest-chain rule lets strangers settle on a single shared history of payments without any boss, and it is now called Nakamoto Consensus.

Why post it to that small list rather than a newspaper? Its readers had spent years debating how money might work online with no bank in charge, so they were the people most likely to find the flaws and actually try running the code.

The paper is short but carefully built. It runs in twelve numbered sections, from the Introduction and Transactions through Proof-of-Work, Incentive and Privacy to Calculations and a Conclusion, and it uses no mathematics harder than probability.

Satoshi ran the mining software heavily in Bitcoin's earliest months, when he had the field almost to himself and new coins came easily. Researchers who study the earliest blocks estimate that about one million bitcoins sit in his addresses, and they have never been spent.

The paper never called itself political, but its deeper meaning grew plain in the years that followed, as governments created trillions of new dollars. A working answer to double-spending meant that money could exist with no central authority to issue it at all.

The network went live in January 2009, and almost at once the respected cryptographer Hal Finney, whose own earlier system of reusable proofs of work was a close cousin of Bitcoin, began running it and received the first transaction Satoshi ever sent. When a respected expert joins a new open-source project early, other skilled people take it as a sign that the system is worth their time.

signature-first-republic-and-the-march-2.context_blurb:
In the spring of 2023 American banks began falling like dominoes. Silicon Valley Bank went first, on Friday, March 10; Signature Bank in New York followed that Sunday; and San Francisco's First Republic limped on until May. The story shows how panic spreads, how rescues work, and how a central bank's own policies can set the trap.

When one bank fails, customers of other banks that look similar get frightened, and they pull out their money too, even before anyone knows whether those banks are sound. That is why a second bank was shut down only two days after the first.

Fear that jumps from one bank to the next, regardless of the second bank's real health, is called financial contagion. It spreads the crisis through rumor and panic rather than through any actual loss.

Signature Bank had a well-known board member: Barney Frank, a former congressman who had helped write the banking rules passed after 2008. Lawmakers or regulators who move into well-paid jobs at the companies whose rules they once wrote are passing through what people call the revolving door.

On March 16, eleven of the largest American banks, the giants of Wall Street, joined forces to steady First Republic by placing deposits with it, $30 billion in all. It was not enough.

On May 1 regulators closed First Republic, and JPMorgan, the nation's largest bank, bought most of what was left. Over four decades of such mergers the number of American banks has fallen from more than fourteen thousand to a few thousand, and as small banks keep being swallowed, the biggest banks grow bigger and customers are left with fewer choices.

Analysts who sifted the wreckage found one shared root cause. All three banks had loaded up on long-term bonds when rates were near zero, many of them labeled held-to-maturity, and those bonds lost much of their value when the Fed pushed rates up hard through 2022 and into 2023.

Federal deposit insurance normally covers $250,000 per account, but in 2023 the government made sure even the largest depositors were repaid. Critics warn of the long-run cost, which is moral hazard: big depositors stop watching how risky their bank is, because they expect to be rescued.

Days before Silicon Valley Bank fell, Silvergate, a California bank whose customers were almost all crypto companies, announced that it was shutting down. A bank whose customers all work in one industry fails faster than a mixed one, because when that industry hits trouble, every customer tries to withdraw at the same moment.

After buying First Republic, JPMorgan's chief, Jamie Dimon, declared that this part of the crisis was over. When a giant bank that everyone considers safe takes over a failing one, depositors calm down and the panic stops spreading.

Bitcoin economists draw a deeper lesson from the sequence. The banks bought those bonds because the Fed's years of bond buying and near-zero rates made them attractive, and then the Fed's tightening turned them into losses. In their reading, the same central bank that creates assets during a cycle of quantitative easing exposes them to loss when the tightening that follows arrives.

solyndra-2011-the-green-loan-guarantee-t.context_blurb:
Solyndra was a California company that made an unusual kind of solar panel. In 2009 the Obama administration backed it with a federal loan guarantee of $535 million, and President Barack Obama later toured its factory. In 2011 it went bankrupt, and it became the most famous failure of Washington's attempt to pick winners in green energy.

When a company like that collapses and cannot repay a government-backed loan, the loss does not vanish. It falls on taxpayers, whose money stood behind the guarantee.

Officials had believed Solyndra would beat its American and Chinese rivals. The general problem is that officials guessing which private companies will succeed rarely guess better than the market, because they risk other people's money and lack the market's knowledge.

Solyndra's panels were tubes coated with a mix of rare metals, unlike the flat silicon wafers used by most rivals, a design that paid off only while silicon was dear. Then silicon's world price crashed, from about $400 a kilogram in 2008 to about $40 by 2011, and cheap Chinese flat panels left Solyndra's design far too expensive.

Private investors had seen the danger. As silicon prices fell and Chinese factories grew, venture investors pulled back from putting more money into Solyndra, yet the Department of Energy stayed committed. Friedrich Hayek's knowledge problem explains why that matters: the bets private investors decline are themselves dispersed information that a central agency does not have.

When Congress held hearings, reporters focused on one private backer, the Oklahoma billionaire George Kaiser, whose firm Argonaut Ventures was Solyndra's largest investor and who had raised campaign money for Obama.

A critic in Bastiat's tradition says the focus on Solyndra alone misses the larger unseen cost. The loan came from a federal guarantee program of about $16 billion, and other firms it backed, such as Abound Solar, also failed. All of that money, committed to companies chosen by officials, could not be doing anything else.

sowells-there-are-no-solutions-only-trad.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell has spent his career teaching one habit: before you cheer a policy, ask what it costs and who pays. He has summed up the habit in a handful of famous sentences, each of which turns a debate about good intentions into a question about trade-offs.

The most famous comes from A Conflict of Visions (1987). Sowell described two competing views of what people are like: an unconstrained vision, in which clever policy can perfect people, and a constrained vision, in which people are flawed, knowledge is limited and every choice is hard. The constrained vision refuses the word politicians love best, and Sowell put the refusal in two short sentences: there are no solutions; there are only trade-offs.

In his essay collection Is Reality Optional? (1993) he paired two propositions. The first lesson of economics, he wrote, is scarcity: nothing exists in quantities large enough to satisfy all who want it. The first lesson of politics, he added, is to ignore the first lesson of economics.

Free college, universal health care, a bigger army: each sounds noble alone. Endorsing any of them without asking at what cost, Sowell says, is not analysis but cheering. That question has a partner, compared to what?, and he treats the two as halves of one test.

In a 1995 book about the self-appointed experts he called the anointed, he mocked their picture of the world, in which answers to hard problems lie about waiting to be collected, like eggs hidden for children at an Easter egg hunt. A world of hidden answers has no trade-offs in it at all.

The two visions read failure in opposite ways. When a program has run fifteen years without delivering, the unconstrained vision blames too little effort and calls for a bigger version. The constrained vision concludes that the fix cost more than it was worth and should be withdrawn.

The same book named the anointed's favorite substitute for analysis. Faced with a hard problem, they reach for a slogan that denounces it, a verbal solution that requires no sacrifice and changes nothing.

Apply the method to rent control. Tenants in capped apartments really do pay less, but Sowell insists we also say what their savings were paid for with. The first cost he names is upkeep: landlords stop maintaining their buildings, because capped rent will not cover repairs.

Price ceilings also breed black markets, and Sowell makes a startling claim about them. Black-market prices run higher than the prices a free market would have set, because the seller must be paid for the risk of prosecution as well as for the goods.

His rule cuts both ways. A student who prices out a proposed subsidy, finds it too costly and then demands that an existing program be abolished is not finished, because repeal is a policy too. He must name what abolition will cost and who will bear that cost.

Even a bearable price proves nothing alone. A student who finds that the country can afford a program has still not shown that no other real arrangement would buy the same result more cheaply.

Sowell never claimed the trade-offs line as a discovery. It compresses the proposition economics has rested on from the start: resources are limited, so every use of them gives up another. Economists call what is given up the opportunity cost.
