tariffs-the-consumer-who-pays-and-does-n.context_blurb:
A tariff is a tax a government charges on goods crossing its own border, and it is economics' oldest laboratory for the gap between what a policy shows and what it hides. The factory with its furnaces still lit is easy to photograph. The cost is just as real, but it arrives as a few dollars on a car, a can of soup, a refrigerator, spread so thinly that the households paying never learn why.

In March 2018 the American government taxed imported steel at a quarter of its value and imported aluminum at a tenth, using a law that lets a president act on national-security grounds. Steel and aluminum are the bones of cars, cans, appliances and skyscrapers, so the bill never stopped at the border: everyday buyers in the country that added the taxes paid it, at the dealership and on the supermarket shelf. Frederic Bastiat, writing in France in the 1840s, had already supplied the method: look past the group a headline names and hunt for the losers nobody counts. By that method the unseen casualties of a steel tariff are American consumers of goods that use steel as an input.

So what did a rescued job cost? Economists at the Peterson Institute for International Economics in Washington, Gary Hufbauer among them, took the extra money American firms were paying for steel in 2019, divided that sum by the count of steel jobs the taxes had created or saved, and came out at about $900,000 for each one, each year. There is nothing clever about the arithmetic; it is simply the honest way to score the policy. Count the jobs saved and subtract the jobs lost at every factory that buys steel, because a mill's good news is an axle plant's higher input bill.

The classic case is older. In May 1930 the New York Times printed an open letter from over a thousand economists, Paul Douglas of Chicago among them, begging Herbert Hoover to kill a bill that raised duties on more than twenty thousand imported articles. Shoppers would pay higher prices for many everyday goods, the signers wrote, and a tariff war would be poor soil for world peace. Hoover signed it in June anyway. Foreign governments then answered the only way politics allows, and they put their own tariffs on American exports in return, and Kansas wheat farmers watched their export markets slam shut.

The damage shows up in the trade figures. Between 1929 and 1934 the value of world trade fell by about 66 percent, each retaliation wiping out somebody's export market. It is tempting to hang the whole Depression on that collapse, and the tariff earned its share of blame. But in 1963 Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz put the slump's unusual depth down to a monetary cause instead: the Federal Reserve's failure to prevent a one-third collapse in the money stock between 1929 and 1933. A trade war makes a monetary contraction hurt worse; it does not make one happen.

Bastiat had compressed the politics of the whole business into a joke back in 1845. His candlemakers petition the French parliament to board up the windows of the nation and shut out the sun, on the grounds that free daylight is unfair competition against honest domestic candles. The shape of the joke is the shape of the real thing: concentrated benefit for a small named group; dispersed cost across every consumer. A few thousand mill workers in two towns can be named and organised into a lobby; the hundred million buyers who each lose a few dollars cannot, which is why Mancur Olson's 1965 account of collective action predicts the tariff wins the vote.

And the 2018 numbers came out the way that method predicts. Two economists, Lydia Cox of Harvard and Kadee Russ of the University of California, Davis, added up both sides in 2020, drawing on a Federal Reserve study by Aaron Flaaen and Justin Pierce: roughly a thousand jobs gained in primary steel, roughly seventy-five thousand lost in the factories that buy steel and now paid more for it. That is about 75 downstream jobs lost per primary-steel job added, a ratio nobody could see from the mill-town headline.

terra-luna-celsius-and-voyager-the-2022-.context_blurb:
In 2022 the industry that calls itself crypto came apart in public over about six months, and the wreckage is the clearest lesson available on the difference between a protocol and a company. Four famous names failed. One thing did not.

The first domino was Terra/LUNA, a South Korean project led by Do Kwon. Its coin, UST, promised to be worth a dollar for ever, and Terraform Labs held no dollars to pay anybody with. Instead a program traded a partner token, LUNA, printing and burning it to nudge the price back whenever it drifted. That works while the drift is small, and it cannot work in a stampede: if everyone tries to sell at once, the program cannot keep the price up, and each new LUNA minted to defend the dollar makes LUNA itself worth less. Over four days in May 2022 both tokens fell to almost nothing and about $40 billion of nominal value disappeared, much of it belonging to small Korean savers.

The panic spread. Celsius Network, run by Alex Mashinsky, had been paying depositors interest no bank could match and advertising itself as safer than a savings account. When confidence drained out of the whole sector, customers came for their cash, and Celsius froze on June 12, 2022 and filed bankruptcy July 13. The court filings showed about $4.7 billion of customer money trapped inside when the gate came down.

Three Arrows Capital, a crypto hedge fund run by Su Zhu and Kyle Davies, had borrowed heavily to bet on the Terra ecosystem and could not pay once the bet died. One of its lenders was the broker Voyager Digital, which never saw the money again, shut its own customers out and went into bankruptcy that July. Economists call the sequence contagion: one failure topples the firm that lent to it, that firm topples the next, and the loans between them are the fuse.

The Terra wreck settled an old argument about what stands behind a coin. A token pegged by nothing but a formula and a sister token has no reserve to sell when the selling starts, so without a real reserve of value, one bad panic can wipe the coin out. Do Kwon left South Korea, was arrested at Podgorica airport in Montenegro in March 2023 carrying false Costa Rican papers, and was handed over to the United States in December 2024.

Mashinsky's own case ended in a New York federal court. In December 2024 he pleaded guilty to fraud and market manipulation of the Celsius token CEL, admitting he had propped up the price of his firm's own coin while telling depositors their money was safe.

Sam Bankman-Fried's exchange FTX went down that November, and by then the pattern was impossible to miss. One group of Bitcoin owners lost nothing in any of it. They held their own bitcoin themselves instead of trusting a company to hold it for them, with the keys on a device in a drawer at home. Andreas Antonopoulos had been teaching that in five words for years: coins whose keys you do not hold are not really your coins. The distinction he pressed is structural rather than tribal. A firm that issues a token or promises a yield is a counterparty that can fail, while bitcoin in a wallet you control has no counterparty to fail in the first place. Through every one of those collapses the Bitcoin software itself kept producing blocks on schedule; the price fell hard, and nothing in the system stopped working.

the-1989-collapse-arc-solidarity-to-berl.context_blurb:
Nineteen eighty-nine is the year the long argument ended. Between June and December the communist governments of Central and Eastern Europe fell one after another, and the thing that pushed the first of them over was not an army. It was a trade union of shipyard workers.

In communist Poland a worker could not start a union of his own. The state insisted that it already spoke for the working class, so no second voice was needed or allowed, and the reason the ban mattered so much is plain: a free union gives ordinary workers real power the government does not control. In August 1980 the Gdansk shipyard men struck anyway, led by an electrician named Lech Walesa, and they called what they built Solidarity. The demand underneath the strike was never mainly about wages. It was the freedom to bargain and choose their own leaders. Martial law outlawed the union in December 1981, and it survived underground for eight years.

By the spring of 1989 the Party agreed to a partly open election, keeping most of the lower house for itself and leaving the brand-new upper house wide open. The result was not close. Solidarity won 99 of 100 Senate seats and every contested Sejm seat, and by August Poland had a prime minister the communists had not chosen.

The fences had been telling the story for forty years. Churchill's iron curtain ran from the Baltic to the Adriatic in wire and concrete, and every gun on it pointed east, back at the population it enclosed, which says exactly who the barrier was built to stop: people trying to leave the communist side for the free side. Hungary began cutting its own wire along the Austrian border in May 1989, and East Germans on holiday there simply walked out. Then on the evening of 9 November a Politburo spokesman, Guenter Schabowski, fumbled a question at a press conference and announced that the crossings were open; nobody had warned the guards. Berliners were dancing on the Wall within hours. What that stampede showed is that many people had wanted out for a long time and could not say so before.

Czechoslovakia went next, and went quietly: marches in Prague, a general strike, crowds jingling house keys instead of throwing stones, no tanks and no shooting, which is why the country named it the Velvet Revolution. The dissident playwright Vaclav Havel was its president before the year ended. Romania was the exception. Elena and Nicolae Ceausescu were caught trying to flee, were tried in an hour by a military court, and were shot by a firing squad on 25 December 1989, Christmas Day, the only communist ruler of that year to end that way.

The centre held for two more years and then let go. On 25 December 1991 Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on television, the hammer and sickle came down from the flagpole above the Kremlin, the walled fortress of palaces and cathedrals that has held the seat of Russian power since the tsars, and the Soviet Union ceased to exist. The verdict that stung most came from the other side of the argument. Robert Heilbroner had spent a career at the New School making the case for planning over markets, and in a New Yorker essay in September 1990 he gave the old calculation debate a three-word obituary: Mises was right.

One coincidence frames the whole year. On 4 June 1989, the day Poles queued to vote the communists out, the Chinese army cleared Beijing's central square with tanks and rifles, and the Tiananmen Square killings stand as the one case that year of a communist government keeping power by shooting its own citizens. Gorbachev, for his part, declined to send tanks west. And the collapse had been forecast long before, though hardly anybody listened: the Austrian economists, Ludwig von Mises from 1920 and Friedrich Hayek from the 1930s, had argued that central planning must eventually seize up, because without real prices the planners work blind.

the-assignat-1789-1796-french-revolution.context_blurb:
France's revolutionary government was broke by the autumn of 1789. On 2 November the Assembly voted to take the lands of the Catholic Church, the largest landowner in the kingdom, and then printed paper notes against them, each one in theory a ticket redeemable for a piece of that property. The paper was called the assignat, from the French verb assigner, because a note was assigned to particular acres.

The hole in the scheme is not the land but the press. The government can just print more whenever it wants, so the money loses value, because the acres behind the notes do not multiply when the notes do. That is exactly what happened. The first issue, in late 1789, ran to four hundred million livres, and the deputies promised there would never be another. Each successive Convention and Directory added more to cover its bills, and by the end of 1795 the face value outstanding had passed over 40 billion livres, roughly 100 times the promised limit.

By the mid-1790s farmers and traders wanted coin rather than paper, and the state's answer was not to slow the press. In 1793 the Convention made it a capital crime to refuse the notes at face value or to price gold above paper, and the punishment was death. Fear did not restore confidence in the currency. Shops emptied instead, and the sellers who stayed open hid their best goods and dealt in secret.

By 1796 an assignat was worth about a thousandth of its face value, so the Directory withdrew the entire issue and began again with fresh paper against the same land: The mandat territorial. It lost nearly everything within months, faster than the money it had replaced, and seven years later Napoleon's government went back to silver and gold coin. France had been here before. In the years up to 1720 a Scottish adventurer in Paris had run the first experiment, John Law's Banque Royale and Mississippi Company, whose notes and shares collapsed and kept the country off paper money for seventy years.

The episode found a chronicler who meant it as a warning. Andrew Dickson White, co-founder and first president of Cornell, published his account in its final form in 1912, under a title that named the thing plainly as fiat money inflation, and he wrote it for Americans tempted by the same shortcut. Writers still point back to the French story because it shows what happens when a government prints too much paper money too fast. White's conclusion is the hard one. Through legal-tender decrees, controls on prices and the guillotine the Revolution tried every instrument it had, and not one of them worked, because no government could make paper worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem.

The playbook repeats itself. Weimar Germany 1921-1923 reached for the same tools, legal-tender rules, ceilings on prices and the prosecution of hoarders, and came apart in the same manner, since none of those tools touched the printing. Frederic Bastiat's test sorts the lesson into two columns. Seen: legal-tender laws and price controls; Unseen: goods vanishing from shops and savers wiped out. The decrees are what a government announces; the bare shelves and the ruined savings of people who trusted the paper are the part no decree reports.

the-bitcoin-fixes-this-subculture-and-st.context_blurb:
Bitcoin grew a culture as well as a price. It lives on social media, in local meet-ups and at enormous annual gatherings, it has its own jokes and its own tests of membership, and nobody designed any part of it.

Around 2019 a three-word reply began turning up under every story about a frozen bank account, a currency collapse or a government printing binge: 'Bitcoin fixes this'. Half joke and half argument, it claims that a surprising share of modern financial misery begins with money a government can make more of whenever it likes. The same crowd works hard at a second distinction. What it insists on being separated from is 'crypto' as an umbrella term including altcoins, because lumping Bitcoin in with thousands of copycat tokens hides the one property its holders care about, a supply that nobody can expand.

The unit matters to the habit. A bitcoin divides into 100,000,000 smaller pieces called satoshis, or sats, named after its pseudonymous creator, so a person with twenty dollars can still buy a meaningful quantity of something. Many holders therefore ignore the price chart and put the same small sum in every payday, whether the price is high or low, a practice the community calls stacking sats. A fund manager would call it dollar-cost averaging; the slang exists because refusing to try to time the market is treated here as a virtue.

The culture has a sharper edge too. 'Have fun staying poor' is what a holder says to people who will not own any, and it is meant as a forecast rather than an insult: inflation slowly eats dollar savings, so refusing Bitcoin leaves them poorer over time, which is a claim about the currency rather than about anybody's intelligence.

None of this was organised from above. The sats, the home nodes, the city meet-ups and the yearly conferences grew out of thousands of separate choices with no committee in charge, which is what Friedrich Hayek's spontaneous order was coined to describe: useful order arising out of dispersed decisions, the way language and the common law did. You can hear the difference at the conferences in Nashville, Prague and Riga, which look like investment events and are nothing of the kind. The main stage runs to talks on monetary history, sound money, and Austrian economics rather than trading tips, and the virtue the speakers praise is patience.

the-calculus-of-consent-1962.context_blurb:
Economists had long treated the state as a referee. Businessmen and shoppers chase their own advantage, the story went, and government steps in above the fray to serve the public interest. In 1962 two economists at the University of Virginia asked what becomes of the analysis once the referee turns out to have interests of his own.

Gordon Tullock and James Buchanan published the answer with the University of Michigan Press under the title The Calculus of Consent, and the book founded a field. Its method is one move applied without flinching: treat Voters, politicians, and bureaucrats as the same self-interested people economics already assumes them to be in a shop or a factory, rather than as servants of a public good nobody can define. A politician wants re-election, an official wants a bigger department, a voter wants the benefit without the bill. None of that is wickedness. It is what people are like, and a theory of politics that assumes otherwise will go on being surprised.

The book's deepest idea is that politics happens on two floors. Downstairs, under the existing rules, people vote on taxes, tariffs and subsidies, each knowing perfectly well which side he is on. Upstairs is where the rules themselves get written, and the two authors called that The constitutional level. The difference matters because of what a rule-writer cannot know. Sitting down to pick rules, nobody can tell whether he will later stand with the majority or the minority on the votes those rules will produce, and that ignorance of one's own future position is The veil of uncertainty. A man who cannot be sure of winning will not hand unlimited power to whoever does. So the authors expect rule-writers to insist on Supermajority rules for the gravest decisions, since a bare fifty-one percent is too thin a margin to let the winners take a losing minority's rights away, even though a higher threshold makes agreement harder to reach.

Nine years later the philosopher John Rawls made a related move from a completely different starting point, asking what rules a person would choose for a society if he did not yet know whether his life would begin rich or poor, strong or sick. His name for that position is a veil of ignorance. The two devices are cousins, although Rawls used his to argue about distribution and Buchanan used his to argue about institutions. What the economists' version did first was puncture a comfortable idea about majorities. A vote of fifty-one percent does not reveal the will of a people. What it reveals is the balance of Interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance: organised groups leaning on legislators, legislators swapping votes across unrelated bills, and citizens who never learn about an issue that costs each of them a few dollars.

The research had a patron. Early money for the Virginia programme that produced the book came from The Ford Foundation, which is a small irony given what the programme went on to say about organised interests. It is worth being exact about what the book did and did not contain. The constitutional and post-constitutional floors are in it, so is the veil of uncertainty, and so is the treatment of vote-trading. The concentrated-benefits / dispersed-costs pattern of collective action is not: that arrived three years later, in Mancur Olson's 1965 study of why small groups with much at stake organise while large groups with little at stake do not.

One distinction has outlasted everything else in the volume: The distinction between the RULES of the game and the choices WITHIN the rules. Two people can quarrel furiously over a tax and still agree about how taxes ought to be decided, and the second agreement is the deeper kind of consent, because it was given before anybody knew who would win. Buchanan built the rest of his career on it and took the 1986 Nobel for the work. His lesson runs to a single line: How the rules are chosen matters more than who wins under the rules.

the-crime-of-73-and-bryans-cross-of-gold.context_blurb:
Money is never neutral between the man who owes and the man who is owed, and American politics spent a quarter of a century proving it. In 1873 Congress passed a Coinage Act that quietly ended the unlimited minting of silver dollars and put the country on gold alone. Debtors and the silver-mining West gave the law a name that lasted a generation: the Crime of '73.

The grievance behind the name was specific. The hardest hit were farmers who had borrowed in Civil-War-era greenbacks, taking out mortgages in the plentiful paper dollars of the 1860s and repaying them in the scarcer gold dollars of the 1880s, while crop prices drifted downward and the debt stayed exactly as large as it had been written. Their remedy was to mint silver without limit alongside gold, which would have put a great deal more money into circulation and sent prices up. The word for lifting prices by adding money is inflation, and in the 1890s it was a farmers' demand rather than a bankers' fear.

Put the question to a Kansas farmer with a fixed mortgage and the arithmetic decides it. He backs the pro-silver side, because more money in the economy raises prices: the price of his wheat rises, his monthly payment does not, and the real weight of the debt falls. The Democratic Party split along exactly that line, and on 9 July 1896, at the convention in Chicago, a Nebraskan of thirty-six called William Jennings Bryan carried the hall with a speech that compared the gold standard to a torture. He closed by warning the gold men that they should not press a crown of thorns upon the brow of labour, and should not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold. He won the nomination the next day, on the fifth ballot. The election that followed was the first fought openly on the currency, and the question before the voters was whether to back the dollar with only gold or also with silver; William McKinley won it for gold by 271 electoral votes to 176.

Then the argument evaporated without being settled. Major new gold discoveries in the Klondike, the Witwatersrand, and Colorado poured fresh bullion into the world's money supply in the late 1890s, prices rose, farm debts eased, and the free-silver movement lost its reason to exist. Congress wrote the gold standard into law in 1900.

The episode left a reasoning move worth keeping. Hard money benefits savers and creditors; inflation benefits debtors, and the effect runs both ways at once, because a dollar that holds its value is good news for whoever is owed one and bad news for whoever owes it. That is why the Austrian answer, argued later by Murray Rothbard, refuses both camps. It wanted neither silver inflation by statute nor falling prices imposed by decree, but a market-determined money supply that neither government nor lobby can inflate to redistribute wealth by decree, so that the quantity of money is not a prize a lobby can win in a vote. The lasting lesson of 1896 is the one the silverites and the gold men both grasped better than later generations: Money policy is always distributional -- there is no neutral choice between hard and soft money.

the-ethanol-mandate-and-the-2007-guatema.context_blurb:
In 2005 Congress wrote a rule called the Renewable Fuel Standard, expanded in 2007, which requires that a set volume of ethanol distilled from corn be blended into American petrol every year. The stated aims were less imported oil and cleaner air. The visible beneficiaries were corn growers in Iowa and the firms that distil the ethanol.

Corn does not care what it is for. Once a guaranteed market existed for fuel corn, farmers moved land and grain into it, and by the early 2010s something like two-fifths of the American crop was going into engines rather than onto plates. It makes food-corn more expensive because so much corn is used as fuel, which is simply what happens when the same bushel has two buyers. Bastiat's rule from 1850 names the half of the ledger that nobody photographs. The crop that was never planted, and the family that could not pay for what was, is the unseen.

The bill arrived in other countries. World corn prices roughly doubled between 2006 and 2013, and January 2007 brought tens of thousands of people into the streets of one capital, banging pots and pans, because the staple they had eaten every day of their lives had almost doubled in a few months: maize tortillas, in Mexico City. Comparable protests broke out in Egypt, Haiti and Guatemala. When the world prices of corn, wheat and rice rose together across 2007 and 2008, the World Bank reckoned the increase pushed more than 100 million people back below the extreme-poverty line, overwhelmingly in countries that import their food.

Inside the World Bank an economist named Donald Mitchell tried to apportion blame for the doubling of food prices between 2002 and 2008. Drought mattered and the oil price mattered, but his own calculation put the largest policy-driven share on biofuel mandates diverting food crops to fuel, and that share could have been undone by a vote in a legislature. That is the whole case in a line. The reasoning move is seen versus unseen: the farm boom is seen, the dearer food abroad is not, because US corn diverted to fuel raises world corn prices and food-importing countries pay the invisible cost, so a law about motor fuel in one country turns up as the price of dinner in another.

the-feds-dual-mandate-and-the-austrian-c.context_blurb:
A central bank with one job can be judged. A central bank with two jobs can always explain itself. In 1978 Congress handed the Federal Reserve two, in the Humphrey-Hawkins Act, named for a senator who had died that January, and the pair is known as the dual mandate.

The goals are maximum employment and stable prices, with the statute adding moderate long-term interest rates, which everyone treats as following from the first two. The difficulty shows the moment they are set side by side. The two goals can pull against each other, so the bank has to choose, and whichever way it chooses it can point at half of its own instructions for cover. Europe wrote its rulebook the other way about. When the European Central Bank was created in 1998 the treaty gave it one primary objective, which is to keep prices steady, with other aims permitted only so far as they do not prejudice that; the design followed the Bundesbank's record against inflation.

The timing of the 1978 law is the awkward part. A decade earlier Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had shown that any lasting trade between inflation and jobs must break down, because once people come to expect higher prices they bargain for them, and the 1970s then delivered high inflation and high unemployment together. So the trade-off assumption had just been falsified by 1970s stagflation at the very moment Congress wrote it into statute. The Austrian objection is about incentives rather than arithmetic. Given two goals and a political system, a central bank will lean one way: the employment side, because unemployment is politically salient in a way low-grade inflation is not. A factory closing leads the evening news; a few extra points on the price of everything is diffuse, delayed, and hard to blame on anybody.

Which inflation the Fed watches matters as well. Since 2012 the two percent target has been stated on the PCE price index, a broad measure of the prices of what American households actually buy, with a 'core' version that strips out the wild swings in food and energy watched alongside it. Austrian critics point out that it counts nothing of what happens to the price of a house or a share. The 2021 episode is the case they cite. Prices climbed hard through that year while the Fed held rates near zero and called the rise temporary, and when the pivot arrived in 2022 it had to be violent. To the critics the miss was not bad luck but the employment-side bias producing predictable inflation error, the mandate's own incentives running exactly on schedule.

Milton Friedman's answer was to take the choice away. He argued for decades that nobody should sit in a room setting interest rates by judgement, and proposed instead a constant money-supply growth rate, one low number held steady from year to year and out of reach of a committee's discretion. The Austrians went further and wanted the money itself out of political hands altogether. Both start from the clash written into the 1978 law: printing more money to lift employment tends to raise prices, which the same law says to keep stable, so the statute instructs one institution to do a thing and to undo it.

the-genesis-block-and-the-times-headline.context_blurb:
A blockchain has to start somewhere. On 3 January 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto ran the software on his own machine and produced the first block of Bitcoin, numbered zero and known ever since as the genesis block. It paid the standard reward of fifty coins to an address written into the program, and then he waited. Block one did not follow for about six days, presumably while he satisfied himself that a live network behaved as the code promised, and after that the blocks arrived on the roughly ten-minute rhythm they have kept ever since.

Inside the block's coinbase transaction, the record that mints new coins, Satoshi put a sentence that had no technical function whatever. It was a headline out of The Times of London, dated 3 January 2009 and printed that same morning. What it reported was the UK Chancellor preparing a second bailout for banks, weeks after the first rescue, which is to say the state preparing to print again to save institutions that had already failed.

The sentence did two jobs at once. Because the block's hash takes in that text, nobody could have produced the block before the newspaper existed, which makes it a timestamp proof that the block was not pre-mined, the same trick as a hostage holding up a dated paper. The second job was political, and the community has never read it any other way: a direct protest against the 2008-09 bank-bailout culture, naming in a single line the thing the system was built to escape.

No government currency had ever been launched with a protest about its own rulers written permanently into its first page: a line that timestamps itself and says plainly what it stands against. The Austrian reading presses the point into monetary theory. What the gesture claims is that a monetary system can bind itself to a rule and refuse to rescue failed banks, giving up at issuance the political discretion a bailout needs. That is the one promise a currency run by a committee can never make, because a committee can always decide otherwise.

One oddity remains in the first block. By a quirk of the original code the fifty-coin reward was written in a form that leaves it outside the ordinary ledger of spendable outputs, so it can never be spent or moved to another address, though every node on the network can see it sitting there. The consequence is small and permanent: fifty coins are permanently locked out of the circulating supply, while the 21-million limit, which falls out of the arithmetic of the halvings, is unchanged.

the-holodomor-stalins-ukrainian-terror-f.context_blurb:
Holodomor is a Ukrainian compound: holod, hunger, and mor, death. It names what Stalin's government did to the Ukrainian countryside in 1932 and 1933, and the word exists because the English word famine suggests weather.

The grain quota set for Ukraine in 1932 could not be met by any village, which was the point of it. Requisition brigades went from house to house and took Everything down to seed grain and food from the shelves, the cured meat in the rafters and the grain put by for spring sowing included. A household with no reserves and nothing to plant does not recover in the spring. Millions starved to death across that winter and into 1933, in one of the richest farming regions in Europe.

Two further measures turned a shortage into a sentence. On 22 January 1933 Stalin signed an order sealing Ukraine and the Kuban from the inside: guards stood on the roads and the railway lines checking papers, and when starving villagers set out for Russian towns to beg for bread They were turned back or arrested. Earlier famines had been survivable because people could leave. The second measure punished whole communities. A village that missed its quota went onto a state register, cut off from all trade, stripped of the food still on its shelves and forbidden to let anybody out; these were Blacklisted villages, marked as such at the boundary.

Counting began in earnest only after 1991, when the archives of the party and the secret police opened. The range the peer-reviewed studies now give is About 3.5 to 7.5 million, with most of them clustering between three and a half and five million. The first substantial Western account had been written without those archives: Robert Conquest published The Harvest of Sorrow with Oxford University Press in 1986, and academic Sovietology treated it with suspicion until the files proved him broadly right. Anne Applebaum's Red Famine, thirty years later, is the standard modern treatment. Ukraine's own parliament gave the famine a legal name on 28 November 2006, voting to call the Holodomor A genocide of the Ukrainian people, and the European Parliament passed a comparable resolution in December 2022.

The name is the point of the whole story, and it is the name Ukrainians use: The Holodomor, the killing by hunger, as distinct from any harvest failure. The same collectivisation hit Soviet Kazakhstan in the same two years, where the herds of the nomads were confiscated and killing an animal privately was made a crime. Roughly a million and a half Kazakhs died, which was About 40 percent of all the ethnic Kazakhs then alive, and it changed the country's demography for decades.

What separates this from a natural famine is the combination of acts, and the combination is worth stating in one line: A deliberately unfillable grain quota, plus border-sealing to prevent escape, plus blacklisting of under-quota villages. No frost and no insect did any of those three things. That is also why the votes in European legislatures matter, Germany's and Poland's and Ireland's among them: It records the deaths as a deliberate crime, not an accident of bad weather, which is exactly what the Soviet state denied for sixty years.

the-lobbying-industry-1-4b-1998-to-4-1b-.context_blurb:
Federal lobbying in the United States is a disclosed industry: anybody paid to press Congress or a federal agency has to register and file reports. The declared total was about 1.4 billion dollars in 1998. For 2023 it was a record of about $4.2 billion, with something like twelve thousand registered lobbyists at work.

The spending is not spread evenly. One industry has led the table for years, laying out about three hundred and eighty-five million dollars by itself in 2023: pharmaceuticals and health products, ahead of electronics and insurance. Among single organisations the biggest spender is usually the US Chamber of Commerce, at close to seventy million dollars in the same year, with the National Association of Realtors its usual rival for first place.

Gordon Tullock gave the activity its economics in 1967, in a paper about what tariffs, monopolies and theft really cost a society. His point was that a government able to grant privileges will attract people who spend real money competing for the privileges, and that money builds nothing at all. The lawyers' hours, the dinners and the advertising produce no goods, and the name for what society loses in the contest is deadweight loss. Four billion dollars a year is not being spent to explain general policy trade-offs to legislators. Money is spent to capture specific rules, exemptions, subsidies, and enforcement decisions, which is a claim about incentives rather than about anybody's honesty.

The revolving door is where the value turns up in a salary. A member of Congress or a senior staffer earns a capped federal wage, and the same person moving to a lobbying firm on K Street typically sees a rise of 500 to 1000 percent, a market pricing what the contacts and the inside knowledge are worth. Matilde Bombardini, Francesco Trebbi and Marianne Bertrand asked in 2014 which of the two a lobbyist is really paid for, and gave their paper a title that puts the question plainly: Is It Whom You Know or What You Know? Their answer was mostly whom.

Foreign lobbying has been regulated separately since 1938, when Congress watched German propaganda agents working inside America and required anybody paid by a foreign government, party or company to register publicly and declare the money. The law goes by four letters, FARA, and prosecutors still use it; those disclosures run to something like half a billion dollars a year on top of the domestic total. The industry's address tells its own story. So many firms and trade associations keep offices on one downtown street in Washington that its name stands for the whole trade, and the clustering is no accident: lobbyists cluster near power because access to lawmakers is valuable.

The public-choice point is a default rather than an accusation. The right to petition the government is protected, and plenty of lobbying is one person explaining his business to a legislator who knows nothing about it. But when a statute is long, technical, aimed at a single industry and heavily lobbied, the Buchanan and Tullock analysis suggests where to look first: the beneficiaries are the concentrated lobbying interests, not the dispersed public. The costs are spread thin across millions of people who will never read the bill.

the-negative-railway-break-every-rail-li.context_blurb:
In the 1840s France was planning a railway from Paris to Madrid, and a Bordeaux newspaper writer, one M. Simiot, argued that the line ought to break at his city. Bastiat answered with a joke, printed in his Economic Sophisms in the mid-1840s and known ever since as the negative railway.

The break would force freight off the train and back on and make travellers stop over at Bordeaux. The work that would create was real and local, and he named trades that would get it, among them boatmen, porters and hotel-keepers. Who gains and who pays is not hard to see once somebody asks: the town's workers win; travelers and both big cities lose time and money, and every ton of freight on the line pays for the handling twice.

Bastiat's reply was to take the argument seriously. If a break at Bordeaux enriches Bordeaux, the same must hold for a break at every town on the route, and if each of them is granted its break what you are left with is a series of unconnected roads that is not a railway at all. The reductio exposes the mistake underneath, which is treating friction as income: delays and extra costs make trade worse, not better, and a railway is valuable precisely because it removes handling that used to be unavoidable.

He made the same point again in 1850 with destruction instead of friction, in the parable where a boy smashes a pane and the neighbours congratulate the glazier: the broken window. The two stories close both doors, since destruction is not creation and delay is not income. Run the make-work argument backwards and it eats the whole history of tools, because if saving labour destroys wealth then humanity should never have taken up labour-saving tools as old as the spade and the wheel.

The shape returns whenever a machine arrives. The newest version is the fear that artificial-intelligence tools destroy writing jobs, which runs the Bordeaux argument almost word for word: the writing a program now does is the seen loss, while the unseen part is whatever the freed hours produce next and the cheaper words everybody else can buy. The general name for any policy that preserves a job for the sake of the job, rather than for the sake of what the job produces, is make-work, and the negative railway is still the shortest refutation of it anybody has written.

the-paradox-of-value-dissolved-diamond-w.context_blurb:
Adam Smith opened the fourth chapter of his first book, in 1776, with a puzzle that defeated him. One thing is as useful as anything on earth and will buy almost nothing; another is of almost no use and will buy a great deal. The pair he chose was water and diamonds.

Smith did not resolve it. He divided the word instead, splitting value into two senses and moving on, and the two he named were value in use and value in exchange. The next generation tried to do better by locating value in production, in the labour that had gone into a thing. The two who pressed that hardest wrote the books of 1817 and 1867: David Ricardo and Karl Marx, the second of whom built it up into a theory of surplus value and exploitation.

Carl Menger's answer in 1871 was to stop looking inside the good altogether. Value, on his account, lives in the ranking a specific chooser assigns to a specific additional unit against alternative uses, which means nobody ever compares water as a class against diamonds as a class; a person compares one more unit, given what he holds already, with the next-best thing he could do instead. His illustration is a farmer with five sacks of grain: one baked into his own bread, one fed to his livestock, one kept back as seed, one brewed into beer, one thrown to his parrots. A rat destroys a sack overnight, and the farmer gives up the parrots -- and that least-urgent use sets the value of any one sack, because the sacks are interchangeable and the use he drops is the one he minds least.

Now the paradox dissolves. Water is abundant so the marginal glass serves only a trivial use; diamond stock is near zero so the marginal stone serves a top-ranked use, which is why a plumbed household will not pay much for one more glass although it would pay anything for the first. The test of the explanation is to reverse the scarcities. Put a traveller in the Sahara with a single canteen and pockets full of stones and the ranking reverses -- one more glass of water now ranks above any additional diamond, which tells you value was never a property of either substance.

Textbooks keep two terms for the two quantities the old puzzle had run together: total utility and marginal utility, the first being everything a person gets from all the water he has, the second being what one more glass adds given what he holds already. Water's total utility is enormous, and its marginal utility in a house with taps is almost nothing. What the move destroyed is bigger than one puzzle. It dislodged the labour theory of value, because it assumed value was a property of the good rather than of a chooser's ranking. And with it went the whole project of locating value in an objective property of the good itself, whether the property on offer was labour-hours, cost of production, or usefulness to survival.

the-powell-tightening-11-hikes-in-16-mon.context_blurb:
The Federal Reserve had not raised its policy rate since December 2018. It moved again on 16 March 2022, by a quarter-point, and the reason is the simplest proposition in monetary policy: when prices climb too fast a central bank will raise interest rates so borrowing money costs more, which cools spending and investment.

The pace then became extraordinary. By the middle of 2022 American consumer prices were climbing at more than nine per cent a year, and the committee moved at four meetings in a row, June, July, September and November, with hikes of 75 basis points each, the fastest tightening since Volcker. Eleven increases in sixteen months carried the rate from almost zero to a range between 5.25 and 5.50 per cent by July 2023. Alongside the rises the Fed stopped replacing the bonds on its own balance sheet as they matured, draining up to ninety-five billion dollars a month of reserves out of the system, a policy it called quantitative tightening, the mirror image of the buying it had done for a decade.

Nothing happened quickly, and that is the nature of the instrument. Prices kept climbing through 2022 after the hikes had begun and slowed clearly only during 2023, which is what economists mean by long and variable lags: rate changes take many months to fully affect prices. Judging whether the slowdown was real meant choosing a measure. Food and energy prices jump about from month to month, so officials watched the version of the consumer index with both stripped out, core CPI, excluding food and energy, and through most of 2023 it stayed stubbornly above four per cent while the headline figure fell towards three.

Something had to break, and in March 2023 it did. A California bank had loaded up on long-dated government bonds during the years of near-zero rates; when rates rose the bonds lost value on paper, the losses were about the size of the bank's equity, and when depositors read about it they came for their money. What killed Silicon Valley Bank was a bank run triggered by rising interest rates. Austrians had been describing that sequence for a century, and they state the Fed's position as a trap with no clean exit: raise rates enough to kill inflation and you break the financial system built on cheap money; hold rates and inflation persists. On their reading the malinvestment built up during the cheap years has to be liquidated, and preventing the liquidation only prolongs the misallocation.

The comparison everybody reaches for is unflattering. Powell's peak of five and a half per cent was the highest in two decades, and Paul Volcker, who chaired the Fed from 1979 to 1987, had taken the same rate to about 20 percent to break the inflation of the 1970s. The reason a modern chairman cannot go near that number is arithmetic rather than nerve. Federal debt stood at about thirty-two per cent of national output when Volcker did it and about a hundred and twenty per cent in the 2020s, so each extra point on the policy rate now adds tens of billions a year to the Treasury's interest bill. A Fed operating alongside 120% debt-to-GDP faces a much lower ceiling on how high it can raise rates than a Fed operating alongside 32% debt-to-GDP, and economists call that constraint fiscal dominance.

the-scholarly-rebuttal-to-macleans-democ.context_blurb:
Public choice is the branch of economics that studies government the way an economist studies a grocery store: by asking what the people inside it are rewarded for. James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock built it in the 1960s, and Buchanan took the Nobel Prize for it in 1986.

Its founding assumption is deflating rather than cynical. A senator wants re-election, an agency head wants a bigger budget, a regulator wants a comfortable job in the industry he oversees, and the sensible move is to expect an official to answer such rewards the way a shopkeeper answers prices, because people in government act on incentives like everyone else. The view the theory was built against is the one older civics textbooks assumed without argument, that government officials always act in the public interest. Buchanan and Tullock never claimed officials are wicked; they claimed that no analysis is honest if it models shoppers as self-interested and the voters' agents as saints.

In 2017 the Duke historian Nancy MacLean recast that project as a conspiracy. Her book Democracy in Chains argued that Buchanan had run a stealth campaign against American democracy on behalf of rich donors, and the publishing world took to it: it was a New York Times bestseller and a National Book Award finalist.

Then specialists read her footnotes. Michael Munger, Peter Boettke, and the pair of Jean-Baptiste Fleury and Alain Marciano, writing from different political corners, converged on one charge: that MacLean quoted Buchanan and his correspondents systematically out of context. Several passages, they showed, reversed the sense of what Buchanan had actually written, and the archive she cited did not carry the segregationist link she drew from it. Fleury and Marciano published their review essay in December 2018, in the journal of record for arguments about the history of the subject, The Journal of Economic Literature.

What a student should carry away from the two stacks of reading is not that acclaim is worthless, nor that critics are automatically right. It is narrower and more useful than either: when a work receives wide media acclaim but is met by systematic detailed rebuttal from experts across ideological lines, that pattern is itself diagnostic.

the-state-is-the-great-fiction-the-most-.context_blurb:
Frederic Bastiat was a French landowner's son turned pamphleteer who spent the 1840s writing short, funny, deadly essays in defence of free trade. His method has a name he gave it himself in the 1850 essay on what is seen and what is not: every time a government acts there is a visible result and an invisible one, the thing that was never built because the cash went somewhere else. He taught his readers to look for both, the seen and the unseen.

In 1848 Paris rose in revolution, a provisional government promised a wave of new programmes, and Bastiat, elected that April to the Constituent Assembly, printed an essay called The State on September 25, in the Paris daily Journal des Debats. It opens with a joke prize, not five hundred francs but a million, with crowns, crosses and ribbons, offered to whoever could set down a clear and honest definition of one word, and the word was 'the State'. Then he submitted his own entry. The State, as he put it, is the great fiction through which each man tries to live at his neighbours' cost, and that middle noun, fiction, is the word everyone quotes. The fiction he names is the belief that a government owns some fund of wealth of its own, when in truth every dollar the government gives out is taken from someone else.

He aimed the essay at one particular room. The Journal des Debats spoke for the propertied liberal middle class that had backed Louis-Philippe, and it was that liberal-Orleanist bourgeois readership Bastiat meant to reach, not the men on the barricades. He also held a seat where the arithmetic landed: through 1848 and 1849 he sat on the Constituent Assembly's finance committee, the body handling the taxes and the spending his famous sentence described. His complaint about its habits was precise, that new benefits went onto the list without the tax or the borrowing that would have to pay for them.

The line is about voting as much as about money. Once a benefit can be legislated, voters can vote themselves benefits paid for by their neighbors, and every group can hope to come out a net taker while somebody else turns out to be the net payer. In a companion pamphlet of 1850, The Law, Bastiat sharpened the same thought: get a statute passed that makes taking your neighbour's property lawful and the taking starts to look respectable and orderly, which he called legal plunder. He died that December.

A century later the recognition came back as a research programme. James Buchanan, who shared with Gordon Tullock the plain observation that voters and politicians and civil servants answer incentives like everyone else, built the field called public choice and took the 1986 Nobel Prize for it, citing Bastiat as the classical statement of the same point. And the recognition, not the quotable slogan, is what a reader gets today: that every promised state benefit must be funded by a transfer from other citizens, seen or unseen. Whether a particular transfer is worth making is a separate argument, and Bastiat's sentence does not settle it.

the-us-sugar-program-candy-jobs-that-fle.context_blurb:
Sugar in an American supermarket costs about double what the same sugar fetches on world markets, and has for decades. Washington holds it there with a quota on how much foreign sugar may enter and with cheap federal loans to domestic growers, machinery built by the Sugar Act of 1934 and renewed in every Farm Bill since. Through the 2010s the American price ran near thirty-five cents a pound against a world price near seventeen, and the food propped up this way is sugar.

Who pays is the first question Bastiat would ask. The growers are helped, and visibly so. The cost falls on American shoppers, who pay a little more for candy, for soda and for food, a few dollars a year each, which nobody notices and nobody organises against.

The second question is who else uses the stuff. In 2003 Kraft shut the plant in Holland, Michigan that had made Life Savers for generations and moved the work to Montreal, because Canadian sugar cost about half as much, and sugar is most of a Life Saver. The reason for the gap is simple: US laws limit sugar imports so American sugar farmers can charge more. Two more candy firms from the Chicago area went the same way in the 2000s and said plainly why: Ferrara Pan and Brach's, both of which shifted much of their production to Mexico. That is exactly what the seen-and-unseen method predicts when a law doubles the price of a factory's main ingredient above the world price: they move production to where sugar is cheap.

So why does the programme survive every Farm Bill? Because of the shape of the arithmetic. About four thousand sugar farms collect large, concentrated gains and pay for lobbyists, while some three hundred million consumers each lose a few dollars and do nothing, so the small organised group beats the big unorganised one, which is Mancur Olson's concentrated benefits and dispersed costs, set out in his 1965 book on collective action. The best-known winners are one Cuban-American family in Florida, whose companies own Florida Crystals and control Domino Sugar; a 1998 estimate built on government figures put their take at sixty million dollars a year or more, and the name is the Fanjul family.

Bastiat had written the parody already, in 1845. French candlemakers, in his tale, petition the government for a law to shut out the sun, since the sun hands out light for nothing and competes unfairly with honest domestic light-makers, and the satire is called The Petition of the Candlemakers. The move to recognise is not that a particular quota is wicked. It is that the beneficiary of a trade restriction is always small, organised and perfectly aware of itself, while the people who pay are many and barely feel the bill.

the-white-papers-twelve-sections.context_blurb:
On 31 October 2008 someone writing as Satoshi Nakamoto posted a paper to a small cryptography mailing list, describing a digital money called Bitcoin that moved from hand to hand with no bank in between. For a proposal with that much arithmetic in it, the document is famously brief: about nine pages of body text, in twelve numbered sections, plus an abstract and a page of references.

It opens by naming the problem rather than the solution. Its first line observes that commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments. Everything after that is an argument that cryptography and a network's own vote can take the middleman out.

The security comes from making cheating expensive. To attach a new block of transactions, a miner has to solve a hard puzzle that burns real electricity, so anyone wanting to rewrite history would have to redo the puzzle for every block after the one he altered. Satoshi called the method Proof-of-Work and credited earlier work for it in the citations. Those citations are short and specific: the reference list names Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money.

Two pieces of engineering make the thing practical. Section 7 explains how a node can throw away old spent records and still prove that nothing has been altered, because each block header carries a short hash summary of its transactions, arranged in a shape that lets any single record be checked on its own: a Merkle tree, named for Ralph Merkle, who patented the structure in 1979. The next section does the same favour for small computers. A wallet can keep only the little block headers plus a short proof that a payment sits inside one of them, which means a small device can verify payments without running a full node. That is what made phone wallets possible at all.

The last section is the shortest thing in the paper. Section twelve is the Conclusion, roughly two paragraphs, recapping the coin as a chain of signatures and the assumption that honest miners hold more computing power than any attacker. Nine pages, no institution behind it, a pseudonym for an author, and a monetary system whose fixed supply has been argued over ever since.

trygve-hoff-and-the-1938-restatement.context_blurb:
Trygve Hoff did not look like the man who would write the decade's best book on socialist planning. He ran a family business in Oslo and edited Farmand, a free-market magazine with a wide readership, and he took his doctorate at the University of Oslo in 1938 with a dissertation on an argument that had been running since 1920.

That argument is the socialist calculation debate. Through the 1920s and 1930s Friedrich Hayek and Ludwig von Mises had asked whether a state committee could price every good in a country, bread and steel and shoes and tractors, with no market of buyers and sellers to set those prices, and their answer was no -- without market prices, planners are flying blind. Hoff's book did what nobody else had attempted. It pulled the entire quarrel into one volume, defended Mises against Oskar Lange in close detail, and drew on German, Anglo-American, and Soviet-planning sources together. The Norwegian original was Okonomisk kalkulasjon i socialistiske samfund; an English translation followed eleven years later, published in London in 1949 as Economic Calculation in the Socialist Society.

His second career cost him. When Nazi Germany occupied Norway, Hoff's outspoken editorials marked him out, and the occupation authorities arrested him for the editorship; he spent much of the war in prison and a concentration camp. He survived it, and Farmand became the leading classical-liberal paper of the Nordic countries.

In April 1947 Hayek called thirty-nine scholars to a hotel on Mont Pelerin, the mountain above Lake Geneva, to test whether classical liberal ideas, limited government and private property and free markets and the rule of law, could still be defended after the war, and Hoff was among the founders of The Mont Pelerin Society. He sat in that first cohort with Mises, Hayek, Friedman, Ropke, Robbins, Popper, Stigler, Machlup and Knight.

The book went out of print, and the Ludwig von Mises Institute, the American centre founded to carry on the work of Mises and Rothbard, brought it back into circulation with a fresh foreword by the Swiss-born monetarist Karl Brunner. Hoff stands for a whole generation of continental liberals whose work the war interrupted and who carried the pre-war Vienna argument into the institutions of the post-war world.

venezuelas-bitcoin-mining-and-the-clap-b.context_blurb:
When a country's prices stop working, its people do not stop allocating; they find something else to allocate by. Venezuela through the 2010s ran two parallel informal economies at once, and watching them side by side is the plainest lesson in the subject anyone has filmed.

The first ran on a subsidy. Nearly everything in the country cost thousands of percent more each year, yet one input stayed almost free, because the state held its household price far under what producing it actually cost: electricity, whose domestic price was set far below production cost. Plug mining rigs into a socket like that during a hyperinflation and near-free power converts into Bitcoin, which keeps its value while the bolivar dies, and by 2018 Venezuela had one of the largest mining populations per head in Latin America. The government did not celebrate. For years the Maduro regime treated miners as a political problem, since savings held in Bitcoin sit outside the state's reach; it sent police to raid mining operations and seize rigs, and in May 2024 it cut mining off the national power grid.

The second ran on loyalty. With private shops unable to stock food at mandated prices, the state began handing out subsidized boxes of rice, cornmeal, cooking oil and canned fish through neighborhood committees, and the four-letter Spanish acronym is CLAP (Comites Locales de Abastecimiento y Produccion). Reporters and neighbors soon noticed which blocks got boxes and which did not, because a household that stopped voting the right way stopped being supplied, which shows that it can be used as a tool to force people to support the ruling party. Opposition figures and journalists at Reuters and the New York Times documented that condition between 2016 and 2019.

The idea that explains the contrast is ninety years older than either economy. In his 1920 essay on economic calculation, Ludwig von Mises argued that without real market prices, a planner cannot figure out what to make, so an economy stripped of prices must grope in the dark. Two writers put the Bitcoin half of the Venezuelan story on the record in 2019 for the Human Rights Foundation, documenting ordinary savers rather than speculators using it to outrun hyperinflation: Alejandro Machado and Jill Carlson. Set the two systems beside each other and you see what replaced the price system in Venezuela: the underground global market via Bitcoin, and political loyalty via CLAP. The Austrian prediction was that a suppressed price would come back as something; Venezuela made the something visible.

wei-dai-and-b-money-november-1998.context_blurb:
Wei Dai, a Chinese-born American cryptographer, was writing serious code long before Bitcoin existed. The library he wrote and still maintains, which other programmers drop into their own applications to get strong ciphers, is called Crypto++. In November 1998 he posted something else: a two-page sketch of a digital cash, sent to a cypherpunk mailing list, which he named b-money.

The cypherpunks had been circling one idea for a decade. Money whose quantity is settled by mathematics and code rather than by anybody's decision cannot be printed at will by a bank or a government, and Bitcoin, arriving in 2009, built straight onto that, because the money's supply is fixed by math, not by a person deciding.

B-money broke with the digital cash that came before it, which had leaned on a trusted issuer. Dai's version had no master ledger on any server. Instead every participant would maintain a separate private copy of every user's balances, updating it as signed transactions were broadcast across the network. New money came into existence when users solved computational puzzles, a technique he took from Hashcash, the anti-spam scheme Adam Back had published the year before, and the technique is proof-of-work.

He was honest about what he had not finished. His first protocol, he wrote, was impractical, because it leaned on a synchronous and unjammable anonymous broadcast channel, and an appendix names money creation as a weak spot, since every account keeper had to agree on a computation's cost while computing raced ahead. That was an invitation for somebody else to solve the rest.

Ten years later somebody did. Satoshi Nakamoto emailed Dai on 22 August 2008, ten weeks before the white paper appeared, to ask the year b-money was published so that he could cite it. That paper's reference list opens with Wei Dai's b-money, cited ahead of everything else. And the gaps Dai had left, agreeing on new money and on a single shared record, are the ones Bitcoin closed with an issue schedule fixed in its code and the longest-chain rule, which is why the b-money sketch reads today as the bridge between the trusted-issuer era and the trustless one.

The debt shows up in the plumbing. Bitcoin's smallest unit is the satoshi; when Ethereum launched in 2015 it named its smallest denomination the wei, one billion billionth of an ether, after Wei Dai, and the habit tells you how the field reads its own past, since cryptocurrencies openly honor the earlier thinkers whose ideas made them possible.

why-the-austrians-won-the-1989-verdict.context_blurb:
For twenty-eight years a concrete wall split one German city, and guards shot people who tried to cross from the eastern side to the free and prosperous west. In November 1989 peaceful crowds took it apart with hammers while the guards stood aside, and the thing they demolished was the Berlin Wall. Two years later the state behind it broke into fifteen countries, and what had failed was a centrally planned command economy, under which Moscow had spent some seventy years setting the output of every farm and factory, down to the number of tractors and the wage in each region.

The prediction had been on the record from the beginning. In 1920 Ludwig von Mises published an essay in a German social-science journal arguing that a fully socialist economy must end in chronic shortage, glut and waste, for want of any real price with which to weigh the cost of making one thing against another, and that essay is Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth. Friedrich Hayek shifted the argument in September 1945: the barrier was not the arithmetic but a kind of information that markets create and no ministry can obtain, namely the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds. English-speaking economists met the 1920 essay only in 1935, in a volume Hayek edited and introduced, and that translation set the terms of the whole planning-versus-markets debate for decades.

Then the evidence arrived from three directions. From December 1978 China's leadership began letting farmers sell on their own account anything they grew beyond the state's required quota, and output jumped within two seasons, for the plainest reason there is: farmers work harder when they get to keep more of what they produce. Vietnam copied the move in 1986, freeing crop sales, scrapping most price controls and admitting foreign investors, and those reforms moved the country from central planning toward a market economy, with income per head rising many times over since. And a team of French historians under Stephane Courtois added up what the regimes had cost, about a hundred million lives across the Soviet Union, Maoist China, the Khmer Rouge, North Korea and the rest, in a 1997 volume called The Black Book of Communism.

The most interesting witness stood on the other side. Robert Heilbroner had taught economic history to millions through The Worldly Philosophers and had been a socialist all his life, and in a 1990 magazine essay he wrote plainly that Mises had been right. He named what Soviet pricing had produced in a phrase worth keeping: grotesque misallocations of effort. Steel plants with no buyer, warehouses of unsellable shoes, and nothing on the shelf that anybody wanted. The question the experiment had answered, at the cost of some hundred million lives by the Black Book's count, was whether human beings could design an economic system rationally from a central point.

One oddity survives the verdict. Don Lavoie argued in 1985, in Rivalry and Central Planning, that the mainstream had answered Mises about prices and never engaged Hayek about knowledge, and Austrians since, among them Guido Huelsmann, Peter Boettke and Joseph Salerno, have described the result: the profession absorbed the empirical result while keeping Lange's blackboard verdict. Which is why, on their reading, market-socialist proposals keep reappearing in every generation.

zimbabwe-2007-2009-the-100-trillion-note.context_blurb:
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe from 1980 to 2017, and the monetary disaster at the end of it started with land. From 2000 his government seized farms from the commercial farmers who had worked them for decades and handed them to political allies, most of whom had never raised a crop, and the country went from feeding itself to needing food aid. With the farms went the tax base.

By 2008 the treasury was empty and the Reserve Bank was printing to pay soldiers and civil servants. That is the whole recipe, and Zimbabwe followed it exactly: a fiscal deficit from collapsed tax base plus central-bank money-printing to close it. In November 2008 the monthly rate of inflation reached about 79.6 billion percent, with prices doubling roughly every twenty-four hours, a figure beaten in recorded history only by Hungary's pengo in 1946. In January 2009 the central bank issued a banknote with a face value of 100 trillion Zimbabwe dollars, one of the largest denominations ever printed, and on its first day it was worth around 30 US dollars.

What rescued daily life was not a policy. Farmers would not sell food for paper that was worthless by evening, so Zimbabweans began trading in money from elsewhere: the US dollar, the South African rand, and the Botswana pula. The order of events is the part worth noticing, because ordinary people spontaneously adopted foreign currencies from below, before the government formally allowed it. In every hyperinflation people at last refuse to hold the dying note, which is a fact about what money is: something accepted rather than something decreed.

The formalities came afterwards. The Reserve Bank demonetised the old currency in June 2015, when it valued a hundred-trillion note at 40 US cents. The notes themselves found a second career, and the hundred-trillion bills now serve as souvenirs selling for a few US dollars each on collector markets, which makes the cheapest monetary-history lesson available anywhere.

The lesson that comes out of it is Bastiat's. Seen: soldiers and civil servants receiving pay; Unseen: every existing citizen's savings destroyed. The visible achievement was that the army and the civil service got paid; the invisible cost was every bank balance and every banknote already sitting in a Zimbabwean pocket.

adam-back-s-hashcash-and-reference-6.context_blurb:
In 1997 Adam Back, a British cryptographer, offered a small fix for junk email that he called Hashcash. Back belonged to the cypherpunks, a scattered online circle of programmers who dreamed of digital cash without banks. Eleven years later his little trick became one of the load-bearing beams of Bitcoin. It rests on one observation: make something costly to produce but cheap to check.

Spam exists because an email costs its sender almost nothing. Back's idea was to make every message carry a stamp of computer effort, a small puzzle that keeps the sender's machine busy for about half a second. A person who writes twenty messages a day spends ten seconds of computing on them and never notices. Multiply that half-second by a million messages, though, and the puzzle work stretches into hours or days. A spammer simply could not afford to keep going, because the puzzles would swallow his machines' time.

Computer scientists call such a lopsided puzzle, slow to solve yet checked by the recipient in a blink, proof-of-work. The idea is a little older than Hashcash; Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor had described something like it in 1993. In the mid-2000s Microsoft's mail servers tried Hashcash-style postmarks against spam through a research effort called Penny Black. The stamps never spread everywhere, because every email program on earth would have had to switch at the same moment.

Other cypherpunks saw money in the stamp. Wei Dai's b-money proposal of 1998 and Hal Finney's Reusable Proof-of-Work, or RPOW, in 2004 both leaned on Hashcash to sketch a currency made of costly computation. In August 2008 a pseudonymous programmer, Satoshi Nakamoto, emailed Back for comments on a draft, and that October he put the same puzzle-work at the heart of Bitcoin's mining. Because each new coin costs real electricity to mint, nobody can flood the network with cheap coins, and that cost is what makes the coins scarce.

Satoshi's nine-page white paper, posted on Halloween 2008, ends with a short list of eight earlier works; Back's Hashcash paper sits in sixth place, as Reference 6, while the very first entry is Wei Dai's b-money. The network that grew from the paper has no owner, no chief executive and no foundation guarding its code. Since the software is public, anyone anywhere can improve the network without asking permission, and rival teams keep one another honest. Back himself co-founded the company Blockstream in 2014, one of many teams that contribute to Bitcoin Core.

Inside Bitcoin the old spam stamp took on a second job it never had in email. Joined to the rule that the longest chain of work wins, proof-of-work became the way thousands of computers settle on one agreed order of transactions without any central coordinator. Bitcoin writers look back on Hashcash as a turning point. Before it, anything digital, a song, a photo or a game, could be copied for free. Back's stamps were the first digital tokens that cost real electricity to make yet could be checked for almost nothing: the first working taste of digital scarcity.

andrew-jackson-vetoes-the-second-bank-of.context_blurb:
Andrew Jackson, the frontier general who rode a populist wave into the presidency in 1828, spent much of his two terms trying to destroy a bank. The Second Bank of the U.S. was the nearest thing the young country had to a central bank. Jackson's war on it is a vivid reminder that a central bank is not a law of nature but a decision made by politicians.

Congress created the Second Bank in the wake of the War of 1812, in 1816, for a twenty-year term, as the successor to Alexander Hamilton's First Bank, whose charter had lapsed in 1811. From its headquarters in Philadelphia it issued notes that passed across the country and held the Treasury's money, and from 1823 Nicholas Biddle ran it. Jackson looked at the Bank's owners, wealthy men of the East and investors abroad, and saw a danger to the republic: a small group holding control over the whole nation's money.

On July 10, 1832, Jackson vetoed the recharter bill. His veto message warned that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to selfish ends; a privilege like the Bank's, he wrote, helped make the rich richer and made the potent still more powerful. The struggle between Jackson and Biddle that followed, lasting until the charter ran out in 1836, is remembered as the Bank War.

Freshly reelected, Jackson began moving the government's deposits out of the Bank in 1833. Biddle fought back with the weapon he had: he squeezed credit hard across the country to bring on a recession, hoping voters would blame the president and force a new charter, a plan his own letters document. Jackson parked the federal money in a handful of state banks friendly to him, and his enemies mocked them as pet banks, political allies rewarded for loyalty.

Tradition says that in 1834, when a delegation of the Bank's directors came to plead with him, Jackson called them a den of vipers and thieves and swore he would rout them out. Historians still dispute the exact source, but the line captures his tone. Jackson won. The charter expired in 1836, and for seventy-seven years, until the Federal Reserve Act of December 1913, the country ran on private and state banks with no national central bank of any kind, though it suffered periodic panics.

Jackson's enemies were not only political. On January 30, 1835, an assailant, Richard Lawrence, came at him at the Capitol with two pistols. Each percussion cap went off, yet neither gun fired its main charge, a double misfire later reckoned at odds of about 125,000 to 1, and Jackson went after his attacker with his cane before bystanders subdued him. Jackson blamed friends of the Bank. The whole episode teaches one recognition about central banks: whether a country has one is a political choice, never a technical necessity. A determined president killed this one, and only a fresh political consensus, generations later, brought a central bank back.
