methodological-individualism.context_blurb:
When a news report says that a country decided something, or that a social class exploited another, economists of the Austrian school stop and ask a question: who, exactly, did it? Their insistence on that question is one of the school's founding commitments.

The rule holds that acting, choosing and deciding are things only individual persons do. A nation, a firm or a class is shorthand for the people within it, and every social outcome must be traced back to what those people did. The Austrian school, from Carl Menger through Mises and Hayek, calls this rule methodological individualism.

The rival camp treats groups, classes or whole societies as units that act in their own right, and Karl Marx's class analysis leans heavily on it. That approach is called methodological holism.

Ludwig von Mises made the rule the foundation of his 1949 treatise Human Action. An economy, on this view, is millions of individuals each pursuing aims of their own, and every price and trade is one of their choices, so economics has to start from what individual people choose to do, and why. By the logic of methodological individualism, a central plan that handles a whole country as if it were a single person cannot see what its millions of citizens actually want and choose. The philosopher Karl Popper endorsed the same rule from outside the school in 1945.

The rule has a practical payoff. When a Marxist writes that the bourgeoisie exploits the proletariat, a Misesian rewrites the sentence to name the specific persons acting in specific transactions, who hired whom, on what terms and for what reason, so the real choices and incentives come into view.

Some critics take the rule to mean that every language, market and custom must have been consciously planned by someone. That is a misreading. Hayek, drawing on Adam Ferguson of the Scottish Enlightenment, stressed that an outcome can arise from people's actions without being anyone's design.

Ferguson made the point in his 1767 Essay on the History of Civil Society: speech, law, money and trade grew from countless actions that no one planned. Hayek built on that line his idea of a spontaneous order, an order that grows without any single planner in charge.

Murray Rothbard carried the rule into his own great treatise of 1962, which begins, as Human Action did, with individuals choosing means to reach the ends they have chosen. That book is Man, Economy, and State.

mises-institute-auburn-alabama-founded-1.context_blurb:
In 1982 Lew Rockwell, a former congressional staffer, opened a small institute beside the campus of Auburn University in Alabama. He named it for Ludwig von Mises, the Vienna-born economist who spent his life fighting central planning. The Mises Institute grew into the main American home of the Austrian school, the tradition of Carl Menger, Mises and Friedrich Hayek.

One of its early champions was Ron Paul, a Texas doctor and congressman who made three runs for the presidency, largely to protest the Federal Reserve. His slogan was three words long, End the Fed. His central complaint was simple: when the Fed creates new dollars from nothing, every dollar already in your pocket buys less as time goes on.

The right to use the Mises name came from Ludwig's widow, Margit von Mises, who gave the founding her personal blessing and sat on the board until her death in 1993.

Since 1998 the Institute has put out the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics, long edited by Joseph Salerno, as the flagship outlet for new research in the school's Rothbardian wing.

Every summer the Institute runs Mises University, a week of intensive teaching for college students who come from all over the world and pay their own way to Auburn. Why make the trip? Most universities teach little or nothing of the Austrian tradition, so for many students the week is the first time anyone lays it out in full.

Rothbard was Mises's leading American student, and after he died in 1995 Auburn became the home of his hard-money branch of the school. That branch's signature reform is 100 percent reserve banking, which means a bank must keep every dollar of its customers' deposits on hand rather than lending some out, together with the abolition of the Federal Reserve.

In 2007 the Institute published the standard modern life of Mises, the work of the historian Jörg Guido Hülsmann. Its subtitle, The Last Knight of Liberalism, pictures Mises as a lone defender of the old liberal creed of private property and free markets in a century of planners.

Its website, mises.org, puts nearly the whole library of the school online for free: Menger, Böhm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Rothbard and modern scholars alike. Free books spread the school further than any advertisement could, because a student anywhere can read the original arguments for himself and make up his own mind, instead of meeting the ideas only through a critic's summary.

mt-gox-the-first-great-custody-catastrop.context_blurb:
Mt Gox began as a site for swapping Magic: The Gathering cards, and its name was short for Magic: The Gathering Online Exchange. By 2013, run from Tokyo, it carried the bulk of all Bitcoin trading on Earth. Its collapse in 2014 became the first great lesson in what can happen when coin owners hand their coins to someone else to hold.

Its customers had left their bitcoin in the exchange's accounts instead of moving it into wallets of their own. In February 2014 about 850,000 bitcoins, worth roughly half a billion dollars at the time, turned out to be gone. Bitcoiners drew a blunt lesson: coins left with someone else are only as safe as that someone.

Out of that wreck came a famous saying: "Not your keys, not your coins." Whoever holds the private keys controls the bitcoin, so coins left on an exchange belong, in practice, to the exchange.

The man running Mt Gox at the end was Mark Karpeles, a Frenchman living in Japan, who had purchased it from the American who started it, in 2011. A Japanese court convicted him in 2019 of falsifying records but cleared him of stealing the coins.

The end came quickly. On February 7, 2014, Mt Gox froze every bitcoin withdrawal and blamed technical problems. The website went dark on February 24, and the company filed for bankruptcy in Tokyo four days later.

Weeks afterward, the company announced that about 200,000 of the missing coins had turned up, sitting forgotten in an old wallet kept offline, the kind called cold storage.

The founder, the American programmer Jed McCaleb, had registered the site in 2007 with card trading in mind, turned it into a Bitcoin exchange in 2010, and sold it the next year. He kept building. He co-founded Ripple in 2012 and Stellar in 2014, two projects that, unlike Bitcoin, do not rely on proof-of-work mining.

The creditors waited a decade. In 2024 the trustee named by the court at last started repaying them from the salvaged coins. One fact softened the long wait: bitcoin's price had climbed so far that the recovered coins were worth many times what they had been worth in dollars in 2014.

nick-szabo-s-bit-gold-1998.context_blurb:
The American Nick Szabo trained as both a computer scientist and a lawyer, and he was one of the cypherpunks who spent the 1990s trying to build money and contracts out of cryptography. A decade before Bitcoin he sketched a digital money called bit gold that came closer to Bitcoin than anything else, and people have wondered ever since whether he invented Bitcoin too.

In the mid-1990s Szabo coined the term smart contract: an agreement written as computer code that carries itself out the moment its terms are met. Pay the rent and the digital lock opens; miss a payment and it locks again, with no lawyer, judge or court involved.

In 1998 he described bit gold. Each new token began as the solution to a costly puzzle, and each solution became the seed of the next puzzle, so bit gold was minted by chaining proof-of-work, computation that is expensive to perform but quick for anyone to check.

What Szabo prized most was the supply. Dollars, yen and euros grow whenever a central bank decides. Bit gold's supply would grow only as fast as the fixed difficulty of its puzzles allowed, so no issuer could ever print more at will.

Bit gold was never built, because one hard piece was missing. When many people across a network are solving puzzles at the same moment, how do they all agree on the order of the new entries, and so on a single shared history? Szabo could not settle that problem of distributed consensus.

Satoshi Nakamoto, the unknown author of the 2008 Bitcoin white paper, supplied the missing rule. When two computers offer competing histories, everyone follows the longest chain, the one with the most proof-of-work behind it, so proof-of-work itself serves as the tiebreaker.

Szabo also trained in law, earning his law degree at George Washington University, and his widely read essays mix computer science, legal analysis and the history of money.

His early design, his style of writing and his lifelong focus on digital money have led journalists and researchers to suspect that Szabo is Satoshi. He has consistently and publicly denied it.

Oddly, the white paper cites Wei Dai's b-money, Adam Back's Hashcash and the timestamping work of Haber and Stornetta, yet it never mentions Nick Szabo's bit gold, the project most people see as Bitcoin's closest ancestor.

Bitcoin historians sum up the relationship in one line: bit gold is Bitcoin minus the consensus mechanism. Szabo already had proof-of-work, chained puzzles, signatures and a plan for issuing coins. The one hard piece the field had left open was agreement across the whole network, and that is the piece Satoshi added.

on-the-origin-of-money--1892---money-as-.context_blurb:
Where did money come from? Many people assume a king or a government invented it. In 1892 Carl Menger, the founder of the Austrian school, gave a different answer in a short essay, "On the Origin of Money," printed in The Economic Journal: money grew up by itself, out of ordinary people's trading.

Picture a village with no money at all, where a cobbler who wants bread must carry shoes to the baker and swap them for a loaf. Trading goods directly for goods like this is called barter.

Menger's answer was that money came from regular people trading with each other, not from any king or government. Over many generations, traders settled on goods such as silver and gold, which were easy to carry, did not rot and were accepted by almost everyone.

He was attacking an old rival theory that reached back to Aristotle. It held that money is whatever a ruler stamps on metal and declares to be money, so in that view money comes from the state. Menger replied that no stamp can make people accept a coin unless they already expect others to accept it too.

Barter has a built-in obstacle. A wheat farmer who needs a plow may find a plowmaker who wants leather this month, not wheat, so the farmer must first hunt down a tanner who wants wheat. Economists call this obstacle a double coincidence of wants: both traders must want what the other has, at the same moment.

Menger's central idea was saleability, meaning how easily a good can be traded away again at little loss. A cow is more saleable than a clay pot, silver more saleable than a cow, and a small silver coin more saleable than a silver bar. The most saleable good of all becomes money.

Nobody planned any of this. No committee sat and no one drew up a scheme; money emerged as countless traders each solved a problem of their own. Friedrich Hayek later made this pattern famous as spontaneous order, for institutions that nobody designs but everyone uses, and he gave money, language and the common law as his examples.

Later writers building on Menger list the traits that fit a good for money: durability, portability, divisibility, sameness from one unit to the next, easy recognition, and scarcity, a supply that cannot be cheaply expanded. Gold won out over copper as money because it is scarcer, and Bitcoin's fans argue that its fixed cap of 21 million coins makes it scarcer than any physical good can be.

The rival view came back in 1905, when the German economist Georg Friedrich Knapp published The State Theory of Money, which declares money a creature of law. Knapp founded chartalism, the doctrine that money's value comes from the state that issues it and accepts it for taxes, and today's Modern Monetary Theory descends from it.

Ludwig von Mises built on Menger in The Theory of Money and Credit (1912). Money's buying power today, he showed, rests on its buying power yesterday, and that chain can be traced back step by step to a time before the good served as money, when people valued it only as an ordinary commodity. This is the regression theorem.

In The Bitcoin Standard (2018), the economist Saifedean Ammous calls Bitcoin a digital replay of Menger's process. He grades money by three kinds of saleability: across space, meaning how far it can travel; across scales, meaning how finely it divides; and across time, meaning how well it keeps its value into the future, which depends on the discipline of its supply.

Menger's English essay boiled down a longer article he wrote for a great German reference work on political science, the Handwörterbuch der Staatswissenschaften. His entry appeared under a single plain heading, Geld, the German word for money.

peter-boettke-and-the-george-mason-schoo.context_blurb:
George Mason University, in the Virginia suburbs of Washington, holds the liveliest academic home of Austrian economics in America, and Peter Boettke is its central figure. A teacher of teachers, he has trained a generation of economists who apply the old Vienna ideas to everything from Soviet planning to pirate ships.

Born in Vienna in the late 1800s, the Austrian school runs from Carl Menger through Mises to Friedrich Hayek. Its economists champion free exchange, honest money and prices formed by actual buying and selling, and the belief they reject most sharply is that a few experts at the center could successfully plan an entire economy.

Hayek, the 1974 Nobel laureate, gave the school its best-known image. In his view a price is a signal carrying information, telling everyone at once which goods are scarce and which abundant.

The school's starting point is praxeology, the study of human action, meaning people choosing ends and the means to reach them; every economic argument, in this view, builds up from there. Boettke carried that tradition forward as a long-time editor of the Review of Austrian Economics.

In 2012 he published Living Economics: Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow, a defense of the older Austrian and market-process tradition. Economics had wandered, he warned, into models built only of mathematics, which cannot capture how actual markets bring people's plans into line.

His students take the method to surprising places. Peter Leeson studied the pirates of the decades around 1700 and found that, with no king, judge or navy over them, crews wrote detailed codes of their own, covering how loot was shared, how captains were chosen and removed, and what a sailor was paid for losing an arm or an eye. His book The Invisible Hook (2009) draws the lesson that rules and order can grow up from below without any boss imposing them.

Christopher Coyne, another of Boettke's students, examined two ways outsiders try to fix other countries: foreign armies installing new governments, as America tried in Iraq and Afghanistan; and aid agencies rushing supplies into disasters. In his books After War (2007) and Doing Bad by Doing Good (2013) the same finding keeps appearing. The outsiders usually do not have the local knowledge it takes to see what will really work.

Boettke's own first book, published in 1990, examined the early Soviet Union from 1918 to 1928, the first decade of communist planning. The troubles of pricing and coordination that the two Austrians had foreseen, he argued, appeared in that experiment from the very beginning.

Behind all of this stands Hayek's central insight. The practical know-how spread among millions of workers, shoppers and owners can never be collected by a small group of planners, and that dispersed knowledge is the very thing that lets a market function. Economists call it the knowledge problem.

In 2010 Boettke edited the Handbook on Contemporary Austrian Economics for the publisher Edward Elgar, and it became the standard one-volume introduction to the living tradition.

George Mason is unusual in one more way. Beside its Austrians it has housed two schools whose founders won Nobel Prizes: James Buchanan's public choice, the study of how governments actually decide things, and Vernon Smith's experimental economics, which runs economics like a laboratory.

political-business-cycles-nordhaus-1975-.context_blurb:
A central bank is supposed to stand apart from the politicians of the day. But a president who wants to be reelected would love cheap money and a booming economy on election day, with the bill arriving afterward. Economists call the pattern that results the political business cycle, and American history offers some famous examples of it.

Public choice, the school James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock pioneered, assumes that politicians respond to rewards the way everyone else does. For most elected politicians the top reward is simple: getting elected again.

In 1975 the Yale economist William Nordhaus, who later shared a Nobel Prize, turned this into careful mathematics in an article titled The Political Business Cycle. Leaders facing reelection, he showed, have reason to time their boosts of spending and easy money to peak just before the vote and let the costs land after it.

The classic case is Richard Nixon. Ahead of his 1972 campaign he leaned hard on Arthur Burns, the Fed chairman he had chosen, to keep interest rates low, and Burns went along; the White House tapes record the pressure. The usual price of that kind of pressure is inflation, arriving soon after the votes are counted.

The key interest rate dropped from around nine percent in 1969 to near three by early 1972, and the money supply grew fast in the election year itself. In November 1972 Nixon won a 49-state landslide, losing only Massachusetts and the District of Columbia. Then inflation climbed, to about 6 percent in 1973 and 11 percent in 1974, opening a decade of stagflation.

Later studies of many countries found the same tilt. Under that kind of pressure, a central bank's policy tends to line up with what helps the government at election time: looser before the vote, tighter after it.

A quieter echo came in 2003. In June of that year Alan Greenspan's Fed cut its key overnight rate to 1.00 percent, the lowest in decades, and held it there for a year, beginning to raise it only in mid-2004, as that year's presidential campaign heated up.

Austrian-school economists warned that so long a stretch of cheap money would inflate a bubble in house prices that must eventually burst, and the crash of 2008 followed.

Central bankers can resist. Paul Volcker tightened hard in 1979 and 1980 even though the recession that followed helped cost Jimmy Carter the 1980 election, proof that a central bank is able to defy the political calendar if it decides to.

The pressure has never gone away. In 2018 and 2019 President Donald Trump publicly attacked Jerome Powell, the Fed chair he himself had appointed, in speeches, interviews and posts, demanding faster rate cuts.

James Buchanan, the father of public choice, would say none of this is a conspiracy theory. His point is that the Fed's independence is a legal structure, not necessarily an incentive structure: the people running it still face reappointments, relationships with Congress and careers after the Fed, and those shape what they do.

price-control-failures-from-diocletian-t.context_blurb:
Few economic lessons have been taught as often, or forgotten as fast, as this one: when rulers push prices under the level buyers would freely pay, the goods start to vanish. The story runs from ancient Rome to Nixon's Washington to modern Berlin, and it always ends the same way.

Imagine a king who orders that no loaf may cost over a single gold coin, when flour, yeast and firewood cost the bakers two coins a loaf. No baker can go on losing a coin on every loaf, so the shelves will soon be empty of bread.

Rome lived it. In 301 the emperor Diocletian fixed maximum prices for more than a thousand goods and wages, on pain of death. Lactantius, an early Christian historian who wrote about Diocletian's reign, reported that goods vanished from the markets, black markets appeared, and many people were put to death over trifles.

In August 1971 President Richard Nixon went on national television and froze almost all American wages and prices for 90 days, a rare peacetime price control, in the same broadcast that closed the gold window. A ceiling below the market price brings shortages, because sellers will not offer as much at the forced low price.

The aftereffects lingered. When Saudi Arabia and other Arab producers halted oil shipments to America in October 1973, federal caps left over from the Nixon era kept gasoline prices from rising, so the shortage showed up as lines at the pump instead. The defining image of that winter was fuel lines with odd-and-even rationing, under which drivers could buy gas only on days matching the last digit of their license plates.

Housing tells the same story. In 1971 the Swedish economist Assar Lindbeck, a Social Democrat and no libertarian, wrote that rent control appeared to be the most efficient known way to destroy a city, short of bombing.

In February 2020 Berlin froze most rents under a law called the Mietendeckel, and in April 2021 Germany's Constitutional Court struck it down. Basic economics predicts what such a cap does to supply over time: landlords list fewer apartments and let some decay, because a capped rent no longer pays for upkeep.

New York City has kept rent control without a break since 1943, when wartime federal price ceilings first reached housing, so its program began in the 1940s and is the longest-running in the country.

Across all these cases one pattern repeats. Set a legal ceiling under the price at which supply meets demand, and you get lines, black markets and shrinking supply: people wait, trade illegally, or find that sellers have simply quit.

Ludwig von Mises's 1920 argument explains why. In a fully socialist state, with no market for factories and land, planners have no prices to tell them whether to put steel into tractors or into bridges. Rent control abolishes nothing, but a ceiling below the market price is enough to break the local price signal, just as full central planning breaks it across a whole economy.

Thomas Sowell's textbook Basic Economics, which first appeared in 2000 and has gone through five editions, walks readers through Diocletian, Nixon and rent-controlled cities to make exactly this point.

proof-of-work-and-the-digital-lottery.context_blurb:
Every ten minutes or so, somewhere in the world, a computer wins the right to add the next page to Bitcoin's shared ledger. The contest it wins is called proof-of-work, and it is the engine that keeps Bitcoin honest with no bank, government or boss in charge.

To win, a miner's machine must hit on one special number which, mixed with all the data in the block, yields a digital fingerprint, the hash, that falls below a target set by the network; in practice the hash must begin with a long run of zeros. That special number is called a nonce, short for "number used once," and finding it takes trillions of guesses.

No machine can reason its way to the answer. It can only guess and check, over and over, at a rate of billions per second, so Bitcoin teachers call the race a digital lottery: every guess is a ticket, and more computing power simply buys more tickets.

Each guess runs the block through a hash function called SHA-256, which reduces any input to a fingerprint exactly 64 characters long. America's National Security Agency designed it, and the US government adopted it as a standard in 2001; Bitcoin later took it over unchanged.

The network wants a new block about every ten minutes however many miners join or leave, so it retunes the puzzle's difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly every two weeks, making it harder when blocks come too fast and easier when they come too slowly.

Anyone wanting to undo an old payment must quietly redo every block since then and keep adding blocks faster than all the honest miners in the world put together. That takes more than half of the total mining power.

This is how Bitcoiners answer critics who call mining's electricity a waste. The burned power is not a side effect but the point: the energy forms a wall guarding every dollar stored on the network, because an attacker would have to burn even more to outrun the honest miners.

For decades computer scientists had wrestled with a famous puzzle about generals besieging a city. They must agree on when to attack by sending messengers, yet some messengers may lie and some generals may be traitors, so how can the honest ones settle on one plan? It is called the Byzantine Generals Problem, set out by Leslie Lamport and two colleagues in 1982, and Bitcoin offered the first practical answer to it among strangers on an open network.

Satoshi Nakamoto's answer combined two rules: adding a block must cost real work, and when two rival chains appear, everyone follows the one with the most total work behind it. Computer scientists now call that combination Nakamoto Consensus.

Critics point to giant mining farms and call them environmental waste. Austrian-school defenders reply that ordinary money burns enormous energy too, only out of sight, spread across bank branches, armored trucks, the printing of cash and the whole regulatory machine that oversees the banks. Bitcoin makes its energy cost visible, while the old system hides its own.

The miner who finds a valid block collects the block reward: newly created coins that the Bitcoin software itself issues, plus the fees paid by everyone whose transaction the block carries. New issuance shrinks toward zero around 2140, after which miners will live on fees alone.

qe2-and-bernankes-washington-post-op-ed.context_blurb:
In the autumn of 2010 the American recovery from the financial crisis was limping, and the Federal Reserve decided to create money and buy bonds again. This time its chairman, Ben Bernanke, also explained the plan to the public in a newspaper column, and in it he said plainly that he wanted stock prices to rise.

On November 3, 2010, the Fed announced it would create $600 billion for purchases of Treasury bonds, roughly $75 billion a month until June 2011. This second round of quantitative easing is known as QE2.

The next day Bernanke defended the program in an opinion piece in The Washington Post.

His argument ran through the stock market. Buying bonds would lift share prices, he wrote, and higher stock prices would boost consumer wealth and confidence, encouraging families to spend.

Economists call that idea the wealth effect: when the value of people's stocks and houses rises, they feel richer and spend more. By naming it, Bernanke made explicit what critics had long suspected, that the Fed was aiming at asset prices.

Abroad, the reaction was sharp. Germany's finance minister, Wolfgang Schäuble, called the American policy clueless in an interview with Der Spiegel. Germans remembered the hyperinflation of the 1920s, and Schäuble worried that the flood of new dollars would push prices up and unsettle other countries' economies.

At home the program became a campaign issue. In August 2011 Rick Perry, the governor of Texas, who was running for the Republican presidential nomination, said in Iowa that printing more money before the 2012 election would be almost treasonous. He was accusing the Fed of bending its money policy to help one side, President Barack Obama, win an election.

Austrian critics saw Richard Cantillon's old point at work: new money helps those who receive it first, before other prices rise. From late August 2010, when Bernanke first signaled the program, to its end in June 2011, the S&P 500, the index of America's largest companies, rose about 24 percent.

Read through Frédéric Bastiat's lens, QE2 had a seen side and an unseen side. The seen was a strengthening recovery. The unseen was the new reserves flowing into the prices of stocks and other assets rather than into wages or productive investment, rewarding those who already owned shares.

The op-ed itself changed something lasting. Once a central bank openly declares that it wants higher stock prices, that goal becomes an openly admitted aim of policy rather than a hidden side effect.

richard-cantillon-the-1730s-essay-on-mon.context_blurb:
Richard Cantillon was an Irish-born banker who made a fortune in Paris during John Law's Mississippi Bubble and was shrewd enough to get out before it burst. Around 1730 he wrote one of the first great books of economics, and in it he explained something that still matters every time a central bank creates money: who gets the new money first.

Picture new money as a stream, not as rain. It flows first into big banks and companies, through loans and bond purchases, and they spend it while shop prices are still at their old levels. By the time ordinary employees see it in their paychecks, groceries and rent have already gone up, so the losers are regular workers, who are reached last, once prices have already climbed.

Cantillon wrote his book in French in Paris, and it circulated in manuscript among French thinkers for two decades. It was finally printed in 1755, more than two decades after his death, under the title Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en Général.

His key insight was that creating money is not neutral. Fresh coin from a mine or fresh notes from a press reach the economy at particular places, and those first receivers can spend at the old prices before the rest of the country's prices adjust.

Austrian economists of our own time, Jesús Huerta de Soto and Murray Rothbard among them, revived the idea, which now carries his name: the Cantillon effect. Rothbard went so far as to hail Cantillon as a founder of economics itself.

Today the Fed makes new reserves when it purchases Treasuries from a short list of Wall Street firms with a special federal designation, the primary dealers. The new money lands first at that meeting point between the Fed and the dealers, in the dealers' own accounts.

The timing Cantillon described shows up in modern data. During the pandemic rescue of 2020 and 2021, share prices and property soared first, while everyday prices rose only later, through 2021 to 2023. The match with his account is that lag between creating money and the rise in consumer prices, with asset prices moving first.

The general rule is simple. The people who benefit most are the ones who receive the new money first, before prices have risen.

Cantillon also gave economics a word. He described the entrepreneur as the person who pays today for materials, tools and labor at known prices, hoping to sell the finished product later at a price no one can know, and who can be ruined if prices fall before he sells. Israel Kirzner later put that figure at the center of Austrian economics.

Ludwig von Mises, Rothbard and their heirs turn Cantillon's insight against today's central banks. In their reading, central-bank money creation systematically benefits Wall Street before it ever reaches Main Street.

Cantillon's own end is a mystery. In May 1734 fire destroyed his London house with Cantillon apparently inside it, and from the start people whispered that the blaze was no accident. The suspicion that has followed the case ever since is murder by a servant he had dismissed, who was thought to have set the fire to cover the crime.

ross-ulbricht-dpr-the-life-sentence-and-.context_blurb:
Ross Ulbricht was a young American with a libertarian streak who, early in 2011, opened a secret online market called the Silk Road. It became the first famous real-world use of Bitcoin, and it ended in one of the harshest sentences ever handed to a first-time offender, followed, eleven years later, by a presidential pardon.

The site lived on the Tor network, which can be reached only with software that disguises where a user is, and people traded drugs and forged papers there without real names or credit cards. To keep payments hard to trace, buyers and sellers paid in Bitcoin.

Ulbricht ran it under the name Dread Pirate Roberts, borrowed from the film The Princess Bride, in which the pirate's name passes from one wearer to the next so that nobody can ever catch the original. For a man running an illegal market, such a name meant investigators could never be sure the person they caught was the real founder.

Ulbricht promoted the site online in late January 2011, and it kept running until federal agents arrested him on October 1, 2013 and took the site down, so the market lasted about two years and nine months.

The arrest was carefully staged. Agents found Ulbricht at work on his laptop in the science-fiction section of the Glen Park branch of the San Francisco Public Library. The machine was protected by full-disk encryption, so if he shut the lid, its secrets would lock away for good. Two agents staged a loud quarrel nearby, and while the commotion physically distracted him, others grabbed the laptop before he could lock it.

In the weeks after the takedown, federal agents seized about 144,000 bitcoins from Ulbricht's computer, and the US Marshals later sold the seized coins at auction.

In early 2015 a federal jury in New York convicted him on seven charges. Judge Katherine Forrest then sentenced the first-time offender to two life sentences plus 40 years, without any possibility of parole.

His mother, Lyn Ulbricht, who had fought for him since his arrest, kept up the public campaign to free him for more than a decade, insisting that the sentence was out of all proportion.

Locking up the founder did not end the trade. Within weeks of the shutdown, copycat markets appeared, because buyers and sellers still wanted to deal with each other, so a new marketplace opened somewhere the law could not see.

On January 21, 2025, his second day back in office, President Donald Trump granted Ulbricht a full pardon, a promise he had made at the Libertarian Party's convention in 2024. Libertarian writers drew a lesson from the eleven-year fight: a sustained public campaign for one specific person can succeed where abstract advocacy fails, even against the largest legal system in the world.

satoshis-disappearance-and-the-untouched.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's inventor, known only as Satoshi Nakamoto, spent about two years guiding the young project: posting on forums, fixing the software and trading emails with the first programmers. Then he went silent and never came back. His disappearance, and the huge pile of coins he left untouched, turned out to be one of Bitcoin's strengths.

The last thing he posted publicly, on the BitcoinTalk forum, is dated December 12, 2010. It was no farewell, just a plain technical note about defending the network's computers against DDoS attacks, floods of junk traffic meant to knock them offline.

He still wrote a few private emails. In April 2011 he told the developer Mike Hearn that he had moved on to other things and left the software in the hands of Gavin Andresen. The network has run without him ever since, and that is a strength: no single person has to be alive, or present, for Bitcoin to keep working.

Bitcoin's code is also open source, published for anyone to read, test and suggest fixes for, unlike a bank's code, which only its own staff can see. Supporters say openness makes it safer, because thousands of eyes can spot problems and no boss can quietly rewrite the rules.

In Bitcoin's first months Satoshi mined about a million coins, which still sit at known addresses. If he returned and dumped them all on the market, the price would most likely fall sharply, as buyers panicked at so much sudden new supply.

Researchers watch those addresses around the clock. In more than fifteen years, not one satoshi, the smallest unit of a bitcoin, has moved out of the early-mined addresses, and that untouched hoard is the strongest sign that he truly walked away.

His restraint also matters for the currency itself. By never selling, Satoshi permanently removed the founder's temptation to get rich at the expense of the people using his money, the temptation that every printing government and every self-dealing founder faces.

Many have tried to claim the title. The Australian computer scientist Craig Wright spent years in court against people who doubted him, until in March 2024 a judge of the High Court in London ruled that he was not Satoshi and had forged documents. An unknown creator is a safer creator: nobody can arrest him, silence him or pressure him to change the rules.

Why did he vanish? Some think he died, others that he hid on purpose so that no government could ever lean on him, and no message bearing his cryptographic signature has ever surfaced. The honest answer is that nobody knows for certain, though the coins remain untouched to this day.

Those coins are worth a staggering sum. Cashed out at recent prices, they would make their owner one of the richest people on earth, a fortune Satoshi has never touched.

silicon-valley-bank-march-10-2023.context_blurb:
Silicon Valley Bank, based in Santa Clara, California, was founded in 1983 to serve the region's technology startups. On March 10, 2023, it collapsed after the fastest bank run in American history, the largest bank failure since Washington Mutual in 2008. Its fall packed several old economic lessons into one frantic day.

The first is about concentration. Nearly all of the bank's customers were startups in one industry and one region, so when the tech boom cooled and many of them needed their savings at once to meet their payrolls, the trouble hit them all together. A bank whose customers are that alike is in more danger than an ordinary town bank.

The bank's boom began with cheap money. When the Fed holds interest rates near zero, safe bonds pay almost nothing, so investors go hunting for anything with a better return, and money floods into risky startups. Venture money poured into tech companies, and they parked it at the bank, whose deposits roughly tripled between 2019 and 2021.

The bank put much of that money into long-term bonds at those very low rates. When rates jumped, the bonds lost value, but under an accounting label called held-to-maturity the bank did not have to write the losses down. It looked healthy on paper while quietly holding real losses; by the end of 2022 they nearly equaled all of its equity.

The rush, when it came, was a bank run: a sudden stampede of depositors trying to get their money out of a bank they fear is failing. On a single day, March 9, customers tried to withdraw about $42 billion, close to one dollar in four that it held.

They did it from their phones. In the past, worried depositors had to stand in line at a teller's window, and runs took days. Now warnings raced through Twitter and group chats, and withdrawals took seconds, so a run can unfold in hours, leaving regulators far less time to react.

The bank's depositors had every reason to hurry. Federal insurance covers $250,000 per account, but startups had parked millions there, so about nine in ten dollars were uninsured. Uninsured depositors have a strong reason to pull their money out at the first sign of trouble, because they stand to lose whatever the bank cannot repay.

On Sunday, March 12, two days after the seizure, the FDIC, the Fed and the Treasury jointly announced that every depositor would be paid in full, even on balances far above the insurance limit.

Inside the bank, a warning sign had been ignored. For about eight months of 2022 the post of Chief Risk Officer, the executive charged with catching risky gaps between money that can leave overnight and investments locked up for years, sat empty.

The biggest bank failure in American history remains Washington Mutual, which collapsed in September 2008. Banks across the country had made huge loans to homebuyers, and when house prices fell, many of those families could not keep up their payments. The banks had lent against home loans that could not be repaid.

The lesson of 2023 is about speed. A digital-age run can empty a bank in a single day, faster than any run in earlier banking history.

soviet-gosplan-and-the-200-000-product-c.context_blurb:
For most of its seventy years, the Soviet Union ran its economy from a single office in Moscow: Gosplan, the State Planning Committee. Its planners tried to decide, year by year, what every factory in a country stretching from Eastern Europe to the Pacific should make. Their troubles turned Ludwig von Mises's calculation problem from a theory into a daily experience.

The task was close to impossible from the start. No small committee can know what hundreds of millions of people actually want, which shoes in which sizes, how much bread in which towns, because that knowledge lives with the people themselves and changes every day.

The list of things to plan was staggering. By the mid-1980s Gosplan itself drew up balances for only about 2,000 goods, but counting the supply agency Gossnab and the industrial ministries, the planners tracked some 200,000 kinds of products, from grades of steel to sizes of screws. Even that was a small slice of the roughly 24 million distinct items the Soviet economy made.

Mises had argued in 1920 that a planner without market prices cannot do the arithmetic. Teachers of the point often add a rough count of their own: to coordinate an economy you must weigh every price against every other, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the number of products: half of N multiplied by N. For 200,000 products that comes to 20 billion relationships, each shifting daily with harvests, tastes and technology.

The plan always had gaps, and ordinary people filled them with blat, the Russian word for getting scarce goods through favors traded with friends, relatives and workmates.

Factories had their own workaround. When Moscow forgot to ship steel to a tractor plant, there was no market where the manager could simply buy it, so he sent traveling fixers to the capital to work every contact and pry the supplies loose. They were called tolkachi, which means pushers.

Planners judged factories by crude numbers, and the results were predictable. In famous Soviet stories, nail factories paid by total weight churned out a few giant, useless nails at month's end, and glassworks paid by the square meter made panes too thin to survive delivery. Paying for weight or count instead of quality yields piles of heavy, badly made goods that nobody wants to use.

Even some socialists conceded the point. In 1983 the British economist Alec Nove, a socialist and a scholar of the Soviet economy, admitted in The Economics of Feasible Socialism that the calculation problem is real and that any large planned economy must face it.

By the late 1980s shortages were everywhere. On December 25, 1991, Christmas Day, Mikhail Gorbachev resigned on television and the red Soviet banner was lowered from the Kremlin; the Soviet Union, and Gosplan with it, came to an end.

Mises's critics had once expected better data and faster computers to rescue the planners. Instead, after 1991 market prices did what Gosplan never could: they coordinated millions of goods with no committee in charge at all.

sports-stadium-subsidies-the-economists-.context_blurb:
Every few years an American mayor unveils plans for a gleaming new stadium for the local team, paid for with public money and sold as a boon for jobs, tourism and downtown business. Few questions in economics produce such agreement among economists: the promised boom almost never arrives. The puzzle is why cities keep paying anyway.

The economists Brad Humphreys and Dennis Coates spent two decades combing data from dozens of cities. Their finding was blunt: publicly funded stadiums leave a region's economy no bigger than before.

Much of the help is hidden in the tax code. Cities borrow for stadiums by selling tax-exempt municipal bonds, whose interest is free of federal income tax for the buyers. That lets cities borrow cheaply and quietly shifts part of the bill to the federal treasury, and so to taxpayers everywhere.

Frédéric Bastiat's seen and unseen explains the missing boom. A family that spends $200 on a day at the ballpark mostly takes that money from what it would have spent at local restaurants, cinemas or bowling alleys. Stadium spending largely substitutes for other local entertainment spending rather than adding new activity.

Mancur Olson's logic of collective action explains who pushes for the deals. The big, concentrated winner is the team owner, whose franchise grows more valuable when the public pays for his stadium, and who can bankroll campaigns and threaten to take the team elsewhere. The cost is spread thin across taxpayers.

Cities are also caught in a trap. Any city that refuses an owner's demands risks losing its team to one that pays. All the cities would be better off refusing together, but none trusts the others to hold firm, so all of them pay, a textbook prisoner's dilemma.

Some cities hide the bill further by taxing hotel rooms. Las Vegas paid much of its roughly $750 million share of the Raiders' new stadium, which opened in 2020 after the team left Oakland, through a hotel tax. The people who quietly foot most of such bills are travelers and vacationers staying in the city's hotels, who cannot vote there.

In 2008 the same two economists reviewed the independent studies, those not paid for by the teams. They found near-unanimous agreement that stadium subsidies produce no positive net effect on a region's economy.

So why do the subsidies keep coming, and why do voters keep approving them? Two forces work together: concentrated benefits with costs spread thin, and a prisoner's dilemma among competing cities.

The case teaches a general rule. When experts nearly all agree that a policy does net harm and yet it spreads everywhere, look first for concentrated beneficiaries with the organizational advantages to defend it.

The honest summary of decades of research follows Bastiat. Money spent on sports mostly replaces other local entertainment, and the multiplier, the extra activity the spending supposedly sets off, turns out to be small.

tarp-700-billion-in-a-3-page-memo.context_blurb:
In September 2008 the American banking system began to lock up. Lehman Brothers had gone bankrupt on the fifteenth, banks had stopped lending to one another, and the Treasury Secretary, Henry Paulson, who had run Goldman Sachs until 2006, went to Congress asking for seven hundred billion dollars to clear the ruined mortgages and mortgage-backed paper out of the banks. What he sent over was less a bill than a note.

Paulson's first draft ran three pages, and for a request of that size the brevity became legendary: even members of Congress who liked the idea were startled to find almost no detail attached. The plain American word for public money spent to keep a failing firm alive is a bailout, and once the newspapers began using it, the politics turned ugly fast.

Buried in those few pages was one clause that drew the sharpest fire. Section 8 declared that the Secretary's spending decisions were committed to his own discretion and could not be reviewed by any court or any administrative agency -- seven hundred billion dollars with no appeal. Congress struck the language out.

On Monday 29 September the House voted the package down. Wall Street had assumed passage was a formality; instead the Dow Jones fell 777.68 points -- the largest single-day point drop in history to that date, roughly seven per cent of the market's value gone between lunch and the closing bell. Four days later a rewritten version carrying limits on the pay of rescued executives, a special inspector general and a congressional oversight panel cleared both chambers, and George W. Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act on 3 October 2008.

The promise had been to buy damaged mortgages. Within a fortnight the plan had changed shape: on 14 October the Treasury pushed a hundred and twenty-five billion dollars of capital straight into the nine biggest Wall Street banks, without going back to Congress for fresh authority. Follow where the money actually went and the honest reading is that it helped the biggest banks and their owners, more than borrowers with bad loans.

Then the rescue spread beyond banking. Roughly eighty billion dollars from the same fund went to General Motors and Chrysler, while Ford refused the help and borrowed on the open market instead. That is where the standing objection bites: other companies expect a rescue too, so they stop being careful with money, and the carelessness is cheapest for whoever is biggest. Paulson had already demonstrated the problem inside banking. He summoned the chiefs of the nine largest firms to a single room that October and made each of them sign for capital, healthy institutions included, so that no outsider could guess which ones were weak. Sheila Bair, who chaired the FDIC through the crisis, made the objection plainly: it treats careful banks the same as reckless ones, so being careful stops paying off.

By 2015 nearly every dollar had come back to the Treasury, often with interest, which is why defenders still call the programme a success. The Austrian and public-choice complaint was never about the accounting. It taught every big bank that a large enough failure will always be met with a public rescue, and that expectation gets carried into the next boom by people who never read a word about 2008. Congress saw the danger well enough to bolt a watchdog panel onto the programme, because the people spending the money have stronger incentives to bend rules than voters have to watch them.

that-which-is-seen-and-that-which-is-not.context_blurb:
Frederic Bastiat was a French landowner turned pamphleteer who spent the last six years of his life writing economics faster than his failing lungs allowed. In July 1850, five months before he died in Rome, he published the short work that carries his whole method. Its French title, Ce qu'on voit et ce qu'on ne voit pas, goes into English word for word: what is seen, and what is not seen.

The opening pages make one move and then keep making it. Every law and every act, Bastiat wrote, has an immediate result that announces itself and a train of later results nobody notices at the time, so the whole of his economics turns on the difference between the seen and the unseen. From there he drew his test for the profession: a bad economist stops at whatever is in front of him, while a good economist takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen.

The work runs as twelve short chapters, each taking one French policy of the day and prising out what it concealed. The chapter nobody forgets is the first, the broken window. A boy smashes his father's shop window; the father, James Goodfellow, pays a glazier six francs to fit a new pane, and the neighbours assure one another that the accident did the town good, since the glazier now has six francs to spend. Bastiat makes them look back at the till. What the crowd forgets is the six francs the shopkeeper cannot now spend on shoes or bread, and the shoemaker's lost sale is no less real for being invisible.

Within a decade a Scottish free-trader, William Ballantyne Hodgson, had put it into English, and only then could British and American readers argue with it. Readers in other languages cannot use the idea until someone translates it, which is why a translator belongs in the history of an idea rather than in its footnotes.

In America the work owes its unbroken print run to a small institute at Irvington-on-Hudson, founded in 1946 by Leonard Read with the journalist Henry Hazlitt among its backers: the Foundation for Economic Education, which has kept Bastiat on American shelves for eighty years. Thomas Sowell later gave the method a plainer name. Stop at the first effect and you are doing stage-one thinking; the discipline he urges is stage-two thinking, the habit of asking 'and then what?' of every policy that sounds generous.

Hazlitt wrote the sequel himself. Economics in One Lesson, published in 1946, walks the seen-and-unseen test chapter by chapter through New Deal and postwar American policy, and Hazlitt named Bastiat as the source of his one lesson.

the-2004-06-rate-hikes-and-the-inverted-.context_blurb:
A central bank can build a bubble, ring an alarm about it, and then fail to hear its own alarm. The American housing crash is the cleanest example on record, and the whole sequence is visible in the path of a single interest rate.

After the slump of 2001 Alan Greenspan's Federal Reserve parked its benchmark overnight rate at one percent and left it there for a year. On 30 June 2004 it finally began to tighten, and the first move was deliberately small: 25 basis points, a quarter of one percentage point, taking the rate to one and a quarter. Then it did the same at the next meeting, and the next, seventeen times in a row, until the rate peaked in June 2006 at 5.25 percent, by which time Ben Bernanke had taken the chair from Greenspan. The Fed had told everybody in advance that it would move at a measured pace, which in practice meant a quarter-point per meeting. That kind of coded, repetitive language is deliberate: the committee uses it to signal its next move without surprising markets, since an unexpected rate is a shock to every loan priced against it.

The quarter-points landed on the kitchen table. Through 2003 and 2004 American banks had sold adjustable-rate mortgages with a cheap teaser rate for two or three years and a reset to market rates after that, and families signed on the strength of the teaser. When those loans reset into the world the seventeen hikes had built, plenty of monthly payments did not creep upward. They doubled or tripled, and subprime foreclosure notices climbed through the second half of 2006.

While that was happening the bond market put up a warning sign of its own. Lenders normally charge more for ten years than for two, because time carries risk; in 2006 the order flipped and short money paid better than long money, which the bond desks call an inverted yield curve. In American history that shape has been the most reliable omen there is of a recession within the next year or two. Two New York Fed economists had measured exactly how reliable, in a 1996 paper the crisis writers later quoted to death: Arturo Estrella and Frederic Mishkin showed that every American downturn since 1968 had been preceded by a sustained inversion.

The flip persisted for most of 2007. The private research bureau that dates American business cycles later fixed the start of the Great Recession at December 2007, two years after the curve first flipped. In between, the news worsened every month: subprime delinquencies rising, two Bear Stearns funds blowing up over the summer. Ben Bernanke and other Fed officials answered with the same adjective all year, assuring Congress and the press that the problems were contained.

Sheila Bair, who ran the federal deposit insurer through the crash, later wrote that no financial crisis in the country's history had been easier to see coming. What anybody could have seen was a rapidly rising housing bubble and a huge boom in loans to people who could not repay them. Put the pieces in order and the recognition is uncomfortable. The Fed can produce a bubble with cheap credit, then produce a warning signal by tightening, and then ignore its own warning signal for over a year. The instrument worked perfectly; the institution reading it did not.

the-austrian-dispute-about-bitcoin-shost.context_blurb:
A serious school of thought argues with itself. Through most of the 2010s the Austrians argued about whether Bitcoin could be money at all, and the quarrel turned on a single claim written in Vienna in 1912.

The claim belongs to Ludwig von Mises, who set it out in his first great book on money and credit. Nothing becomes money out of nowhere, he argued: whatever ends up serving as money must have been wanted for some other purpose first, since on the opening day nobody could price a unit that had never had a price. Gold was ornament and jewellery for centuries before it was coin. Austrians call the argument the Regression Theorem, because it traces a money's value backwards to a demand that existed before anyone spent it.

Frank Shostak, long a scholar at the Mises Institute, applied the test to Bitcoin in the 2010s and found it wanting. A string of digits had never been jewellery or salt or cattle, so there was no earlier demand to trace, and his conclusion followed directly: that Bitcoin was a speculative bubble that would eventually collapse. What happened instead is the interesting part. A thing with no physical use at all held its value through crashes, bear markets and a decade of official hostility, which suggests that digital scarcity alone can give something monetary value.

Younger Austrians answered that Shostak had read the history too narrowly. Saifedean Ammous, the Lebanese economist whose 2018 book The Bitcoin Standard made the case at length, and the writer Peter St Onge put it the other way round. Bitcoin did have a prior non-monetary use: in its earliest days it was a cypherpunk collectible, prized by cryptographers as a technical achievement in itself, which is exactly what the theorem asks for. Bitcoiners mark one milestone on the way from collectible to money with a famous meal: the 10,000-BTC pizza purchase of May 22, 2010, when a programmer handed over ten thousand coins for two pizzas and a digital curiosity bought a physical good for the first time on record.

The argument did not end in a debating hall. It ended in the record. In the years that followed, a number of Austrian economists came round to the Ammous reading, while Shostak kept his position. The puzzle that forced the rethink is easy to state. On Shostak's reading, Bitcoin had no other use before people started trading it, yet it still became money, and a theory about how money arises has to account for the one case that turned up after the theory was written.

Two lessons came out of the dispute. The first is about the school rather than the coin: even a rigorous school can disagree internally about how to apply its own theorem, and the resolution comes by looking harder at the historical record rather than by re-reading the founder's text one more time. The second is why Bitcoiners think the old hard-money argument has found a new home. For a century the Austrians had warned that a government eventually debases whatever paper it issues, and that a saver is protected only by something genuinely scarce and hard to counterfeit. Bitcoin's claim to that job rests on its fixed 21-million cap plus proof-of-work, which makes it costly to create and impossible to inflate by decree.

the-bitcoin-pizza-10-000-btc-for-two-pie.context_blurb:
On 22 May 2010 a programmer living in Jacksonville, Florida, had two pizzas delivered and paid for them in a currency almost nobody had heard of. Laszlo Hanyecz had offered ten thousand bitcoins on a web forum to anybody willing to order him a meal, and another user took the deal, buying the food from Papa John's with ordinary dollars.

What he asked for was two large pizzas, with enough left over, he wrote, to eat the next day. Bitcoin traded then at something like four-tenths of a cent, so his ten thousand coins came to about $41, which works out at roughly twenty dollars a pizza and was a perfectly ordinary price for dinner.

Coins had changed hands before, for cash and for other tokens, but nothing physical had ever been bought with them, which makes that meal the first documented purchase of a physical good with Bitcoin. The date is now a holiday in the Bitcoin world. Every 22 May holders order pizza, post photographs of it and call the whole thing Bitcoin Pizza Day.

Hanyecz had already left a larger mark than the dinner. Mining in the first year ran on everyday desktop processors and yielded a trickle of coins, until he worked out that the chip built for drawing video-game graphics could hash far faster, and in 2010 he posted the first software that let a graphics card (GPU) mine Bitcoin. That code began the arms race that led to purpose-built mining machines and to the industrial hashing farms of today.

The arithmetic afterwards is what makes people wince. Those ten thousand coins would be worth hundreds of millions of dollars within a decade of the order. At the prices Bitcoin reached in the 2020s, above a hundred thousand dollars a coin, the same two pizzas come to over one billion US dollars. Hanyecz has said in interview after interview that he has no regrets, and his reason is the serious one: the trade proved bitcoin could really be spent on real goods, and a money nobody ever spends is not yet money.

The meal carries weight in an argument among economists too. Austrians who doubted that Bitcoin could be money pointed to Mises's rule that any money must begin as something wanted for another purpose, and its defenders answered that Bitcoin began as a collector's item among cryptographers and grew into money from there. On that reading the pizza order is the dateable hinge: the moment Bitcoin crossed from cypherpunk collectible to a medium of exchange for goods.

the-classical-gold-standard-1815-1914.context_blurb:
For a century after Waterloo the money of the industrial world was a weight of metal. Each major currency was defined as a fixed quantity of gold and could be exchanged for the metal on demand, which is why the years from 1815 to 1914 are called the classical era of The gold standard. Britain led it: the Bank of England resumed paying gold out for paper pounds in 1821, at the Mint price Isaac Newton had fixed back in 1717.

Because every currency was pegged to the same metal, the rates between them barely moved. One pound bought About 4.86 dollars decade after decade, a figure quoted in the trade press the way a constant is quoted in a physics text. The reason is mechanical rather than diplomatic: both currencies were redeemable for gold at fixed ratios, so their exchange rate was essentially fixed, and a labourer in London could post five pounds home to Naples knowing the lire that arrived would be worth what he had sent. Imbalances between countries settled themselves in shipments of the metal.

The system spread by accident of war. Bismarck's newly unified Germany wanted to leave silver for gold in 1871 and needed an enormous hoard to do it, which arrived as The French war reparations after the Franco-Prussian War: five billion francs of indemnity, paid by the loser, converted into the reserves behind the new German mark. What the arrangement bought, across the whole century, was a price level that went nowhere. A pound in 1914 bought roughly what a pound had bought in 1821, through the railways, the steamships and the factories, which is the plainest way of saying that prices under the standard were Stable.

Contemporaries called the last stretch of it the belle epoque, and the economic memory of the years from 1871 to 1914 is of Rising trade, a growing middle class, and long stretches of stable prices, with capital and people crossing borders on private savings rather than government schemes. The Austrians prize the arrangement for a political reason more than an economic one. Writing after the Second World War, Ludwig von Mises argued that gold discipline restrained the state more effectively than any written constitution. In that tradition the standard is The most important instrument of the constitution of freedom, because a government that cannot print has to persuade taxpayers or lenders to fund whatever it wants.

The hard part of the arrangement is also the point of it. Paper was redeemable on demand, so no government could quietly print its way to a larger budget, and it imposed a hard budget constraint on the state and made war spending painful. Wars had to be funded by taxes a parliament would vote or loans a market would buy, and neither scales to industrial slaughter, so what the standard made unaffordable was Fighting long industrial wars by inflation. The standard did not fail, then. It was switched off. Germany suspended gold payments on the fourth of the month and the other belligerents followed within the week, and that is when the classical gold standard ended: August 1914.

the-cultural-revolution-1966-76.context_blurb:
In May 1966 Mao Zedong announced that class enemies had worked their way into the Communist Party at every level, and for ten years China tore itself apart on his instructions. The Cultural Revolution ended only with his death in 1976.

What Mao launched was a purge of his own party and his own country, carried out largely by teenagers. He told millions of students, who wore red armbands and called themselves Red Guards, that their teachers and local officials were enemies of the revolution. He gave them permission to act on that. The lesson about one-party rule is unmistakable: One party with total power can turn on its own people, because there is nobody left outside the party to stop it. What follows when adolescents are handed authority over adults is just as predictable, and it is what happened: widespread violence and settling of personal grudges, old scores paid off in political language.

The movement had its ritual. A target, a teacher or a doctor or a shopkeeper or a monk, was dragged in front of a crowd, made to stand or kneel with a placard round his neck listing his supposed crimes, and shouted at for hours; beatings were routine, and so were suicides afterwards. The name for it is a struggle session. Mao also handed his followers a list of things to smash, old customs, old habits, old culture and old ideas, which he called the Four Olds, and in their name temples came down, libraries burned and family heirlooms went into the street.

Loyalty was no protection. Liu Shaoqi was president of the People's Republic and had once been Mao's designated heir; he was arrested, paraded in front of crowds, beaten, labelled the country's leading capitalist roader, and left to die in a cell at Kaifeng in November 1969 with pneumonia and no treatment. His fate says what everyone around Mao learned: Even top loyal officials could be destroyed if Mao wanted them gone. The thing ended as abruptly as it had begun. Mao died in September 1976, and a month later the police arrested the four who had run the movement's last years, Mao's widow Jiang Qing among them: the Gang of Four, tried and blamed for the whole decade in 1980 and 1981.

The accounting is grim and imprecise, as it always is where the state keeps the records. Serious estimates of those killed outright across the decade run from about 500,000 to 2 million, with millions more imprisoned or sent down to the countryside for years of manual labour. The Party gave its own verdict five years after Mao died, in a formal 1981 resolution on its history: the Cultural Revolution, it said, was responsible for the most severe setback and heaviest losses since the founding of the PRC, and that judgment is still official doctrine.

Deng Xiaoping, purged himself in 1966 and sent to work in a tractor factory, came back after Mao's death and began in December 1978 to undo the economics of it. A farmer could keep and sell part of his own crop, and small shops and workshops were allowed to open in the cities again, which is some room for markets and private incentives alongside heavy state control. Over the following decades hundreds of millions of Chinese climbed out of extreme poverty. The tradition that argues hardest against a project like Mao's is Austrian economics: no planner can know a whole society, so forcing change destroys huge knowledge. The knowledge destroyed here belonged to the teacher who was beaten, the engineer sent to the fields and the shopkeeper whose trade was smashed.

the-faa-and-boeing-737-max-certification.context_blurb:
In December 2010 Airbus launched a re-engined version of its A320 that burned markedly less fuel, and airlines began ordering it in place of Boeing's 737. A firm in that position has one obvious answer, which is to redesign its own plane to be more fuel-efficient rather than start a new aircraft from a blank sheet, because a derivative can be built and approved far faster. Boeing built the 737 MAX, and it entered service in May 2017.

Larger engines sat differently under the wing and changed how the aircraft pitched when the nose rose steeply, so Boeing added software, called MCAS, to push the nose back down by itself, and kept the system out of the manuals so that airlines would not have to put pilots through a simulator. The price of that decision is the lesson: cutting corners to save money can cost lives. A Lion Air MAX went into the Java Sea off Jakarta in October 2018 with 189 aboard, and an Ethiopian Airlines MAX came down six minutes out of Addis Ababa in March 2019 with 157. Both had the same automatic nose-down trim firing on one faulty sensor, and the two crashes killed 346. Regulators grounded the model worldwide in March 2019, and the American ban lasted about twenty months, until November 2020, while the software was rewritten and the approval done again.

Then the investigators looked at how the aeroplane had been approved in the first place. For nearly two decades the Federal Aviation Administration had delegated much of the certification work to Boeing's own engineers under a scheme called Organization Designation Authorization, and the choices about MCAS, one sensor and no mention in the manual, were made under that delegated authority with no outside review. The difficulty is not that such engineers are dishonest. It is that the reviewer's paycheck depends on the product passing, which bends judgement at the margin in a predictable direction. A House committee spent eighteen months on the question and used a phrase in its 2020 report that stuck to the company: a culture of concealment.

In January 2021 the company settled with the Justice Department for about $2.5 billion, admitting that it had misled the regulator about the flight-control software, in one of the largest settlements in the history of aviation. Three years later, on 5 January 2024, a door plug blew out of a MAX 9 climbing over Portland at sixteen thousand feet; the cabin lost pressure, the crew landed it, and nobody died. Investigators found bolts missing, which revived the worry that cost cutting had undermined factory quality control, a problem on the production line rather than in the certification paperwork.

Public-choice writers call this a structural failure rather than a scandal, and the distinction matters. Nobody needed to take a bribe: the people who know enough to check the design work for the company being checked, because the engineering depth required to certify a modern airliner exists in a handful of firms and almost nowhere else. George Stigler predicted the general pattern in 1971, that a regulator comes to serve the industry it supervises, and aviation is the limit case, where the expertise itself sits inside the regulated company. Congress answered in December 2020 with a law on aircraft certification and accountability whose central requirement is stronger independent FAA review of a manufacturer's own safety sign-offs, together with new protections for whistleblowers.

the-five-sowell-questions-a-distillation.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell has written about politics and economics for more than fifty years from the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and his method can be compressed into five questions. The compression is a reader's, not a list he ever published in one place; the questions run through A Conflict of Visions, Knowledge and Decisions, The Vision of the Anointed, Applied Economics and hundreds of newspaper columns.

Underneath the questions sits a claim about why political argument never ends. When people fight over school rules, tax rules, gun rules and welfare rules, Sowell says they are really disagreeing about something prior: what human beings are capable of. One side treats human limits, selfishness and scarcity and patchy knowledge, as permanent, so every arrangement buys one good thing by giving up another; the other treats those limits as the fault of bad institutions that clear-sighted people could design away. Sowell belongs to the first camp, and his most quoted line says there are no solutions, only trade-offs. His 1980 book Knowledge and Decisions took Hayek's 1945 argument about scattered knowledge and stretched it far past markets, and when Hayek reviewed it in Reason magazine in December 1981, the review ran under the title 'The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year'.

The first question is about evidence. A column that proves a program works by printing three warm interviews has given you nothing, since the people the program missed or harmed were never interviewed, so the question to press is What hard evidence is there? -- anecdotes are not data. The second is about cost, which is not the same thing as price. A city that announces four thousand new flats has counted what the program made and nothing of what it used up, because the money, the land, the timber and the builders' hours were all doing something else before. Hence At what cost? -- name what the resources were doing before.

The third question is the famous one. Someone lists the real failures of a private insurer, denied claims and stranded customers, and concludes that the state should take it over; Sowell answers that the insurer exists and the state he is comparing it with lives only in his head, so he presses Compared to what? -- name the body that would actually run it. The fourth follows the chain. A rent cap does just what it promises in year one, because landlords and builders have had no time yet to respond, and Applied Economics carries a subtitle about thinking beyond stage one for precisely that reason: And then what happens? -- follow the chain past move one. The fifth refuses the free lunch. A politician who promises to end homelessness at no cost to anybody is not offering a bargain a human being can strike, which is why the last question is What are the trade-offs? -- every gain is bought with a loss.

Applied Economics, in 2003, drew a line between how a politician assesses a policy and how an economist does, and he does not say that politicians are stupid. It is that the analysis reliably stops at the policy's first, immediate result, while the later repercussions, often very different and much longer-lasting, go uncounted. Sowell's own addition to Hayek is a question about institutions rather than prices. For any arrangement, a market or a court or a firm or a family or a legislature, he asks how each one puts right a choice that turned out to be mistaken. A firm that misjudges its customers loses money and must change; an agency that misjudges its clients may be handed a larger budget.

Run the fourth question on a proposal to cancel student debt and its authors are right about the immediate result: the people who owe money stop owing it. What the question puts next is the change in behaviour, because colleges and future students borrow expecting another cancellation, and that alters what people do from now on rather than redistributing what has already happened. Notice what the questions do not do. A student can run all five honestly on tariffs, on the minimum wage, on rent control, and finish by disagreeing with Sowell on each, and the method has still worked, because what it yields is an account of what a policy costs and causes, for each person to weigh.
