the-great-leap-forward-1958-62-the-deadl.context_blurb:
In 1958 Mao Zedong told China it would overtake Britain in steel output inside fifteen years. The Great Leap Forward is what followed, and it produced the deadliest famine in recorded history.

Private land went first. Families were pushed into enormous farming units of five thousand households and more, each of them economic unit and local government at once, and the name for them is people's communes. The incentive problem is the whole story in a line. Farmers were forced off their own plots and had no reason to work hard, because the harvest no longer belonged to the household that raised it and the tools no longer belonged to the man who used them.

The industrial half of the plan asked peasants to make the steel themselves. Door hinges, cooking pots and farm implements went into village kilns called backyard steel furnaces, which turned out pig iron that was almost all unusable, and the implements were melted exactly when the fields needed them. The agricultural half was worse, because it rested on a theory that was not true. Mao followed the Soviet pseudo-scientist Trofim Lysenko, whose rejection of real genetics had already been forced on Russian farming, and ordered seeds planted crammed together and soil ploughed very deep. It collapsed, and tens of millions starved, and no official in China dared say in public what any farmer could see in his own field.

Then the reporting system did its work. Commune officials who missed a quota were in danger, so they wrote down harvests that had never been gathered, and Beijing believed the paper. Acting on figures for grain that did not exist, the state exported it to earn foreign currency, drawing on reserves that were real only in the files while the village granaries emptied.

One man said it aloud. At the Lushan conference in 1959 Marshal Peng Dehuai, one of Mao's own commanders, sent him a private letter criticizing the campaign, its inflated harvest reports and the hunger spreading through the villages. In a state where nobody may contradict the ruler the result was the usual one. Mao had the letter handed round the meeting and had Peng denounced, and he chose to defend the campaign rather than repair it, which kept it running through the worst of the famine; Peng was jailed and beaten in the Cultural Revolution and died in prison in 1974.

Counting the dead took fifty years and two determined historians. Yang Jisheng, a Xinhua journalist, worked through provincial party archives county by county and published his count in Hong Kong in 2008: about 36 million. Frank Dikotter, working in the same newly opened records, put the figure near forty-five million in a 2010 book, and the reason modern numbers run so far above the Cold War guesses is simple: local Communist Party archives, once opened, showed the true numbers were hidden for decades. The demographic methods differ and so do their answers, so the honest way to state the scholarly result is as a range: about 15 to 45 million.

Mises had explained the mechanism in 1920, thirty-eight years before the campaign began. Take away private ownership of land and factories and there are no market prices at all, and with no prices a planner cannot tell a wasteful use of steel or grain from a productive one. So, with no market prices and nothing to check them against, false grain reports ran on until granaries emptied. The party formally wound the campaign up in January 1961, and the retreat that followed was run by two more practical men who let peasants sell some of what they grew and reopened small markets: Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping. Mao's answer, five years later, was the Cultural Revolution, which destroyed them both.

the-khmer-rouge-and-year-zero-1975-79.context_blurb:
On 17 April 1975 the Khmer Rouge marched into Phnom Penh and ended Cambodia's civil war. Pol Pot, born Saloth Sar, called the year that followed Year Zero: Cambodian history was to begin again from his victory, with the religion, the schooling, the money and the family cleared away first.

A regime that means to wipe the slate clean has one practical difficulty, which is the people already standing on it. In practice that meant destroying the people and traditions that did not fit the plan, and it began within days. The capital held about two million people. The regime force-marched all of them into the countryside on foot, emptying hospitals of patients, monasteries of monks and lecture rooms of professors, and abolished money and blew up the central bank building for good measure.

The targets were chosen by the marks that education leaves. Clerks, engineers, doctors and teachers were hunted down, and one everyday object was enough to have a man shot, because it implied he could read: glasses. Soft hands or a word of French did the same work. The regime turned a Phnom Penh high school into the interrogation centre known as S-21, now the Tuol Sleng museum, where some fifteen thousand people were tortured and killed, and the choice of building says something exact about the rulers: they saw ordinary life and learning as threats to their power.

Execution was done out in the open country, at hundreds of sites now called the Killing Fields, the best known of them at Choeung Ek. Killing on that scale needs a particular political arrangement, and the arrangement is the lesson: a government with total power and no check on its rulers. The accounting done by Ben Kiernan and by the genocide programme at Yale puts the dead at about 1.5 to 2 million out of a population of seven or eight million, proportionally the worst killing by a government of its own people in the century.

The men who ran it had met as students. Ieng Sary, Khieu Samphan, Son Sen and Pol Pot himself belonged to the same Marxist circle on French scholarships in the early 1950s, in Paris, and came home with a vision of a purely agrarian utopia. The regime fell to an invasion rather than a revolt: Vietnamese troops crossed the border on Christmas Day 1978 and held Phnom Penh by 7 January 1979, which settles a question people once argued about, because being communist did not prevent wars between them. Justice came slowly. A hybrid court seated inside Cambodia with United Nations backing, the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, convicted the S-21 commandant Kaing Guek Eav in 2010 and later two of the surviving leaders; Pol Pot had died under house arrest in 1998 without ever being tried.

The whole episode fits in one sentence if it has to: trying to erase a whole society and start over causes mass death, because a society is not a blank sheet and the people in it do not survive being treated as one. Between a fifth and a quarter of the Cambodian people died in four years.

the-marginal-revolution-as-parallel-inve.context_blurb:
Three men in three countries had the same idea inside three years, and not one of them knew what the others were doing. Carl Menger published in Vienna in 1871, William Stanley Jevons in Manchester the same year, and Leon Walras in Lausanne in 1874. Historians of the subject call the cluster the marginal revolution, and parallel invention has rarely come tighter.

The idea itself can be taught with a glass of water. Dying of thirst, a man will trade almost anything for the first glass; offered a fifth, he hardly cares, and the reason is not chemistry: each extra glass meets a smaller need than the one before. The same point holds about people rather than goods. Two men find identical coins on a beach, one a collector with a drawer full of them and the other a boy who needs his bus fare, and the coin is worth more to the poor kid, because he needs it more right now. Value, then, is not a property of the thing. It is a ranking by a particular person of one more unit, and the name for that is marginal utility.

The three took the insight in different directions. Walras, at Lausanne, went furthest into mathematics, building a model in which the price of everything in every market settles at the same instant, all of it locked together in one system of simultaneous equations; he called that general equilibrium. It is beautiful, and it has a difficulty no computer repairs: real people change their minds and new products appear every day, so the economy will not hold still while the equations are solved.

Menger read Walras and objected at the root rather than to the technique. Economics for him was no branch of mechanics: economics studies purposeful human choice, which is not reducible to physics-style equations, because a person deciding is not a particle obeying a law. The two agreed about marginal utility and disagreed about method, and that disagreement is still open; it is why Austrians quarrel with modern macroeconomic modelling itself and not merely with its conclusions.

Somebody had got there first and nobody noticed. The German Hermann Heinrich Gossen set out diminishing marginal utility in a book of 1854 that almost no one read; a Manchester scholar turned up a surviving copy in 1878 and Jevons acknowledged the priority in his own second edition. What the episode shows is that big ideas often show up in more than one place before the world is ready to hear them. What the revolution destroyed matters as much as what it built. Once value is a ranking of the next unit by a chooser, it can no longer be a property that production puts into a good, and the casualty was the labour theory of value shared by Ricardo, Mill and Marx.

The three roads became three schools, Austrian and Cambridge and Lausanne, agreeing about the marginal insight and disagreeing about everything to do with how economics should be written: as prose about human action, as supply-and-demand diagrams, or as systems of equations. That split is still there, which tells you something about the subject: its identity is at least as much about method as about content.

the-nixon-shock-august-15-1971-and-the-b.context_blurb:
On the evening of Sunday 15 August 1971 American viewers watching Bonanza found the programme interrupted by their president. Richard Nixon announced three things at once, and the package has been called the Nixon shock ever since.

The first was the end of gold convertibility. Since 1944, when delegates from forty-four countries met at a hotel in New Hampshire and tied every major currency to the dollar, and the dollar itself to gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce, a foreign central bank could hand dollars to the Treasury in Washington and take metal away; that arrangement was Bretton Woods. What Nixon shut was the mechanism itself, known as the gold window. From that evening onward the dollar was backed only by trust in the government, not by gold, which is the condition every major currency has been in ever since.

The second announcement was domestic and unprecedented in peacetime: a 90-day wage-and-price freeze, extended afterwards in phases into 1974, which held the appearance of calm prices through the 1972 election and then came apart. The third was aimed abroad, at West Germany and Japan, which Nixon said were holding their money cheap to undercut American exports: a surcharge on imports, set at 10 percent and lifted that December once the Smithsonian agreement had adjusted the exchange rates.

The decision had been taken over the weekend of 13 to 15 August at Camp David, in a small group dominated by the Treasury Secretary, John Connally, with the Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns, George Shultz and a young Paul Volcker in the room. What the change meant in principle is plain enough: the government can print far more money without a hard limit, since nothing now had to be redeemed in anything. Connally supplied the other half of the lesson in Rome that November, telling European finance ministers who complained about the flood of unredeemable dollars that the dollar was America's currency and their problem. The privilege he was describing is real: the country that issues it can print more and let others feel the pain.

Why the system broke is a question about budgets. Through the 1960s the United States ran two enormous commitments at the same time, and the Austrian account of the strain names them: the Great Society and the Vietnam War, which together produced deficits that could not be settled in metal at thirty-five dollars an ounce. The broadcast made the failure official. Counting from that August to the present day, the dollar has been pure paper for more than half a century, longer than any earlier American peacetime stretch; the greenback interruption of the Civil War years ran seventeen.

One chart gets passed around more than any other. Plot American output per hour against the typical worker's pay and the two lines climb together from 1948 into the early 1970s, after which output per hour kept rising, but pay almost stalled. Bitcoiners read the bend as the mark of the broken gold link; economists still argue about how to measure the gap and how much of it the monetary change explains, so the chart raises the question rather than settling it. One last interval is worth holding onto. From Nixon's broadcast to the Bitcoin white paper, posted under the name Satoshi Nakamoto in October 2008 and proposing a money whose supply no government could expand, is thirty-seven years.

the-peltzman-effect-safety-regulation-an.context_blurb:
A protective device changes the thing it protects, and it also changes the person using it. The earliest written notice of the problem is an 1908 letter from Colonel Willoughby Verner to The Times of London, about country lanes whose hedges had been cut low so that motorists could see round the bends. What he reported was not what the trimming had promised: Drivers went faster, and crashes became more common.

The American story starts with Ralph Nader's book of 1965, which argued that Detroit cared more for power and styling than for surviving a crash. What turned public opinion was the response to it rather than the book: General Motors Hired private investigators to dig up personal dirt on Nader, the Senate heard about it, and Lyndon Johnson signed the first federal vehicle-safety act in September 1966. From the 1968 model year every new car carried belts, a padded dashboard and a collapsible steering column. In 1975 Sam Peltzman of Chicago looked at what followed. Deaths per crash fell exactly as the engineers had predicted, and total highway deaths did not, because Pedestrian and cyclist deaths rose, and crashes grew more frequent.

The pattern is not confined to roads. American football gave up leather headgear for the rigid plastic shell in the late 1940s, skull fractures duly fell, and neck injuries rose, because players began Leading the tackle with the crown of the helmet, a technique the old leather had made too painful to attempt. The Food and Drug Administration required child-resistant caps on aspirin from 1972. Kip Viscusi checked the figures afterwards and found aspirin poisonings flat and poisonings from other painkillers up, because parents were Leaving the caps off, or leaving trusted bottles within reach; he called it the lulling effect.

The reasoning move is about people rather than devices. Put a helmet rule before a city council and the laboratory number, how much a helmet cuts head injury in a hard fall, is the wrong figure to plan on, because That cyclists and drivers will adjust to the new protection, shrinking the gain. The engineering estimate describes the equipment, not the person wearing it. Market-supplied safety shows the same thing. Airbags and antilock brakes get bought first by careful drivers, which flatters them in aggregate data; a 2006 study by Winston, Maheshri and Mannering used disaggregated crash records and found Nothing measurable, because drivers had traded the protection for speed.

Peltzman's result did not stand unchallenged, and the challenge was about measurement. Leslie Robertson reworked the same American data in 1977, reporting that belts cut deaths among car occupants with no matching rise outside the cars, and he attacked the model on the ground That it left vehicle miles travelled and driver experience out of the estimate. Later critics pressed the same line. Where researchers have gone looking for the offset elsewhere they have not always found it: helmeted skiers turn out not to ski any faster or crash any harder, and head injuries on the slopes fell by a third to a half without any rise in reckless riding. What that shows is That the offset is a hypothesis to test case by case, not a general law. A review of twenty-three cycle-helmet studies points the same way, with two finding more risk-taking, eighteen finding none, and ten finding helmeted riders more cautious.

A stronger claim exists and should not be confused with this one. The psychologist Gerald Wilde proposed risk homeostasis in 1982, the claim That each person holds a target level of risk and steers back to it, which predicts that a safety measure is cancelled out entirely unless the appetite for risk is itself addressed. That is a far larger assertion than Peltzman's and much harder to defend. The press tends to report the whole literature as proof that safety rules never save anybody, and David Henderson has pointed out at Econlib that this overstates what the economics supports. If a study shows that a belt law reduced deaths and that belted drivers drove faster, then Both results stand: an offset occurred, and the law still produced a net gain. The move earns its keep by telling a reader that the engineering figure is an upper bound and that the human response has to be measured; it hands nobody a verdict.

the-rise-and-decline-of-nations-1982.context_blurb:
Mancur Olson spent his career on one asymmetry: a small group with a great deal at stake organises itself, and a large group with a little at stake does not. His 1982 book carried that insight from committee rooms to whole countries, and Yale printed it under the title The Rise and Decline of Nations. The subtitle names what it was written to explain: economic growth, stagflation and social rigidities.

The mechanism is accumulation. Give a country decades of political stability and the organised interests pile up, unions and trade associations and farm lobbies and licensing boards, each holding a privilege written into law, and Olson's name for them is distributional coalitions. Each coalition is small enough to act together, and the cost of its privilege is spread thin enough that nobody fights it. Add them up across fifty years and growth slows because too many groups protect their own turf, which is why the oldest and most peaceful democracies often move the slowest.

The uncomfortable implication is what happens when that accumulation is destroyed. An occupation, a lost war or a revolution that smashes the old cartels and guilds leaves the rebuilt economy without the encrustation, which is why the shocks smash the built-up interest groups blocking growth and the growth that follows looks miraculous. The comparison Olson drew is the obvious one from the 1950s and 1960s: West Germany and Japan, whose pre-war arrangements had been destroyed by defeat, grew markedly faster than victorious Britain, whose coalitions survived intact from the Industrial Revolution onward.

He tested the pattern inside one country as well. The American case he developed at length pairs a region physically ruined by a war on its own soil against a rival the fighting never touched, which grew more slowly afterwards: the postbellum US South versus the industrialized Northeast. The puzzle he claimed to solve was the one the Keynesians could not. Prices kept rising through the 1970s while growth stalled and unemployment climbed, a combination the standard models ruled out, and Olson's accumulated coalitions offered an account of stagflation -- high inflation coexisting with slow growth, because a thicket of privileges raises costs and slows every adjustment.

Olson did not think decline was fated, and the book's final chapter is about peaceful ways out. Later scholars point to two programmes of the 1980s as the textbook cases of a government dismantling entrenched interests without a war: Thatcher's Britain 1979-90 and Roger Douglas's New Zealand 1984-88, both of which took on unions and licensing guilds and subsidy recipients head-on. The misreading to avoid is the obvious one. Critics said he was glorifying war, and he spent years refusing the charge: he explained a structural pattern; he never advocated destruction as policy.

The reason reform is so hard in an old democracy is the asymmetry he began with, written across a whole country. Every coalition fights fiercely to keep its privilege; no cross-society force fights back. The subsidy recipient has everything riding on one line of a statute, while the taxpayer who funds it has a few dollars riding on the same line and a life to get on with.

the-so2-acid-rain-program-1990-coasean-t.context_blurb:
Through the 1970s and 1980s the rain falling on New England and the Adirondacks turned sour enough to kill fish and strip spruce forests bare. Most of the blame lay with coal-burning power plants upwind, and the clean-up Congress finally chose in 1990 became the first large test of a very different idea about how a rule should be built.

The idea grew from the work of Ronald Coase, a British-American economist who wrote in 1960 about the real cost one man's smoke imposes on his neighbours, and who took the Nobel Prize in 1991. A regulator in Washington can order every plant to bolt on an identical scrubber, but he cannot know which plant can strip a ton of sulfur for forty dollars and which would spend four hundred. Let plants buy and sell the right to emit, and whoever cleans cheaply has a reason to cut deeper and sell what he no longer needs, so the clean-up arranges itself around the dispersed knowledge utilities have about their own abatement costs.

The Clean Air Act Amendments that President Bush signed in November 1990 went after sulfur dioxide, the gas behind the acid rain. Congress set a national ceiling on total emissions, handed out allowances adding up to that ceiling, and let utilities trade them, which is cap-and-trade, as against the older habit of telling each firm which machine to install. Robert Stavins of Harvard had directed a bipartisan study of market-based designs, Project 88, sponsored by Senators Timothy Wirth and John Heinz, and its proposals shaped the 1990 statute.

Emissions from American power plants came in about a third below their 1990 level by 2005. The bill was the surprise. Compliance costs came in at the low end of the forecasts and allowance prices far below them, and economists who studied the program reckoned it far cheaper than a fixed-rule approach would have been. So the live choice for a designer is not rules against no rules, since both are regulation, but command-and-control versus property-rights-plus-trading: the first assumes the regulator knows each plant's costs, the second admits he does not. Stated as a claim about who holds the facts, utilities know their own abatement costs; the regulator does not.

The design travelled. The European Union opened its own market in carbon dioxide permits on the first day of 2005, capping the emissions of power stations and heavy industry and letting the permits change hands, which is cap-and-trade on a continental scale. California's 2006 climate law authorised the same machinery behind a ceiling that shrinks a little each year, and the state's cap-and-trade market opened for business in 2013.

The design also has a soft joint, and Washington found it. A 2009 bill from Representatives Henry Waxman and Ed Markey would have built a national carbon market, with most of its permits given away rather than auctioned. Who received that free paper was worth billions, lobbyists fought each other over the allocation, and the bill died in the Senate. The scramble showed that free-permit allocation attracts rent-seeking capture, which is exactly the prize Gordon Tullock had described in 1967. Coase would not have been surprised. He spent years protesting that textbooks had boiled his paper down to a slogan about costless bargaining, when his actual move was comparative: compare institutional forms on their real, transaction-cost-inclusive terms, counting the frictions and the capture risk each one carries, instead of measuring a real institution against a perfect imaginary one.

the-subjective-theory-of-value.context_blurb:
Before 1871 the best economists held that value was a property of the thing. Adam Smith, David Ricardo and then Karl Marx all took a good to be worth the labour poured into it, so ten hours of work ought to fetch twice what five hours fetched. Then in the early 1870s three men reached the opposite conclusion separately and almost at once: Carl Menger in Vienna, Leon Walras in Switzerland and William Stanley Jevons in England. Value comes out of how much the person choosing it wants it right now. Historians named that cluster of near-simultaneous discoveries the Marginal Revolution, and it sits beside Darwin and Wallace on natural selection as a case of parallel discovery.

Menger's own illustration is a farmer holding five sacks of grain with no market to buy more. One sack is his own food, a second is extra food, a third feeds the chickens, a fourth goes to the still for whisky, a fifth feeds his pet parrots. Robbers take a single sack, and the use he gives up is the least important one, parrot feed, which means the worth of any one sack is set by the lowest use it would have served, not by the average of the five.

The same move dissolves a puzzle Adam Smith raised in 1776 and then walked away from. Water keeps us alive and costs almost nothing, while a stone with hardly any use in life sells for a fortune, and the costly item in his pairing was diamonds. The riddle only looks hard while you weigh all the world's water against all its gems, because nobody ever chooses in those quantities. What a chooser ranks is the next unit added to what he already has. A city dweller with a tap running ranks his next glass near zero, his thirst already met, while the next stone stays scarce and ranks high; the usefulness of the whole class runs one way, usefulness at the margin the other, and price follows the margin. That is also why your fourth glass of water pleases you less than the first did, a principle called diminishing marginal utility.

Menger attached a condition to the whole theory. Mountain air and seawater satisfy real human wants and are still not economic goods, because no one is ever made to weigh this breath against the next; before any ranking can happen, the good must be scarce relative to the wants it can satisfy.

The sharpest test is a pair of suits. One tailor spends ten hours and turns out a badly cut, badly sewn garment that hangs like a sack; a second spends five and turns out one that fits beautifully. Counting labour, the first ought to be worth double. Counting rankings, the well-made 5-hour suit is worth more, because no chooser ranks the badly-made one higher, and labour spent on what nobody wants is labour wasted rather than value created.

That is why Austrians treat this as more than a technical repair. Ricardo's 1817 Principles had made labour the source of value; half a century on, a German exile living in London built an entire account of exploitation on that base, holding that socially necessary labour time fixes what a good is worth and that whatever the worker is paid below it is surplus pocketed by the owner. The argument belongs to Karl Marx, in Das Kapital vol. 1 of 1867. And the subjective theory is what makes the later Austrian case against planning bite: if the ranking lives inside a chooser's head and shows itself only when he actually chooses, no central board can hold the information in a file, which is how subjective value feeds straight into Mises's socialist calculation argument.

the-use-of-knowledge-in-society-1945.context_blurb:
In September 1945, from a London professorship he had held since 1932, Friedrich Hayek published eleven pages that became the most-cited paper in the modern Austrian tradition. The journal was the flagship of the American economics profession, The American Economic Review.

Its question is a reframing, and the reframing is the whole essay. Economists arguing about planning in the 1930s had treated the matter as a sum to be solved: given the resources and the wants, allocate. Hayek said they were answering the wrong question, because the real problem is how to make use of knowledge that is not given to anyone in its totality. No one person can know which warehouse has spare nails, what a shopper two towns over will want on Friday, or which sizes a shoe shop should stock. What puts all that scattered knowledge to work, with no official ever learning any of it, is prices in a free market.

Hayek splits knowledge in two. There is the kind written in textbooks, scientific and general, and a planning office could in principle gather that. Then there is the kind that actually runs an economy, held by particular people about their own customers, warehouses, ships and jobs: the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place. That a certain ship is half empty, that a store room is overstocked, that a foreman on the night shift has found a way to save two hours, none of it survives being summarised and posted to a ministry.

His running example is a metal, and the metal is tin. A new use turns up somewhere, or a mine seam fails, and the price rises; every user of tin on earth then economises on it, including the ones who never learn what moved the number. A single price has carried the planet's changing knowledge about tin to everyone who touches it. Hayek's own image for this is mechanical. He called the price system a machinery for registering change and, more memorably, a system of telecommunications, in which each producer need only watch a few pointers, as an engineer watches the hands of a few dials.

The move goes one step past Ludwig von Mises. Mises had argued in 1920 that lacking market prices a planner cannot calculate; Hayek added that a planner cannot even acquire the dispersed local know-how that prices summarise, however honest and clever he may be, and that addition is the knowledge problem. Chicago's university press gathered the essay with his related papers in 1948 under the title Individualism and Economic Order. He came back to the argument in December 1974, in his Nobel Memorial lecture at Stockholm, which he called The Pretense of Knowledge, an attack on an economics that had borrowed the manner of the physical sciences while claiming a grasp of the whole that no mind can hold.

Carry the move, not a verdict. It is a claim about what can be known rather than about anyone's motives: the knowledge needed to plan an economy is dispersed and cannot be gathered up to any central board. A reader can accept that much and still argue about any particular policy. And the essay's closing note is astonishment, because a shortage of one raw material can set tens of thousands of strangers using the stuff more sparingly, with no order issued and almost nobody knowing the cause, which Hayek calls a marvel.

thomas-sowell-harlem-to-hoover.context_blurb:
Thomas Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina on 30 June 1930, into a house that had neither electric light nor running water. His father died before he was born and his mother a few years later, so a great-aunt and her two grown daughters raised him, and the family moved to Harlem when he was nine. His contact with white people was so slight in those early years that he did not know that blond was a hair color.

He won a place at Stuyvesant, one of New York's best public high schools, and was the first in his family to stay in school past the sixth grade. At seventeen he walked out, short of money and tired of a quarrelsome house, and took a job delivering telegrams for Western Union. He tried out for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1948. Then the Marines drafted him for Korea, trained him as a photographer, and discharged him in 1952 without a promotion past private first class.

The explanation he reached for first was Marxism. On the daily ride back from his downtown school, the bus went past expensive shops, a concert hall and comfortable streets before crossing the bridge into his own tenement blocks, and the contrast would not add up. The thinker who seemed to explain it was Karl Marx. He stayed a Marxist through his twenties, writing a Harvard senior thesis on Marxian economics and a Columbia master's thesis on Marxian business cycles. The GI Bill paid for Harvard, which he finished magna cum laude in 1958, and he liked to say afterwards that the best thing about the place is that you are never again intimidated or impressed by people who went there.

The break came from data rather than from reading. In the summer of 1960 he took a job at the Department of Labor studying the Puerto Rican sugar industry, where the wage floor was set in Washington, and the numbers showed payrolls shrinking as that floor rose. He brought the finding to his colleagues, and what they would not do was test whether the law was helping the workers; their business was to enforce it. He drew the lesson wider: that agencies have their own self-interest to look after, whatever the program was set up to do. It is also why he presses hardest on a wage floor pitched above the value of a beginner's labour, since the people it prices out are young workers with no experience, who can no longer get their first job.

He followed George Stigler to Chicago in the autumn of 1959 and took his doctorate there in 1968, and what Chicago taught him was that prices do a better job of steering an economy than any plan drafted in a ministry: the price of goods and labor in a free market. Teaching a course on the Soviet economy finally made Hayek's 1945 essay on dispersed knowledge click, and he compressed the failure of central planning into a line about who held what: those with the power didn't have the knowledge, and those with the knowledge didn't have the power.

In 1980 he left teaching at UCLA for Stanford's Hoover Institution, where scholars are paid to publish studies on public questions from a classical-liberal and free-market standpoint. An outfit of that kind is a policy think tank. That same year he published Knowledge and Decisions, carrying Hayek's scattered-knowledge argument into the workings of courts, firms, schools and legislatures. Hayek reviewed it himself and gave the review a title that settled the matter: The Best Book on General Economics in Many a Year. Sowell's own summary of the whole subject is that solutions do not exist, only trade-offs do, meaning that every choice gives up something else -- you can't get all good and no cost.

tullocks-1967-paper-rent-seeking-as-dead.context_blurb:
In 1967 Gordon Tullock published nine pages in a minor journal, the Western Economic Journal, after better-known journals turned the paper down. His complaint was that the standard textbook cost of a monopoly, the small shaded triangle in every introductory chapter, was far too modest a number, and he made the point by yoking three unlike things together in one title: The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft.

Start with the burglar, because the burglar makes it obvious. What he carries off is a transfer, moving wealth from one pocket to another without changing the total, so that is not where society's loss shows up. The loss is the resources spent on locks, alarms, security guards, and burglary tools, on both sides of the contest, bought with labour and steel that could have built something.

Now run the same accounting on a privilege. Suppose Congress is about to pass a steel tariff worth a hundred million dollars a year to one firm. How much would that firm pay out to lawyers, to Washington representatives and to campaign funds, to be sure the vote went its way? Tullock's answer is up to $100 million per year, because a rational bidder will pay anything less than the prize is worth. With several firms bidding, and rivals spending to stop them, what the contest burns up on average is the full value of the rent being sought. The old calculation had counted only the consumer surplus lost on units the monopolist never produces; Tullock's rectangle adds everything spent fighting over the privilege itself.

The waste has a name. When companies and lobbyists pour money and talent into lawsuits, advertising and political persuasion in order to win or keep a protected position, economists call it rent-seeking. A car maker that hires expensive representation in Washington to block foreign rivals, instead of building cheaper and better cars, is rent-seeking in its plainest form. Anne Krueger gave the term its currency in a 1974 paper and tested it on India and Turkey; India's licence system made the right to import or to operate a business enormously valuable, with firms spending nearly as much to win licenses as the licenses were worth. The job that is the pattern's classic illustration is held by lobbyists, skilled and well-paid people whose whole working day produces no crop, no house and no medicine, only a rearrangement of who is allowed what.

What links the tariff, the monopoly grant and the burglary is a single feature: each attracts real-resource competition for a redistributive prize. Put as one sentence, every government-granted privilege attracts wasteful real-resource competition for it, which is a general result about prizes rather than a claim about anybody's politics. And it points at a design rule that James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock pressed in the 1960s: the policies that invite least of this waste are broad-based rules that apply equally to all firms and citizens, since a rule with no carve-outs leaves nothing worth lobbying for.

venezuelas-fair-price-law-and-the-empty-.context_blurb:
Tell every grocer in a country that milk must be sold for a dollar a gallon when the farmer's feed and labor and refrigerated trucking already cost more than that, and a grocer who obeys loses money on every gallon. Grocers are not stupid, so there will be a shortage -- milk will disappear from shelves. That sentence is the story of Venezuela between 2013 and 2016, run at the scale of a country.

The caps grew out of Hugo Chavez's controls and were tightened after Nicolas Maduro won the special election of April 2013. Queues were already forming that year, and the item that became the world's symbol of the crisis was neither bread nor petrol but toilet paper, filmed in lines that ran around the block. In January 2014 Maduro's government gave the policy its fullest legal form, capping retail prices across hundreds of goods and making an overcharge a criminal matter, under a statute whose Spanish name is Ley Organica de Precios Justos. A new agency, SUNDDE, existed to enforce it.

Frederic Bastiat's rule fits the law exactly. What was seen was the cheap mandated price printed on the package in the state supermarket, where a television crew could film it. What went unseen was the shelves themselves -- basic goods disappeared and Venezuelans queued for hours, because a supplier who cannot cover his costs withdraws rather than sell at a loss.

Each patch created the next problem. A black market grew, called bachaqueo, in which people bought capped goods at state stores and resold them outside at real prices; rather than lift the caps, the government installed a fingerprint-indexed rationing system at state checkouts so that each household could draw its quota only once. When the ordinary grocery trade broke down altogether, the state took over feeding people through cardboard boxes of rice and flour and cooking oil, handed out by neighborhood committees of the ruling party and skipping households that were not loyal, and Venezuelans came to call them the CLAP boxes.

The money collapsed alongside the goods. The government covered its bills by printing, prices doubled every few weeks, and the central bank's own figure for the 2018 peak is roughly 130,000 percent a year, with the IMF's estimate about ten times higher. And the people left: by 2024 the count of Venezuelans who had emigrated stood at roughly 7.7 million, about a quarter of the pre-crisis population and the largest peacetime migration Latin America has recorded.

Two lessons come out of it, one narrow and one broad. The narrow one is Mises's, and the chain of moves makes it visible: when market prices are abolished, something else allocates -- and that something becomes political power. The broad one is honesty about causes. Price controls were not the only blow, and the standard accounting also counts the oil-price collapse 2014, sanctions from 2017, monetary chaos, with the shortages beginning before the sanctions and tracking the enforcement of the law itself.

weimar-hyperinflation-1921-1923-the-whee.context_blurb:
Germany lost the First World War and owed reparations it could not raise in taxes, so the Reichsbank printed paper marks instead, and by 1923 the presses ran day and night. Prices went up so fast that money became almost worthless. In January 1922 a dollar bought about 190 marks; twenty-one months later, in October 1923, a dollar bought about 25 billion marks, and at the peak prices were doubling every few days.

The pictures from those months are the ones everybody remembers. Pay came twice a day so that a worker could reach the shops at midday, ahead of the afternoon price, and the photograph that became the standard image of a currency collapse is a wheelbarrow of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread. People burned notes for heat because paper cost less than firewood, and children stacked bundled hundred-thousand-mark notes like building blocks. The anecdote that compresses it best is the woman who set her shopping basket down on the pavement for a moment: the basket was stolen; the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk.

The suffering was not spread evenly, and that is the economically interesting part. A day laborer paid on Friday could spend his wages before the prices moved, a farmer with land and livestock held real things, and a man with a mortgage watched his debt melt. The people destroyed were the middle class -- professionals and small savers who held bonds and cash, whose accounts and pensions and life policies were all counted in old marks. Austrian economists give the pattern a name and a mechanism: it is Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction, playing out in real time, since newly created money reaches some hands long before others, and whoever receives it last loses the most. Hitler took power ten years later, with Weimar's political centre already gutted.

Bastiat's distinction fits the episode in one line. Seen: money still being paid; Unseen: a generation's savings evaporating. The wage still arrived on Friday in nominal terms while every mark already saved was being destroyed.

The end came fast, and not through restraint. In November 1923 the currency commissioner Hjalmar Schacht issued a new note, the Rentenmark, backed by claims on German farmland and industry and issued in strictly limited quantity, while the old marks were withdrawn. The remedy was a scarce new currency that replaced the old one and ended the demand for the old paper. Germans trusted it almost at once because the new currency was tied to something real and could not just be printed at will. The exchange rate Schacht had to set on day one tells you how far the old mark had fallen: one Rentenmark equaled one trillion Papiermark.

william-niskanen-bureaucrats-maximize-bu.context_blurb:
Picture a government department whose funding rises every year whatever the quality of its work. Its head gets a wider office and more people under him whenever the budget rises, and he never has to win a paying customer. When he sits down to fill in next year's request, what he asks for is an even bigger budget.

William Niskanen turned that observation into a theory. Chicago-trained and a veteran of Nixon's budget office, he published the book that founded the public-choice account of public offices in 1971, and its title is Bureaucracy and Representative Government. It built on Gordon Tullock's earlier work and it dropped the assumption everyone else began from. Rather than ask what officials are supposed to want, Niskanen asked what actually rises across their careers: salary, staff, prestige, perquisites, promotion prospects. Every one of those rises with the size of their agency's budget.

The claim is impersonal, and Niskanen was careful about that. He never argued that civil servants are bad people, and many of those he studied were dedicated. He argued that the career incentive structure rewards budget-expanding behavior, whatever the official mission says. Anthony Downs had reached the same place from the other end in 1967, sorting the people inside a bureau into climbers and conservers and zealots and advocates and statesmen, and the lesson from his classification is that people inside government act on their own goals, just like people outside it.

The model makes predictions a reader can check. An agency almost never reports that its mission is finished, discovering fresh priorities and fresh problems to take on instead, and the reason is that announcing mission completion would justify budget and staffing cuts. The bureaus that expand fastest are the ones whose results nobody can measure, since where failure is visible a bigger budget becomes hard to argue for, so the claim that agencies with clearly measurable failure tend to grow fastest is exactly backwards. Ronald Reagan's administration arrived in 1981 promising to shrink the federal government, fought for cuts and freezes and reorganisations, and attacked bloat in speech after speech; across eight years the headcount of federal civilian employees barely moved despite the political pressure.

Niskanen watched that from the inside, as a member and then acting chairman of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers. He left in 1985, after he had said, in front of the President and Treasury Secretary Donald Regan, that a Treasury tax plan was something Walter Mondale would love; Regan, soon chief of staff, blocked his path to the chair. He spent the rest of his career at the Cato Institute. The payoff of the whole argument is a point about method, which a reader can accept without agreeing about any particular agency: assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions about agency behavior.

zimbabwes-june-26-2007-price-halving-ord.context_blurb:
Zimbabwe in mid-2007 had prices rising by thousands of percent a year, because the Reserve Bank was printing money to pay the government's bills. On 26 June 2007 Robert Mugabe answered that by blaming shopkeepers. His executive order told every retailer to cut prices roughly in half, and police and army units enforced it in the supermarkets of Harare and Bulawayo, arresting those who did not comply. Ask a shopkeeper to sell a loaf for less than the flour in it cost him and the outcome is not mysterious: shelves empty because selling below cost bankrupts stores.

The speed is what makes the case famous. Buyers poured in for meat and bread and milk at the bargain prices, the goods went into private hoards and onto black markets, and the stores across Zimbabwe ran bare within days. The damage then moved up the supply chain. The Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries had warned that the cuts would deepen manufacturers' troubles, and within weeks factories (meat processors, dairies, bakeries) began shutting down because they could not produce at below-cost mandated prices. Nobody can bake a loaf for less than the flour and the fuel cost.

The order did not hold. By late July the government had already raised the official price of cooking oil about fourfold, and in August it began approving rises on other basics, the bare shelves and shut factories having made the cuts impossible to defend. The inflation it was aimed at carried on and accelerated, which was always likely, since the price of bread was the symptom while the disease lay elsewhere: the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe was printing money to finance the government's budget. By January 2009 the same bank was issuing a single note with a face value of 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollars, and that year the country gave up its own currency for the US dollar.

What a Hayekian points out about the episode is its compression. Most price-control failures take years and leave room to argue about other causes, while here the whole chain from decree to empty shelves ran in days, not years. Decree, then the low legal price on the label, then the goods vanishing, then the queues, then the closures, all within a few weeks. Suppressing the signal did nothing whatever to the scarcity the signal was reporting.

agency-budget-maximization-tsa-irs-and-t.context_blurb:
William Niskanen was an American economist who worked inside the federal government in the 1960s and noticed something odd: the agencies around him kept growing even when their work did not improve. His 1971 book Bureaucracy and Representative Government gave the public-choice school its model of why. The model accuses no one of corruption. It simply asks what the people inside an agency want.

Niskanen asked which single quantity a bureau acts as though it is always trying to enlarge, and his answer was its own budget. An official's salary, prestige, staff and chances of promotion all rise with the size of the agency, so career-minded bureaucrats push to expand it, quite rationally. Take the Transportation Security Administration, which Congress set up in November 2001, in the wake of the September 11 attacks, to screen bags at every airport. Two decades on it was bigger, not smaller, with some 60,000 employees and a budget near $10 billion a year, because new agencies almost never shrink.

Size is not the same as results. In 2015 undercover inspectors from the Department of Homeland Security tried to carry fake guns and bombs through airport checkpoints, and the screeners reportedly missed about 95 percent of them; a 2017 follow-up found little improvement. In August 2022 the Inflation Reduction Act handed the Internal Revenue Service, the national tax collector, some $80 billion spread over a decade, mostly for people rather than machines. The money was meant to pay for about 87,000 new hires.

Congress tends to answer a problem that grips the nation with a new department, and over the following decades the department's budget, staff and offices swell. Yet the problem it was built to solve often does not clearly get better. Jimmy Carter signed the Department of Education into being in October 1979; Ronald Reagan campaigned to abolish it, and it survived and grew. Real spending per pupil in American public schools more than doubled between 1970 and 2010, but the national long-term tests of reading and math for students finishing high school stayed roughly flat from the early 1970s to 2012, the last year those tests were given. Set airport screeners, tax collectors and school officials side by side and one pattern repeats: staff and budget grow, while the results each agency exists to deliver do not clearly improve. Niskanen's model predicts exactly that.

Tie an office's budget to how many people it employs rather than to anything it finishes, and over a decade it will hire more people and invent new tasks so the budget keeps climbing. Public-choice economists such as James Buchanan spent careers tracing incentives like these, and the political scientist James Q. Wilson's 1989 book Bureaucracy showed how much an agency's behavior turns on whether its output can be measured at all. Niskanen's framework hands citizens a test for any agency that asks for more: show that the last ten percent of its old budget bought roughly ten percent of its output. If the last dollar bought far less than a dollar of results, the next dollar is even less likely to pay off, which is why Niskanen predicted agencies would resist any measurement that allowed the comparison.

Picture a school lunch service that swells from 100 staff to 400 in a decade while the number of children eating stays the same. A Niskanen reader presumes the growth reflects what the workers themselves want rather than what the job needs: internal incentives, not rising demand. After winning the 2024 election, Donald Trump put Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy in charge of a drive to find bureaus bloated in just this way. He named it the Department of Government Efficiency, and its initials, DOGE, winked at a famous internet meme of a Shiba Inu dog. Bastiat would have recognized the move: grand buildings and busy hearings are easy to see, while the flat line of actual output takes effort to look up.

anne-krueger-1974-rent-seeking-gets-its-.context_blurb:
In the early 1970s the American economist Anne Krueger looked hard at two developing economies, India and Turkey, whose governments rationed the right to import foreign goods through licenses. What she found was whole departments of companies devoted not to making anything but to chasing permits. Her short 1974 paper in the American Economic Review gave that waste the name economists still use.

Picture two rival firms fighting for the only license to import some product, each spending a million dollars on lawyers and lobbyists. One wins, one loses, and nothing new has been made. The country is no richer, because the money produced nothing; it only paid for a fight over a government favor. The same thing happens when an industry, rather than making better products, pays lobbyists to persuade lawmakers to keep its foreign rivals out. Economists call that kind of profit-hunting rent-seeking. Gordon Tullock had described the mechanism in 1967, in a paper on the costs of tariffs, monopolies and theft, but Krueger gave it its permanent name.

Krueger put numbers on the waste. She estimated that the hunt for licenses swallowed about 7 percent of India's national income in 1964 and about 15 percent of Turkey's national output in 1968: effort spent courting officials, hiring lobbyists and standing in queues instead of making goods. She called that wasted effort rent-seeking, and the name stuck.

In Turkey an import permit could be worth more than the very goods it admitted, so firms behaved rationally. They staffed entire departments to lobby for licenses, cultivated officials and made side payments, and every hour spent chasing a permit was an hour not spent producing. Krueger's title named the whole pattern, The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society: a rent-seeking society is one organized around that waste.

Before Krueger, the usual explanation for poverty among nations was a shortage of capital or of schooling. She added a new reason: in state-led economies, a large share of what gets measured as economic activity is really unproductive rent-seeking, ingenuity pointed at permits instead of production. Fix the rules that create the rents, her work implied, and the wasted effort turns back toward real work. India became the test. From independence in 1947 onward, for decades, its License Raj demanded official approval before a factory could expand, change what it made or grow, and businessmen haunted ministries in New Delhi instead of serving customers. In 1991 India's finance minister, Manmohan Singh, led reforms that tore down most industrial licensing and cut away the rents that fed all that lobbying, and growth sped up within a few years.

Her paper became one of the most-cited articles in economics, and others built on it. In 1982 the Indian economist Jagdish Bhagwati widened the idea into directly unproductive profit-seeking, or DUP activities: every way of earning an income without producing goods, from theft to tariff-hunting to lawsuits.

argentinas-2020-rent-control-law-and-its.context_blurb:
Argentina, a country with a long history of high inflation and populist politics, ran a rare experiment in the early 2020s. In June 2020, in the middle of the COVID lockdowns, its Congress clamped national controls on apartment rents; at the end of 2023 a new president tore them away. Because both halves happened within four years, economists could watch one market react in both directions.

The law, numbered 27,551, rewrote every lease in the country. It required leases of at least three years and allowed rents to change only once a year, by a Central Bank formula tied to wages and inflation. Within a year, brokers in Buenos Aires reported that new long-term listings had fallen by roughly 40 to 50 percent, and rents on the apartments still offered climbed steeply, tripling or more in pesos by 2023. Rather than lock an apartment into a three-year contract at a controlled rent while inflation ate the payments, landlords moved units to short-term tourist rentals on Airbnb, to unfurnished monthly lets, or onto the sale market, and some simply left them empty.

In November 2023 Argentines elected Javier Milei, an economist who campaigned brandishing a chainsaw to show how hard he would cut the state and promised to end price caps, slash spending, tame inflation and scrap the rent law. He named his school openly: the Austrian school of small government, sound money and free prices. In late December, less than three weeks after taking office, Milei issued a sweeping emergency order, a Decreto de Necesidad y Urgencia, or DNU, numbered 70/2023, that repealed or rewrote hundreds of laws at a stroke, the rent law among them. It took effect on December 29. Within a few months, new rental listings in Buenos Aires roughly tripled, and rents on new listings fell after inflation as landlords competed for tenants again.

Put the two halves together, supply shrinking with the caps on and returning with them off, and the plain lesson shows: any rule that makes supplying rental housing less profitable will shrink the amount of housing supplied. That is why the episode matters. Most studies of rent control see only the years under the caps, followed by decades of decay, which leaves defenders free to insist that removing the caps would never repair the harm. In Argentina the ceiling was removed completely and supply bounced back within months.

Opponents challenged the decree in court, and judges froze parts of it, but the section ending rent control survived every challenge. The rent law stays repealed, and Argentine leases now fall under ordinary contract law, with terms negotiated freely. Milei proudly calls himself an anarcho-capitalist and an Austrian-school economist, and he cites Rothbard, Mises and Hayek in his speeches. Frédéric Bastiat would know the shape of the story: a visible cap, invisible apartments never offered, and those apartments reappearing once the cap was gone.

bastiat-and-cobden-the-anti-corn-law-fri.context_blurb:
In the 1840s Britain's Corn Laws taxed grain brought in from abroad, keeping prices high for the landowners whose fields grew the wheat. From the factory city of Manchester rose a mass campaign to repeal them, and across the Channel a French essayist, Frédéric Bastiat, followed it with mounting excitement. The friendship that grew between them carried the free-trade argument from one country to another.

Wheat makes bread, and bread was on every table at every meal. So the grain tax fell hardest on poor families, who paid extra for every loaf while the landlords pocketed the higher price. Two Manchester cotton merchants, Richard Cobden and John Bright, led the fight through their Anti-Corn Law League and spent seven years touring the country with speeches, and both became famous names in Parliament. The families who rallied to the League wanted the grain duties gone for the plainest of reasons: the tariffs made bread dearer than it needed to be.

Their victory came in 1846. On June 25 the Conservative prime minister, Sir Robert Peel, carried repeal through Parliament against the fury of his own party's landowners, and he was out of office within days. The episode showed what a tariff really is: a help to a small group that hurts millions of ordinary buyers.

Bastiat crossed to England in the summer of 1845 to study the League's methods at its Manchester headquarters and met its leaders. Back in Paris that same year, the publisher Guillaumin brought out his book introducing the campaign to French readers, Cobden et la Ligue, packed with translations of the League's speeches and pamphlets. In February 1846 Bastiat founded a French free-trade association in the port city of Bordeaux, and it spread to Paris later that year. Its central argument was that a tariff helps a few producers a great deal but raises prices for everyone else, so most people end up worse off.

From November 1846 Bastiat edited the association's weekly paper, Le Libre-Échange. Its favorite example was a tariff on foreign shoes, under which every family pays more for its shoes so that a few shoemakers can charge more. The French campaign never won a law the way the British one had, but Bastiat's writings became its lasting legacy, and he wrote to his English friends for the rest of his short life. History named the English wing after its industrial home: the Manchester School, still a byword for classical-liberal political economy.

benjamin-strong-and-the-coup-de-whiskey-.context_blurb:
Benjamin Strong, a New York banker who had attended the secret 1910 meeting on Jekyll Island that sketched out the Federal Reserve, became the first governor of the New York Fed in 1914. Until his death in October 1928 he was the strongest personality in the young central bank. Austrian economists later saw his easy money as a root of the 1929 crash.

The Fed's chief power is over how much money circulates. When it creates a great deal of new money and pushes it into the economy, prices in the shops tend to rise, because more money is chasing the same goods. Strong pioneered the Fed's most important everyday tool, open market operations: buying Treasury bonds from banks to add reserves and push rates down, and selling them to drain reserves away.

His closest friend in finance was Montagu Norman, who governed the Bank of England for twenty-four years, from 1920 to 1944, one of the longest reigns of any central banker, and together they shaped world monetary policy through the decade. In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, went back onto gold at the prewar parity of about $4.86 to the pound. That rate overvalued the pound and brought painful deflation, strikes and unemployment, and John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a famous pamphlet. To help his friend, Strong kept American rates low so gold would not drain from London to New York.

In July 1927 Strong gathered Europe's central bankers in secret at an estate on Long Island. Montagu Norman of the Bank of England and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany's Reichsbank came in person, and the Bank of France, governed by Émile Moreau, sent its deputy governor, Charles Rist. Days later the Fed trimmed its discount rate, the price of its loans to banks, by half a point to 3.5 percent, to help the Europeans keep their currencies tied to gold. In private, Strong reportedly said the cut would give the stock market a little coup de whiskey. The phrase survives through the later Senate testimony of Adolph Miller, the one Fed Board member who opposed the cut.

Austrian economics explains why such a cut is dangerous. An interest rate held below the level where saving and borrowing would naturally meet tells a business owner, falsely, that people want to save more, so long-term projects such as new factories look profitable. Murray Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) traced the crash to the Fed's credit expansion from 1921 to 1929, when the money supply grew by roughly 60 percent, and once Strong died nobody at the Fed could rein it in. Austrians call the wasteful projects that cheap credit funded, ventures doomed once the boom ended, malinvestment.

Those who fault the 1927 cut argue that the cheap money that poured into New York fueled a stock-market bubble that burst in October 1929 and opened the Great Depression. The episode teaches one move about central banks acting in concert. When they ease together to defend a fixed exchange rate, the country doing the easing can get inflated asset prices even if its own economy needs no easing at all: Strong eased Britain's problem and created America's.

bootleggers-and-baptists-bruce-yandle-19.context_blurb:
Bruce Yandle, an economist from Clemson University, served as executive director of the Federal Trade Commission in the early 1980s and kept noticing an odd alliance behind new regulations. In 1983 he described it in a short essay for Regulation magazine, subtitled The Education of a Regulatory Economist. His two-word name for the alliance became one of the most-cited ideas in political economy.

Two groups with clashing motives can end up quietly wanting the very same rule for opposite reasons. Yandle's model case came from old Sunday liquor bans. Church members backed them because they believed drinking on the Sabbath was wrong, and illegal moonshine sellers backed them because, with the legal stores shut, thirsty customers came to them instead. Yandle named the pattern after that unlikely pair: Bootleggers and Baptists.

In the American South, devout Baptists campaigned loudly for Sunday closing as a moral crusade, while bootleggers profited quietly, because on Sundays their illegal liquor faced no legal competition. The Baptists were the moral partner and the bootleggers the profit partner. Each side needed the other. The bootleggers gained profits and helped pay for the fight, while the Baptists gave the rule moral cover, so that lawmakers could defend it without blushing.

Once seen, the coalition turns up everywhere. When a city tightens the rules on where Uber and Lyft may pick up riders or what they may charge, taxi-medallion holders, who profit from keeping rivals out, usually stand at city hall beside pedestrian-safety advocates, who supply the moral cover. Environmental rules work the same way. Sincere environmentalists support a rule to protect the planet, while domestic producers cheer it on quietly when it burdens foreign competitors more than themselves, so a green rule doubles as a trade barrier.

Economists read the nationwide alcohol ban of the 18th Amendment, which lasted from 1919 to 1933, as the biggest case of all. On one side stood moralists such as the Anti-Saloon League and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union; on the other, organized-crime beneficiaries who ran the black market and grew rich while it lasted. In 2014 Yandle expanded the idea into a full book with a co-author confusingly named Adam Smith, a present-day scholar rather than the Scot of 1776. The Cato Institute published it as Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics.

Yandle turned the insight into a habit for reading the news. In a working coalition the moral side does the visible lobbying and holds the microphone, while the profit side quietly supplies the resources and signs the checks. Regulatory economists, he wrote, spend years learning to look past the moral rhetoric to find the bootlegger.

bryan-caplan-education-signaling-and-rat.context_blurb:
Bryan Caplan teaches economics at George Mason University and has built a career on book-length arguments against ideas most readers assume are settled. He writes plainly, for educated general readers, and starts from a specific puzzle in the data rather than from a slogan. His targets have included voters, parents, colleges and the rules that keep houses scarce.

His best-known claim concerns college. The bulk of a graduate's higher pay, Caplan argues, comes not from what was learned in class but from what the diploma tells employers: that its holder can finish hard, dull tasks. Economists call this signaling, and The Case Against Education, his book of 2018, presses it hard. If he is right, students will pay a great deal for the degree itself, even when the classes taught them nothing useful, because the paper is what employers reward.

His evidence includes a jump in the data. Someone who quits one class short of graduating earns far less over a lifetime than a classmate who finished, though their coursework barely differs, so the diploma by itself seems to be worth a small fortune. Economists call that jump at the finish line the sheepskin effect. Caplan estimates that roughly 80 percent of the college wage premium is signaling, a claim that is heterodox even among friendly economists, and from it he draws his main policy recommendation: cut education subsidies. The signaling story changes what taxpayers buy. If a degree mostly shows that a student is bright and diligent, then grants, cheap loans and state universities pump up the signal without producing matching productive skills, and as more people hold the same diploma its premium wears away.

His 2007 book, The Myth of the Rational Voter, argued that voters hold systematically biased views on economics, suspicious of markets, of trade with foreigners and of saving, and keep them because a mistaken ballot costs the person casting it nothing. Caplan named the pattern rational irrationality. A shopper who believes nonsense pays for it at the checkout, but a voter who believes nonsense pays nothing, so clear thinking about politics is personally costly and privately worthless. The idea extends an older public-choice claim. In 1957 Anthony Downs argued that voters barely study the issues since one ballot in millions hardly ever decides anything, and he called that rational ignorance; Caplan's addition is that voters not only skip the homework but also indulge comfortable errors.

In 2011 Caplan used research on twins and adopted children to argue that how grown children turn out owes much less to their parents than most people believe, so raising children can be more relaxed than people fear, and he titled the book Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids.

His case for freer immigration rests on a startling gap. With an ox and hand tools, a farmer in a poor land might raise some $500 of crops a year; move that same man to a wealthy nation of tractors, good roads and reliable power, and similar work could pay around $40,000. Where people work, not just how hard they work, sets what they can produce. His 2024 book Build, Baby, Build turned to housing. When a booming city such as San Francisco smothers construction in permits, zoning and neighborhood vetoes while new jobs keep drawing residents, home prices climb steeply, because supply cannot keep pace with demand. Unusually for a tenured professor, Caplan made both of these books nonfiction graphic novels, Open Borders (2019) drawn by Zach Weinersmith and the housing book drawn by Ady Branzei. The comic form solves a problem scholarly prose cannot, reaching general readers who never open an academic book.

capitalism-and-freedom-1962-and-free-to-.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman, the University of Chicago economist who won the Nobel prize in 1976, wrote two books for ordinary readers that went on to change American policy. The first, in 1962, argued that economic and political freedom are bound together and offered a list of reforms that sounded eccentric at the time. The second, in 1980, written with his wife Rose, carried the case to television.

The 1962 book began as talks Friedman delivered in 1956 at Indiana's Wabash College, and Rose helped turn them into plain English. He called it Capitalism and Freedom, and over the years buyers took home upward of 500,000 copies. Its central claim runs in one direction only: economic freedom is necessary for political freedom, though it is not enough by itself. Once a government controls the jobs, the press and the currency, a dissenter cannot hold out, because he cannot even eat.

The book's proposals included vouchers that parents could spend at any school, a negative income tax in place of the tangle of welfare programs, an army of volunteers, floating exchange rates, and an end to licensing rules that kept newcomers out of trades. Universal single-payer health insurance, the Canadian model, was never among them. Ending the draft was the proposal that produced the sharpest exchange. In the late 1960s, at hearings of a presidential commission on the draft, General William Westmoreland objected that he had no wish to lead mercenaries, and Friedman asked whether he would rather have an army of slaves. Congress let the draft authority lapse in 1973.

Free to Choose made the same case through everyday scenes. A shopper choosing freely among thousands of items buys what her family really wants; hand the same budget to a committee of nutrition experts, and many shoppers would end up with food they did not want while the shelves filled with things nobody bought. The 1980 book accompanied a ten-part public-television series shot on location from Hong Kong to Chicago and Washington, and it reached number one on the New York Times best-seller list that year. According to Friedman's memoirs, it was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in underground translations, and the Czech reformer Václav Klaus later credited it as a source of his country's reforms after 1989.

The voucher idea was older than either book. Friedman first set it out in 1955 in an essay, The Role of Government in Education, in a volume edited by Robert Solo, and later folded it into Capitalism and Freedom. He had argued since 1953 for letting currencies float freely against one another. When Richard Nixon closed the gold window in August 1971, the fixed-rate system of Bretton Woods fell apart, and by 1973 the world's major currencies were floating against each other.

Looking back, historians note how many of the 1962 proposals that seemed eccentric at the time became mainstream policy: the volunteer army in 1973, floating currencies in the early 1970s, and state voucher programs from the 1990s on.

ceausescus-romania-and-the-1989-executio.context_blurb:
Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled Romania for twenty-four years from 1965, first as head of its Communist Party and later as head of state as well, with his wife Elena at his side as co-ruler. His regime joined a cult of personality to ruinous central planning. It held together for decades, then collapsed in about a week in December 1989, and he became the only communist leader shot in that year's revolutions.

By the late 1980s Romanians lived with empty shops, secret police everywhere, and heat and electricity doled out for only a few hours daily; what they threw off that December was a communist dictatorship. Ceaușescu's monument was a colossal palace in central Bucharest for the party's ruling bodies, built in the 1980s as the House of the People by 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. Only one office building on earth has more floor space, and a great stretch of the old city, churches included, was flattened to make room. Today it is called the Palace of the Parliament and houses Romania's legislature.

In October 1966 Ceaușescu banned abortion and contraception, both legal since 1957, to drive the birthrate up by command. The order, Decree 770, also taxed unmarried adults and childless couples over twenty-five, and births nearly doubled within a year. The state could not care for the babies it had ordered into the world. When foreign reporters entered Romania's state institutions in 1990, they found about 100,000 children in appalling orphanages, and the footage drove reform of international adoption for decades.

In the 1980s his program of systematization bulldozed thousands of farming villages and herded families out of their old houses into identical concrete blocks near state factories. It was central planning in miniature: one small group decides how everyone should live and ignores what people actually want. The hardship had another cause too. Through the decade Ceaușescu insisted on paying off every dollar of foreign debt, exporting grain, meat and fuel for hard currency, while at home Romanians endured rolling power blackouts and rationed food, queues for meat, sugar and cooking oil, and cold apartments winter after winter.

The end began in the city of Timișoara. On December 16, 1989, townspeople gathered to stop the eviction of a pastor, László Tőkés; troops fired on them, and within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. It showed how fast public obedience can vanish once people see their neighbors dare to defy a dictator. On December 21 Ceaușescu ordered a mass rally beneath the balcony of the party's Central Committee building, carried live on national television. In mid-speech, for the first time in his rule, the crowd turned on him: boos and jeers rose, his face froze in shock, and every home in Romania watched it happen on state TV. He fled by helicopter and was caught, and on December 25, 1989, Christmas Day, a military tribunal at Târgoviște tried him and Elena in about an hour and had them shot by firing squad.

Like East Germany's Stasi, the Soviet KGB and Albania's Sigurimi, Romania's Securitate was a secret-police force with a wide network of neighborhood informants, enormous for the size of the country, built to defend the state against its own people.
