politics-without-romance-buchanans-nobel.context_blurb:
James Buchanan, the American economist who won the 1986 Nobel Prize, helped build the public-choice school, which studies politicians and officials with the same tools that economists apply to buyers and firms. In 1979, in a lecture in Vienna, he gave the school a three-word motto that has been reprinted ever since: politics without romance.

The romance he wanted to strip away was a warm assumption hidden in many textbooks, the belief that people in government act out of pure public spirit. Buchanan saw no reason to think a person becomes a saint the day he enters government.

That assumption had let older welfare economics play a trick. It compared a real, messy market with an imagined, perfect government and concluded that the government should step in. Buchanan said an honest comparison must weigh the market's real failures against the government's real failures, like against like.

The school also made a matching term its own. Economists had long spoken of "market failure"; public choice answered with government failure, policy that breaks down because of the rewards and pressures the people running it face.

The public-choice toolkit lists the ways that happens: regulatory capture, rent-seeking, agencies that grow their own budgets, and voters who rationally stay uninformed. Adam Smith's invisible hand does not belong in that kit at all, because it describes how markets coordinate people, not how governments fail.

The essay's key idea is simple. Politicians act on their own incentives just as everyone else does.

From that idea comes the school's central move. Buchanan and his allies Tullock and Olson refused to judge two groups by different standards, treating market actors as self-interested while treating political actors as noble stewards. Both, they insisted, must be studied the same way, as self-interested human beings.

The motto works as a test in real debates. When someone says that the market has failed and the government must therefore act, the test makes the listener ask what reason there is to believe that the actual politicians and bureaucrats who would run the fix will do any better.

Buchanan's motto is often grouped with the sayings of other free-market thinkers, so it helps to keep the owners straight. The line that there are no solutions, only trade-offs, belongs to Thomas Sowell, not to Buchanan.

price-gouging-laws-the-generator-that-ne.context_blurb:
After a hurricane, prices for ice, water, fuel and generators shoot up, and most American states make that a crime called price gouging. The laws feel like simple fairness. Economists in the Austrian tradition, Duke University's Michael Munger loudest among them, argue that the laws make disasters worse, because the high price is the very signal that brings help.

In September 1996 Hurricane Fran knocked out power to about a million people around Raleigh, North Carolina. Four young men rented freezer trucks, bought ice in a town that still had power, sawed fallen trees off the road to get through, and sold the bags in the dark city for several times the old price. Police arrested them and seized the truck, and the people waiting in line clapped and cheered as the sellers were handcuffed.

Munger told the story in a 2007 essay for the Library of Economics and Liberty. Its title, They Clapped, came from the crowd, and its subtitle asked whether price-gouging laws can prohibit scarcity. His answer was no: a law can forbid a price, but the ice is no less scarce for the ban.

Florida's law works differently from most. It is not always on: it switches on when the governor declares a state of emergency, and from then on a price breaks the law when it runs grossly higher than what the same seller charged, on average, in the month before.

In 2005 a Kentucky man named John Shepperson watched the news from Hurricane Katrina, loaded nineteen generators he had bought into a rented truck, and drove roughly 600 miles south to Mississippi, where buyers would pay about twice what he had paid. He spent four days in jail, and the police held on to the generators, which sat in custody instead of powering anyone's home.

Friedrich Hayek explained why the price matters in his famous 1945 essay on knowledge. Suppose tin suddenly grows scarce, so that a vast crowd of its users must make do with less. They need to know nothing beyond the new, higher price they face; whether a mine closed or a war broke out makes no difference to what they should do.

A critic in Bastiat's tradition grants that an anti-gouging threat means well. He points instead to a cost that arrives the moment the threat is announced: every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away stays where it is, because no trucker will load, drive and sell at a price that could land him in jail. Shepperson's generators at least reached Mississippi; the ones that never left Georgia never made the news.

Florida's thirty-day benchmark carries a hidden assumption, a Hayekian critic adds: that the pre-storm price is still the right price after the storm. On Hayek's account a price is news about present conditions, so pinning it to last month tells the market to act as though the storm changed nothing.

On Russ Roberts's EconTalk podcast, Munger has boiled the whole case down to one sentence: the only way to guarantee low prices, he said, is to let sellers charge high prices. The high price pulls truckers and supplies toward the disaster, steers the scarce stock to the people who need it most, and makes everyone already holding ice or fuel stretch it.

proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake-the-ethe.context_blurb:
Bitcoin's proof-of-work makes miners burn electricity to add blocks. On September 15, 2022, Ethereum, the second-largest cryptocurrency, abandoned that method in an upgrade called the Merge. The switch set up the biggest live experiment in crypto: two great networks secured in two opposite ways.

Why burn power at all? The designers of proof-of-work chose the cost on purpose, so that no single group can easily fake or take over the money. Rewriting its history would cost more real electricity than any attacker could afford, which is why Bitcoin needs no boss.

Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake. Instead of burning electricity, the block-makers, called validators, put up a pile of coins they own as collateral, and a validator caught cheating forfeits it. Overnight the network's electricity use fell by roughly 99.95 percent, the strongest argument supporters make for the change. Ethereum's founder, Vitalik Buterin, who published its white paper in late 2013, had pushed for the switch from the start.

Bitcoin's defenders press two main complaints. First, they say, proof-of-stake revives something from traditional finance that proof-of-work set out to destroy: concentration of power in the hands of those who already hold the most tokens. The biggest holders get the biggest voice over new blocks and rules, with no outside cost to check them.

Second is the nothing-at-stake problem. A miner can spend his electricity on only one chain at a time, but a validator spends no real resource on a signature, so he can costlessly sign several competing chains at once. Defenders of proof-of-stake answer with penalties called slashing.

Proof-of-stake also drew legal trouble. Gary Gensler, then chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, suggested that many proof-of-stake tokens might count as investment contracts under the Supreme Court's 1946 Howey test, which would bring heavy registration rules.

Bitcoin still runs on proof-of-work, and its community insists the energy cost is a feature, not a bug. They call it a commitment made in the physical world, outside the network, that ties digital money to reality in a way no promise written purely in software can.

Which bet was right? Neither argument can settle it on paper. The answer will come from whether each network survives decades of live attacks, crashes and stress; Bitcoin has run on proof-of-work since 2009, while Ethereum's proof-of-stake has run only since 2022.

Proof-of-work did not vanish with the Merge. Litecoin, launched in 2011 as the silver to Bitcoin's gold, and Dogecoin, born in 2013 as a joke, with a Shiba Inu dog for its mascot, both descend from Bitcoin's code and kept on mining.

rai-stones-of-yap-the-sunken-money-still.context_blurb:
On the small Pacific island of Yap, east of the Philippines in Micronesia, people used one of the strangest monies ever recorded: rai, giant round discs of stone with a hole in the middle. The largest stood taller than a grown man and weighed as much as a car. They show, better than any coin, what money really is.

The islanders left the biggest stones sitting outside houses and along paths. Yap is the island famous for this stone money.

Yap itself had no suitable stone. Crews sailed to Palau, about 250 miles away, carved the discs by hand from its limestone, and hauled each one home lashed to an outrigger canoe across the open sea. That hard journey was part of what made each stone valuable.

Once a big stone was set up in a village, nobody moved it again. Yet stones still changed hands. When a stone was traded, the villagers simply agreed in public that it now belonged to someone else, and the stone itself stayed exactly where it was.

One story shows how far the idea went. A canoe crew towing a huge new stone home was caught in a storm, and the stone broke loose and vanished into the deep. The crew testified to its size and quality, and the islanders agreed that the lost stone was still valuable, still owned and still tradable, though it lay on the seabed where nobody would ever see it again.

In 1991 Milton Friedman retold the tale in an essay, "The Island of Stone Money," later collected in his book Money Mischief. Modern money, he pointed out, works much the same way: almost nobody ever sees the gold or the reserves that stand behind it, but everyone agrees on who owns them.

His favorite example came from 1932 and 1933. France asked to convert its dollar holdings into gold, and rather than ship the metal across the Atlantic, clerks at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York moved gold bars into drawers marked as French inside the same vault. Ownership crossed the ocean; the gold never moved.

Friedman, and later the cypherpunks, drew the same lesson from Yap. Money is a ledger, a shared record of who owns what; the stone, the gold bar or the paper note is only a container for that social agreement.

On Yap the ledger lived in the villagers' memories. Bitcoin hands that task, keeping track of which coin belongs to whom, to the blockchain, a shared record book secured by mathematics and held in copies by thousands of computers worldwide.

Seen that way, Bitcoin is not a break from monetary tradition. A purely digital ledger is a natural next step in it, moving the record from human memory to cryptographic memory.

The rai and Bitcoin share one more feature that ordinary money lacks. Kings could stamp new coins and governments print new notes at will, but each rai had to be quarried and carried across the sea, and each bitcoin must be mined with real electricity. As the cypherpunk Nick Szabo pointed out, both demand costly proof-of-work to create every new unit.

right-to-try-and-the-fda-from-peltzman-t.context_blurb:
The Food and Drug Administration decides which new medicines Americans may use. Every rule it adds can stop a dangerous drug, but every month of delay also keeps good drugs from sick people. Economists from Sam Peltzman to the oncologist Vinay Prasad have asked how to count both kinds of harm, the one everyone sees and the one nobody sees.

The story starts with thalidomide, a sedative that doctors in Europe and beyond prescribed to expectant mothers in the late 1950s. Before it was withdrawn in 1961, more than ten thousand babies had been born with severe deformities. Congress answered in 1962 with the Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which made drug makers prove their medicines worked. Stricter rules carry a trade-off: fewer bad drugs get through, but good drugs also arrive much more slowly.

After the new rules, approvals took years longer. Fewer harmful drugs reached the market, a real gain, yet the slower pace carried a price that is easy to miss: sick people died waiting for medicines that would have saved them.

In 1973 Peltzman measured that trade-off in the Journal of Political Economy. The seen benefit was fewer thalidomide-style tragedies. The unseen cost was patients dying while safe and effective drugs sat in a longer approval line, often drugs already in use in Europe or Japan, and Peltzman argued the unseen cost was the larger one.

For dying patients the stakes are starkest. Someone with a fatal disease and no approved treatment left gains nothing from being told to wait: the practical outcome of waiting is death. The Right to Try Act, signed on May 30, 2018, lets such patients use drugs that have passed early safety trials. Its moral argument is that dying patients have little to lose and should decide the risk for themselves.

Prasad, a California cancer doctor, worries about the opposite error. On fast-track programs, he says, the agency often clears cancer drugs on early lab signals, such as a scan showing a tumor getting smaller, and treats those signals as proof the drug saves lives, though many such drugs never help patients live longer. He made the case in his 2020 book Malignant.

His fix is not less FDA but a better one: judge drugs by results, not by intentions or by surrogate markers, the lab numbers that merely stand in for survival.

Milton Friedman pointed out that a drug regulator can make two kinds of mistake. Approving a harmful drug, as with the painkiller Vioxx, withdrawn in 2004, makes headlines name by name. Blocking a good drug almost never gets noticed, because the people who would have been saved are never seen.

The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 widened the fast-track paths partly for that reason. When a promising drug takes ten years to clear review, the cost easiest to miss is the lives lost by patients who would have been saved had it arrived sooner.

An honest scorecard for the FDA must therefore count both mistakes: the seen one, a bad drug approved, and the unseen one, a good drug blocked.

The COVID-19 pandemic tested the balance. In December 2020 the FDA used an Emergency Use Authorization to allowed the earliest COVID vaccines into people's arms months ahead of full approval. Such authority trades faster access in an emergency for less complete safety data at first.

saifedean-ammous-the-bitcoin-standard-th.context_blurb:
Saifedean Ammous is a Lebanese-Palestinian economist with a doctorate from Columbia University who spent years as a professor in Beirut, at the Lebanese American University. He became one of the most widely read writers arguing that Bitcoin is sound money in the Austrian tradition, money that no government can inflate at will to cover its spending.

What makes Bitcoin sound, in this view, is one hard rule written into its code: no more than 21 million coins can ever exist, and nobody, not even its creator, can raise that limit.

In 2018 the publisher John Wiley and Sons brought out his book, The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking. It argued that Bitcoin may be the hardest money ever created and that fiat currencies have historically lost most of their value, and it has since become one of the most widely read books about Bitcoin, translated into dozens of languages.

Its central tool is the stock-to-flow ratio: the amount of a good already in existence divided by the amount newly produced each year. Throughout history, Ammous argues, money has formed around whatever scores highest on that ratio, which is why gold kept becoming money among physical goods.

Applied to Bitcoin, the ratio climbs in steps. Every 210,000 blocks, about every four years, the halving cuts the reward for new coins in half while the existing stock keeps growing, so Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio roughly doubles every four years and heads toward infinity as new issuance approaches zero.

His 2021 sequel, The Fiat Standard, looks at what happened after the last link between money and gold was cut in 1971. When a central bank can print as much as the government asks for decades on end, the predictable long-run result is a steady climb in prices and a steady loss in the value of savings.

Ammous draws on an old Austrian distinction. Easy money can be multiplied cheaply, with a printing press, a keystroke in a central bank's computers or a lucky strike at a mine. Gold and Bitcoin, whose supply resists any quick increase, are what economists call hard money.

He later left university teaching and set up a website of his own and sold his courses and writing straight to students, thousands of whom signed up. His move shows what the internet allows: buyers and sellers of teaching can now connect directly, cutting the middleman out.

The deepest argument of The Bitcoin Standard is about politics as much as scarcity. Fiat currencies have lost value through rulers' freedom to expand the supply whenever it suits them, and a fixed supply takes that political discretion to debase away entirely.

school-choice-milton-friedmans-1955-vouc.context_blurb:
Most American children attend whichever public school their street address assigns them. In 1955 Milton Friedman asked why that should be so. His answer, the school voucher, became the reform he cared about most, and seventy years later it had spread across much of the country.

His essay "The Role of Government in Education," later a chapter of Capitalism and Freedom (1962), drew a sharp line. Government might reasonably pay for schooling, Friedman wrote, but that did not mean government had to run the schools. He proposed giving parents a voucher they could spend at any accredited school they chose.

Friedman's critics of the old system point to a striking pair of numbers. Since 1970, American spending per public-school pupil has roughly tripled after inflation, yet the national test that tracks seventeen-year-olds' reading and math, the long-term trend survey known as NAEP, has stayed essentially flat over the same half century.

Under a school voucher program, a city gives families, often poor ones, a voucher good for tuition at any school willing to take their child, whether public, private or religious, so schools must compete for students instead of receiving them by district assignment. The first big urban program began in Milwaukee in 1990, pushed by a Democratic state legislator, Polly Williams, a former welfare mother, and signed by a Republican governor, Tommy Thompson.

In 2002 the Supreme Court ruled five to four that Cleveland's voucher program did not break the First Amendment's ban on an established religion, even though parents could use the money at religious schools, because the aid reached those schools only through the parents' own choices. The case is Zelman versus Simmons-Harris.

Defenders of choice answer critics with a simple analogy. A grocery store that kept nine in ten customers by force, not by quality, would slowly get worse, because nothing would push it to improve. That is the competitive-pressure argument: a monopoly provider loses the discipline to improve when its customers cannot leave. John Chubb and Terry Moe built the empirical case in Politics, Markets, and America's Schools (1990).

In 1996, near the end of his life, Milton Friedman and his wife Rose founded an organization devoted to school choice for children from kindergarten to twelfth grade, through vouchers and later education savings accounts; in 2016 it was renamed EdChoice.

Education savings accounts carried Friedman's idea further. An account holds public money that a family can spend on private tuition, tutoring or homeschool supplies. After Arizona opened its program to every family in 2022, a wave of states followed in 2023 with universal or near-universal programs, among them Iowa, Arkansas, Florida and Ohio.

silk-road-bitcoins-first-widely-known-us.context_blurb:
From February 2011 to October 2013, a secret website known as the Silk Road sold drugs and other contraband to buyers around the world. It ran on the Tor network, which hides users' locations, and the only money it would take was Bitcoin. It became the first famous use of Bitcoin beyond a small circle of hobbyists, and an uncomfortable test of what the new money could do.

Why Bitcoin? Because Bitcoin can be sent from one person to another without any bank or government approving the payment, so there was no card company to refuse it and no bank to report it.

A fair defender of Bitcoin has to admit something here. The same freedom that lets people in poor countries escape currency controls also let criminals sell drugs online; any tool that gives people more freedom can also be used to do wrong.

The site's founder, a young American libertarian named Ross Ulbricht, ran it as Dread Pirate Roberts, a name from The Princess Bride. On October 1, 2013, FBI agents wanted his laptop while it was open and logged in to the site's controls. They caught him among the science-fiction shelves of a San Francisco public library, the Glen Park branch, after staging a distraction nearby.

A jury found him guilty in February 2015 of seven crimes, among them money laundering and conspiring to traffic drugs. That May the judge gave him life behind bars with no chance of parole, two life terms plus 40 years in all, and his case became a cause for libertarians and Bitcoiners for a decade.

Arresting the boss did not end the trade. Copycat markets, starting with Silk Road 2.0 a few weeks later, sprang up and drew the same customers, because while people still wish to buy and sell, someone will open a new place to do it.

The episode split the early Bitcoin community. Some cheered that the technology worked exactly as designed; others feared the link with drugs would taint Bitcoin forever. Either way, the Silk Road showed off Bitcoin's most important trait: electronic payments resistant to censorship, which no middleman could block.

In January 2025 President Donald Trump pardoned Ulbricht. A public-choice analyst would warn a student not to read that as a verdict on drug markets. The sound reasoning move is to weigh the arguments of this one case, such as whether the sentence fit the crime, without turning it into a universal endorsement of the market Ulbricht ran.

sowell-on-discrimination-and-disparities.context_blurb:
For decades the economist Thomas Sowell has challenged a claim common in news reports and courtrooms: when two groups end up unequal, someone must have treated one of them worse. In Discrimination and Disparities (2018) he argued that the claim skips a step.

Sowell agrees that gaps are real. His point is that a gap, on its own, shows only that something differs between the groups, and not yet what that something is. Age, geography, family size and inherited culture are all causes to be tested.

His favorite evidence comes from minorities shut out of occupations, restricted by law and attacked by mobs, who nonetheless grew wealthier than the majorities around them. His main example is the overseas Chinese of Southeast Asia, in countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines.

Indonesia is his sharpest case. Chinese families were only a small share of its people and suffered bans and deadly riots, yet by Sowell's figures they held about eighty per cent of the country's wealth. Severe hostility and great success sat side by side.

He pairs the Chinese with Lebanese traders in West Africa and Indian merchant families in East Africa. Both arrived poor and resented, and both came to run much of the local commerce. The common cause, Sowell argues, lies not in the countries where they landed but in what they brought: trading skill and business habits that kept working in a new land. Economists call such skills portable human capital.

Between 1994 and 1998 he published three linked books on race, migration and conquest, after fifteen years of research that took him around the world twice. Their common theme is that groups carry their own ways of life with them, so their economic histories cannot be understood without those cultures.

He also separates two meanings of one English word. Discrimination I is the ability to tell real differences in quality apart and to choose accordingly, ideally judging each person as an individual. Discrimination II is harming people because of baseless assumptions or dislikes about their group, the kind the law forbids. Public arguments, he says, blur the two.

To show how large gaps can be with no group cause at all, he cites a study of National Merit Scholarship finalists from families with exactly five children. Siblings share parents, home, schools and income, yet the eldest child turned out to be the finalist more often than all four younger siblings put together.

His prerequisites argument extends the point. Getting into a demanding engineering program may require good schooling, the right language, family support, mobility and money, all at once. If one of five is missing, having the other four is worth nothing, so an even spread of success across regions or groups would be the astonishing result, not the normal one.

Suppose a regulator shows that mortgage applicants in one district are turned down more often and blames biased lenders. A reader trained by Sowell accepts the figures, but he first asks that the two groups of applicants be compared on the things the lender actually looks at, such as credit records and income, before the gap is allowed to mean anything.

Critics accuse Sowell of calling discrimination a myth; he answers that they mistake the kind of claim he makes. His is a claim about what evidence it takes to prove a cause, not a denial that the cause exists; discrimination must be shown by evidence about treatment, not assumed from the size of a gap.

His travels gave him a test that a single snapshot cannot. Following the same people over generations and into the different countries where they settled reveals whether a pattern travels with them under different institutions. If a group does well in Lagos, London and Chicago alike, its treatment in any one place cannot fully explain it.

The distinction between the two discriminations predicts collisions. Imagine a law banning any sorting of applicants by a trait that comes out unevenly across groups. An airline hires pilots by their hours in the air and a bank lends by repayment history, and both come out unevenly, so such a rule would catch sorting on real qualifications along with sorting driven by arbitrary aversion.

spot-bitcoin-etfs-approved-january-10-20.context_blurb:
For a decade, anyone who wanted bitcoin had to open an account at a crypto exchange or learn to guard his own keys. On January 10, 2024, that changed. The Securities and Exchange Commission, the federal regulator of the stock market, approved a new kind of fund, and Bitcoin walked onto Wall Street.

That day the SEC approved eleven spot Bitcoin ETFs at once. An exchange-traded fund trades like a share on the stock market, and a spot fund holds actual bitcoin rather than futures contracts on its price, so big investors could at last own genuine bitcoin from the same brokerage account they used for stocks.

Bitcoin's fans saw why it mattered. Buying bitcoin became as easy as buying a share of Apple: no wallet, no exchange, no secret phrases to guard.

For years the SEC had refused such funds, so most retirement savers stayed out rather than open a crypto account. Now ordinary savers and retirement accounts could own bitcoin far more easily, through the same accounts that held their other investments.

The approval was forced. In August 2023 a federal appeals court ruled in a case brought by Grayscale that the SEC could not approve Bitcoin futures funds, as it had in 2021, while rejecting spot funds built on the same market. The commission's vote was three to two, with Chairman Gary Gensler, who made clear he was not enthusiastic, joining the two Republican commissioners. A split that close shows that even the experts inside one agency disagreed deeply about whether to allow the new technology.

Money poured in faster than skeptics predicted, with BlackRock's fund, ticker IBIT, growing fastest of all. By December 2024, about eleven months after launch, the funds together held about 1.1 million bitcoin, roughly five percent of the 21 million that can ever exist.

Richard Cantillon's old rule says that whoever gains access to something new first tends to profit most, buying before prices are bid up. Individuals who already kept coins in their own wallets were in already; in this reading, the earliest winners from the new product were the big pension and endowment funds that could pile in from the first day, once fiduciary rules no longer kept them out.

Not every Bitcoiner cheered. Critics in the tradition of Andreas Antonopoulos warn that holding bitcoin through a fund on Wall Street falls short of owning it, because a custodian holds the keys. What you give up is the feature that makes Bitcoin distinctive: the ability to hold your own money without trusting any bank.

Michael Saylor, whose company MicroStrategy was the first big American firm to swap much of its cash for bitcoin, welcomed the funds anyway, because they let millions more people buy bitcoin easily and so widened its reach.

In December 2024, about eleven months after approval, Bitcoin's price passed $100,000 for the first time. The funds were one cause among several, alongside the April 2024 halving and the wider economy.

It helps to be clear about the limits of the approval. It made it much easier for big investors to buy in, but it did not touch Bitcoin's code: the 21-million cap, the open network and the option of self-custody stayed exactly as designed. The fund wrapper is a regulatory invention, not a change to the money itself.

tarp-and-bailouts-moral-hazard-and-the-2.context_blurb:
A rescue has two prices. The first falls due at once and everybody sees it. The second falls due years later, and it is paid by people who were never in the room. The autumn of 2008 set the first price; the spring of 2023 presented the bill.

By October 2008 Lehman Brothers had failed on bad housing loans and Citigroup looked ready to follow. On the third of that month George W. Bush signed a seven-hundred-billion-dollar programme letting the Treasury buy damaged loans and take stock in large banks to keep them upright: TARP, short for the Troubled Asset Relief Program. Economists already had a name for the trap it set. Moral hazard is what appears when a climber knows somebody will catch him if he slips, so he climbs with less care than before; once a bank's creditors expect a rescue, they demand a smaller premium for risk, and the risk duly grows.

Frederic Bastiat's rule from 1850 is to hunt for the cost nobody photographs. In a bailout that cost does not fall in the year of the rescue at all; it waits in the next crisis. Future bankers take bigger risks because they now expect a rescue when things go wrong, and no camera can catch a risk that has not yet gone bad.

Fifteen years later the sequel arrived. Silicon Valley Bank had put the bulk of its deposits into long-dated Treasury bonds and government-backed mortgage securities bought when rates sat near zero, and when the Federal Reserve raised rates hard in 2022 those bonds sank in value. Depositors read the news and tried to get out on the same morning. A bank run is precisely that, a crowd demanding its cash at once, and no bank holding long bonds can pay a crowd. Silicon Valley Bank failed on 10 March 2023, with the great majority of its deposits above the insured ceiling, most of the money belonging to technology companies and venture funds.

The ceiling is the thing to watch. American deposit insurance normally stops at $250,000 per account, and the market's own signal to a saver holding more is simple: spread the money over several banks, or watch your bank like a hawk. Two days after the failure the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC announced jointly that every depositor would be paid in full, uninsured balances included, under a systemic-risk exception. To a wealthy saver the lesson comes through as: do not worry about the limit; the government may cover you anyway. What gets erased is the useful lesson, the one the market had been teaching for free: splitting your money across many banks was the safe move; the bailout hides that lesson.

Walter Bagehot, the Victorian editor who wrote Lombard Street in 1873, had set out the rule a central bank should follow in a panic. It was to lend freely to any sound bank, take nothing but good collateral, and charge a high, punishing rate. The sting is the whole point: a bank that can borrow cheaply in an emergency will come for the money whether the emergency is real or not. The 2023 rescue did the opposite and handed large depositors a free option. Read the two episodes side by side and the shape is plain: TARP 2008 as precedent; SVB 2023 as institutionalization.

Anna Schwartz, who had written the 1963 monetary history with Milton Friedman that pinned the Depression on the Federal Reserve, left a last warning in her old age. The Fed, she argued, had quietly changed jobs and was now preserving asset values, not merely stabilizing money, and the cost of that drift would surface in the crisis after next.

thatcher-reagan-and-the-1980s-hayekian-p.context_blurb:
A grocer's daughter from Grantham and a film actor from Illinois spent the 1980s running two of the world's largest economies, and both took their bearings from the same Austrian emigre. Margaret Thatcher had led the Conservatives since 1975 and walked into Downing Street in 1979; Ronald Reagan, once governor of California, was sworn in as the fortieth American president two years later.

Britain in the late 1970s owned its coal mines, its steel mills and its telephone network outright. Handing a state industry back to private owners is privatization, and from 1979 Thatcher did it on a scale no government had attempted before. Reagan's instrument was the tax code: he cut the top rate of federal income tax from 70 percent to 28 percent over eight years, on the argument that lower rates would get people working longer, saving more and starting firms, which is supply-side economics.

The Austrian was Friedrich Hayek, and the scene everybody tells, which rests on one later account rather than a record of the meeting, is set in the summer of 1975. A speaker at the Conservative Research Department was urging a middle way between the parties when Thatcher reached into her handbag and produced Friedrich Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty, his long and radical book of 1960. She brought it down on the table and told the room that this was what the party believed. Hayek had been building that network for decades. In April 1947 he gathered a few dozen free-market scholars at a hotel on a Swiss mountainside above Lake Geneva, Milton Friedman, Karl Popper, Lionel Robbins and Ludwig von Mises among them. The society they founded there took the mountain's name: the Mont Pelerin Society, which held free-market thinkers together for the next forty years.

The selling began in earnest in November 1984 with shares in British Telecom, the national phone company: more than two million applications poured in, many from small savers who had never held a share before, and that flotation is the best-remembered privatisation of them all. The same years brought the hardest fight. For a year from March 1984 the mineworkers' union under Arthur Scargill struck against the closing of pits that lost money, and the government, which had spent years quietly stockpiling coal, simply waited. With no strike pay and their savings gone, the men went back with nothing to show for it, and the year taught the plainest lesson about the weapon: a strike only works if the workers can outlast the losses they take from not being paid.

On 27 October 1986 the London Stock Exchange opened under new arrangements: fixed commissions abolished, foreign firms admitted, the shouting floor giving way to screens. Stripping old rules off a market to open it up is deregulation, and the day the papers called the Big Bang made the City of London one of the world's two great financial centres. British taxes came down too, from a top rate of 83 percent in 1979, when the taxman took all but seventeen pence of an extra pound, reaching 40 percent in the 1988 budget. The chancellors, borrowing the argument of the American economist Arthur Laffer, said that people work and invest more, so the government can still collect a lot of tax at the lower rate.

Underneath all of it sat the argument Hayek had been making since the 1930s, when planning was the mainstream view in nearly every economics faculty. No planner, however clever or well intentioned, can gather the prices and the practical know-how that millions of separate people carry in their heads and act on hourly, and that is the knowledge problem, a claim about information rather than about motives. Stockholm agreed far enough to give Hayek the Nobel in 1974, and Reagan had him to the White House in November 1983, at eighty-four.

One more piece explains how the argument reached a cabinet room. A former RAF fighter pilot named Antony Fisher read a condensed version of Hayek's wartime book in 1945, sought the author out and asked how to fight back. Hayek told him to stay out of elected office and win the argument from outside it, and Fisher duly founded a free-market institute in London in the mid-1950s that turned out short, sharp pamphlets. The reasoning behind that advice is the lasting part: politicians usually only vote for what voters think is possible, so the ideas must be won first.

the-2008-great-financial-crisis-peter-sc.context_blurb:
On 15 September 2008 a Wall Street house older than the Civil War went to court for protection from its creditors, listing something like six hundred and thirteen billion dollars of debts. Lehman Brothers was 158 years old and the fourth-largest investment bank in America, and it had stuffed its books with bonds built out of American home loans. When a firm owes more than it can ever pay and goes through that court process, the word is bankruptcy, and this was the largest one in the country's history.

The ingredients had been assembled years earlier. After the dot-com bust Greenspan's Fed cut its benchmark rate to 1 percent in June 2003 and left it there for a year. Cheap money made mortgages easy, and from roughly 2003 to 2006 banks lent to buyers who could not really carry the payments. More borrowed money bidding for the same houses pushes prices up without improving a single house, and a price rise that comes from borrowed enthusiasm rather than from anything real is a bubble.

Not everybody missed it. Peter Schiff, a stockbroker with a small firm in Connecticut, spent 2006 and 2007 on cable news insisting that the housing boom was a creature of Federal Reserve credit and would end in a crash. In early 2007 he published the forecast as a book, Crash Proof: How to Profit from the Coming Economic Collapse, which predicted, in order, a housing collapse, then a banking crisis, then a sinking dollar. The studio panels laughed at him on air. A compilation of that laughter went round the internet after the crash, and the lesson it carries is uncomfortable for anyone who trusts a panel: even experts can miss huge risks that a few outsiders see.

Then the Fed reversed. From June 2004 it pushed the rate up in seventeen quarter-point moves that brought it to 5.25 percent two years on, and that lifted the payments on a great mass of adjustable mortgages at once; house prices turned down and defaults climbed. To an Austrian economist that is not bad luck but the second half of a known pattern, the one the Austrian Business Cycle Theory calls malinvestment revealed. Cheap credit had made long-dated projects look profitable, and the return of normal rates exposed the fact that the savings needed to finish them had never existed. Friedrich Hayek had set the mechanism out in four lectures in London in 1931. Push rates below what savers would really accept, he argued, and firms begin long projects that real saving cannot sustain, and when the easy money stops many of them cannot be finished and are abandoned as wasted investment.

The people in charge did not see it. In the spring of 2007 Ben Bernanke told Congress that the trouble in the risky end of the mortgage market looked likely to stay there, and eighteen months later the system nearly stopped. The honest conclusion is not that he was lying: even the top experts often cannot see a crisis coming, which is an argument for humility in anyone pricing credit for a whole country. One congressman had seen it. In 2003 Ron Paul of Texas told a House committee that the two enormous mortgage companies with quiet federal backing were inflating an artificial boom in house prices. An implied government guarantee lets the company take huge risks because taxpayers will cover the losses, so the profits stay private while the downside does not. Paul's bill to strip the guarantee went nowhere.

The Fed's answer to the crash was to take rates to the floor and buy bonds with freshly created reserves, three rounds of it between 2008 and 2012, which carried its balance sheet from under a trillion dollars to more than four trillion by 2014. The name for buying long-dated government and mortgage paper on that scale is quantitative easing. Austrians read the whole sequence as one case study, and the book that made it for the general reader was Thomas Woods's Meltdown: A Free-Market Look at Why the Stock Market Collapsed, written by a Mises Institute senior fellow and published in 2009. It blamed cheap Federal Reserve credit and the political push to put families into mortgages, rather than markets, and it reached the New York Times list of bestsellers.

the-bank-term-funding-program-stealth-qe.context_blurb:
On Sunday 12 March 2023, the weekend regulators seized a second American bank, the Federal Reserve opened a new window for banks whose bond holdings had sunk underwater. A rescue is usually judged by whether the panic stopped. This one is better judged by how it priced the collateral.

What the Fed set up was an emergency lending facility: a programme that lets banks borrow cash from the central bank for a year at a time against assets they pledge, so that a wobbling institution need not dump bonds into a falling market. What made it unusual was the valuation. At the ordinary discount window, collateral is valued at market price, typically with a haircut, a deliberate trim below today's price so that the Fed always lends less than the security would fetch. The new facility took long Treasuries and mortgage bonds at their original face value instead. A ten-year Treasury bought when yields sat at one and a half percent might fetch only eighty cents on the dollar once yields reached four percent, and the Fed accepted it at a hundred. Critics called that a hidden bailout for a plain reason: the central bank is pretending the bonds are worth more than the market says, and the difference is a gift to whoever made the losing bet.

Sound-money analysts had a nickname ready within days. The Fed was supposed at that moment to be shrinking its balance sheet, and each loan from the new window swelled it again, so Peter Schiff, Lyn Alden, Jim Bianco and others called the programme QE by another name. Use of it grew all year. Borrowings peaked at about $167 billion in early 2024, and every dollar was a rate-cycle loss quietly carried by the central bank rather than by the bank that had bought the bond.

The legal authority is itself a signal. The Fed may open a facility of this kind only under a clause added to the Federal Reserve Act in 1932, which permits emergency lending in unusual and exigent circumstances. Reaching for that power therefore announces that something is seriously wrong and the Fed is trying to stop a panic, which is why its use in March 2020 and again three years later rattled people who read the fine print.

Two objections run deeper than the nickname. The first looks forward: banks may take bigger risks in the future, expecting another rescue, because a mismatch between short deposits and long bonds is a cheaper gamble once the central bank has shown it will cover the loss. The second is about the present: pricing a damaged bond at its old value hides real losses and lets weak banks keep going instead of failing, leaving the system carrying institutions the market would have shut.

Bastiat's two columns sort the episode cleanly. Seen: it steadied the banks. Unseen: it subsidized losses the Fed's own low-rate policy had caused. The banks had loaded up on long bonds at low yields because the same institution had made those yields look attractive, and when its own tightening turned the bonds into losses, the facility quietly made the losses good. The programme closed on 11 March 2024, and the Austrian objection is that closing it changes nothing, because every bank now knows the Fed will lend against bad bond portfolios in the next crisis too, and moral hazard accumulates one precedent at a time.

the-black-book-of-communism-1997.context_blurb:
In 1997 the Paris publisher Robert Laffont brought out nine hundred pages of accounting that nobody could have written before 1991. Six European historians, with Stephane Courtois as lead editor, worked through the archives that opened as the Soviet Union fell and counted the dead of communist rule, country by country, from Pol Pot's Cambodia to Mao's China to Lenin's Russia. The short name of the volume is The Black Book of Communism. Harvard University Press issued the English edition two years later, and the figures entered American scholarly argument from there.

The number they reached is among the largest in modern history. Setting the country chapters side by side, the shootings under Stalin, the famine of Mao's Great Leap Forward, the deaths in the camps, the Cambodian killing fields, the volume arrives at about 85-100 million. The rounded version that has entered general use is around 100 million, and it is quoted in that form in nearly every serious argument about the twentieth century.

The breakdown is where the opened archives did their work. Nicolas Werth wrote the Soviet chapter from the new files and set that country's total at about 20 million, taking in the camps, the Great Purge shootings and the Ukrainian terror-famine of the early 1930s. The chapter on China carried the largest total in the book, about 65 million, counting the famine of the Great Leap Forward between 1959 and 1961, the Cultural Revolution that followed it, and the deaths in the laogai labour camps. Smaller totals followed for Cambodia and North Korea, at two million each, and for Africa, Afghanistan, Vietnam and Eastern Europe.

Then the book's own authors fell out in public. Courtois had opened the volume with an introduction on the crimes of communism, and two of his collaborators, Jean-Louis Margolin and Nicolas Werth, published open letters distancing themselves from a single claim in it: the equation of communist and Nazi crimes. Both men stood by the chapters they had written themselves. The comparison Courtois pressed rests on arithmetic nobody disputes: standard scholarly figures put the killings of Nazi Germany, the Holocaust and the rest, at some twenty-five million. That is about one-fourth of the communist total in his book, and his introduction asked why the public memory of the two is so unequal.

Later work has filled in the two biggest chapters. Anne Applebaum's history of the Soviet camp system, published in 2003 and awarded the Pulitzer Prize for general non-fiction the following year, was the first full English-language history of a network that ran from 1918 into the 1950s, and she reckoned that about 18 million people passed through it across the system's whole life. On China, the Xinhua journalist Yang Jisheng spent years in provincial archives and published his account in Hong Kong in 2008; his estimate for the Great Leap Forward alone, the worst famine ever recorded, is about 36 million dead. The book that began the argument has travelled a long way itself: about 26 language editions have appeared, and first-year sales in France alone passed two hundred thousand copies.

the-cobra-effect-british-delhi-and-the-b.context_blurb:
A bounty is the simplest policy there is: pay people for the thing you want and you get more of it. The German economist Horst Siebert gave the opposite result a name in 2001, borrowing a story about colonial India for the title of a book about policies that bite back.

The story is set in British-ruled Delhi, though no archive has ever confirmed that the scheme really ran. In the telling, the administration wanted fewer venomous snakes in the capital and announced a cash payment for each dead cobra brought in. So far the logic is impeccable: kill more cobras, collect more money, and the snake population falls. What the officials had not priced in was enterprise. Delhi residents worked out that farming snakes beat hunting them and Began breeding cobras in their back yards for the bounty, so the payments climbed while the wild population did not drop. When the government noticed and cancelled the scheme, the stock in the yards was suddenly worth nothing, and the breeders Released the now-worthless cobras into the streets, leaving the city with more snakes than it had before anybody was paid a rupee.

A better-documented version happened in French Indochina. In 1902 the administration in Hanoi paid a bounty for each severed rat tail, and the rat-catchers obliged by snipping tails from live rats and letting them go to breed, or by farming rats outright in the suburbs.

The general rule was spotted in 1975 by Charles Goodhart, a British economist studying the Bank of England's attempts to steer the money supply. Pick a number to be judged by, he noticed, and the number stops measuring what it used to measure, because everybody starts managing the number itself. Hence the rule everyone now quotes: once a measure becomes A target, it stops telling anyone the truth. Modern examples are everywhere. Wells Fargo told its staff in the mid-2010s to hit monthly quotas for new accounts or lose the bonus, and the staff opened millions of accounts no customer had asked for. The lesson runs to one line: reward a target instead of the real goal and people will hit the target in harmful ways. American schools went through the same machinery from 2001 to 2015 under the federal law called No Child Left Behind, which made funding partly conditional on test scores and produced the practice teachers named teaching to the test.

Hospitals got the same treatment and answered the same way. A 2010 American health law fined a hospital when a discharged patient came back inside thirty days, so some hospitals Held patients in the emergency department under observation rather than formally admitting them, since an observation stay is not counted as an admission. The measured number improved. Whether the patients did is a separate question, and that is the whole lesson of the cobra: pay for a measured number and you will get the number rather than the outcome.

the-cypherpunk-lineage-digicash-b-money-.context_blurb:
Bitcoin did not arrive out of nowhere. It arrived at the end of a twenty-year argument among cryptographers who had decided that privacy was something to build rather than something to petition for. They met near San Francisco from 1992, first in Eric Hughes's house in Oakland and then on a mailing list, and the hacker Jude Milhon gave them the name that stuck: the cypherpunks.

Digital money had one problem that would not go away, and it is not a problem gold ever had. A digital file can be copied and spent twice, since a copy is indistinguishable from the original, so any coin made of bits can be handed to two people at once unless something prevents it. Every design in the lineage is an attempt on that problem.

David Chaum, the American cryptographer often called the father of digital cash, founded DigiCash in Amsterdam in 1989 to sell the blind-signature method he had invented in 1982, and the anonymity part worked: a payment could be made without the bank learning who made it. By 1998 the company was bankrupt, and the flaw later designers fixed on was structural rather than mathematical. The money still had to be issued by a trusted bank that could be shut down, and one issuer is one choke point.

Adam Back, a British cryptographer, attacked a different nuisance with the same tool in 1997. His scheme, Hashcash, made a computer solve a small puzzle before it could send an email: half a second for one message, unnoticeable to a person writing to a friend. For a spammer pushing out a million a day, the puzzles would take days, so spamming stops paying, which is the whole trick of putting a price on an action that had been free. One property of the puzzle mattered far more than spam ever did. Solving one puzzle is expensive but verifying a solution is instant, which is exactly what a money needs if strangers are to check one another's work without trusting anybody.

Two designs from 1998 went after the issuer itself. In November the Chinese-American cryptographer Wei Dai posted two pages describing a currency with no bank at all, in which every user keeps his own copy of a ledger recording each transaction; he called it b-money. Dai was candid about what he had not solved, and that gap is the one Satoshi closed ten years later: how to reach network consensus when different users see different transaction orderings, because two honest copies of a ledger can disagree about what happened first. The same year Nick Szabo, a legal scholar and computer scientist who had given the world the phrase smart contracts in 1996, described a scheme in which puzzles chained one to the next produced tokens nobody could issue at will: bit gold.

On 31 October 2008 a nine-page paper under the name Satoshi Nakamoto drew the threads together, and its short reference list names two of the four ancestors: B-money and Hashcash. Chaum's company and Szabo's design go uncited, though the debt is universally acknowledged. What had held the whole twenty-year effort together was a sentence Eric Hughes wrote in March 1993, opening the movement's manifesto by declaring privacy necessary for an open society in the electronic age, not a privilege to be granted by a legislature but a condition to be built in software.

the-farm-bill-and-snap-urban-rural-logro.context_blurb:
The United States Farm Bill comes up for renewal about every five years, runs to many hundreds of pages, and is not mostly about farms. Of the ten-year spending in the most recent version, scored at something like a trillion and a half dollars, roughly three-quarters goes to a single programme: SNAP (formerly food stamps), which helps low-income households buy groceries. The farm side proper, price supports and crop insurance and conservation, divides the remaining quarter between them.

Why are those two things in one bill? Picture a senator from Ohio who wants money for a bridge and one from Texas who wants an army base: neither project could pass by itself, since most members care about neither, so the two are written into a single bill and each man votes for the other's. The old name for that trade is logrolling. The Farm Bill is its grandest standing example. The votes for food assistance belong to city and suburban members while the votes for farm payments belong to rural ones, so the coalition that carries the bundle is urban Democrats plus rural Republicans. The architecture goes back to 1973 and a friendship across the aisle between a Kansas Republican and a South Dakota Democrat: Bob Dole and George McGovern.

The numbers explain the strength of each half. About 42 million Americans were drawing food assistance each month as of 2023, most of them in cities and suburbs, a constituency no urban legislator will cross. The test came in 2013, when the House voted to carve food assistance into a statute of its own. The split failed and the two programs were bundled back together in conference, and the 2014 law looked like every one before it, because separation dissolves the coalition each half depends on.

A bundle is hard to attack from outside. Congress tried in 1996 with the Line-Item Veto Act, which let a president strike individual provisions out of a bill without vetoing the whole thing. When Bill Clinton struck out a health-care payment destined for New York, the city sued, and on 25 June 1998 the Supreme Court threw the whole statute out as unconstitutional in Clinton v. City of New York. So the bundling continues, and the same mechanics appear wherever a bill must pass. A legislator with a minor local project to fund attaches it to the annual defence authorisation, which nobody dares vote against, and a provision carried that way is called a rider.

Buchanan and Tullock described the mechanism in 1962 and treated it as a defining feature of majority rule rather than as corruption. The public-choice reason for an odd-looking bundle is simply that each half alone could not get a majority, so bundling them creates one. The theory also makes a testable prediction, which 2013 duly confirmed: unbundle a logrolled bill and the voting coalition collapses and neither half passes. That leaves a reader a diagnostic for any bill that looks strangely assembled, which is to ask what would become of the votes if the halves were separated.

the-fomc-who-actually-decides-us-monetar.context_blurb:
The Federal Reserve is an institution, but the decision belongs to a committee. Eight times a year, on a calendar published well in advance, a group of officials meets in Washington and votes on whether the target interest rate goes up, down or nowhere, and the committee's name is FOMC, short for the Federal Open Market Committee. Those eight meetings, roughly six to eight weeks apart, each produce a short statement, a press conference and, three weeks later, the minutes.

More officials attend and argue than ever cast a ballot. There are twelve voting seats, seven belonging to the Board of Governors in Washington and five to the presidents of the regional Reserve Banks. Of the twelve regional banks, eleven take turns through four of those seats on annual rotations while one votes at every meeting: the Reserve Bank of New York, whose permanent seat was made official in 1942 and which carries out the committee's trades in the markets.

The Washington governors are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate, and each serves a single term of fourteen years, which cannot be renewed and is the longest fixed term in the federal government outside the Supreme Court, where justices stay as long as they wish. The length was Congress's attempt in 1935 to put the Board beyond the reach of a four-year political cycle. What the committee actually votes on is narrower than people suppose. It does not set the rate on your mortgage or your card; it sets a target range for the federal funds rate, the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to one another, and the rest of the economy's rates are priced off that one.

Who sits on the committee matters as much as what it decides. Alan Greenspan chaired it from 1987 to 2006, through the crash of 1987, the rescue of a large hedge fund in 1998, the dot-com bust and the rate cycle of 2004 to 2006, and he cut rates so reliably after a market fall that investors learned the habit: they take bigger risks, expecting the central bank to bail them out. The regional presidents arrive by a different door. They are not nominated by a president or confirmed by the Senate; each is chosen by the Class B and Class C directors of that regional bank, the non-banker members of a nine-person local board, with the Board of Governors signing off. Public-choice critics call that a governance gap, since private member banks have a hand in picking officials who vote on the price of credit.

The Austrian objection to the whole arrangement is not that the twelve are foolish. In his 1945 essay on how knowledge spreads through a society, Hayek argued that the facts an economy runs on are held in millions of separate heads and communicated by prices, which no committee can gather in time. Applied to a rate-setting committee, that argument is the knowledge problem: twelve people cannot know the right price of credit for a country of hundreds of millions. Meanwhile an entire profession has grown up to read the committee's prose. Change one adjective in the statement, from patient to measured, and billions of dollars move within seconds, which is why the economists, reporters and analysts who do nothing else are known as Fed watchers.

the-great-terror-1936-38-the-yezhovshchi.context_blurb:
Between July 1937 and November 1938 Joseph Stalin's secret police shot some seven hundred thousand Soviet citizens, more than a thousand a day for eighteen months. Russians call that year and a half the Yezhovshchina, after the man who ran it. The English word for a government that destroys its own people and its own party is a purge.

The instrument was the NKVD, the interior ministry's police arm, which answered to Stalin and to no one else. Its agents could take a man from his flat at night, hold him without charge and put him on a train to Siberia, and no court could ask them why. The name for a force like that is secret police. When the archives opened after 1991 the arithmetic became firm. The NKVD's own records count nearly 700,000 people shot in those eighteen months, out of roughly a million and a half arrested.

How the killing was organised is the detail that tells you most. On 30 July 1937 the NKVD issued a numbered order giving each regional office a figure for how many people in its area were to be shot and how many sent to the camps for ten years. That is a quota to fill, guilty or not, and officers who exceeded their figure were rewarded, so they filled the numbers with whoever was nearest to hand.

The men destroyed first were the ones who had made the revolution. Nikolai Bukharin, whom Lenin had called the party's favourite, went on trial in March 1938 and was shot; Trotsky had been exiled in 1929 and was murdered in Mexico in 1940. The pattern recurs after every successful revolution, with Mao turning on his Long March comrades and Robespierre guillotining his own colleagues, and the reason is unsentimental: they know his weaknesses and might replace him. The scholarship carries its own lesson. Robert Conquest laid the whole thing out in a 1968 book that many Western academics mocked, and the archives of the 1990s bore out the broad lines of his account. His critics had made the standing mistake of people defending a system they admire: they were more loyal to the theory than to the facts.

The army was a particular target. Stalin accused his senior officers of plotting with Nazi Germany, and the purge ran from marshals down to colonels: three of the five Marshals of the Soviet Union died, two shot and one in custody after torture; the purge also removed thirteen of fifteen army commanders, eight of nine fleet admirals and some thirty-five thousand officers in all, many of them shot, which is why the Red Army was still rebuilding when Germany invaded in June 1941. The enforcers were not exempt either. Nikolai Yezhov, who had run the campaign, was replaced by Lavrentiy Beria in November 1938, arrested in 1939 and shot in February 1940, his face scratched out of the official photographs; Beria in his turn was arrested and shot in 1953. Even the enforcers get killed once their work is done, so no one is ever safe, which is a feature of such a system rather than an accident in it.

Whole communities were taken for their ancestry. An order of August 1937 directed the arrest of ethnic Poles across the Soviet Union, and about a hundred and eleven thousand were shot in that operation alone; similar orders followed for Germans, Koreans, Latvians, Greeks and Finns living near the frontiers. It could target people just for who their grandparents were, not for anything they had done, which is as plain a definition of state terror as the century offers. Timothy Snyder's Bloodlands, published in 2010, sets Stalin's killing beside Hitler's in the same stretch of Ukraine, Belarus and Poland, where the two regimes deliberately killed around fourteen million civilians between 1933 and 1945. Reading the two tolls together shows two very different ideologies turning to the deliberate killing of ordinary people in the same lands.

the-latin-american-debt-crisis-and-brady.context_blurb:
On 12 August 1982 Mexico's finance minister telephoned the United States Treasury to say his government could not pay what it owed. The banking word for that is a default, and this one came close to taking several of the largest American banks down with it.

The lending had looked safe for a decade, and the man who said so most often was Walter Wriston, chairman of Citibank from 1967 to 1984. His line was that countries don't go bankrupt, since a sovereign can always tax its citizens or print its own money, and he put it in print in a New York Times column that September, as the crisis broke around him. The flaw sat in the currency. These were dollar-denominated loans to sovereign borrowers, so the printing press a government does control was no help whatever: the debt had to be paid in a money Mexico could not issue.

Then Paul Volcker changed the price of dollars. To break American inflation he drove short-term rates above nineteen per cent in 1981, which worked at home and detonated abroad, because the Latin American loans carried floating rates tied to American policy: their debt payments exploded and many countries went bust. By 1982 the nine biggest American banks held Latin American loans worth about a hundred and seventy-six per cent of their combined capital, so a full write-down would have left several of them insolvent. What followed in Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile and Peru was ten years of stagnation, bank failures and inflation running into the thousands of per cent, remembered as the Lost Decade: income per head in Mexico did not regain its 1981 level until the middle of the 1990s.

The official response was not to let the loans fail. The Federal Reserve and the International Monetary Fund pressed the banks into what was called concerted lending: fresh credit advanced so that the old loans could be counted as current. Pretending a bad debt is healthy has a predictable result, which is that the pain is spread out but the bad loan never really goes away, and here the waiting was done by Latin American workers rather than by bank shareholders.

The way out came in 1989 from Nicholas Brady, the American Treasury Secretary. His plan was a swap: the banks would hand over their unsellable loans and receive new tradable bonds with part of the principal guaranteed, which is to say: turn unsellable bad loans into bonds that can be sold, spreading the loss. The guarantee had to be something nobody doubted, so the collateral was US Treasury zero-coupon bonds, which pay nothing until maturity and then hand over their full face value, giving a holder a hard floor under the principal while the rest of the bond traded at whatever the market thought it was worth.

The moral-hazard reading of the episode is about who was made to wait. Latin American publics bore stagnation; US banks were shielded from failure. The same critics saw that pattern again in 1998, in 2008 and in 2010: the gains from the lending stayed private, while the cost of the mistakes moved onto people who had made no loans at all.

the-methodenstreit-1883-1893-menger-vs-s.context_blurb:
Carl Menger had founded a school with one book in 1871. Twelve years later he wrote a second one in order to fight with Berlin. The quarrel that followed has a German name in every history of the subject, Methodenstreit, meaning method-fight, and what was being fought over was The right method for doing economics.

The other side was the German Historical School, led from the chair at Berlin by Gustav Schmoller, and its programme was to build economics up out of national statistics and particular historical cases. That way of reasoning, from a pile of particular cases towards a general rule, is Inductive. Menger's answer in 1883 was that cases alone cannot do the job, and that economics also needs Basic ideas about how people choose that are true in every country. His model was geometry: start with a few truths about a person acting to satisfy a want, and reason From general first principles down to specific cases, which is deduction rather than induction.

Schmoller reviewed the book with contempt and gave Menger's circle a sneering label, a Vienna sect, which the accused promptly adopted and have worn ever since: The Austrian School. Menger replied in 1884 with a short, furious pamphlet written as open letters to a friend, on what he called historicism's errors in the German economics of his day. The move he pressed is precise: That economic laws are universal and hold in every age and country, so history can illustrate them but cannot create them. A scarce thing will be economised in ancient Rome and in modern Vienna alike. He never denied that history was worth studying; he denied that it could replace theory.

The fight had consequences well beyond the journals, because Schmoller was more than a professor. From the Berlin chair he controlled Prussian academic appointments, edited the leading journal and chaired the national economics association, and when he declared Vienna-school men unfit for German posts the result was A generation-long exclusion of Austrian economists from German academic appointments. Menger kept his own chair in Vienna, and his pupils carried the argument on: Eugen von Boehm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser were the school's second generation, with Hayek and Mises arriving after them as the third.

Schmoller's death in 1917 ended the personal feud. The split outlived him. What began in Berlin in 1883 is with the profession still as Methodological individualism versus historical-institutional analysis: on one side the individual chooser as the unit of analysis, on the other the rules and habits and organisations that shape what he chooses. Both traditions re-argue it in each generation. It is worth being accurate about what that quarrel did and did not produce, though. Subjective value, the denial that value is a property production puts into goods, and the demand for universal laws all come from Menger in 1871 and 1883. The socialist calculation critique of central planning does not: that is Mises in 1920, thirty-seven years later, a daughter of the founding method rather than its mother.

the-nyc-taxi-medallion-1-3m-to-100k-afte.context_blurb:
New York has capped the number of yellow cabs since the Haas Act of 1937, holding the total near twelve thousand for decades while the city grew around it, and near thirteen and a half thousand by 2014. The licence itself, a small metal plate known as a medallion, became a tradable asset, and the arithmetic of fixed supply against rising demand is not subtle: the price of a license rises very high because new ones cannot be made.

The figures tell the story by themselves. A medallion went for two and a half thousand dollars in 1947, two hundred thousand in 1997, and at the peak in 2013 and 2014 one changed hands at about $1.3 million, more than a house in most of America. Then a San Francisco startup arrived. Uber launched in New York in 2011 and registered its drivers as for-hire black cars rather than taxis, which put them outside the medallion cap altogether and let supply grow with demand. By 2019 a medallion fetched about $100,000, a fall of some ninety-two per cent in six years.

The human cost landed on the drivers who had bought at the top. Brian Rosenthal's investigation for the New York Times in May 2019, which won the Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting in 2020, traced roughly nine hundred and fifty bankruptcies among medallion owners. The series' subject was exactly that: how reckless loans devastated a generation of taxi drivers, who had borrowed at peak prices against an asset whose price the lenders had helped inflate.

Bastiat's method asks who had been paying for the seventy-six years before the crash. The visible party was the medallion owner, whose disc was worth a fortune; the invisible ones were the riders who cannot find a cab and walk, wait, or drive drunk, along with the drivers who would have worked if a licence had been available. That invisibility had a geography. Yellow-cab economics ran on street hails, so cabs clustered in Manhattan and shunned long trips with empty returns; testers sent out under Mayor Bloomberg found the same places passed by again and again, which were the outer boroughs like the Bronx and southeast Queens.

So the collapse reads differently under Bastiat's method than it did in the headlines. The crash was painful for the people holding medallions, and what it revealed was the capitalized value of the harm the cap had been extracting from riders and blocked drivers for 76 years. The price of the licence had always measured a transfer running one way; when the cap stopped binding, the transfer stopped with it.

the-petition-of-the-candlemakers-a-law-a.context_blurb:
In 1845 Bastiat published a mock petition to the French Chamber of Deputies, over his own name, as a chapter in his collection of satirical pieces about trade and industry: Economic Sophisms. The petitioners are the makers of lamps and candles and tallow, and they write with perfect gravity to complain of a foreign rival whose cheap output is flooding France and ruining honest domestic producers.

The rival is named in the second paragraph, and the naming is the joke, because it is the sun. What the petition demands is a statute requiring every window, skylight, shutter, curtain and blind in France to be closed during daylight hours, so that people must burn candles at noon. Bastiat is not mocking windows. He is mocking businesses that beg the government to hurt competitors so they can charge more, and the piece works by letting them say out loud what such a request actually asks for.

The petition's best stretch is its list of everybody who will prosper once the sun is shut out. Tallow farms must expand, which means more cattle and more pasture; whaling fleets will sail for oil; forests will come down for the ships; carpenters will be set to work on shutters. That chain of blessings parodies a real argument for tariffs, the multiplier argument for tariffs, which counts every job upstream of the protected industry and no job anywhere else.

The technique has a name that goes back to the Greeks. Bastiat takes the protectionist principle entirely seriously, that domestic producers deserve shelter from cheaper foreign competition, and follows it to a conclusion nobody will defend, which is reductio ad absurdum. Done well it is the most economical form of argument there is, because the opponent's own premise does all the work: reductio ad absurdum -- pushing the other side's logic until it looks silly. Jonathan Swift had used the same instrument in 1729, taking the logic of Irish policy seriously enough to propose eating Irish children.

What Bastiat was attacking has a name too, and it is the one the petition was written against: protectionism. Milton Friedman used the petition in 1980, in the book and television series he made with his wife, to press a diagnostic question at modern trade policy. The pair to look for is abundance treated as a threat, scarcity treated as a benefit: if a policy treats more goods for less work as a problem, it is the candlemakers' argument in modern dress. That is why the phrase has become standing shorthand in economics writing, applied to cheap imports, cheap solar panels, robots and foreign labour alike. It flags any argument that treats free abundance as a threat requiring policy remedy.
