the-road-to-serfdom-1944.context_blurb:
In March 1944, while the bombs were still falling on London, Routledge published a slim book by a Viennese economist who had taught in Britain since 1931. Its warning to Britain was that keeping the wartime economic controls after the peace would start the country down the road German-speaking Europe had already travelled, from reformist planning in the 1920s to dictatorship. What Hayek warned against is a government that plans and controls almost every part of daily life. The dedication names the readers he was aiming at: To the socialists of all parties.

The country whose path he had watched in person was Germany, which had moved from wide-ranging state planning in the 1920s to outright dictatorship by 1933. The American edition nearly did not happen. Macmillan, Little Brown and Harper all turned the manuscript down, and one of the rejections called him a man standing outside the stream of present-day thought, before it was finally taken by the University of Chicago Press, which published it in September 1944.

The argument is about mechanism rather than motive. When a government sets out to plan what gets made, who does which job and what things cost, it must override millions of individual choices, and overriding them means silencing the people who would have chosen otherwise, which is why central planning of the economy tends to end personal freedom too. The book then did something no academic economics book does. A mass-circulation American digest condensed it as the lead item of its April 1945 issue, in a condensation by Max Eastman, and the Book-of-the-Month Club sent that version to more than six hundred thousand subscribers. A picture magazine went further still in February 1945 and turned the argument into a comic strip, frame by frame, which General Motors reprinted as a pamphlet and pushed out to its workers by the million: the magazine was Look.

The core warning states in a line, and it is the line the book is remembered for: central economic planning slides toward political tyranny. George Orwell reviewed it in the Observer on 9 April 1944 and summarised the thesis in a sentence of his own, that socialism leads inevitably to despotism, while adding the worry that the collectivism Hayek feared was a real danger and so was the alternative on offer. What citizens lose, on this argument, is concrete: they lose the freedom to choose their own work, prices, and daily lives, because one plan has replaced millions of private decisions.

Keynes read it and wrote to Hayek on 28 June 1944, calling it a grand book and saying the world had every reason to be grateful for its being said so well. His reservation was not about the moral warning: he disagreed with Hayek about where the line of state action should be drawn, which is the whole quarrel in one sentence, since Hayek never held that the state should do nothing at all. Thirty-one years later the woman newly elected to lead the Conservatives pulled Hayek's longer book of 1960 from her handbag at a research-department meeting and told the room that this was what the party believed, an anecdote her own foundation flags as perhaps too neat to be literally true, and one that still shows a political party can be reshaped when a leader takes a set of ideas seriously. The move worth recognising in the book, though, is narrower than its reputation: that comprehensive economic planning requires progressively more coercive power to override the individual choices it must direct. That is a claim a reader can accept or reject on the evidence. It is not a verdict on anybody's motives, and it is not a forecast about which system produces more output.

the-socialist-calculation-debate-the-40-.context_blurb:
Vienna, 1920. The First World War had just ended, four empires had fallen, and serious people across Europe were saying the market's days were numbered and the state would soon own the farms and the factories. Ludwig von Mises, an Austrian economist then in his late thirties, published a long essay in a German social-science journal to argue that it could not be done, not because socialists were wicked but because of an information problem.

His argument runs in steps a teenager can check. The price of steel or land or machine time comes out of real owners bargaining with one another. Abolish private ownership of the farms and factories and no owners are left to bargain, so no real prices exist for producer goods. Lacking those prices, a planner has no common measure and cannot tell whether a bridge built of steel costs the country more than the same bridge built of concrete. That is the socialist calculation problem.

The reply came from Oskar Lange, a young Polish economist teaching at Chicago in the 1930s. A planning board needs no traders, he said: it can chalk up a price for every good, see whether stockrooms clog or counters empty, and move the number until the guessing settles, so central planners can copy what markets do for prices. Because the scheme kept public ownership and bolted a trial-and-error price mechanism onto it, it earned a name of its own, market socialism, and Abba Lerner polished the blueprint in 1944. Mises against Lange, Austrians against socialists, for roughly forty years: the socialist calculation debate.

Friedrich Hayek then shifted the ground. In an essay that ran in September 1945 in the American Economic Review, he granted the arithmetic, allowing that a board might in principle grind through the sums. What no board could do was gather the facts the sums require, because the useful facts are small, local and perishable: which seam in the mine has thinned, who has a lorry standing idle this afternoon, which customer will accept a substitute today. Markets manage the one thing no planning office can imitate, aggregating the dispersed knowledge of time and place held in millions of minds.

Mises left Vienna for Geneva in 1934, ahead of Nazi rule, reached New York in 1940, and there in 1949 restated the whole case in a thousand-page treatise called Human Action, with a long section on the economic calculation problem. For decades most economists scored the paper argument for Lange. Then the evidence arrived: on the night of November 9, 1989 the fall of the Berlin Wall opened the border, and inside two years every planned economy in Eastern Europe had given up and turned toward markets. Robert Heilbroner, who held the Norman Thomas chair at the New School and whose bestselling history of economics had left Mises out of its first edition altogether, wrote in a 1990 magazine essay that Mises, it turned out, had been right. The lesson is not about scoring points: even honest people can look at hard evidence and change their minds about big questions.

Don Lavoie recast the quarrel in 1985, arguing that Mises's missing prices and Hayek's missing facts are one objection with two faces, the knowledge problem, that no central office can collect all the scattered facts guiding daily choices.

the-theory-of-money-and-credit-1912.context_blurb:
In 1912 a thirty-one-year-old economist in Vienna published his first big book and handed the same manuscript to the university as the thesis that would license him to lecture. He was Ludwig von Mises, and the book founded the Austrian tradition in monetary theory. Its German title is Theorie des Geldes und der Umlaufsmittel; that last word means means of circulation, which an English publisher sensibly shortened to Money and Credit.

Carl Menger had left a hole in 1871. If a good's value comes from how useful its next unit is to some person, money looks circular, since money is useful almost entirely because other people take it. Mises answered with the regression theorem. What you will hand over for a coin today rests on what you know it bought yesterday, and that on the day before, and if you follow the chain backwards it must land on a day when the money-good was not yet money but was valued for a direct non-monetary use. Ask a shopkeeper why a silver coin is worth anything and the honest answer waits at the far end of that chain: a time when silver itself was a useful thing people wanted for jewelry, tools, and trade. Gold had been wanted for ornament and dentistry, cattle for meat and haulage, salt for keeping food through winter.

The same book planted the seed of the Austrian account of the trade cycle. When a bank makes credit artificially cheap, firms launch long projects that only look profitable at that rate, and some years on the half-built projects are abandoned, which is the boom-bust cycle caused by cheap credit, worked out in full by Friedrich Hayek in his 1931 London lectures. Mises added the uneven arrival. New money does not lift all prices at once; it enters at particular points, so whoever stands near the spigot spends it before the prices move, and the ones hurt first and worst are savers and people on fixed incomes. Murray Rothbard's short 1963 booklet for the general reader called the old practice by its plain name: shaving the metal out of a coin, or printing extra notes to dilute the ones already in circulation, is currency debasement.

A century later the theorem became a live quarrel. The first Bitcoin was mined in January 2009, purely digital, backed by no state and never traded as anything else, so a few Austrians promptly argued that Mises had ruled it out, pointing to the regression theorem's requirement of a prior non-monetary use. Konrad Graf replied in 2013 that the requirement had been met before any price existed, because the earliest users were cypherpunks who wanted the protocol for its use as a means of censorship-resistant value transfer across a peer-to-peer network, something no other technology could do. Robert Murphy and Silas Barta refused the hunt altogether. Reading the theorem as a strictly historical explanation with no bearing on whether Bitcoin becomes money, they held that Mises had been explaining how commodity monies emerged, not setting a condition on future ones. Which reading is right is still argued in Austrian circles.

the-vienna-diaspora-of-1934-1940-how-the.context_blurb:
Mises ran a private seminar in Vienna through the late 1920s and the early 1930s, in his office at the Chamber of Commerce, and most of the young economists who later carried the Austrian School into the English-speaking world passed through it. The crossing began as ordinary academic travel and ended as flight.

Hayek went first. Lionel Robbins, then rebuilding the economics department of the London School of Economics, brought him over at the end of January 1931 for four lectures, printed that year as Prices and Production, and they landed so well that the school offered him a permanent post. From 1932 he held its senior professorship in economics, named for the nineteenth-century monetary writer Thomas Tooke: the Tooke Chair of Economic Science and Statistics. He stayed almost twenty years, became a British subject in 1938, and left for Chicago in 1950.

Others followed on fellowships. Fritz Machlup, who had studied under Mises in the 1920s, used a Rockefeller grant in 1933 to tour American universities and settled in 1935 into a twelve-year chair at the University of Buffalo, before later moves to Johns Hopkins and Princeton. Gottfried Haberler spent 1934 to 1936 as an economist in Geneva for the League of Nations, work that produced Prosperity and Depression, his survey of the theories of the trade cycle, and then took a Harvard professorship in the autumn of 1936. Karl Menger, the mathematician son of the school's founder, left a full year before the political end came, reaching South Bend, Indiana in the autumn of 1937 and resigning the Vienna chair in March 1938: his refuge was the University of Notre Dame.

Oskar Morgenstern's escape was luck of the calendar. He directed Vienna's institute for business-cycle research and sat in the seminar, and on 13 March 1938, when German troops crossed the border in the Anschluss, he was on a lecture tour of the United States; he stayed and took a Princeton appointment, choosing a three-year lectureship out of six offers and simply never going home.

Mises himself had gone in 1934, to a paid professorship his own city never gave him, Vienna having granted him only an unpaid lecturer's title, at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva. He held it until July 1940, when he and his wife Margit fled the German advance through France. Spain refused them three times before a consulate at Toulouse issued the visa; they crossed by train to the Portuguese coast and sailed from Lisbon, the neutral port that took in Europe's refugees that year. The ship reached New Jersey on 2 August 1940. He was a few weeks short of fifty-nine, and no American university offered him a paid chair for the rest of his life. From 1945 to 1969 he taught at New York University as an unpaid visiting professor, his stipend covered by private donors.

Then came the rebuilding. On 10 April 1947, two years after the Nazi collapse, Hayek gathered thirty-six scholars at a hotel on Mont Pelerin, the mountain above Lake Geneva, with Robbins, Popper, Friedman, Stigler, Machlup and Mises among them, to ask whether classical liberal thought could be put back together, and the group founded there is the Mont Pelerin Society. The vindication came in 1974, when Stockholm gave the economics Nobel, in an odd pairing with Gunnar Myrdal, a Swedish social democrat, to the one man out of that Vienna seminar ever to win it: Friedrich von Hayek.

tim-may-s-crypto-anarchist-manifesto-198.context_blurb:
Timothy May was a physicist at Intel in the 1970s who helped solve a flaw that was ruining memory chips, cashed enough stock to retire young, and moved to the hills above Santa Cruz to write. In November 1988 he carried photocopies of a short essay to the annual CRYPTO conference at Santa Barbara, handed them round and read the thing aloud, and he read it again later to the first cypherpunk gathering near the bay.

He opened with a theft. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels had begun an 1848 pamphlet by announcing a spectre haunting Europe, the spectre of communism; May changed the noun, and in his version a specter was haunting the modern world, and that specter was crypto anarchy. His specter was not a political party. He meant a bundle of powers he expected the mathematics to hand to ordinary people, namely communication, contracting and trade among people who could not be seen or stopped by any government. The sentence that follows says computer technology is on the verge of providing the ability for individuals and groups to communicate and interact with each other in a totally anonymous manner.

The whole bet rests on one tool: strong encryption -- math that scrambles the message, which anyone can run and nobody can unpick by force. May's guess in 1988 was that once that math reached ordinary hands, no state could read its citizens' letters or block their payments, so what would grow up instead is private communication and private trade between strangers.

He also listed the tools he expected the math to allow, and the list was uncannily good: anonymous networks, digital pseudonyms, electronic contracts, and digital money. By the early 1990s a group around San Francisco Bay was meeting in person and arguing on a mailing list about exactly these things, calling themselves cypherpunks, with Eric Hughes, John Gilmore and May among them, and holding one belief in common about what any citizen should be free to use without a government's leave or a bank's: strong encryption for private messages and digital cash. May followed the manifesto in 1994 with a book-length question-and-answer document that circulated inside that community for years.

The digital-money item took twenty years. Almost exactly two decades after the essay, on Halloween of 2008, nine pages appeared describing money that moves straight from one person to another, with no bank between them and no government able to watch or halt a payment, matching May's sketch point for point: Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin white paper of October 31, 2008. May never claimed to be Satoshi, and when he died in 2018 at sixty-six the crypto press settled on calling him one of the fathers of the movement Satoshi wrote from within.

What makes the essay remarkable is what it did not have. In 1988 there was no code, no infrastructure and no working anonymous system of the sort May described, so the honest way to read it is as a physicist's forecast of what the mathematics would eventually let ordinary people do, before any of it existed in software.

universal-basic-income-milton-friedmans-.context_blurb:
In chapter twelve of Capitalism and Freedom, published in 1962, Milton Friedman proposed replacing the whole stack of American welfare programmes with one payment. Nobody would queue at an office to prove eligibility; everyone would file an ordinary tax return, and anyone earning less than a set figure would receive a cheque from the tax authority instead of paying one. Running the income tax backwards like that is a negative income tax. The design mattered: the payment shrank gradually as earnings rose, at a known constant rate, so that taking work always left a family better off.

The idea was actually tested. Between 1968 and 1979 four large randomised experiments ran in the United States and Canada, in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, in Seattle and Denver, and in Manitoba. Critics had warned that the cheques would send recipients off the job in droves, and what the trials found instead was modest reductions (~5-13 percent for primary earners) rather than the catastrophic labor-supply collapse critics had predicted, alongside large savings in administration.

The modern cousin goes by another name. In the 2020 presidential race the New York entrepreneur Andrew Yang built his campaign on a thousand dollars a month for every adult, no strings and no phase-out, which he branded the Freedom Dividend and which belongs to the family called universal basic income. It has been tried privately at scale as well: a study funded by Sam Altman's OpenResearch gave a thousand dollars a month for three years to a thousand people across Illinois and Texas, and when the results appeared in August 2024 recipients reduced work hours by roughly 1.3 to 1.4 hours per week, with modest health gains and no clear employment benefit.

Here is the distinction the shared label hides. The older plan replaces the old programs; the newer plan is added on top of them, which changes both what the state does and what marginal rate a family meets as it earns more. Charles Murray's version, in a 2006 book, would send every adult ten thousand dollars a year, and it replaces almost all existing welfare programs with one cash payment, from food aid and housing help through to the old-age and health programmes.

One real programme has run for decades. In 1976 a Republican governor persuaded voters to lock a share of the state's oil royalties into an investment fund, and from 1982 it has paid every resident, children included, a yearly dividend that has ranged from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars: the state is Alaska, and the payment is the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend.

So when a student asks whether a universal payment is obviously a good idea, the public-choice answer is a refusal to answer yes or no. Set Murray's plan beside Yang's and you have one label, opposite machinery, opposite consequences. Read the actual law, not the label; same-name plans with different rules give different results.

vietnam-after-1975-re-education-camps-an.context_blurb:
Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, the war ended, and the city was renamed for Ho Chi Minh the following year. What the victors did next can be checked against every other communist takeover, beginning with Russia in 1917, where the state took over the shops and decided what each would sell and at which price: shelves get emptier and lines get longer.

The new government in Hanoi arrested the officials, soldiers, teachers, journalists and Catholic priests of the defeated south and sent them to camps in the jungle for forced labor, political lectures and hunger, a few weeks for some and more than fifteen years for others. The official name was re-education camps, hoc tap cai tao in Vietnamese, and an estimated one to two and a half million people passed through them between 1975 and the middle 1980s, with Vietnam's own government admitting over 165,000 deaths.

Then came the seizure of the south's private economy. Across 1977 and 1978 the state took over family shops and small factories, and the ethnic-Chinese merchant families of the Cholon district were hit hardest; a shopkeeper in that position had three choices, all bad, which is why the owners flee, lose everything, or go underground. About eight hundred thousand Vietnamese left by sea between 1975 and 1990, most of them in the panic of 1978 and 1979, packed into wooden fishing boats aimed at Thailand, Malaysia or Hong Kong, and the world called them the Boat People. The UN refugee agency puts the deaths at sea at two hundred thousand or more, because a crowded boat on open water meets storms, thirst, and pirate attacks that kill many at sea. From 1979 an Orderly Departure Program, set up under the UN refugee agency, let people with family abroad or American ties leave with paperwork instead, and from 1980 to 1997 more than six hundred thousand left that way, most of them for the United States.

Central planning did the rest. Farmers in the Mekong Delta, one of the great rice regions of the world, were told what to plant, who to sell it to, and at which price, and a decade later the country was buying rice from abroad. Prices rose more than fivefold in 1986 alone, the year after a failed reform of prices, wages and money. In 1986 the Communist Party admitted that the Soviet model could not feed the country and launched the market reforms it called Doi Moi, meaning renovation or renewal. The change that mattered most was letting farmers grow, sell, and price their own rice. Within three years Vietnam had become a rice exporter, and by the 2000s it stood among the top three in the world.

Same land, same farmers, opposite result. For the long argument Mises and Hayek had with the planners, the Vietnamese record makes one narrow and testable point: the same farmers can go from famine to export within a few years once prices return.

welfare-cliffs-the-effective-marginal-ta.context_blurb:
A welfare cliff is a point on the income scale where one more dollar of wages costs a family more than a dollar. Take a single mother earning thirty thousand dollars a year with about ten thousand more in food aid, Medicaid and a housing voucher. Her employer gives her a two-thousand-dollar raise, the raise carries her over a cutoff, and the whole ten thousand stops, so she is worse off by about $8,000. Smaller version, same shape: four hundred dollars a month of help that ends the moment anyone earns more than two thousand a month, set against a promotion from nineteen hundred to twenty-one hundred, means the extra $200 in pay would cost the family $400 in help -- a net loss.

The cliff is nobody's plan. A 2015 government audit, drawing on congressional researchers' lists, counted more than 80 separate federal programs for people with low incomes. They were written at different times by different committees, each with its own income cutoff, so the cliff is a mechanical consequence of stacking multiple means-tested benefits without coordinating their phase-outs. The Atlanta Fed has published a calculator since 2018 that maps the cliffs facing one particular family across the whole stack, and its name says what it looks for: the CLIFF tool.

One of the biggest cliffs is famous. One sat where a family's income reached four times the federal poverty line, above which it lost every dollar of help with health-insurance premiums at a stroke, and the 2010 law that created it is the Affordable Care Act. A gentler design runs the other way: the Earned Income Tax Credit, in place since 1975, pays a bigger credit the more a low earner works, up to a limit, because the point of that shape is to make working pay more than not working.

Milton Friedman had proposed a way around the whole problem in 1962, in chapter twelve of Capitalism and Freedom: scrap the stack and pay one benefit that tapers off at a single known rate, so that no family ever loses money by earning more. He called it the negative income tax.

Thomas Sowell catalogued cases of this kind in 1995, in a book whose title names the people he holds responsible for them, The Vision of the Anointed. One of his examples is a family-structure measure from long before the Great Society. Before the Second World War, a larger share of black women than white women were married, and that marriage rate, which dropped hard once the 1960s began, is the number Sowell points at. Sowell and Friedman put the cliff to the same broader use, and it is a rule of method rather than a verdict: judge policies by their results, not their intentions.

ww1-and-the-collapse-of-the-classical-go.context_blurb:
In the last days of July and the first of August 1914, as Europe mobilised, every major belligerent treated its money the same way within days of the others. Russia moved on 27 July, Germany on 4 August and France on 5 August, with the others close behind, and what each of them did was that it suspended the redemption of paper money for gold. The classical gold standard, under which anybody could walk into a bank and exchange notes for coin at a fixed rate, was gone inside about ten days.

The reason was arithmetic. While the promise to pay gold still held, a government could fund a war in only two honest ways, by taxing citizens or borrowing from lenders, the first unpopular and slow, the second limited by what lenders were willing to hand over. Off gold, a central bank could simply print notes and settle the armament orders directly. Over four years of war the money circulating in Germany roughly quintupled, which planted the seed of the hyperinflation that followed the peace. British prices roughly doubled and French prices roughly tripled, while the rouble went to nothing in the revolution; only the United States, in the war from April 1917 and so two and a half years late, held much discipline. The mechanism is the same in every war of the century, because fresh currency bids for goods that factories cannot turn out any faster: inflation, because more money is chasing the same amount of goods.

The most striking claim about all this came out of Vienna in 1919, in a book titled Nation, State, and Economy. Its author called inflation an indispensable intellectual means of militarism, because without it the cost of a war would become obvious much sooner and war-weariness would set in much earlier. The author was Ludwig von Mises.

Going back proved as painful as leaving. In 1925 Winston Churchill, as Chancellor, restored convertibility at the prewar 1914 parity of $4.86, which left sterling overvalued and forced deflation, wage cuts and unemployment onto miners and factory hands. Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet that named the Chancellor in its title, The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill, echoing his own 1919 attack on the Versailles treaty. A weaker compromise had already been sketched at the Genoa Conference of 1922, which proposed that only central banks hold metal while other countries held pounds and dollars as reserves, and that arrangement is the gold-exchange standard.

Two conclusions follow in the Austrian reading, and both are offered as a reading rather than a proof. The first is about power: sound money limits state power, and war-making states always want to escape that limit. The second is about how the century's history fits together, because the industrial-scale wars and the abandonment of gold discipline were the same event, not two separate tragedies to be filed under politics and money.

zoning-the-housing-that-glaeser-and-gyou.context_blurb:
American cities can tell you what to build on your own land because of a lawsuit a village won in 1926. Euclid, Ohio had written rules assigning each lot to houses or shops or factories; a real-estate company called Ambler Realty sued on the ground that a village had no business controlling private land that way; and the Supreme Court sided with the village, in the case of Village of Euclid versus Ambler Realty. Nearly every large American city has used that authority since. Most of Houston never did, and land use there is handled instead by private agreements written into each home's deed.

In 2002 two economists measured what the codes cost. They compared what it actually costs to build an apartment in a constrained city with what that apartment fetches on the market, and the gap, often half the price or more, is the charge the rules lay on everybody who rents or buys. The pair were Edward Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko. They called the gap a zoning tax, and in a 2005 study of Manhattan, written with Raven Saks, they found apartments selling for more than twice what they cost to build, while across much of the country prices sat close to construction costs.

Bastiat's method is what the measurement makes concrete. A homeowner says the code protects the character of the street, and that is visible, as are the existing houses and their prices. Bastiat's question is what a rule costs that nobody can see because the thing never came into existence, and here that means the apartments and houses the code prevented from being built, along with the families priced out of the city and the hours they now spend commuting. Put the same town in front of decades of newcomers drawn by jobs and schools, keep the single-family rule in place, and home prices go up, because the rule blocks builders from adding more homes.

Why does it last? Because of who votes. Current homeowners vote in local elections; would-be residents cannot, since the people a tight code prices out do not live in the city yet and hold no ballot there. That is the concentrated-benefit, dispersed-cost pattern with a franchise twist.

The politics have begun to move. Minneapolis voted in December 2018 to end single-family-only zoning across every neighborhood, the first large American city to do it. California's Senate Bill 9, signed in 2021, let an owner split a single-family lot and put up to four homes on it in most residential zones, overriding the local ban, and on ordinary supply-and-demand reasoning that should push prices down over time by allowing more homes to be built where demand is highest.
